EU to press UK and Canada to boost Ukraine aid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:01:23 UTC
19:01:23 KST

The European Union is increasing pressure on Britain, Canada, and other international partners to give more financial support to Ukraine.
In a speech to the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Wednesday, European Council President António Costa said non-EU partners must pay a larger share.
“The EU and its member states now account for 80 percent of the external support for Ukraine,” Costa said.
“Our international partners must also step forward and increase their contributions,” Costa said.
The call comes after officials in Brussels realized that Ukraine faces a budget gap of 70 billion EUR in 2027. That amount is equal to about 520 billion DKK. The gap is so large that European leaders are asking international partners to help pay for it.
Both Britain and Canada have said they want closer cooperation with the EU. EU leaders plan to present their funding request during upcoming summits with both countries.
The EU has expected from the start that countries outside the bloc would help pay for the war. Last year, EU countries could not agree on using frozen Russian funds to help Ukraine. Instead, 24 of the 27 EU member countries agreed to give Ukraine a loan of 90 billion EUR.
Under the original plan, the 90 billion EUR loan was only meant to cover two-thirds of Ukraine’s defense and civilian spending for 2026 and 2027. International partners such as Britain and Canada were expected to provide the remaining one-third. That money has not arrived.
The European Commission estimates that the EU loan will cover Ukraine’s needs this year, but more funding will be needed next year for Ukraine to continue the war.
“Our willingness to support Ukraine and its people is greater than ever. 16 billion euros have already been paid out this year from the EU loan for use in Ukraine’s defense,” Costa said.
“An additional 17 billion euros in budget assistance will be paid out this year if Ukraine makes the necessary reforms. We will fulfill our obligations,” Costa said.
Both Britain and Canada are facing serious economic problems, as are several EU countries.
Britain’s public net debt has passed 3 trillion GBP for the first time. That is equal to about 94 percent of the country’s gross domestic product.
Canada is dealing with a tariff dispute with the United States under Donald Trump. The United States usually buys more than two-thirds of Canada’s exported goods.
EU leaders believe they can pressure both nations because both look to the EU to buy more of their exports and help their economies. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said it is “possible” that the Labour Party will include a new vote on rejoining the EU in its next election manifesto.
The first talks will take place on October 29 and October 30, 2026, in Montreal, Canada. Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will meet with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney to discuss trade, energy, and a closer partnership.
The summit with Britain is scheduled for November 20 in Brussels.

US invokes rarely used torture law in revamped case against Maduro
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:01:20 UTC
19:01:20 KST

US invokes rarely used torture law in revamped case against Maduro
- US prosecutors have expanded the case against Nicolás Maduro and Cilia Flores with rare torture charges, saying they conspired to torture political opponents to stay in power.
- The case is a landmark because it is the first US prosecution of a head of state for allegedly authorising torture at home, and it could bring stronger witnesses and more detailed evidence.
- Maduro and Flores deny the charges and are due for trial in June 2027, while lawyers say the new case is a major escalation and may reshape the trial around human rights abuses.
AI generated
NEW YORK – Nicolas Maduro is one of just a handful of people to be charged in the US with violating a federal law criminalising torture committed overseas, a Reuters review of court records found, as prosecutors seek to broaden their criminal case against the ousted Venezuelan president.
Maduro, 63, and his wife Cilia Flores, 70, pleaded not guilty last week to an expanded indictment accusing them of conspiring to torture political opponents to remain in power, in addition to the drug trafficking charges they already faced.
They are scheduled to go on trial in June 2027.
Maduro and Flores, captured in January during a US military raid in Caracas ordered by US President Donald Trump, are just the seventh and eighth people Reuters identified who have been charged with violating a 1994 law criminalising acts of torture.
The law defines torture as an act intended to inflict severe physical or mental pain or suffering on a person in custody.
Four people have been convicted under the statute, including members of paramilitary forces in Liberia and Gambia, the head of a Syrian prison under ousted President Bashar al-Assad, and a US citizen who developed an illegal arms factory in Iraq.
The Maduro case marks the first time the United States has prosecuted a head of state for allegedly authorising the use of torture in their country, according to Michel Paradis, a partner at the Steptoe law firm.
“This really is a landmark case,” said Paradis, who previously represented detainees at the Guantanamo Bay US naval base.
The torture charges mark a substantial shift in the focus of the case against Maduro and Flores.
While they remain accused of abusing their power to help drug traffickers and enrich themselves, the new charges mean that alleged human rights abuses during the political upheaval that often marked Maduro’s 13 years in office will become central to the trial.
‘A significant escalation’
The torture charge could strengthen the hand of prosecutors by allowing them to tell a more comprehensive story about how Maduro allegedly employed a wide range of criminal activity to stay in power, and by enabling them to call more sympathetic witnesses, legal experts said.
“The torture charge is really a significant escalation,” said Artie McConnell, a former federal prosecutor focused on national security issues.
“It puts these torture and political repression elements at the centre of the government's theory,” McConnell added, referring to the prosecution.
Lawyers for Maduro did not respond to requests for comment.
Mark Donnelly and Andres Sanchez, lawyers for Flores, said she is “completely innocent” of all charges. They said they would revise a motion they previously made to dismiss the indictment on the basis of sovereign immunity – protection from prosecution as the head of a sovereign country – to account for the new charges.
A spokesperson for the Manhattan US Attorney’s office, which brought the charges, declined to comment.
Cooperating witnesses
The 1994 law was passed by Congress to make good on US obligations under the United Nations Convention against Torture, signed during former president Ronald Reagan’s tenure.
Under the law, each torture count is punishable by up to 20 years in prison, or by a life sentence or the death penalty if the victim dies due to the torture. People convicted of multiple acts of torture can receive longer sentences. Those convicted under the statute so far have received prison sentences of 60 to 97 years.
Maduro and Flores are not eligible for the death penalty because they are charged with torture conspiracy, not with carrying out torture themselves.
US prosecutors can bring torture charges only against defendants who are US nationals or who are physically present in the United States. The charges against Maduro and Flores came after they were brought to New York following the raid in Caracas.
Many of the other defendants in US torture cases had moved to or attempted to enter the United States after the alleged torture.
McConnell, a partner at law firm BakerHostetler, said the new indictment was more detailed than the previous one, citing the descriptions of alleged torture victims and incidents.
In one 2018 incident described in the indictment, prosecutors said Venezuelan military officers hit a detainee with a machete and sprayed him with a chemical irritant while interrogating him about the whereabouts of a Maduro political opponent.
Jurors could find testimony from alleged torture victims to be powerful, said Shane Stansbury, a former federal prosecutor in Manhattan.
Three of the alleged torture victims in the indictment are American citizens, and their testimony could resonate particularly strongly among the jurors, McConnell said.
A trial on the drug trafficking charges alone likely would have relied heavily on the testimony of cooperating witnesses, who may have played a role in the alleged crimes themselves. Defence lawyers often question cooperating witnesses sharply about their own criminal histories on cross-examination to try to undercut their credibility.
To be sure, cooperating witnesses are still likely to prove critical in helping prosecutors link Maduro and Flores to the alleged torture, experts said.
Kevin Sullivan, a prosecutor with the Manhattan US Attorney’s office, said in an Oct 8 court hearing that cooperating witnesses would testify about alleged involvement by Maduro and Flores in the torture conspiracy.
Acquittal in Tennessee
Not every torture case the US has brought has resulted in a conviction.
One defendant, an upstate New York resident named Sulejman Mujagic who was charged in the US in 2012 with torturing a soldier after the breakup of the former Yugoslavia, was instead extradited to Bosnia for trial in 2013.
Another defendant charged over alleged torture in Bosnia, Sead Miljkovic, was found not guilty of US torture charges by a jury in Chattanooga, Tennessee, in 2025 but later pleaded guilty to passport fraud. He has since left the US, according to his lawyer, Bryan Hoss.
Hoss said the accounts given by the alleged victims who testified in the case had shifted over time, undercutting their credibility, and that the abuse allegedly committed by his client did not rise to the level of torture. Hoss also said that jurors may have questioned why the US government was prosecuting the case.
Jurors in the Maduro trial may not have similar concerns.
“The fact that these are filed against the former head of the country allows people to understand it a little better,” Hoss said. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

UN report warns world is now certain to exceed 1.5-degree warming limit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:01:09 UTC
19:01:09 KST

Decades of poor action on climate change mean global warming will unavoidably pass 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial times, according to a report from the United Nations Environment Programme, known as UNEP.
The findings come from UNEP’s “Emission Gap Report 2026: The Point of Return,” which measures global temperature trends. The report states that the chance to keep warming under 1.5 degrees without ever passing that mark has slipped away. The main job now is to keep the temporary temperature jump as small as possible and bring warming back down to 1.5 degrees later.
In the best-case scenario described in the report, there is a 66 percent chance that global temperatures will peak at around 1.7 to 1.8 degrees in the middle of the century. After that, there is a 50 percent chance that temperatures will slowly fall back to 1.5 degrees or lower by the year 2100.
To reach that goal, global greenhouse gas emissions must drop quickly compared to 2025 levels. The report states that emissions must fall by 18 percent by 2030, by 45 percent by 2035, and by 69 percent by 2040. At the same time, nations must remove more and more carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.
The best-case path will disappear quickly if countries do not act immediately. For every five years that carbon dioxide emissions stay at current rates, global temperatures rise by about 0.1 degrees.
Under the current policies in place around the world, temperatures are set to rise by 2.8 degrees by the year 2100, and warming will continue to increase after that.
If all countries meet their national targets, warming would be held to 2.6 degrees by 2100.
If countries hit all of their national targets and also fulfill their net-zero promises, warming would reach about 2.1 degrees by the end of the century. Net-zero means that any carbon dioxide released is matched by an equal amount taken out of the air.
The new projections are worse than the ones in last year’s report. One reason is that the United States pulled out of the Paris Agreement. Furthermore, new climate promises submitted by governments since last year’s report have made almost no difference to the overall numbers.
The report also points to some positive developments, stating that the world has more tools than ever to speed up its work.
Renewable energy such as wind and solar power has grown faster than experts expected. In addition, the use of coal and oil has grown at a slower rate than predicted. Burning coal and oil is the biggest source of carbon dioxide emissions.

boss design turns outdated furniture into timeless pieces with circular initiative

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:00:48 UTC

boss design turns outdated furniture into timeless pieces with circular initiative
the british furniture brand gives old pieces a new lease of life through a circular initiative and a chair built to last.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
Boss Design’s The Loop revives discarded furniture
When planning a space, Boss Design knows that an interior design studio considers more than its architectural characteristics. The furniture used to populate that room is as much a part of the design as the walls surrounding it.
Yet we often encounter the dilemma of interior designs that systematically discard existing pieces to create a space better suited to current needs. Whether due to natural wear from use or changes in furniture trends or personal tastes, hundreds of recoverable pieces are discarded every year in favor of new furniture. This behavior generates a carbon footprint that is both significant and avoidable.
Boss chooses most effective way to protect environment
Today’s society expresses its interest in protecting the planet through the way it consumes. According to Simon Kucher, more than 70% of Europeans say they want to adopt sustainable solutions, and that social awareness involves choosing environmentally responsible products. Yet the most sustainable decision when decorating is not to replace furniture in the least harmful way possible, but to keep it.
For this reason, Boss has introduced The Loop, an architectural service framework created to extend the life of furniture. Through this initiative, Boss works to prevent quality furniture from ending up in landfills through four pillars: ReNew focuses on repairing and reupholstering outdated or damaged furniture; ReUse will see the design team collaborate with owners to intelligently relocate products and restore their purpose within the overall scheme; RePurpose focuses on responsible clearance through donations to initiatives such as WastetoWonder; and ReCycle involves the controlled separation of materials so they can be used in new pieces in the future.
As a finishing touch, this initiative is not limited to Boss Design furniture. The brand has opened The Loop to a wider audience to repair, renew, redistribute, and recycle pieces from both Boss and other manufacturers.
History and technical expertise in service of the planet
This proposal comes from a brand with considerable knowledge. Boss has 40 years of experience, investigation, and aesthetic training underpinning the technical expertise needed to restore furniture to its original factory condition.
These four decades have allowed the brand not only to refine its craftsmanship, but also to research solutions that help protect the planet from the production stage. Examples include the integration of its BioPUR foam, low-VOC components and responsibly sourced materials that help protect indoor air quality while reducing the carbon footprint of large-scale projects.
At the same time, The Loop is connected to Boss’s Plan Zero, an initiative that provides architects with verifiable environmental documentation and certifications (Declare labels, Clean Air certification, lifecycle carbon reporting) needed for LEED, WELL v2, SKA, and BREEAM credits.
Sustainability from factory: how Lucy chair was created
To demonstrate that sustainability can be achieved at every stage of a piece of furniture’s life cycle, Boss has introduced Lucy, a chair designed not to be discarded.
With its modular design, the structure has been developed to adapt over time, even surviving drastic changes in spatial layout. Its removable cover system requires no tools and allows a complete aesthetic transformation of the space without altering the architecture or replacing the piece.
On a technical level, its internal construction combines the aforementioned BioPUR foam, a recyclable internal steel frame and responsibly sourced plywood, demonstrating that sustainability is a decision that begins when a piece is first conceived. Finally, a structure with minimal fixings was chosen to simplify assembly and disassembly at the end of its useful life.
Lucy embodies what Boss has called ‘circular engineering.’ If The Loop demonstrates that it is possible to extend the life of our furniture, whether made by the brand or not, thanks to four decades of expertise in quality and finishes, Lucy is proof that a piece can be conceived from the outset to combine architectural integrity, ergonomic design and timelessness, creating a responsible design at every level.

‘Apartheid automation’: How Israel uses AI to monitor Palestinian land, movement and lives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:00:44 UTC
19:00:44 KST

From detecting changes to Palestinian homes through satellite imagery to scanning faces at military checkpoints and identifying people for deadly strikes, Israel's expanding use of artificial intelligence is raising concerns about how automated technology is being used to control Palestinian lives.
In the occupied West Bank, AI-powered systems are helping Israeli authorities monitor land, buildings and movement, raising fears that the technology could facilitate demolitions and accelerate displacement.
In Gaza, investigations have documented accounts of AI-generated lists of suspected targets being used to inform military strikes, with Israeli intelligence officers describing approval processes that sometimes took just seconds.
"it's all apartheid automation," Mustafa Jarrar, professor of AI at Hamad Bin Khalifa University, and director of SinaLab, told Anadolu.
"What is new now is that the AI is not only collecting and analyzing, but also can make orders," he said.
Palestinian researcher Jalal Abukhater warned that the expanding surveillance systems were helping reinforce Israeli control.
"The pattern of behavior, the movement, the people you speak to, it's all monitored and going to one purpose: to aid the Israeli occupation in dominating and controlling this population," Abukhater, the policy manager for Palestinian digital rights organization 7amleh, told Anadolu.
A Sept. 17 report by Al Jazeera highlighted ImiSight, an AI-powered tool reportedly used to identify changes to buildings and land, helping Israeli authorities detect structures they consider unauthorized and target them for enforcement.
Initially used in the Naqab desert, where Palestinian Bedouin citizens of Israel face restrictive building policies and demolitions, the technology has reportedly been introduced in the occupied West Bank, raising concerns about the use of automated surveillance to expand Israeli control over Palestinian land.
Israeli media reported in January 2025, citing Israel Land Authority figures, that ImiSight helped survey about 10,735 square kilometers (4,145 square miles) in 2024.
The authority said it opened about 495 enforcement proceedings following detections by the system and inspections on the ground. Enforcement operations contributed to the eviction of thousands of Palestinian Bedouin citizens of Israel.
Jarrar explained that AI systems can compare satellite images taken at different times to detect changes to structures and flag them for further inspection, allowing authorities to identify buildings for potential enforcement action.
Researcher Abukhater said that before such systems were deployed, the process required officials to inspect sites in person before authorities sent forces and bulldozers to demolish structures.
“It would require, you know, human individuals going in to check and verifying,” Abukhater warned, adding that such technologies could accelerate demolitions and deepen Israeli control over Palestinian communities.
The technology's reported expansion comes amid rising demolitions of Palestinian structures in the occupied West Bank.
Across the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, more than 1,100 structures had been demolished in 2026 by the time of UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)'s September reporting, displacing more than 1,500 Palestinians.
According to OCHA data, the annual average number of structures demolished by Israel in Area C over lack of building permits rose about 80%, from 537 in 2010-2022 to 966 in 2023-2025.
Area C accounts for roughly 60% of the West Bank and remains under full Israeli administrative and security control. Palestinians face severe restrictions on obtaining construction permits, leaving many structures vulnerable to demolition.
In April 2025, an Israel Land Authority enforcement unit was established to operate in the West Bank, according to the UN.
Israeli rights group Peace Now described the move as a step toward annexation, while the UN warned it would intensify discriminatory building-permit enforcement and deepen Palestinian displacement.
In March 2025, ImiSight said its technology helped the authority identify unauthorized land use through satellite imagery, drones and aerial photography, reducing delays in enforcement.
“Years of AI-driven insights have transformed enforcement operations, reducing delays and enabling rapid, effective action in the field!” the company said in a blog post.
Abukhater estimated that the number of demolitions carried out since the introduction of these AI-supported systems has doubled.
"These entire systems are designed in a way to entrench the occupation, to empower the occupation with tools that could accelerate its actions against Palestinian communities," he added.
Surveillance extends beyond land and buildings to the people living in the occupied territory.
In a May 2023 report, Amnesty International documented Israel's use of Red Wolf, a facial recognition system deployed at military checkpoints in Hebron.
Red Wolf scans Palestinians' faces without their consent and compares them with biometric databases to help determine whether they can pass through checkpoints.
Amnesty also documented the Blue Wolf smartphone application and Wolf Pack database, which Israeli forces use to collect and access information about Palestinians.
The organization said the systems reinforced restrictions on freedom of movement, particularly in Hebron's H2 area, which remains under Israeli control.
It also documented extensive camera surveillance in occupied East Jerusalem, warning that facial recognition technology undermined privacy and discouraged political activity.
Abukhater said Palestinians were being photographed at both checkpoints and during military raids on homes.
"They just take a phone and take a photo of the person's face," he said, describing instances in which soldiers photographed Palestinians at checkpoints even when they did not present identification.
He also described nighttime raids in which soldiers photographed residents, including children.
"The soldiers have targets, and they are told that you should photograph 100 Palestinians a day," he added.
Abukhater said the information gathered could be used to build extensive profiles of Palestinians, including their movements, relationships and personal histories.
He described the wider system as "a big prison" and said Palestinians were subjected to surveillance that restricted their fundamental rights.
Jarrar said information from cameras, smartphones and vehicle identification systems could be combined to build detailed profiles of individuals.
He also said that Israeli forces hack Palestinians' private cameras.
"You identify human, you identify car … different kinds of objects," he said. "You monitor them all the time and so you identify targets."
He explained that AI could also detect unusual travel patterns, such as someone taking a different route between Ramallah and Nablus.
“AI will detect a new pattern and will quickly, basically click alarms,” he said.
Along with the system documented in the occupied West Bank primarily that involve monitoring and surveillance, investigations into Israel's operations in Gaza have raised separate concerns about AI-assisted military targeting.
An April 2024 investigation by +972 Magazine and Local Call, based on interviews with six Israeli intelligence officers, reported that an AI system known as Lavender identified suspects as potential bombing targets, and marked as many as 37,000 Palestinians during the early stages of the war.
One intelligence source described personnel acting as a "rubber stamp" for the system's recommendations, sometimes spending only about "20 seconds" reviewing a target before approving an attack.
Jarrar warned that such rapid approval processes could leave little room for meaningful scrutiny.
"It's all fully automated," he said of the process he described, calling it "machine killing, basically."
The investigation also identified a system known as Where's Daddy?, reportedly used to track suspected targets and determine when they entered their family homes. With the system, according to the award-winning NAZA documentary, a phrase as simple as “daddy’s home,” can trigger a bombing.
Jarrar said the wider use of such technologies should concern governments and researchers beyond the region.
"Israel is actually pushing and encouraging other countries to do the same," he said. "It's being a model."
Abukhater warned that the spread of such technologies could accelerate violations against Palestinians in the West Bank as well.
"My concern is that these tools are accelerating the plans of ethnic cleansing, of entrenching the occupation, of solidifying the annexation of Palestinian territory in the occupied West Bank," he said.
The expanding use of surveillance technology has also raised questions about international companies providing digital services to Israeli security agencies.
Microsoft came under scrutiny in 2025 after The Guardian reported that an Israeli military intelligence unit used its Azure cloud platform to store recordings of Palestinian phone calls collected through surveillance in Gaza and the West Bank.
On Sept. 25, 2025, Microsoft said a review had found evidence supporting elements of the reporting, including the use of Azure storage in the Netherlands and AI services.
The company disabled specified cloud-storage and AI services used by a unit within Israel's Defense Ministry, saying its terms prohibited mass surveillance of civilians.
"This is a direct complicity by private company actors with Israeli state actors who are directly violating rights," Abukhater said. "It's something that these companies should be held accountable for."
Jarrar also urged stronger international rules governing the use of AI in military operations.
"We need really a new international law regarding the use of AI in automated killing," he said.

Long-term care minister Mirjan Sterk has refused to launch an independent investigation into a Dutch youth care scheme in which children are sent abroad, despite revelations about exploitation and harsh treatment.
An investigation by news programme Nieuwsuur found that the “family home” in the Valencia region, which has been running for over 20 years, subjected children living there to cruel physical and psychological punishments.

Experts described the conditions as “torture”. Huize Soria was ordered to close down in September after evidence of abuse was first uncovered.
Sterk, from the centrist Christian Democrat CDA, has urged youth care organisations to stop placing Dutch children abroad where possible said there was no need for her to order an investigation.
In a letter to parliament, she said it was up to local councils, child protection agencies and care providers who placed the children to make sure the home met the rules.
She also said she did not know which organisations had sent children to Huize Soria, apart from one child protection agency, because there is no central record.
MPs from across the political spectrum said that was exactly why an investigation was needed. Far-right JA21 MP Ingrid Coenradie said refusing one was “running away from your responsibilities”.

Neuroscientists uncover brain clues to why some people with childhood trauma struggle to look forward to things
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:00:39 UTC
19:00:39 KST

A new brain imaging study published in The Journal of Neuroscience indicates that the way a memory-related brain region communicates with the brain’s reward centers is linked to motivational difficulties in young adults with a history of childhood trauma. Among individuals who experienced higher levels of early life adversity, weaker activity and connectivity in the hippocampus were associated with a reduced ability to look forward to pleasurable experiences. These findings suggest that targeting memory and novelty-processing circuits could offer a new avenue for addressing motivational symptoms in trauma-exposed populations.
Anhedonia is a psychological condition defined by a reduced ability to experience pleasure or a lack of motivation to pursue rewarding activities. It is a common symptom across several mental health conditions, including major depression and schizophrenia. Psychologists typically divide anhedonia into two categories: consummatory anhedonia, the inability to feel pleasure in the moment while engaging in an enjoyable activity, and anticipatory anhedonia, a diminished capacity to feel excited about or motivated to pursue future rewards.
To understand the biological roots of anhedonia, neuroscientists often examine the mesolimbic dopamine system, a network of brain structures that release and respond to the chemical messenger dopamine to drive reward-seeking behavior. Two central hubs in this network are the ventral tegmental area, a cluster of dopamine-producing neurons in the midbrain near the top of the brainstem, and the nucleus accumbens, a deep forebrain structure within the ventral striatum that processes reward and motivation. For instance, a longitudinal study covered by PsyPost in 2015 found that adolescents who experienced emotional neglect in childhood showed a drop in ventral striatum activity when receiving rewards over a two-year period, which predicted an increase in depressive symptoms.
While human brain imaging studies of anhedonia have largely concentrated on the striatum, animal research points to the hippocampus as an upstream regulator of this reward network. The hippocampus is a seahorse-shaped structure tucked deep within the temporal lobe on each side of the brain. Although best known for forming and retrieving memories, it also acts as a novelty detector. When an organism encounters something unfamiliar, the hippocampus sends signals through a multi-step neural circuit to the ventral tegmental area and the nucleus accumbens, triggering dopamine release that encourages exploration and goal-directed action.
Because the hippocampus contains a dense concentration of receptors that bind to stress hormones like cortisol, exposure to childhood abuse or neglect can alter how this structure develops and functions. In humans, a 2026 brain-mapping preprint from members of the same research group, which has not yet been peer reviewed, reconstructed the physical nerve tracts connecting the hippocampus, ventral tegmental area, and nucleus accumbens, providing structural evidence that these regions form an integrated loop supporting adaptive behavior. A study covered by PsyPost in 2022 found that people with moderate to severe childhood trauma reported more social anhedonia, a reduced interest in social connection, alongside differences in brain structure.
The research team behind the new study, led by first author Kathleen J. O’Brien of Temple University and senior author Vishnu “Deepu” Murty of the University of Oregon’s Adaptive Memory Lab, wanted to test whether disruptions in hippocampal-reward communication interact with childhood trauma to explain why some people struggle with anhedonia.
“This study was motivated by a large animal literature that suggests that regions implicated in novelty processing, like the hippocampus, are critical for anhedonia, but characterization of this circuit had not been translated into the human literature,” Murty told PsyPost.
To investigate this question, the researchers recruited participants from the Philadelphia site of a broader project examining psychosis risk in young adults, ensuring the sample included a wide range of anhedonia severity. Out of 102 individuals who completed functional magnetic resonance imaging scans, the final sample included 92 participants with usable resting-state brain scans (37 males and 55 females) and 80 participants with usable task-based scans (34 males and 46 females). The participants ranged in age from 18 to 30 years old, with an average age of about 21.
Participants completed a modified version of the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire Short-Form, a self-report survey assessing experiences of emotional abuse, emotional neglect, and physical neglect before age 16. They also filled out the Temporal Experience of Pleasure Scale, which uses separate subscales to measure anticipatory pleasure and consummatory pleasure. Lower scores on these scales indicate higher levels of anhedonia.
Inside the magnetic resonance imaging scanner, which measures brain activity by detecting changes in blood flow, the researchers focused on the anterior hippocampus, the front third of the structure that connects most densely with reward circuits. First, participants underwent a 5.8-minute resting-state scan while looking at a cross on a screen. This allowed the scientists to measure baseline functional connectivity, meaning how closely activity in the anterior hippocampus synchronized with activity in the nucleus accumbens and ventral tegmental area while at rest.
Next, participants completed a target-detection task designed to measure how the brain responds to novelty and pursues goals. An hour before entering the scanner, participants had been familiarized with 80 outdoor scene photographs, viewing each one six times. Immediately prior to scanning and again inside the scanner, participants were shown a single specific target landscape. During the brain scan, participants watched a sequence of images flash on the screen for two seconds each and had to press a button every time the target landscape appeared.
Mixed in with the 40 target trials were the 80 familiar scenes and 80 completely new outdoor scenes the participants had never seen before. Using this setup, the researchers measured how strongly the anterior hippocampus activated in response to the novel images compared to the familiar ones. They also used a forward-prediction model to test whether heightened hippocampal activity during novel scenes predicted stronger activation in the ventral tegmental area when the target image appeared shortly afterward.
In their statistical analyses, the researchers controlled for participant age, as age was correlated with baseline connectivity between the hippocampus and the ventral tegmental area, and they verified in follow-up tests that accounting for psychosis-risk status did not change the outcomes. Across all four brain measures, the authors found no statistically significant links or trauma interactions related to consummatory anhedonia. In other words, hippocampal circuit function did not explain differences in the ability to enjoy pleasurable activities in the moment.
For anticipatory anhedonia, however, interactions emerged between childhood trauma and three of the four hippocampal circuit measures. Resting connectivity between the anterior hippocampus and the ventral tegmental area showed no such interaction. Among individuals with higher levels of childhood trauma (defined as one standard deviation above the sample average), weaker resting-state connectivity between the anterior hippocampus and the nucleus accumbens was associated with greater anticipatory anhedonia.
Similarly, in this high-trauma group, a blunted response in the anterior hippocampus when viewing novel scenes, as well as a weaker link between hippocampal responses to novel scenes and later activity in the ventral tegmental area during subsequent target detection, were both linked to worse anticipatory anhedonia. Among participants with lower levels of childhood trauma (one standard deviation below the average), these brain measures showed no statistically significant relationship with anticipatory pleasure.
To determine whether each of these neural measures contributed independently rather than reflecting the exact same underlying brain process, the scientists ran a machine-learning variable selection technique that removes redundant predictors and retains only the strongest ones. The resulting combined model accounted for 24 percent of the total variance in anticipatory anhedonia scores, or 20 percent after adjusting for the number of predictors in the model.
Even when evaluated simultaneously alongside overall trauma severity, both the interaction between trauma and resting hippocampus-accumbens connectivity and the interaction between trauma and task-based hippocampus-to-ventral-tegmental-area signaling remained independent predictors of anticipatory anhedonia. The interaction involving the hippocampus’s response to novel scenes was retained by the selection procedure but fell short of statistical significance in the final model, while higher trauma levels were themselves associated with greater anticipatory anhedonia.
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2025, which found that chronic stress in mice weakened connections from the hippocampus to the nucleus accumbens and reduced reward-seeking, and that a single dose of ketamine restored both. That work examined stressed animals directly rather than brain scans and self-reported trauma in people. The authors suggest that when early life adversity coincides with weakened communication between the hippocampus and dopamine centers, the brain may struggle to use novel environmental cues to spark motivation and update expectations about future rewards.
“The average person should take away that early life stress may make you vulnerable to anhedonia, a lack of pleasure, but that engagement of circuits centered on novelty and exploration can minimize that risk,” Murty explained. “Sometimes there is a misinterpretation that these mesolimbic systems are just there for reward processing, but rather they are sensitive to motivation and behaviors like novelty, information seeking, and perhaps even curiosity.”
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these results. Because the study is cross-sectional, meaning all data were collected at a single point in time, it cannot establish that childhood trauma or hippocampal alterations directly cause anhedonia. It is possible that preexisting differences in brain circuitry make certain individuals more sensitive to the emotional fallout of early stress, or that prolonged exposure to childhood stress gradually wears down hippocampal pathways over time. Longitudinal studies that track children and adolescents across development will be necessary to determine the exact sequence of events.
The study does have some other limitations. The researchers also did not test whether engaging these circuits, for instance through novel experiences, would actually lower anhedonia in people with a history of trauma. The trauma measure relied on young adults recalling their childhoods, and due to the online nature of the initial screening survey and ethical constraints regarding mandatory reporting without direct participant contact, the researchers excluded questions about physical and sexual abuse, meaning the findings specifically reflect emotional abuse and emotional or physical neglect.
In addition, the sample was drawn from a psychosis-risk study in which 22 participants met criteria for clinical high risk, so the results may differ in a general population of young adults, and replication in larger samples will be helpful given the modest statistical strength of the interaction findings.
The resting-state brain scans lasted just under six minutes, whereas recent neuroimaging standards suggest that longer scan times can yield more stable estimates of baseline brain connectivity. Future research could also expand beyond the hippocampus and midbrain to examine how other brain regions involved in emotion and decision-making, such as the amygdala and the prefrontal cortex, work together to influence motivation after early life stress.
Looking ahead, the research team plans to examine how these brain mechanisms connect to personal recall and everyday emotional life. “Our long-term goal is to try to understand how these findings relate to subjective experience of anhedonia, and how those might relate to memories of the past,” Murty noted.
The study, “Functional Integrity of Mesolimbic-Hippocampal Circuits Is Associated with Anhedonia in Individuals with Early Life Stress,” was authored by Kathleen J. O’Brien, Blake L. Elliott, Ian O’Shea, Jason Schiffman, Vijay A. Mittal, Lauren M. Ellman, and Vishnu P. Murty.

Unproductive hours on submarine contract more than halve
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:00:25 BST
19:00:25 KST

The prime contractor on a nuclear submarine contract recorded almost forty thousand unproductive hours in 2025-26, down from more than ninety four thousand the year before, with the losses arising where government furnished assets were not available to the supply chain when required, according to answers given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked how many unproductive hours there were and, in a second question, for what reason those hours were unproductive, following an answer given on 23 September.
Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, gave the same answer to both: “The Prime Contractor recorded 39,872 unproductive hours in 2025-26, a significant reduction from the 94,640 hours recorded in 2024-25. This equated to around 6% of the contract value in 2025-26.
“These hours arose where Government Furnished Assets (GFA) were not available to the supply chain when required, and where contractual arrangements for coordinating provision across multiple industrial partners were still being refined. Mitigating action has since been taken, including a recruitment pause and the adoption of agile courseware development, which has contributed to a significant reduction in losses in 2025-26 compared with previous years.”
Government furnished assets are the equipment, data, facilities and material the department supplies to a contractor so the contractor can do the work, and a supplier whose people are waiting for them is paying staff who cannot start. Six per cent of contract value lost in a single year is a substantial figure for a programme inside the nuclear enterprise, and it came down from a worse one.
Courseware puts this work on the training side of the submarine programme, where simulators, course material and qualification pipelines have to be built alongside the boats themselves. A recruitment pause closes the loss by stopping the hiring of people the contractor could not usefully employ, and it leaves the supply of government furnished assets where it was.

How America's AI Trust Issues Could Impact the Midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:00:03 UTC
19:00:03 KST

From social media to sports betting, Americans have become remarkably willing to adopt new technologies without necessarily believing they're good for us or our health, our society, or our planet. Artificial intelligence may be the clearest example yet.
Just 39% of Americans say AI has a positive impact on society, compared with 44% who believe its impact is negative, according to a national survey conducted this month by my company, Outward Intelligence. Only 15% say they're excited about AI's growth.
But here’s the disconnect: While 58% of Americans don't trust the leaders of AI companies to make decisions in society's best interests, 41% say they use AI chatbots every day. Among Americans who believe AI harms society, roughly half use AI chatbots at least weekly.
In some ways, this shouldn't surprise us. People can appreciate the convenience of social media while questioning its effects on children. They can participate in the boom in sports betting while worrying about its consequences, from addiction to financial hardship. They can shop online while worrying about the decline of local businesses. And they can rely on smartphones while believing those devices have undermined attention and human connection.
But AI tests the limits of the U.S. consumer’s appetite for holding two contradictory ideas in their minds at once. And the implications are political as much as economic: What happens when Americans embrace a technology but don't trust the institutions responsible for creating it as well as overseeing and pacing its development?
In our survey, about two-thirds of Americans said a candidate's position on AI could influence their vote in the upcoming Midterm elections, although most acknowledged that other issues matter more. Roughly one in six said it could actually determine their vote.
Neither party appears to have established much credibility with independent voters on the issue. Nearly two-thirds of independents say they don’t trust either party to handle AI responsibly, or that they trust both equally, or that they’re unsure.
Data centers are where the broader debate over AI becomes much more concrete, and where opposition becomes more unified. More than half of respondents say they would oppose construction of a large data center near where they live. Nearly four in ten would strongly oppose it.
Their concerns are practical. Electricity costs rank first, followed by water usage and environmental impact. America's ability to compete internationally, which has become a central argument for expanding AI infrastructure, ranks much lower.
To a tech company, building a data center may represent an investment in America's economic future. To someone living nearby, it may mean worrying about electricity bills, local resources, and whether the community has much say in the decision. The result is a growing chasm between how the people building AI think about its benefits and how ordinary Americans think about its costs.
The associated political costs are significant, too. When asked about candidates who strongly support building more data centers, 42% of voters say that position would make them less likely to vote for a candidate, vs. 27% who say it would make them more likely. Among independents, the gap is even wider: 49% to 19%.
So while AI may not be a top issue for all voters in November, their attitudes toward AI expose a tension in the politics of technological progress. Promising innovation and economic growth doesn't answer questions about electricity bills and corporate accountability, and expressing concern about the technology doesn't explain how to capture its potential benefits.
AI companies now ask for an enormous amount of public faith. They're developing systems that could reshape employment, education, and the economy, while making major infrastructure investments that will affect communities across the country. Americans, meanwhile, are weighing who benefits, who bears the costs—and who is accountable when things go wrong.
Americans have already shown they're willing to use AI. The harder challenge, for Silicon Valley and Washington alike, is earning, and deserving, their trust.

Press review: Putin-Trump-Xi summit prospects rise as Witkoff met Zelensky in Oslo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

MOSCOW, October 21. /TASS/. The chances of a trilateral meeting between the presidents of Russia, the United States and China are rising, as a Ukrainian delegation led by Vladimir Zelensky met with US special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo. Meanwhile, the global fuel crisis has given a boost to the market for electric vehicles. These stories topped Wednesday's newspaper headlines in Russia.
Kommersant: Likelihood of Putin-Trump-Xi meeting increases
A historic meeting between the leaders of Russia, the United States and China could take place on the sidelines of the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China’s Shenzhen on November 18 or 19. A summit in this format has never been held before, and some experts have already called it a new Yalta, even as no direct parallels can be drawn with the meeting between the three major powers in the anti-Hitler coalition in February 1945. However, the Russian and US leaders are expected to attend the same event alongside China’s president for the first time in some time. And even as neither side has yet formally confirmed that a separate trilateral meeting will be held in Shenzhen, the prospects for such a meeting are growing.
On Monday evening, US President Donald Trump said, when reporters asked him whether he was ready to meet with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping: "I would do it if they want to have it." "Not so much for Ukraine because Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine," the US leader said. "We would schedule a meeting based on denuclearization," he added.
Trump did not clarify what he meant by denuclearization. He has repeatedly used this term when discussing Russia and China before, though the latest application of the concept was atypical. According to the latest data from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), Russia possesses 4,400 operational nuclear warheads, the United States has 3,700, and China has 620.
According to Vladimir Orlov, PIR Center director and Moscow State Institute of International Relations professor, from the perspective of Russia’s national interests, trilateral agreements on strategic nuclear arms control, as well as a moratorium on new nuclear tests between Moscow, Washington and Beijing, would be "a step in the right direction," albeit in principle, as neither of the three sides, primarily China, "is currently ready for that" for a variety of reasons, the expert told Kommersant.
"Moscow has no reason whatsoever to put pressure on Beijing in these circumstances, especially since the issue has not been examined at an expert level," Orlov said. "Therefore, Trump’s remark that he would like to discuss ‘denuclearization’ could be anything - another bout of ‘verbal diarrhea’ or a good intention on the part of the president who views himself as a global figure or even an echo of discussions he might have had with his inner circle at the White House - but certainly it is not a reality at present," he argued.
At the same time, the expert noted that a potential trilateral summit would be "a good venue and rostrum for the three nuclear powers to issue a non-specific and brief statement, as broad as possible, on three points of nuclear weapons." It is equally important, Orlov continued, that such a statement would help reopen professional, expert dialogues on these issues. "I mean dialogues, mostly between Russia and the United States, as the only nuclear superpowers today. Alternative formats have not matured yet," the expert concluded.
Vedomosti: Why Ukraine needed Oslo meeting with Witkoff
On Tuesday evening, a Ukrainian delegation led by Vladimir Zelensky met with a team of US negotiators, led by US leader Donald Trump’s special envoy, Steve Witkoff, in Oslo, Norway. The other top US negotiator, Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, could not attend in person for health reasons but joined via video link. Zelensky, for his part, was accompanied by EU and NATO officials, including Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store and Finnish President Alexander Stubb. In addition, the Ukrainian media said, Zelensky’s delegation included Ukrainian Foreign Intelligence Service head Rustem Umerov, Kirill Budanov, the head of the presidential office, designated as a terrorist and extremist in Russia, first deputy head of the presidential office Sergey Kislitsa and Pavel Palisa, a deputy head of the presidential office.
Witkoff arrived in St. Petersburg following the Oslo talks, where he could potentially hold another meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin. On Tuesday, The New York Times reported that Kushner and Witkoff might visit St. Petersburg on October 21. NYT reporters said the meeting would most likely take place there.
The meeting between Zelensky, the European officials and Witkoff shows how the peace negotiation process has gathered pace under pressure from Trump, Pavel Koshkin, a senior researcher at the US and Canadian Studies Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences, told Vedomosti. Trump is using the diesel deal with Russia and the suspension of the Graham bill sanctions as leverage to pressure Kiev, he argued. As for the likelihood of a deal materializing, it is lower than last year because the current diplomatic structure of these talks remains very fragile. "Trump is not in a position to overcome the differences between Russia and Ukraine," the expert maintained. Amid the escalation over the past few weeks, Koshkin continued, finding compromises has become more difficult. According to the expert, Norway was selected as a venue because of its relative neutrality in terms of its association with European bureaucratic elites: the country is not an EU member but is a NATO ally. Given the fragility of the current stage of the negotiation process, Ukraine might have used the Oslo meeting as a pretext to buy time, Koshkin emphasized.
All the latest statements from Zelensky, including his criticism of Trump and the US as a whole, as well as his overt attempts to address the American president’s political opponents in Congress without going through him, do not suggest that Zelensky will make the necessary concessions, including the withdrawal of Ukrainian troops from the rest of Donbass, or that he would accept other proposals put forward by the Trump administration, Dmitry Suslov, deputy director of the Center for Comprehensive European and International Studies at the Russian National Research University Higher School of Economics, told Vedomosti.
There is an assumption that all those positive proposals put forward by Witkoff, including proposals to restore energy cooperation with Russia or provide partial sanctions relief, are aimed at persuading Russia to drop its demand for the complete liberation of Donbass: Moscow will not accept that. "Given this, these American proposals will prove unacceptable to both Ukraine and Russia. But it would be better for us if the first No comes from the mouth of the Europeans or the Ukrainians, so Washington could blame them for disrupting talks," Suslov said.
Nezavisimaya Gazeta: Fuel crisis accelerates EV market
The Middle East war and the resulting rise in oil prices have had an unexpected effect, spurring electric vehicle (EV) and hybrid car sales. European countries and Russia, where consumers are facing fuel shortages and rising prices, are seeing a surge in demand for EVs. The climate agenda failed to achieve what has now happened due to disruptions to global hydrocarbon supplies, namely a reduction in the share of gasoline-powered vehicles sold worldwide.
In Europe, EV sales rose by 70% year-on-year in September. More than 300,000 new electric vehicles were registered across 17 European countries, bringing their share of the European market to nearly 33%. According to Western news agencies, nearly 2 million new electric vehicles were registered in the EU in the first nine months of this year, up 38% from the same period last year.
According to experts, higher hydrocarbon prices and fuel shortages have driven up the share of electric vehicles in the global new-car market. In the first half of 2026, the share of gasoline-powered cars with internal combustion engines in the global new-car market fell to 49% from 52% a year earlier, data from Mobility Global showed. Moreover, it dropped below 50% for the first time since the 1920s, when automobiles began to spread widely across the globe. In 2021, they accounted for 73%.
Russia is also experiencing rapid growth in EV sales. In September, 3,184 new battery electric vehicles (BEVs) were sold in Russia, a 155% increase from the same month of 2025, according to data from the Avtostat analytical agency. More than 11,500 new EVs were sold in the first nine months of this year, up 44% from the previous year. However, the share of EVs in the broader Russian passenger car market stands at just 2.6%.
Vladimir Chernov, an analyst at Freedom Global, told Nezavisimaya Gazeta that demand for hybrid cars will grow even after the fuel crisis ends. "Hybrid cars make it possible to save on gasoline while still enabling drivers to refuel at conventional gas stations, which is extremely convenient for long-distance trips. However, much depends on the car price and the distance driven, as the extra cost of a hybrid car could take years to pay off," he argued.
Meanwhile, in the EU, steady demand for EVs and hybrids is driven not only by the current fuel market situation but also by energy policy, Pavel Griboc, an associate professor at the Presidential Academy, noted.
Rossiyskaya Gazeta: Suspended US sanctions fail to narrow discount on Russian crude
Trump’s move to suspend the imposition of the "sanctions from hell" and the diesel deal between the United States and Russia have not reduced the discount on Free-on-Board (FOB) prices of Russian oil at ports of loading: Russian oil prices are growing alongside global oil prices. Moreover, the Cost, Insurance and Freight (CIF) price of Russian crude often trades at a premium to Brent at ports of destination.
According to data from Argus, the discount on Urals oil to Brent at Baltic ports expanded to $25.3 per barrel by mid-October from September’s $22.6, while at Black Sea ports it reached $28.4-$29.3 per barrel (compared with $26.9-$27.8 last month).
Sergey Frolov, a managing partner at NEFT Research, told Rossiyskaya Gazeta that the discount on Russian oil is gradually increasing amid higher freight costs and mounting shipping risks at Black Sea ports. However, positive news related to the suspension of US sanctions could spur interest in Russian crude and reduce the discount range. This is unlikely to constitute a sustainable trend, though, as reactions to statements from politicians are usually short-lived, while the discount depends more on fundamentals, the expert argued.
Shipping risks now reach beyond the Black Sea to the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a waterway used by vessels transiting the Suez Canal that is relevant for tankers leaving Russia’s western ports. While the Houthis have not yet targeted tankers carrying Russian oil, this has not lowered freight and insurance expenses for such vessels.
Finally, Russian National Energy Security Fund head Konstantin Simonov told Rossiyskaya Gazeta that the United States has temporarily suspended sanctions only on Russian diesel exports. No other sanctions relief has been granted, including in relation to Russian oil exports.
Vladimir Chernov, an analyst at Freedom Global, shares this view. The executive order issued by the White House on October 16 left existing restrictions unchanged, while the imposition of new measures was suspended, pending a possible future review, he explained. Should the situation stabilize, the economic rationale for maintaining this relief might weaken. However, this does not necessarily mean an automatic tightening of restrictions, the expert added. Both scenarios remain possible, Chernov believes.
If demand for Russian oil from China and India remains steady and the pool of available carriers grows, the discount will narrow, but the sustainability of this effect will depend on specific US licenses, export routes and the geopolitical situation, Dmitry Tyun, CEO of DA Consulting, said.
Rossiyskaya Gazeta: Experts assess factors driving USD depreciation
The official dollar exchange rate has slipped below 83 rubles per $1 for the first time in two months, while the yuan rate has declined below 12.4 rubles to a new record low. The trend toward moderate ruble appreciation prevailed throughout last week, which experts interviewed by Rossiyskaya Gazeta attributed to favorable oil market conditions, the approaching tax payment period, and a slight improvement in the geopolitical climate.
The ruble largely appreciated amid elevated oil prices that have persisted in the market since August, Natalya Vashchelyuk, a senior analyst at Pervaya brokerage, told Rossiyskaya Gazeta. According to the Russian Economic Development Ministry, average Urals prices rose 37% in September to $92 per barrel from $67 in August. By mid-October, they had climbed above $115 per barrel, which, Finam analyst Nikolay Dudchenko said, is 25% higher than the previous month’s levels.
Geopolitical developments have also bolstered the Russian currency. Earlier this month, the US and Russian presidents reached an agreement on Russian diesel supplies to the global market. "This means that the sanctions rhetoric has softened rather than intensified. Trump, for one, put on hold the so-called ‘sanctions from hell’ bill against Russia in his latest executive order, providing support for the ruble," Dudchenko explained.
Although the diesel deal does indeed expand export opportunities, the announced volumes of 300,000 metric tons in October, 500,000 metric tons in November and 1 million metric tons in December are not particularly significant for the ruble exchange rate. According to Mikhail Vasilyev, a lead analyst at Sovcombank, this will contribute only 0.4% to the ruble’s appreciation by year-end.
"The market has calmed somewhat following a series of fluctuations, including sharp movements last summer and at the beginning of the fall. However, this does not mean that volatility has fully subsided. The main driver of the ruble’s appreciation is high oil prices rather than positive geopolitical signals," said Valeria Popova, a senior analyst at Ricom Trust.
According to Vashchelyuk, in the second half of October, the USD rate could settle within a range of 80-84 rubles per dollar and 11.9-12.6 rubles per yuan, assuming no major changes in external conditions. Dudchenko expects the US currency to trade between 82 rubles and 87 rubles in the fourth quarter.
