The Turkic world: From shared history to a shared future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:34:44 UTC
18:34:44 KST

Ambassador Kubanychbek Omuraliev is the Secretary General of the Organization of Turkic States.
There are critical moments in the life of nations and states when shared history ceases to be merely a memory and becomes a force shaping the future. I believe the Turkic World is living through such a moment today.
Across a vast geography connecting East and West, the Turkic World brings together a population of around 180 million people, bound by deep historical and cultural ties and increasingly connected through trade, transport, investment, education, technology, and people-to-people cooperation. What for centuries was sustained through common language, culture, traditions, and collective memory is increasingly taking institutional and practical form under the family umbrella of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS).
The transformation has been remarkable. Since its establishment in 2009, the OTS has evolved from a platform focused primarily on political dialogue and cultural affinity into a comprehensive and action-oriented framework of cooperation.
As I approach the completion of my tenure as secretary general, I see this moment not simply as an occasion to look back at what has been accomplished. More importantly, it is an opportunity to reflect on what makes our cooperation distinctive, what it can offer to our peoples, and what kind of Turkic World we wish to build together in the decades ahead.
The OTS possesses a quality that is rare among international organizations. International institutions are often created in response to a particular political challenge, economic necessity, or security concern. The foundation of the OTS is different. Our cooperation rests upon something that existed long before the establishment of the organization itself: centuries of shared history, linguistic affinity, common cultural traditions, values, and a profound sense of belonging to the same civilizational space. Common history, language, identity, and culture are not simply references to our past. They provide a foundation of trust upon which strong and sustainable cooperation can be built. Few, if any, international organizations enjoy such a natural foundation. Yet, heritage alone does not guarantee a shared future. The responsibility of our generation is to transform this historical closeness and affinity into opportunities, connectivity, and cooperation that respond to the realities and challenges of the 21st century.
There is a simple expression that captures this idea particularly well: "Biz Birlikte Daha Güçlüyüz" – Together, We Are Stronger. Remarkably, these words, written using letters that form part of the Common Turkic Alphabet, are understood across the Turkic World and require almost no translation, reflecting the deep linguistic and cultural bonds among our peoples. Today, "Together, We Are Stronger" is not merely an expression of solidarity, but a guiding principle for practical cooperation.
One of the most important transformations of recent years has been the gradual conversion of this natural affinity into institutional capacity. Today, the OTS continues to make significant strides in strengthening cooperation among its member states. Currently, 65 cooperation mechanisms exist under the OTS umbrella, which range from economy, trade, transport, and customs to energy, digitalization, industry, science and technology, health, education, youth, agriculture, labor and social protection, intellectual property, space, and many others. Since 2023 alone, 32 new mechanisms have been established – matching the total number created by the end of 2022. This reflects not only the expansion of our agenda, but also the growing determination of our member states and observers to translate shared priorities into concrete institutional cooperation.
What matters even more than the numbers is a change in how we work together. Political consultations have become more frequent and substantive; ministries and specialized institutions are in closer contact; and our ability to think together, plan together, and act together has grown. I would describe this stage of our development in three words: implementation, transformation, and institutional deepening.
As chair of the Coordination Committee of the Turkic Cooperation Organizations, the OTS maintains close and structured cooperation with affiliated and related organizations, including the Parliamentary Assembly of Turkic States (TURKPA), the International Organization of Turkic Culture (TURKSOY), the Turkic Academy, the Turkic Culture and Heritage Foundation, the Turkic Investment Fund (TIF), and the Union of Turkic Chambers of Commerce and Industry (TCCI). Together, these institutions contribute to a multidimensional framework of cooperation, strengthening institutional ties and advancing shared priorities across the Turkic World.
The establishment and operationalization of the Turkic Investment Fund represent an important milestone in this evolution. For the first time, the Turkic states have created a joint financial institution designed to mobilize their economic potential, support investment and entrepreneurship, strengthen small and medium-sized enterprises, and facilitate joint projects. The Council of Central Banks, the Turkic Green Finance Council, and the Turkic Investment Promotion Network (TurkIPAnet) further reinforce this emerging financial and investment architecture.
Yet among the most encouraging developments I have witnessed during my tenure is the emergence of cooperation networks beyond governmental and formal institutions, including within the private sector and professional communities.
Notaries, auditors, engineers, trade unions, and representatives of other professions are establishing contacts, creating networks, and exploring institutional forms of cooperation within a broader Turkic framework. This growing cooperation is also reflected in initiatives such as the Union of International Road Transport Associations of the OTS, the Union of Turkic Ski Resorts, and the Turkic Red Network, bringing together stakeholders across transport, tourism, and humanitarian cooperation. Business communities, universities, young people, experts, and professional associations are finding their own reasons – and increasingly their own ways – to connect.
When people and professional communities begin building connections on their own initiative, cooperation acquires a life beyond institutions. It becomes rooted in society itself.
For me, this is one of the clearest signs of the growing maturity of Turkic cooperation.
The growing importance of the Turkic World is shaped not only by our shared heritage, but also by the scale of our collective economic and strategic potential. According to figures reported for the end of 2025, the combined GDP of OTS member states and observers exceeded $2.4 trillion, while their aggregate trade turnover reached approximately $1.27 trillion. Taken as a single entity, the Turkic states would represent the world’s 11th-largest economy and third-largest energy provider. With substantial reserves of oil, natural gas, coal, and critical minerals, including over 40% of global uranium production, our countries possess significant energy potential while increasingly investing in renewable energy development.
In a time of rising demand and rapid changes in global energy systems, working together is not optional – it is a necessity. Recent OTS summits have stressed the importance of energy security, which depends on connecting pipelines, power grids, storage, and transport routes to ensure stable supply, increase trade, and strengthen economic and geopolitical stability.
The Turkic states are strengthening regional and international energy connectivity through major infrastructure projects, including the Southern Gas Corridor, the Central Asia-Azerbaijan Green Energy Corridor, the Kambarata-1 Hydropower Plant, and the Black Sea Submarine Cable. These initiatives reflect the growing role of the Turkic World in enhancing energy security, diversifying supply routes, and advancing renewable energy cooperation. In this regard, the Turkic World Vision–2040 provides an important strategic framework. It calls on us to deepen economic integration, improve connectivity, strengthen institutions, invest in knowledge-based industries, and promote sustainable and inclusive growth. Perhaps nowhere is this logic more visible than in connectivity.
The Trans-Caspian International East-West Middle Corridor is becoming an increasingly important link between Asia and Europe, with freight volumes potentially reaching 11 million tons by 2030. The China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, with a projected capacity of up to 15 million tons annually, will further strengthen regional connectivity and expand trade opportunities across Eurasia. But a modern corridor is more than railway tracks, roads, and ports. Goods must cross borders efficiently; information and documentation must move with them.
The OTS is complementing physical infrastructure with customs and digital solutions, including the Simplified Customs Corridor, e-Permit, e-CMR, and digital TIR, to facilitate cross-border trade and reduce administrative barriers. The Digital Economy Partnership Agreement and ongoing efforts to conclude a free trade agreement in services and investment will further strengthen economic integration among our countries.
We also welcome the recently established cooperation among competition authorities, financial intelligence units, investment promotion agencies, supreme audit institutions, and tax administrations. These partnerships strengthen institutional connectivity and improve economic governance across the Turkic World. The digital economy remains at the center of this agenda. Digital trade platforms, interoperable e-customs systems, fintech cooperation, secure data exchange, and common approaches to digital regulation can make economic relations more efficient and accessible. Digital transformation is not simply a technical matter. It is one of the foundations of modern economic integration. The objective is straightforward: to make connectivity work better for those who actually use it.
Taken together, these developments point towards the gradual emergence of a more connected Turkic economic space – one in which infrastructure is reinforced by efficient borders, trade is supported by investment, and the strengths of individual countries increasingly become sources of shared opportunity.
For the younger generation, the Turkic World should be a living space of opportunity. The Turkic Universities Union (TURKUNIB) and the Orhun Exchange Program help bring students, academic staff, and universities closer together. Youth initiatives, including the Youth Volunteering Educational Program, the Multilateral Youth Exchange Program, and the International Youth Camp, further promote people-to-people contacts, mutual understanding, and a sense of shared identity among young people across the Turkic World. Meanwhile, initiatives under discussion, such as the Turkic ID and Common Museum Card, aim to facilitate travel and access to our shared cultural heritage.
A transport corridor becomes more valuable when businesses use it. Business cooperation becomes stronger when supported by investment. Investment becomes more productive when connected with technology and human capital. And all of these become more sustainable when our societies participate in and benefit from the process. The future of the OTS therefore lies not simply in expanding the number of areas in which we cooperate, but in bringing existing mechanisms together into a more coherent space of opportunity.
Our strength lies precisely in building upon our unique foundations while remaining open to the wider world. Our long-term direction is set out in the Turkic World Vision-2040. Deeper connectivity and integration, pursued with full respect for the sovereignty and national priorities of our States, should strengthen our common capacity to address climate change, food and health security, emergencies, and other cross-border challenges.
A stronger Turkic World should also mean a more connected and outward-looking Turkic World. Our geography gives us a natural role in this regard. For centuries, the lands of the Turkic World have connected peoples, cultures, markets, and ideas across Eurasia. Today, we have an opportunity to give this historical role a modern meaning. By improving transport links, facilitating trade, connecting energy networks, encouraging innovation, and strengthening contacts among societies, the Turkic states can contribute not only to their own prosperity, but also to greater connectivity and cooperation across the wider Eurasian region.
This approach is reflected in the OTS’s growing engagement with the United Nations system and other international and regional organizations, as well as in the development of the OTS+ format, which provides a flexible platform for cooperation with countries and partners beyond the Organization. Our aim is to develop mutually beneficial, practical partnerships that contribute to peace, stability, connectivity, sustainable development, and dialogue. Our objective is not to build walls around the Turkic World, but to build bridges that connect it with the wider world. A Turkic World that is more connected within can also be more open, more relevant, and more capable of contributing to dialogue, development, and shared prosperity beyond its own borders.
Over the past years, I have had the privilege of witnessing the Turkic World move closer together -- and making my humble contribution to this progress -- in ways that are increasingly diverse and increasingly tangible. Yet perhaps the most important conclusion I draw from these years is that we are still at the beginning of what is possible.
The foundations have been laid. The commitment of our member states is strong. The institutional architecture has expanded. Our collective economic and strategic potential is increasingly recognized. And our societies themselves are discovering new ways of connecting with one another. The forthcoming 13th OTS Summit in Ankara -- to be held under the theme “Turkic Century: Unity in Language, Thought and Deed” and marking the beginning of Türkiye’s Chairmanship -- offers an important opportunity to carry this momentum into the next phase of our common work. Looking ahead, the success of our cooperation must be measured not only by the agreements we sign or the mechanisms we establish, but by the tangible benefits we deliver to our peoples. Our priority must remain to translate our collective ambitions into meaningful opportunities and lasting progress for future generations.
I remain deeply grateful to the heads of state of our member states and observers for their vision and unwavering support, as well as to our governments, institutions, Permanent Representatives, experts, and colleagues at the OTS Secretariat. Their dedication, professionalism, and shared commitment have been indispensable to every step of our collective progress. It has been a great honor to contribute to this journey as secretary general. Although my tenure as secretary general is drawing to a close, my commitment to the unity, cooperation, and prosperity of the Turkic World will remain unchanged. I will always regard it as a privilege to have contributed to this common endeavor and will continue to believe in the extraordinary potential of our shared future.
The Turkic World must continue its journey from affinity to connectivity, from potential to capacity, and from cooperation to tangible benefits for its peoples. Our ancestors gave us a shared heritage. What we leave to future generations must be more than the memory of that heritage. It must be a shared future built upon it. Across our languages and across our geography, the following message should continuously resonate: Biz Birlikte Daha Güçlüyüz - Together, We Are Stronger.

Ambassador Fontana Inaugurates First Section of the Aqar Quf Archaeological Park in Baghdad
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:31:14 CEST
18:31:14 KST

The first section of the Aqar Quf Archaeological Park (ancient Dur-Kurigalzu) was inaugurated in the presence of Italy’s Ambassador to Baghdad, Niccolò Fontana. This marks the opening to the public of one of the most significant sites of Mesopotamian heritage and represents a step forward in its preservation and promotion.
                                    
The initiative is part of the site’s growing international recognition; its inclusion on UNESCO’s Tentative List is the result of collaboration between the University of Bologna and Iraq’s State Board of Antiquities and Heritage. The complex includes the imposing ziggurat, the remains of the ancient Kassite royal city, and the monuments that bear witness to its urban organization and historical-cultural landscape.
                                    
The project combines archaeological research, innovative technologies, conservation and restoration, specialized training, and the involvement of local communities. Activities include surveys using drones and photogrammetry techniques, high-resolution documentation, and diagnostic analyses, along with interventions to protect ancient structures, improve safety, and enhance public access to the site.
                                    
These activities are part of ArTourBagh, a three-year Italian cooperation project worth 3 million euros, implemented through the Italian Agency for Development Cooperation (AICS) in collaboration with the University of Bologna, the University of Catania, CRAST, and AVSI. The initiative aims to preserve Iraq’s archaeological heritage and promote a model of sustainable cultural tourism in the Baghdad area. The project combines heritage conservation efforts with training and awareness-raising activities. 156 people have acquired theoretical knowledge or technical skills through courses, seminars, and conservation workshops, while approximately 320 young people have participated in 30 educational initiatives targeting schools and local communities. ArTourBagh also aims to foster new employment and entrepreneurial opportunities in the sectors of guided tours, crafts, hospitality, and tourism services, with a particular focus on young people, women, and local communities.
                                    
The inauguration reaffirms Italy’s commitment to working alongside Iraqi institutions to protect and promote a heritage of exceptional historical and cultural significance. By sharing expertise and strengthening local capacities, the embassy emphasizes, Italian cooperation helps make culture a resource for sustainable development, community growth, and the strengthening of ties of friendship between Italy and Iraq.

German Army gets its first heavy-lift cargo drone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:30:45 UTC
18:30:45 KST

- The German Army’s 131st Supply Battalion in Bad Frankenhausen received its first TEKEVER heavy-lift drone to test autonomous cargo delivery to troops.
- TEKEVER is opening a German subsidiary in Munich to support the Bundeswehr and work with German industry.
The German Army has received its first heavy-lift cargo drone, with the 131st Supply Battalion in Bad Frankenhausen, Thuringia, taking delivery of an uncrewed aircraft from Portuguese manufacturer TEKEVER to test how drones can haul equipment and supplies to troops in the field.
The Bundeswehr in Thuringia announced the handover on Oct. 13, describing it as the first heavy-lift drone in the German Army and the start of a new chapter for uncrewed cargo transport in its logistics units.
Unlike the small quadcopters now common on the battlefield, the new aircraft is designed to carry heavy loads, and the Bundeswehr said it is meant to move materiel and supplies quickly to where they are needed, including places where roads are difficult or only partly accessible. That is a practical problem for supply units, since trucks heading to forward positions are exposed to drones, artillery and mines, and an aircraft that can deliver ammunition, spare parts or medical supplies without a driver could take some of that risk off the road.
The battalion, commanded by Lt. Col. Sojka, will now run further testing and training to work out what jobs the drone can take on and how autonomous cargo flights could fit into the German Army’s logistics system. TEKEVER said the evaluation will help the Bundeswehr decide what role autonomous transport should play in supporting future operations, and the company described the delivery as an important step in Germany’s assessment of autonomous military logistics.
The handover coincides with TEKEVER setting up a German subsidiary headquartered in Munich, which will serve as the company’s regional hub for engineering, customer support and industrial cooperation in Germany, Austria and Switzerland. Founded in Portugal, TEKEVER has grown into one of Europe’s best-known military drone makers on the back of its AR5 surveillance aircraft, which Ukraine’s armed forces have flown against Russia and which the British Army selected in July to replace its Watchkeeper fleet, as we reported.
The company moved into the heavy-lift market this summer when it unveiled its AR6 family at the Farnborough International Airshow in July. TEKEVER says the AR6 can carry about 200 kg (440 pounds) of cargo over 500 km (310 miles) and that its military version can operate without satellite navigation, with production due to start by the end of 2026 at the company’s manufacturing site in Swindon, England.
Germany is one of several NATO armies now testing cargo drones for frontline resupply, a role shaped by the war in Ukraine, where both sides have used uncrewed aircraft and ground robots to move supplies to troops in areas too dangerous for vehicles. The Bad Frankenhausen battalion is the first German Army unit to receive a heavy-lift system, and the results of its trials will help decide whether more units follow.

Kazakhstan-Uzbekistan trade rises 29% as countries target $10 billion
Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan plan to increase bilateral trade turnover to 10 billion US dollars in the near future, Kazakh Finance Minister Madi Takiyev said on Wednesday, Qazinform News Agency correspondent reports.
Trade turnover between the two countries reached 4.7 billion US dollars last year. In the first nine months of this year, it amounted to 3.7 billion US dollars, marking a 29 percent increase, Takiyev said at a briefing following a meeting of the Qurultay.
The minister said last year, Kazakh-Uzbek trade turnover reached 4.7 billion US dollars, and in the first nine months of this year, it amounted to 3.7 billion US dollars, up 29 percent, adding that the countries aim to increase it to 10 billion US dollars in the near future.
He also noted that an agreement had been signed to open representative offices of the customs services of both countries to help achieve this target.
These offices will provide practical and theoretical assistance to domestic and foreign entrepreneurs to help increase trade turnover. For example, they will help prevent goods from being held up at the border, while other issues will be addressed jointly with our Uzbek colleagues, said Takiyev.

ST PETERSBURG, Russia – Russian President Vladimir Putin hosted US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff in a grand imperial palace on Oct 21 to review new ideas on ending the war in Ukraine amid Washington’s latest push to stop Europe’s bloodiest conflict since World War II.
The talks in St Petersburg, the ninth time that Witkoff has met Putin in person, began with a goodwill gesture from Russia – the release of a retired US school teacher held in Russia.
The encounter comes amid concerns in Kyiv and among its allies that the United States is backing away from Ukraine, at times holding back real-time intelligence on Russian attacks and hobbling Ukraine’s military communications.
The latest talks came more than two years since US President Donald Trump promised in his successful election campaign to end the Ukraine war within 24 hours.
Witkoff flew into Russia’s second city on the morning of Oct 21, a day after conducting what a US official called “constructive” talks in Oslo with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, the leaders of Finland and Norway and European and NATO representatives, as US President Donald Trump said it was time for Ukraine to end the war or face “a very bad thing”.
US-Ukraine ties have deteriorated sharply since Trump announced a diesel export deal with Russia earlier in October to help lower prices in the United States. High fuel costs since he launched strikes on Iran have hurt his Republicans ahead of November legislative elections.
Since the diesel deal, Ukraine has complained of disruption to some intelligence sharing and to its use of the Starshield military satellite system, though Zelensky said that the Oct 20 Oslo meeting had reached an agreement to resolve those issues.
Starlink speeds
Citing US officials and people familiar with the matter, the Wall Street Journal reported on Oct 21 that billionaire Elon Musk had last week ordered the slowdown of a military-grade version of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite service that Ukraine relies on to track Russian ballistic missile strikes.
Reuters could not immediately verify the report.
Musk has said any such decision is taken by the US military or the President. Trump has said he was not responsible.
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Oct 20 signalled the problem lay with the terms of service Kyiv needed to comply with.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Oct 21 that Witkoff’s meeting with Zelensky was positive and that Witkoff would share the results with Russia. He also reiterated that Washington had not pulled back Kyiv’s ability to access Starlink.
“He will now, armed with those ideas, be able to go to St Petersburg and share them with the Russian side, and let’s see if we can make some progress,” he said.
Trump pressure
Despite the apparently cordial nature of the Oct 20 meeting in Oslo, Trump, as he showed in comments in the White House on Oct 20, remains frustrated with Zelensky, whom he has repeatedly rebuked and suggested needs to be replaced.
“He’s going to have to want to make a deal, because I don’t think his people are going to stand for it any longer,” Trump told reporters on the eve of the talks in Russia.
Putin, who has shown few signs of compromising on his central war aims, which include full Russian control of the Donetsk region in eastern Ukraine and no NATO membership for Kyiv, will receive Witkoff in the Constantine Palace, a grand imperial edifice in what is the Kremlin chief’s home city.
Kirill Dmitriev, Putin’s special investment envoy and his main point man for potential economic and financial deals with the US, would also be present at the meeting with Witkoff, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said.
A US official said Ukraine had brought new ideas and proposals to the Oslo talks, which had made “meaningful progress” toward a coordinated approach to engaging with Russia.
The official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said the talks covered “key elements of a comprehensive peace framework,” including security guarantees for Ukraine, a post-war economic plan and a broader European security architecture.
Witkoff would aim to “create a pathway toward direct trilateral and broader multilateral negotiations,” the official said. Zelensky said he hoped to discuss key issues on how to end the war during a trilateral meeting with Putin and Trump.
The Kremlin has repeatedly said that any Putin-Zelensky meeting would need to be painstakingly prepared in advance by aides to make it worthwhile and that a lot of the legwork required for an overall agreement would need to be in place.
Trump said on Oct 20 he had raised the idea with Putin of freeing Stephen Hubbard – a 74-year-old retired US school teacher being held in Russia on mercenary charges he denies.
Putin told Witkoff that Hubbard was at the airport waiting to fly back to the United States with him. Witkoff thanked Putin for the goodwill gesture.
Hubbard was first detained in April 2022 and was later sentenced to six years and 10 months on charges whose veracity his family and US-based lawyer question. REUTERS

six decades of irving penn’s fashion photography are now on view in paris

six decades of irving penn’s fashion photography are now on view in paris
the american photographer transformed editorial assignments into an exploration of silhouette, texture, and the relationship between the body and the image.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
IRVING PENN’S FASHION PHOTOGRAPHY AT THE MEP
The Maison Européenne de la Photographie (MEP) in Paris presents PENN & FASHION, a retrospective of American photographer Irving Penn, tracing six decades of his work for Vogue from September 30th, 2026, to January 17th, 2027. Bringing together photographs from the MEP, the Nicola Erni Collection, and The Irving Penn Foundation, the exhibition examines how Penn moved beyond the demands of fashion publishing to develop a distinct photographic language, in which he reduced his compositions to their essentials, allowing garments and the people wearing them to become the focus.
Penn’s approach took shape at a moment when fashion photography was helping shape the visual culture of the postwar period. After joining Vogue in 1943 at the invitation of art director Alexander Liberman, he initially produced still lifes and cover concepts before establishing himself as one of the leading photographers of the magazine. His training in graphic design under Alexey Brodovitch informed his precise handling of space, while his interest in modernist painting and European Surrealism contributed to images that balanced restraint with unexpected visual tension.
a studio stripped back to its essentials
The exhibition at MEP follows Penn’s career chronologically, opening with two photographs from 1947: Theatre Accident, a still life, and 12 Models Moving Their Heads, a group portrait commissioned by Vogue. In 1950, Penn traveled to Paris to photograph the latest haute couture collections. There, he established a naturally lit studio on Rue de Vaugirard and photographed designs by Cristóbal Balenciaga, Lafaurie, and Rochas against an old theater curtain. With Lisa Fonssagrives as his principal model, he concentrated on the relationship between the clothes and the body. The images he created changed how couture was presented in fashion magazines. The absence of distracting props or narrative settings made the construction of a garment more legible, drawing attention to its silhouette and texture. Penn’s photographs of Balenciaga, whose sculptural designs he regarded as the work of a master architect of clothing, demonstrate how fashion photography can communicate the logic of a design as much as its appearance. The exhibition also includes facsimiles of Vogue, showing how Penn’s photographs appeared in the magazine and how his artistic vision shaped its fashion imagery.
from haute couture to everyday life
Alongside his Paris assignments, Irving Penn developed Small Trades, a series portraying workers and tradespeople in their professional clothing. Photographed in the studio with the same attention given to celebrated models, these sitters occupied a similarly controlled visual environment. The juxtaposition reveals a consistent interest in how clothing communicates identity. Whether photographing a couture gown or the work clothes of a street vendor, Penn approached garments as objects shaped by use, construction, and social context.
Penn’s restrained compositions created a visual continuity between subjects who occupied very different positions within the hierarchy of the fashion industry. He extended this approach to portraits of artists, designers, and cultural figures, including Christian Dior, Pablo Picasso, Jean Cocteau, and Elsa Schiaparelli. Using simple screens, a worn carpet, and carefully controlled lighting, the photographer stripped the studio back to its essentials, placing emphasis on the posture, expression, and presence of each subject. The exhibition also includes facsimiles of Vogue, showing how his photographs appeared in the magazine and how they shaped its visual language.
the dialogue between the photographer and issey miyake
Another section of the exhibition examines Penn’s collaboration with Japanese designer Issey Miyake, which lasted from 1986 to 1999. Their working relationship developed without Penn attending Miyake’s fashion shows. Instead, the designer sent garments to New York, where Penn photographed them in his studio before returning the transparencies to Tokyo. The distance between the two artists did not prevent a close exchange of ideas. Miyake’s sculptural garments, often defined by their manipulation of fabric and volume, aligned with Penn’s interest in reducing an image to its essential forms.
Between 1987 and 1992, graphic designer Ikko Tanaka created more than 60 posters for Issey Miyake using Penn’s color images. Twelve of these posters are included in MEP’s presentation through loans from The Miyake Issey Foundation, showing how the photographs circulated beyond the pages of Vogue and became part of the designer’s broader identity.
beauty, artifice, and the photographic print
Penn continued to explore the relationship between clothing, the body, and the way fashion is presented. His photographs of designs by Yves Saint Laurent, Karl Lagerfeld, Christian Lacroix, and John Galliano kept the focus on shape and texture, even as fashion became more theatrical. His beauty photographs for Vogue gave him another way to experiment. Made with fashion editor Phyllis Posnick, these images used humor, Surrealist ideas, and unusual treatments of the face. In works such as Red-Lacquered Lid (1994) and Bee on Lips (1995), the face becomes a surface for experimentation, moving away from the usual rules of beauty photography. The American photographer also paid close attention to how his images were printed. He later made platinum-palladium printing an important part of his practice, valuing the depth of tone and the physical quality of the finished image. For Penn, making a photograph did not end when he pressed the shutter; the printing process was just as important.
Tracing Penn’s career from his early assignments for Vogue to his later fashion and beauty photographs, PENN & FASHION explores how he balanced commercial work with his own artistic ideas. His photographs show how assignments for a fashion magazine could become opportunities to experiment, looking beyond the clothes to the people wearing them and the way they appear in front of the camera.

 name: PENN & FASHION
photographer: Irving Penn | @the.irving.penn.foundation
venue: Maison Européenne de la Photographie (MEP) | @mep.paris
location: Paris, France
dates: September 30th, 2026–January 17th, 2027

Russia Makes Largest Gold Sell-Off Since 1998 Default to Fund Putin’s War Budget

- Category

Russia Makes Largest Gold Sell-Off Since 1998 Default to Fund Putin’s War Budget
The Central Bank of Russia has been unloading gold from its state reserves for ten straight months to plug a budget shortfall expected to reach 7.3 trillion rubles ($81.1 billion) this year, double initial projections, The Moscow Times reported on October 20.
September statistics released by the regulator show holdings fell by another 0.2 million troy ounces (around 6.2 metric tons), driving total reserves down to 72.8 million ounces—the lowest level recorded since late 2019.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Since December, when the central bank initiated its largest liquidation effort in decades, total holdings have dropped by 2 million troy ounces, or roughly 62 metric tons.
International Monetary Fund data indicates that Russia has only offloaded gold at a faster pace once in modern history. During the 1998 financial crisis, which featured a sovereign default, currency collapse, and the breakdown of the state treasury bill pyramid, the central bank sold 3.8 million troy ounces (118 metric tons) over three months.
By the end of that year, authorities repurchased a portion of the bullion, bringing the net annual reduction to 1.6 million ounces (about 50 metric tons)—a smaller total drop than the current year's decline, according to The Moscow Times.
Following that late 1990s period, the Kremlin steadily expanded its stockpile, increasing reserves more than fivefold. By early 2022, holdings reached 74 million troy ounces, or 2,300 metric tons, representing the fifth-largest gold reserve globally.
Finam analyst Alexander Potavin noted that the Finance Ministry draws on accumulated reserves, including gold, to fund budget shortfalls when revenues lag, The Moscow Times reported. With oil and gas revenues declining in 2026, asset sales from the National Wealth Fund, including bullion, have intensified.
Potavin also highlighted that central bank gold sales help address foreign currency liquidity shortages, adding that strong global gold prices likely supported the decision to step up bullion sales.
The Kremlin’s fiscal stability has faced unprecedented pressure as the 2026 budget cycle projects a deficit nearly double that of the previous year. In early March, Russian war spending officially surpassed all social welfare allocations, forcing the government to tap into the National Wealth Fund at a record pace.
Currently, as Russian leader Vladimir Putin seeks to maintain the offensive in Ukraine, the depletion of liquid assets in the “war chest” has left the Russian Central Bank with few options beyond the liquidation of its gold holdings and the remaining yuan reserves.

Attack on Australian MP Haines: How threats against legislators have soared

Attack on Australian MP Haines: How threats against legislators have soared
Abuse and threats against Australian lawmakers are rising in a country where political violence has historically been rare.
An Australian independent lawmaker, Helen Haines, has had both legs amputated after being struck by a car outside her office in Wangaratta, Victoria state, in what Prime Minister Anthony Albanese called “a deliberate attack”.
The MP’s right leg was amputated on Wednesday, two days after her left leg was amputated at a hospital in Melbourne, where the 65-year-old politician has been receiving treatment after being flown by helicopter.
“The good news in all this is that Helen is alive and she’s stable. That is the most important thing for our family,” her husband, Phil Haines, told reporters outside the Melbourne hospital.
“We are grateful and thankful that, at this stage, both her heart and her mind are in good shape,” he said.
The Australian police said it was a “targeted attack” and warned of growing “online extremism” and recorded a rise in abuse, threats and intimidation targeting lawmakers – steadily growing in a country where political violence has been rare.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has led an outpouring of support for Haines. “It’s a reminder that the world is a more dangerous and divided place than it was a generation ago,” Albanese told ABC Radio on Wednesday.
“I think that Australians do want to see their politicians be able to go about their business, to be able to get something from the back of their car, for goodness sake.”
So, why have threats against Australian lawmakers risen?
What do we know about the alleged attack?
On Monday, Haines, who entered parliament in 2019, was struck by an SUV in Wangaratta in the afternoon, sending the rural Australian town into a mix of horror and disbelief.
Haines was getting something from the boot of her car when her alleged attacker drove past in a Toyota Land Cruiser. Authorities said the 43-year-old man turned the car around before veering at Haines and pinning her against her vehicle. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said the driver then reversed before ramming her again.
Police named the suspect in the attack as Brendan Nugent, who appeared in court on Wednesday but did not apply for bail or enter a plea.
He was charged with three offences: dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury, and causing harm to a public official. Additional charges of cannabis cultivation and possession have also been laid against him.
Nugent will remain in custody until his next court appearance in February.
The Australian Federal Police received no warning of any imminent danger from the alleged attacker, Commissioner Krissy Barrett told reporters.
“What I can say is we didn’t have any specific intelligence that would have indicated something as atrocious as happened on Monday afternoon,” she said.
Victoria Police Chief Mike Bush said the state police could not find any direct past contact between Haines and the accused.
“Motivation is one of these things that we absolutely need to explore. His motivation for this, what we allege is a deliberate attack, is very much a centrepiece of the investigation,” Bush said.
Who is Helen Haines?
Haines entered parliament in 2019 after working as a nurse and midwife, becoming known for stances such as supporting stronger climate action. She retained the rural seat of Indi in 2022 and 2025.
She was widely praised for her efforts to increase transparency in politics and crack down on corruption.
“My background in nursing guides my work. As a nurse and a midwife, you’re with people in their most joyous and difficult moments. It’s taught me that life is precious, that everyone deserves dignity and respect, that good policy starts with listening, and – as a health researcher – that facts matter,” she describes herself on her website.
“Every day, I work to be a strong, independent voice – guided by common sense, decency and a commitment to delivering for our community and your family.”
In parliament, she pushed for a national anticorruption body. She introduced a bill in 2021 for a federal integrity commission, but it was defeated.
A year later, the Australian Parliament passed the National Anti-Corruption Commission Act 2022, leading to the formation of the National Anti-Corruption Commission (NACC).
Haines, who played a major role in the passing of the bill, served as the deputy chair of the parliamentary committee on the NACC.
Why are threats against lawmakers rising?
The Australian Human Rights Commission said the attack happened “against a backdrop of increasing polarisation and threats against politicians” that could undermine democracy.
Threats against Australian lawmakers and electorate offices doubled between 2021 and 2025, with 1,067 incidents reported to police last year.
The police also charged 41 people with offences relating to threats against parliamentarians last year, after the Australian federal police formed a National Security Investigations team described by police commissioner Barrett as a “flying squad of hate disruptors”.
In the 2025 election, threats to candidates jumped 17 percent from the previous campaign.
Earlier this month, police charged three men over separate threats to politicians and government officials, and three others were sentenced by courts.
Senior opposition politician James Paterson on Wednesday called for a review of personal security in response to the alleged crime. “The reality is that Australian parliamentarians by global standards are uniquely accessible to the public and that’s a good thing,” Paterson told the Australian Broadcasting Corporation.
“But we can’t have a situation where shocking attacks like this take place because that will fundamentally change our democracy forever if it becomes a serious risk to your life to be a member of parliament,” he added.
Australian Security Intelligence Organisation Director-General Mike Burgess warned last year that politically motivated violence was among the agency’s fastest-growing security concerns, driven by “grievance narratives, conspiracies and online echo chambers”.
Antiterrorism police are among the agencies investigating the attack on Haines, but the police maintain that they believe it was an isolated incident and there was “no intelligence to suggest any threat to Haines”.
What do we know about the attacker?
Nugent, a 43-year-old resident of the rural town of Tarrawingee within Haines’s electorate, has been charged with offences that carry a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison.
The motive remains unknown, and authorities have refused to speculate while the investigation takes place.
But police said on Wednesday they were examining all possible leads, including that Nugent may have held radical antigovernment views.
“Like everyone, we’re examining social media associations, talking to witnesses, friends and colleagues,” Bush, the Victoria police commissioner, told journalists.
During the brief court appearance on Wednesday, Nugent’s lawyer said his client suffers from a rare neurological condition called idiopathic transverse myelitis and that it was his first time in custody.
Meanwhile, Wangaratta’s Mayor Irene Grant said a sombre mood has settled over the town of about 30,000 people, a regional hub about 250km (155 miles) northeast of state capital Melbourne.
“What has happened to Helen has caused the community to step back in utter disbelief. We can’t believe it; people are horrified by what has happened,” she told AFP news agency.

Damaged Nord Stream lines can technically be repaired — Novak
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:24:38 UTC
18:24:38 KST

ST. PETERSBURG, October 21. /TASS/. The damaged lines of the Nord Stream gas pipeline system can be repaired from a technical standpoint, while supplies through the intact pipeline could resume in the near future, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told reporters.
"One of the four lines is operational. If European consumers - or European countries and politicians - are willing, gas could certainly be supplied through this line. It is up to the Europeans, primarily Germany, since the pipeline runs to Germany. As for the other three lines, as previously mentioned, they can technically be repaired if there is a need, rationale, or necessity," he said.
Novak pointed out that restarting supplies through the sole surviving Nord Stream line would probably not require much time from a technical perspective.
On September 26, 2022, an unprecedented act of terrorism hit the Nord Stream and Nord Stream 2 gas pipelines, leaving only one of the system’s four lines - a Nord Stream 2 pipeline - intact. The 1,224-kilometer Nord Stream pipeline, running along the Baltic Sea bed from Vyborg, Russia, to Greifswald, Germany, has an annual capacity of 55 billion cubic meters. Construction of Nord Stream 2, which has an identical capacity, was completed on September 10, 2021, but the pipeline was never put into operation. The Russian Prosecutor General’s Office has initiated a criminal case into an act of international terrorism.

U.S. Air Force sets new 1,509-fighter goal for 2035
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:23:43 UTC
18:23:43 KST

- The U.S. Air Force now targets 1,509 combat-coded fighters by 2035, with F-35s making up about 40 percent of the fleet.
- The F-47 would replace the F-22 roughly one-for-one, while F-15s and F-16s would together account for about 40 percent.
The U.S. Air Force plans to grow its fighter force to 1,509 combat-coded jets by 2035, with the F-35 becoming its most numerous fighter and the new F-47 taking over from the F-22, under a revised force structure plan the service sent to Congress on Oct. 16. Lt. Gen. David Tabor, deputy chief of staff for plans and programs, laid out the numbers at a Pentagon roundtable on Oct. 20, describing a fleet in which F-35s make up about 40 percent of the force, F-22s and F-47s about 20 percent, and F-15s and F-16s share the remaining 40 percent roughly evenly.
That mix would reshape a fleet that today, not counting the A-10 attack jet, is about 45 percent F-16s, 30 percent F-35s, 15 percent F-15s and 10 percent F-22s, so the F-16 that has dominated U.S. Air Force flight lines for four decades would give up its top spot to the F-35 within the next nine years. Tabor said the growth would come from a combination of F-35A, F-15EX and F-47 purchases, and that the service redid its analysis because the data behind the previous force structure report was “pretty old.”
Hitting 1,509 jets means adding well over 200 fighters to the roughly 1,271 combat-coded aircraft the Air Force projected for 2026, and it goes 140 jets beyond the 1,369 the service had set as its 2030 goal in last year’s report. The new target is slightly below the 1,558 crewed fighters by 2035 called for in the previous long-term fighter plan, and because it counts all combat-coded aircraft, including backup and attrition reserve jets, it is a broader measure than the 1,145 primary mission aircraft that federal law sets as the Air Force’s minimum, a floor the service told Congress in May it had slipped below with 1,098 jets.
The F-15EX is the fastest way to add new airframes, and Boeing is already building them in numbers after the Air Force ordered 22 more of the jets for $2.38 billion on Sept. 30. The service has said it could buy up to 104 of the fighters to replace its aging F-15C/D fleet, as we reported last year, while the F-35A remains the backbone of the plan, with the Air Force previously saying it could buy about 100 a year by 2030 if funding and production capacity allow.
The F-47, the sixth-generation fighter Boeing is developing under the Next Generation Air Dominance program, is due to make its first flight in 2028 and is meant to replace the F-22 roughly one for one. The Air Force built 186 operational F-22s, and Tabor said the service still expects to field about the same number of F-47s as the Raptor fleet it will succeed.
Collaborative Combat Aircraft, the uncrewed jets designed to fly alongside crewed fighters, sit outside the 1,509 count, even though the Air Force is aiming to field 500 of them by 2032. Tabor said the drones are not yet changing how many crewed fighters the service needs but could reduce that number in the future, and he made clear that reaching the 2035 target depends on industry delivering the F-35s, F-15EXs and F-47s it has promised on schedule.

Unknown Publisher

US citizen Stephen Hubbard freed by Russia and 'on his way home', Trump says
- Published
Russia has agreed to release a 74-year-old American citizen who was jailed for allegedly fighting on behalf of Ukraine.
Stephen Hubbard has been taken to Pulkovo Airport, Putin said during talks with US envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg, according to state media.
President Trump said Hubbard was "on his way back home" and "there was no 'swap' necessary for this release".
Hubbard, a former teacher originally from Michigan, was sentenced to almost seven years in a penal colony in 2024.
Prosecutors had accused him of serving in a defence unit in the eastern city of Izyum when he was captured by Russian forces, shortly after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine two years earlier.
Writing on social media after Russian state media reported the release, Trump said it had followed a request he "made directly" to Putin last week.
"There was no "swap" necessary for this release," Trump said.
The US State Department had previously classified Hubbard as "wrongfully detained" and Trump had suggested on Tuesday that his release may be imminent.
"Watch what happens," Trump told reporters, "we have been focused on Hubbard".
CBS News, the BBC's US media partner, reported that Hubbard had been in poor health and was expected to be flown to Texas for treatment.
Russian state media reported that Witkoff had thanked Putin for Hubbard's release and, on Trump's behalf, for the deal struck with Washington earlier this month to import Russian diesel.
The first shipment under the agreement will leave Russia "in two to three days", Putin said during the meeting, as quoted by state news agency TASS.
The diesel deal infuriated Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky and triggered a tumultuous few weeks of deteriorating relations, during which Trump suspended several Russian sanctions and said it was time for Ukraine to elect a new leader.
Kyiv meanwhile accused Washington of halting intelligence sharing on deadly Russian strikes, causing Ukrainians to lose their lives - an allegation Washington rejected as "scandalous".
The Ukrainian president said on Tuesday that such information sharing had resumed, following talks with Witkoff in Oslo described by the US as "positive".
During Wednesday's meeting in St Petersburg, Witkoff was filmed by Russian TV saying the diesel deal was an example to Ukraine of what could be achieved by working together.
"Your decision to remove export controls on diesel oil from Russia, not just to the US but also to the world at large in the midst of an economic shock, I think that was really important that that happened," he told Putin.
"I know [President Trump] is deeply grateful for it."

UK approves Jackdaw gas field after years in limbo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:21:00 UTC
18:21:00 KST

UK approves Jackdaw gas field after years in legal limbo
October 21, 2026
The UK government gave its approval for drilling to begin in the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea on Wednesday following years of legal and political problems that had blocked the controversial fossil fuel venture.
The Labour government justified the move saying it would strengthen the UK's energy security amid rising energy costs due to the US-Israeli war against Iran.
The gas field had previously been approved by the previous Conservative government, but wes held up by a Scottish court that said the approval had failed to consider carbon emissions.
The field lies about 150 miles (240 kilometres) east of Aberdeen in Scotland.
What did the UK government say about the Jackdaw approval?
Labour Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who has been under pressure from US President Donald Trump to increase drilling in the North Sea, said the new gas field would "protect hundreds of jobs and help keep millions of homes warm this winter."
"At a time when people are really struggling, it's right that we look in a responsible way at maximising the existing energy reserves we have in Britain that could help," he said.
"We're committed to moving towards renewable energy and reaching net zero by 2050. But even on our ambitious climate path, we'll still require oil and gas as part of our energy needs for decades to come. That's why we're taking a pragmatic approach to the North Sea," Burnham added.
Energy Minister Miatta Fahnbulleh said gas could start flowing to British houses and businesses by the end of the month. It is expected that Jackdaw will increase domestic gas production by 6% and run for 11 years.
What has been the reaction to the UK's new gas project?
Shell, which is part of the Adura joint venture along with Norway's Equinor, welcomed the decision.
"Long-term energy projects depend on a competitive and stable investment environment, alongside timely and predictable regulatory decisions," Shell said.
However, the move has also been met with strong criticism. The Green Party called it "climate vandalism," while Greenpeace said the approval showed "the toxic grip fossil fuel lobbyists still hold over our energy policy."
"True pragmatism means severing our reliance on expensive oil and gas that leaves British households broke, supercharges extreme weather, and leaves our energy security at the mercy of petrostates," said the environmental group's Ami McCarthy.
Critics have also questioned whether the new project would indeed have an impact on British gas bills since prices are determined by global energy markets.
In an attempt to show the government's commitment to its climate targets, alongside the Jackdaw approval, it announced the set up of a new Energy Wealth Fund, with an initial £2 billion ($2.7 billion), aimed at channeling oil and gas revenues into funding the transition to cleaner energy.
The UK is targeting net zero emissions by 2050, although this target must be examined under the realities already facing the planet, with a new UN report saying the world is heading for 2.8 degrees of warming, way beyond the 1.5 degrees target set in the Paris Climate Agreement.
It also comes after the UK experienced its hottest ever summer on record, with temperatures hitting previously unheard of 38 degrees in some areas in June, according to the Met Office.

Belgium’s police oversight body, Committee P, has received 26 complaints over alleged police misconduct during youth protests in Brussels, following two weeks of unrest that resulted in more than 250 arrests, news portal Bruzz reported on Wednesday.
The complaints concern police conduct during demonstrations on October 9 and 17, according to Committee P.
The unrest erupted amid protests against federal government austerity measures and cuts to French-speaking education.
On October 9, trade unions ACV and ABVV organised a nationwide day of action, joined by student movements.
Police estimated that around 1,000 people were involved in the unrest, during which public transport buses, shared vehicles and street furniture were damaged. Protesters also threw bricks and pyrotechnic devices at police officers.
Police arrested 110 people, including 30 in judicial arrests. Of those, 21 were brought before the public prosecutor’s office over alleged offences including weapons possession, violence and vandalism.
Further clashes erupted during another youth demonstration on October 17, resulting in widespread property damage and 152 arrests, including 19 in judicial arrests.
Rights groups raise concerns
Rights groups have reported allegations of disproportionate police force during the demonstrations, including violence against minors.
Pierre-Yves Rosset, director of the Service Droit des Jeunes (SDJ), said his organisation had received testimonies alleging that police officers injured young protesters.
“One minor was hit on the head with a baton. Another had to be hospitalised with a broken collarbone after being struck with a baton,” Rosset said.
The SDJ has received several testimonies concerning the events of October 9 and 12, while reports relating to the October 17 demonstration are still coming in.
The SDJ and the French-speaking human rights organisation Ligue des Droits Humains (LDH) have also questioned police tactics, particularly the frequent use of tear gas at demonstrations attended by minors and children.

====================================================================================================

Censoring Palestine: Who gets to tell its story and how?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:15:27 UTC
18:15:27 KST

Who will tell Palestine’s story? It is a million-dollar question begging an answer.
From editorial disputes over Palestinian history to the legal consequences of supporting Palestine, the struggle extends beyond what can be said and who gets to decide how it is heard.
A people can lose their homes, their land and the security of their future. But another struggle follows: telling the world what happened, why it happened, and who bears responsibility.
For Palestinians, this struggle increasingly extends into publishing houses, literary events and the institutions that determine which stories reach the public.
Their suffering may be acknowledged, but the historical context that explains it can become contested. Their writers may find opportunities to publish, but disputes over language and framing can determine how much of their intended message survives.
Two recent controversies in the literary world illustrate different dimensions of this problem: the withdrawal of a Palestinian children's book from Penguin Random House following an editorial dispute, and the decision by Irish novelist Sally Rooney and her publisher to withdraw her books from the British market amid the legal consequences of her support for Palestine Action.
The cases are not identical. One concerns editorial disagreements over historical representation; the other concerns how Britain's terrorism legislation affects a writer's earnings and the distribution of her work.
But both raise a question that deserves greater scrutiny: who gets to determine the boundaries of acceptable expression about Palestine?
When history becomes contested
In October, Palestinian-American writers Alana Hadid and Jenan Matari withdrew their forthcoming children's book, ‘Displacement and the Palestinian American Story’, from Penguin Random House after months of disagreement over editorial changes.
The book was intended for readers aged 10 to 13 and would have introduced them to Palestinian history, the 1948 Nakba, Israeli occupation, resistance, and diaspora experiences.
The authors argued that proposed changes would distort their account, including passages concerning the Hamas-led blitz of October 7, 2023, and descriptions of Zionist militias involved in the displacement of Palestinians in 1948.
According to The Guardian, the publisher added language describing the October 7 blitz as violations of international law, while the authors objected to changes they believed contradicted their narrative.
Penguin Random House defended its editorial process as standard practice. The authors ultimately withdrew the manuscript, which is now expected to be published by Interlink Books in 2027.
Publishers have a responsibility to ensure accuracy and provide age-appropriate context. But whose history receives that context, and whose suffering is subjected to endless qualifications?
If children are expected to learn about October 7, they must also be taught about the Nakba, the mass displacement of Palestinians in 1948, and the decades of occupation, dispossession and violence that followed.
Palestinian history cannot be understood through isolated events stripped of their historical context, nor should political sensitivities shape the telling of that history by determining which truths can be expressed and which must be softened or left out.
The question is not whether editors can challenge an author's interpretation. They can, and sometimes should. It is whether editorial intervention improves an account or fundamentally changes what its author is trying to say.
The authors' withdrawal of the book demonstrates the stakes of that disagreement. They concluded that the manuscript being prepared for publication was no longer the book they had written.
This is where the politics of publishing becomes a question of narrative control. A story can remain technically publishable while its historical interpretation is progressively altered.
Suffering can be acknowledged while responsibility becomes less explicit. Displacement can be described without adequately explaining the events that produced it.
Such sanitisation does not necessarily involve a formal ban. It can occur through omissions, selective framing and decisions about which words require qualification and which historical claims are allowed to stand without challenge.
The cost of expressing solidarity
Rooney’s case is distinct from the dispute over Hadid and Matari's manuscript.
Nevertheless, the outcome raises questions about the boundaries of political expression and the consequences of Britain's approach to Palestine-related activism.
The distinction matters. It would be inaccurate to describe every consequence of a legal restriction as equivalent to a conventional book ban.
But it would be equally inadequate to ignore the implications for cultural expression when a writer's political commitments affect whether her work can continue to circulate.
The broader question is how far restrictions intended to address security concerns can affect artistic freedom, political solidarity and the willingness of other writers to express controversial views.
When cultural participation carries significant legal or professional risks, the consequences can extend beyond the individuals directly affected.
Others may become more cautious about the causes they support, the language they use and the subjects they address.
These controversies point towards a broader problem: narrative control does not always require a single authority to prohibit a story outright.
It can emerge through the cumulative decisions of publishers, institutions and legal systems that shape which accounts reach audiences and under what conditions.
Each decision may have its own justification, and each case must be examined on its own evidence. But their combined effects on public discourse deserve scrutiny.
For Palestinians, representation is inseparable from history.
The Nakba was not simply a humanitarian tragedy; it involved the displacement of hundreds of thousands of Palestinians and the destruction or depopulation of hundreds of Palestinian localities.
The subsequent history of occupation, illegal settlement expansion and recurring violence cannot be understood without examining the political and military structures through which these realities developed.
Yet public discussions of Palestine can become detached from that historical continuum.
Particular acts of Palestinian violence may be examined in isolation, while the conditions surrounding them receive less attention.
Palestinian suffering may be presented as a regrettable consequence of conflict rather than an experience that requires sustained examination of power, responsibility, and historical continuity.
Beyond the visible act of censorship
The problem is not simply that Palestinian suffering is denied, but that it is also detached from the history that gives it meaning.
The Nakba becomes a tragedy without perpetrators, displacement becomes a condition without a cause, and resistance becomes an isolated act stripped of the historical realities against which it emerged.
The language of neutrality can itself become a means of obscuring these relationships, particularly when the demands for qualification and restraint fall disproportionately upon those attempting to document Palestinian dispossession.
This is how narrative control operates: not always through the outright denial of history, but through the gradual narrowing of what can be said about it.
A story may be permitted to circulate so long as its political implications remain muted, its account of responsibility softened and its challenge to established power sufficiently diluted.
The result is a version of Palestine that can be mourned but not fully understood, acknowledged but not allowed to disrupt the narratives through which its dispossession is justified or normalised.
Children's literature makes these questions especially important.
Books help shape how young readers understand history, responsibility and the experiences of people beyond their own communities.
If Palestinian history reaches children only after its most contested dimensions have been softened, their understanding of the conflict will inevitably be incomplete.
The issue, therefore, is not merely whether Palestine can be mentioned in a book. It is whether Palestinians can participate in defining how their own history is told.
The withdrawal of a manuscript and the withdrawal of an author's books from a national market reveal different pressures operating on cultural expression. Neither case alone establishes a universal policy of suppressing Palestinian narratives.
Together, however, they invite a serious examination of the institutions and rules that shape what readers can access and what writers can say.
The struggle over Palestine is fought over land, sovereignty and political freedom.
It is also fought over memory, language and representation. A people whose history is contested must be able to challenge not only the denial of their suffering, but also the selective telling of it.
The answer is not to replace one sanitised narrative with another. It is to defend the conditions in which historical accounts can be examined, challenged and debated without the removal of essential context or the unnecessary restriction of political expression.
Palestine should not have to become a more comfortable story to become a publishable one. Its history, with all its complexities and uncomfortable truths, deserves to be told in full.

Unknown Publisher

TOKYO, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- As Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi marks one year in office, criticism is growing over her push to expand the country's military capabilities, revise its pacifist Constitution and consider introducing nuclear-powered submarines, with politicians, protesters and nuclear experts warning that the moves could heighten regional tensions and undermine Japan's postwar pacifist principles.
Former Japanese Prime Minister Shigeru Ishiba recently expressed concern over Takaichi's political course in a television program, criticizing her government and right-wing forces for a lack of honesty in addressing Japan's wartime history.
In the program aired by BS-TBS on Monday, Ishiba said that Japan launched wars that resulted in tens of millions of deaths, questioning whether a country that failed to fully acknowledge these historical facts could establish solid diplomatic relations.
Ishiba also questioned Takaichi's pledge to make Japan "strong and prosperous," noting that the country's gross domestic product could fall to sixth place globally next year; in other words, the so-called "Sanae-nomics" has failed to bring prosperity to the country, adding that Takaichi's political course "will not make people happy."
On Monday evening, Japanese citizens gathered in front of the National Diet in Tokyo to protest against the government's military buildup and moves to revise the Constitution, calling for the preservation of peace.
Taku Yamazoe, policy chief of the Japanese Communist Party, said the government's continued deployment of missiles and pursuit of increasingly advanced weapons had not brought peace, warning that Japanese politics is now showing signs of a dangerous, full-scale revival of militarism.
Mizuho Fukushima, leader of the Social Democratic Party, called for efforts to prevent the House of Representatives from beginning work on drafting proposed constitutional amendments. She also criticized attempts by the Takaichi government to pave the way for constitutional revision by reducing the number of seats allocated through proportional representation.
Pointing to the large-scale Japan-U.S. joint military exercises that began Monday, Fukushima said they demonstrated the continued advance of Japan's militarization, stressing that what the country truly needed was peace.
Concerns have also mounted over the Takaichi government's consideration of introducing nuclear-powered submarines, as it prepares to revise Japan's three key security documents by the end of this year. Nuclear experts and peace advocates warn that the move could undermine Japan's longstanding exclusively defense-oriented policy and weaken the international nuclear nonproliferation regime.
At a seminar held in Tokyo on Monday, participants highlighted policy, financial and nuclear safety challenges associated with introducing such submarines, warning that the move could aggravate regional tensions and increase the risk of nuclear conflict.
Tatsujiro Suzuki, a visiting professor at Nagasaki University, said Japan's move could encourage other countries to follow suit, undermining international nuclear nonproliferation efforts, warning that such a trend could intensify regional tensions and ultimately increase the risk of nuclear war.
Sumiko Hatakeyama, co-representative of the Japanese nongovernmental organization Peace Boat, said Japan must not abandon its postwar principles of exclusively defense-oriented policy and the peaceful use of nuclear energy, stressing that the government should not introduce nuclear-powered submarines.
Hajime Matsukubo, secretary-general of the Citizens' Nuclear Information Center and a member of the Nuclear Energy Subcommittee under the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, said that nuclear-powered submarines could enable Japan to operate for extended periods across wider maritime areas, significantly affecting the regional security environment.
Matsukubo also noted that previous Japanese governments had explicitly stated that using nuclear energy to power military submarines did not qualify as the peaceful use of nuclear energy when nuclear-powered vessels had yet to become widespread.
The Takaichi cabinet's discussions on introducing nuclear-powered submarines therefore represented a clear contradiction with the government's previous position, he said, calling it a serious issue. ■

China Focus: China's Long March legacy endures from trek to tech
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:13:57 CST
18:13:57 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- One of the most visible legacies of the Red Army's Long March, a roughly 12,500-km military odyssey that ended 90 years ago, may well be an active rocket family that bears the same name.
Among the world's busiest launch vehicles, China's Long March rockets have for more than half a century carried satellites, crewed spacecraft and scientific probes into orbit and beyond, helping open the country's path to space.
This name for the rocket was suggested by several pioneers of China's aerospace industry. "It meant that the development of the rockets would overcome all difficulties and achieve victory, just as the Red Army had done during the Long March," said Han Houjian, a general designer of the Long March-1 rocket, which made its maiden flight in 1970.
On April 24, 1970, the Long March-1 lifted off carrying Dongfanghong-1, China's first satellite, into orbit. Since then, this rocket family has grown into a diverse fleet of launch vehicles with increasing payload capabilities. As of October 10, 2026, it had completed 671 orbital launches.
The journey behind these Chinese rockets echoes that of the Red Army: both were marked by immense hardships, determined perseverance, and the resolve to press ahead against the odds.
In October 1934, the Communist Party of China (CPC) was forced to retreat from the Central Soviet Area in east China's Jiangxi Province and move northwest after enduring a series of encirclement campaigns by rival forces of the Kuomintang party. The CPC-led Red Army broke through enemy blockades, crossed rugged terrain, and endured fierce battles and immense hardship. Tens of thousands of soldiers lost their lives along the way.
Few people represent the connection between these two journeys better than Sun Jixian. During the Long March, Sun, as a Red Army officer, led his men across a major river under enemy fire, helping the Red Army break through a dangerous bottleneck in 1935. More than a decade later, after the founding of the People's Republic of China, he took on a different mission -- building the country's first missile and satellite launch site in the remote Gobi Desert. His team battled sandstorms, drank alkaline water, lived in tents and caves, and transferred equipment by hand across the barren landscape.
"I remember once when my father returned from the desert, he reached into his coat pocket to look for candies for me, but what he touched was a handful of rough, cold sand," recalled Sun Dongning, his 75-year-old son.
In the 1960s, when China began developing its first rocket, the country had a weak industrial base and was cut off from access to many key foreign technologies. Scientists performed calculations using hand-cranked computing machines and worked day and night in poor workshops.
China's first nuclear-powered submarine emerged from similarly difficult conditions and relied on technological self-reliance to overcome obstacles. Commissioned on Aug. 1, 1974, it was also named Long March-1. Subsequent generations of Chinese nuclear submarines have continued to carry the Long March name.
The epic trek's legacy has since spread across military and technology sectors. Naval vessels such as Zunyi and Chishui bear the names of places associated with the historic march. Loongson, a major Chinese chipmaker, also gave two generations of its chips the project codes CZ70 and CZ80 in 2006 and 2016, respectively. CZ stands for Changzheng, the Chinese name for the Long March.
For Chinese scientists and engineers, the legacy is not simply a name but a determination to persevere in facing daunting challenges, maintain faith in eventual success, and grow more resilient with every setback.
Long Lehao, a leading Chinese rocket designer, cited the launch failure of Long March-3B as an example. As the rocket's first chief designer and chief commander, Long recalled that his hair "turned white overnight."
"There was no time to think about personal honor or disgrace. I threw myself into the new battle of tracing faults," Long recalled at a recent press conference.
After 30 days and nights of continuous work, his team identified the cause of the failure. Some 551 days later, the Long March-3B successfully delivered its payloads into orbit.
The Long March-5, designed to carry lunar and Mars probes, suffered a rare setback when its second flight failed in 2017. The failure marked the darkest chapter in this rocket's development. The research team carried out painstaking reviews and repeated trials to resolve the technical problem. On Dec. 27, 2019, the rocket completed a successful third flight and subsequently launched several spacecraft, including the Chang'e-6 probe for a far-side lunar sample-return mission.
And the journey continues. In July 2026, the Long March-10B completed China's first controlled recovery of a rocket's first stage, marking a step forward in reusable launch technology. Meanwhile, development of rockets with greater capability is being accelerated.
China aims to land astronauts on the moon before 2030 and launch a Mars sample-return mission around 2028. Additionally, it is pursuing the broader goal of becoming an innovative nation and a world-class science and technology power.
For generations of Chinese researchers, the Long March is a journey that never ends. From rugged trails to the frontiers of technology, its legacy is continuing to inspire further exploration and innovation. ■
