MOSCOW, October 21. /TASS/. Artificial intelligence in the Citadel air defense missile system achieves a 99% target engagement rate, the state corporation Rostec said.
"The system is equipped with an AI-based fire control system. Machine learning algorithms enable a 99% target engagement rate," Rostec stressed.
The corporation noted that the system is already deployed to safeguard critical facilities and can engage both small FPV drones and heavy unmanned aerial vehicles, as well as cruise missiles.
The state corporation said that Citadel learns in real combat conditions. "If the first round misses the target, the system assesses the error and adjusts its next shot. Target recognition and trajectory calculation take only seconds. There is no need to fire in bursts. A projectile with a programmable fuse detonates at the required location, covering the drone in a cloud of shrapnel. As a result, several times fewer projectiles are needed to destroy a target," Rostec said.
It added that military personnel confirm that it takes no more than four shots to neutralize a single target.
Citadel can operate independently or as part of a layered air defense system. By intercepting drones, the system reduces the workload of heavy anti-aircraft missile systems, allowing them to concentrate on priority targets.

Poland’s 360-degree Patriot radars move closer to fielding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:11:53 UTC
18:11:53 KST

- The Defense Logistics Agency asked Raytheon to price production of support hardware for Poland’s LTAMDS radars, with proposals due Dec. 18, 2026.
- The work will be ordered under a new LTAMDS contract vehicle, and DLA did not disclose its estimated value or quantities.
The Defense Logistics Agency has asked Raytheon to price the production of support equipment for Poland’s new LTAMDS radars, the 360-degree sensors that will replace the old Patriot radar in Warsaw’s air and missile defense network, under a sole-source request for proposal posted on U.S. government’s contracting website on Oct. 20.
The agency wants the hardware added to a new LTAMDS contract vehicle that is still being set up, with the Polish production and hardware work to be awarded as a standalone delivery order once that umbrella contract is in place, and it has given Raytheon until Dec. 18 to submit its offer.
The request, issued by DLA Aviation in Huntsville, Alabama, on behalf of the U.S. Army’s STARE (Search Track Acquire Radiate Eliminate) project office, covers several items listed only by their abbreviations, including a BMC and an SRPT, along with frequency converters and non-recurring engineering work. The frequency converters will need both design and development, paid on a cost-plus basis, and production under a fixed price, while the other hardware is also planned as fixed-price work, and DLA asked Raytheon to propose its own line-item structure for the deal.
DLA did not disclose an estimated value for the work or the number of equipment sets involved, and the draft statement of work attached to the request also covers engineering services that are not part of this proposal. The agency said it posted the notice publicly so that, if another company shows interest after reading it, a formal competitive solicitation can be issued to give that supplier a chance to bid.
Poland became the first foreign buyer of the Lower Tier Air and Missile Defense Sensor when it signed for 12 of the radars in 2023 as part of the second phase of its Wisła air defense program, a package that also includes 48 more Patriot launchers and a large stock of PAC-3 missiles in deals worth more than $15.5 billion. The radars are meant to give Poland’s Patriot batteries full coverage against aircraft, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles, with the first Wisła Phase 2 batteries scheduled for delivery in 2026 and 2027 and the program planned for completion in 2029.
LTAMDS uses three active electronically scanned array faces built with gallium nitride, a main forward array and two smaller rear arrays, to watch the full circle around a battery, while the legacy AN/MPQ-65 radar it replaces can only look in one direction at a time. The U.S. Army moved the radar into low-rate initial production in April 2025, and in September that year Raytheon won a $1.7 billion contract for nine radars for the U.S. Army and Poland.
Production has kept growing since then, and in April the U.S. Army awarded Raytheon a $904.6 million modification for five more radars and six spare systems, pushing the program’s total contract value past $5.35 billion, as we reported at the time. Polish industry is also part of the supply chain, with state-owned Military Electronic Works (WZE) in Warsaw building energy storage modules for the radar under a subcontract that made it the first foreign supplier on the program.

U.S. Army awards $308M for digital investigation software
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:06:54 UTC
18:06:54 KST

- The U.S. Army awarded Authentic8 a $307.7 million modification to set up a department-wide contract for its Silo digital investigation software.
- The Army solicited a single bid for the sole-source deal, which covers secure browsing tools used for open-source intelligence and dark web research.
The Pentagon is spending up to $307.7 million on software that lets its analysts browse the darkest corners of the internet without leaving a trace, after the U.S. Army awarded California-based Authentic8 a department-wide deal for its Silo platform on Oct. 20.
Silo is designed for the kind of online detective work that military intelligence now depends on, from monitoring Telegram channels and extremist forums to tracking weapons sales on dark web marketplaces, while hiding the fact that the person on the other end works for the U.S. government.
The problem Silo tries to solve is simple: every time an analyst opens a website from an official network, that site can log the visit, fingerprint the browser and, in the worst case, push malicious code onto a military computer. Silo moves the whole browsing session onto Authentic8’s own cloud servers, so nothing from the website ever reaches the user’s machine, and it lets investigators choose where they appear to be connecting from, so a visit from an Army analyst in Virginia can look like an ordinary user in another country.
That capability has become more valuable as open-source intelligence has grown into a core part of modern warfare, with Russia’s war against Ukraine showing how much can be learned from soldiers’ social media posts, geolocated videos and commercial satellite images. Analysts who dig through that material regularly visit sites run by hostile governments, militant groups and criminal networks, where a careless click from a government address can tip off the target or expose the analyst’s own network to hackers.
The Army ran the purchase as a sole-source deal and received a single bid, after telling industry in August that its requirement was specific to Authentic8’s product and that it planned to buy directly from the company unless another firm could show it offered the same capability. The award gives commands across the Department of War one place to order Silo licenses, add-on tools and support, with the amount and location of the work decided order by order rather than fixed up front.
Authentic8 is already a familiar name in federal law enforcement and financial investigations, with the Department of the Treasury, the Internal Revenue Service and the U.S. Secret Service among the agencies that have bought Silo for secure browsing and dark web research. The new contract expands an initial award made in September into a much larger vehicle that the whole department can use, which puts the Redwood City company’s tools on track to become a standard part of the military’s online investigation kit.

====================================================================================================

Trump's push for Israel-Saudi relations faces obstacles amid elections, Houthi attacks - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:05:20 UTC
18:05:20 KST

US President Donald Trump’s renewed call for Saudi Arabia to accept Israeli assistance against Yemen’s Houthis has revived questions about whether shared security threats could bring Riyadh and Jerusalem closer to normalization. But mounting attacks on Saudi infrastructure, Israel’s approaching election, and unresolved disagreements over Palestinian statehood continue to complicate the prospect of formal relations.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
Asked on October 16 whether Saudi Arabia should accept Israeli help, Trump replied: “I do, I think they will. Israel’s been very helpful to Saudi Arabia.” He also suggested that Saudi-Israeli normalization could be back on the table, “maybe more than ever.”
His comments did not establish whether Riyadh had requested Israeli military assistance or agreed to any overt security partnership.
Saudi Arabia is confronting an intensified campaign by the Iran-backed Houthis, whose missiles and drones have targeted airports, oil facilities, and shipping. An attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport killed 13 people, while repeated strikes have disrupted aviation and raised concerns about the kingdom’s ability to protect infrastructure central to its economic development plans.
For Riyadh, however, accepting Israeli military assistance would carry political consequences at home and throughout an Arab region deeply affected by the wars since October 7, 2023.
“Since the Yemen war, there have been contacts with Israel. Israel wanted to assist with the Houthis, but the Saudis, because of public opinion, did not guarantee any open contact,” Dr. Yoel Guzansky, senior researcher and head of the Gulf Program at Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), told The Media Line.
A September 30 incident illustrated the limits of cooperation. Following the emergency landing in Saudi Arabia of a flydubai aircraft bound for Israel after an attack in its cockpit, Riyadh refused an Israeli request to allow military aircraft to retrieve the Israeli passengers, according to Reuters. The passengers instead returned on another flydubai plane.
“Saudi Arabia did the minimum and didn’t want any normalization,” Guzansky said, referring to the refusal to permit Israeli aircraft to land.
Before the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023, Saudi Arabia and Israel had been moving toward a possible US-brokered normalization agreement. The subsequent wars and destruction in Gaza have made formal recognition considerably more contentious.
Riyadh has maintained that any agreement must include a credible pathway toward an independent Palestinian state, a condition Israel’s current government has resisted.
“Since October 7, the Arab world is very much against Israel. The Palestinian issue is formally at the center because it helps maintain a form of stability for Arab governments,” Guzansky said.
He argued that public opposition to Israel would remain a substantial obstacle even if the two governments identified additional areas of cooperation.
“There is no common ground between Israel and Saudi Arabia in terms of societies. Public opinion is against Israel in Saudi Arabia, and it will be hard to shift that.”
Saudi crown prince politically challenged by ongoing security crisis
For Dr. Cyril Widdershoven, senior advisor at Blue Water Strategy, the security crisis also presents an economic and political challenge for Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.
Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030 development program depends heavily on foreign investment, infrastructure expansion, and the kingdom’s reputation as a stable destination for international business. Continued attacks on airports, ports, and energy facilities threaten those ambitions while increasing defense and reconstruction costs.
Widdershoven warned that mounting expenses and persistent insecurity could fuel domestic criticism of the crown prince, making an openly acknowledged relationship with Israel even more politically sensitive.
The economic consequences of the conflict are already apparent. On October 19, organizers announced that Saudi Arabia’s flagship Future Investment Initiative conference, originally scheduled for October 26–29, would be postponed until 2027. The decision followed deadly Houthi attacks and growing security concerns, although organizers did not explicitly cite the attacks as the reason.
Military considerations present another obstacle. Saudi Arabia has fought the Houthis for more than a decade, yet repeated air campaigns have failed to eliminate the group’s ability to strike across the border or threaten shipping through the Red Sea.
“I don’t think that Saudi is militarily able to crush the Houthis. Hurt them, yes. But to go inside Yemen is something else,” Widdershoven said. “I would say it’s like a potential Afghanistan or Vietnam scenario.”
He also warned that direct Israeli military involvement could expand the confrontation by provoking responses from Iran and allied armed groups elsewhere in the region.
“I would say to the Israelis, I would offer my help, but I would keep my soldiers out. Let’s have the Arabs deal with the Arabs.”
Saudi Arabia is meanwhile seeking assistance from regional partners whose involvement may be more politically acceptable.
On October 18, Egypt’s National Defense Council, chaired by President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, agreed to support Saudi Arabia in defending itself against Houthi attacks. The Saudi defense minister also met the president of the United Arab Emirates as the two governments sought closer coordination despite longstanding differences over Yemen.
Turkey submitted the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan to its parliament for ratification on October 20.
Signed in August, the three-country pact provides for mutual defense if a signatory comes under armed attack. Turkish officials have indicated that assistance to Riyadh could include military equipment and intelligence sharing, while any Turkish troop deployment abroad would require parliamentary approval.
Britain also announced Tuesday that Royal Air Force Typhoon jets would conduct defensive patrols over Saudi territory, expanding British military support against Houthi missile and drone attacks.
“The Saudis need the Emiratis now in terms of Yemen. It is temporary, not fixing their competition,” Guzansky said, distinguishing immediate security needs from the continuing rivalry between Riyadh and Abu Dhabi.
Widdershoven similarly identified Egypt and the Emirates as potential partners while questioning how far arrangements involving Turkey and Pakistan would translate into operational commitments.
He also distinguished official diplomatic relations from informal contacts, suggesting that Saudi and Israeli representatives might continue discussions without public acknowledgment.
“So to expect that officially there will be a discussion between Riyadh and Jerusalem, I think that will not happen officially,” he said.
Change in Israel leadership could improve potential Saudi relations
Israel’s October 27 election adds another layer of uncertainty.
The vote, the first national election since the October 7 attacks, will determine whether Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu can assemble another governing coalition or whether opposition parties can form an alternative government.
Guzansky believes a leadership change could improve prospects for renewed contact with Riyadh.
“The elections are crucial in this situation, since a new government, the current opposition, would help a lot in terms of rapprochement,” he said.
Netanyahu, Guzansky added, “is not well seen in the Arab world.”
Widdershoven offered a similar assessment, suggesting that Saudi opposition to closer relations with Israel is tied partly to Netanyahu personally.
“I don’t expect that as long as Bibi Netanyahu is in power, that this will happen,” he said. “The current feeling in Saudi is not that they are anti-Israeli. I think that they are anti-Bibi Netanyahu.”
Yet a change of government would not necessarily remove Riyadh’s principal diplomatic condition.
Gadi Eisenkot, a prominent opposition contender, has avoided endorsing a two-state formula, while other parties seeking to replace Netanyahu hold substantially different positions on Palestinian statehood, settlements, and negotiations.
An opposition coalition united around replacing the prime minister would therefore not automatically agree on a policy capable of satisfying Saudi demands.
Washington faces its own political pressures ahead of the November 3 congressional midterm elections.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll published October 20 placed Trump’s approval rating at 31%, the lowest of either of his presidential terms, as Americans expressed growing frustration over high gasoline prices and the economic consequences of the war with Iran.
Trump endorsed Netanyahu’s reelection campaign on October 18, even as both experts interviewed by The Media Line suggested that a different Israeli government might be better positioned to improve relations with Saudi Arabia.
The endorsement highlights a potential conflict between Washington’s immediate political alliances and its longer-term ambition to expand the Abraham Accords.
“Trump may keep pushing rhetorically for normalization with Saudi, but in practice it is very different,” Guzansky said.
Iran extending US negotiations to deny Trump pre-midterm success
The approaching US elections are also influencing calculations in Tehran. Senior Iranian officials told Reuters that Iran had deliberately prolonged negotiations with Washington partly to deny Trump a political success before the midterms.
Widdershoven argued that Iran could continue pressuring its adversaries through threats to shipping, rising insurance premiums, and regional instability without necessarily launching another major military offensive.
“They are playing the long game,” he said. “Iran can play this for another two, three, five years. We cannot.”
For Saudi Arabia, continued instability increases the incentive to strengthen regional security arrangements. But neither common threats nor a possible change in Israeli leadership would necessarily overcome the diplomatic barriers to normalization.
“A new government in Israel may push new talks with Saudi Arabia, but still the opposition won’t guarantee a Palestinian state,” Guzansky said.

Taiwan reports 18 mpox cases in October
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:02:38 UTC
18:02:38 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan has reported 18 confirmed mpox cases so far in October, the highest monthly total in two years, the Centers for Disease Control said Tuesday.
Sixteen patients had clade Ib infections, according to a CDC press release. They were in their 20s to 40s and had engaged in higher-risk sexual behavior, while only two had previously received an mpox vaccine.
Taiwan recorded 52 confirmed cases this year as of Oct. 19, including 41 locally acquired and 11 imported infections.
The CDC urged eligible people to complete the two-dose vaccination series. As of the end of September, 31,927 people, or 28% of those who had received at least one dose, had yet to receive their second shot.
Two doses provide about 90% protection, compared with 40% to 80% for one dose, the agency said. Vaccination can also reduce the severity of symptoms if infection occurs.
Free vaccination is available at 327 medical institutions nationwide. Eligible recipients include people who have engaged in higher-risk sexual behavior in the past year, those with a history of sexually transmitted infections, and people whose sexual partners meet either criterion.
Mpox has an incubation period of up to 21 days, and some infected people can transmit the virus one to four days before symptoms appear, the CDC said. Symptoms include fever, swollen lymph nodes, rashes, blisters, and pustules.
Young children, pregnant women, and people with chronic diseases or weakened immune systems may face a greater risk of severe illness.
Further information is available on the Taiwan CDC website or through the toll-free epidemic prevention hotline at 1922 or 0800-001922.

Current DPP mayoral candidate Su Chiao-hui (蘇巧慧) also raised waste disposal concerns while serving as a legislator. During the review of the 2023 national budget, she proposed freezing NT$2 million (US$63,000) in funding for the Environmental Protection Administration until it reported on efforts to legalize waste sorting facilities and prevent illegal dumping, per The Reporter.

Blast heard in Yemen’s Aden as Houthis claim attack on military camp
Smoke seen rising near airport in Aden as Houthis say they attacked a military camp with a ballistic missile.
A powerful explosion was heard in Aden in southern Yemen, an Al Jazeera journalist and police have said, as the Houthis claimed a ballistic missile attack on a military camp in the city.
A police official said on Wednesday that smoke was rising near the international airport in Aden, the seat of power of Yemen’s internationally recognised government.
Yahya Saree, spokesman of the Houthi armed group, also known as Ansar Allah, meaning Supporters of God in Arabic, said in a statement the attack targeted a military camp used by the Saudi-led coalition, which has been battling the Houthis since a 2022 ceasefire in Yemen’s war collapsed earlier this year.

A day earlier, the group launched a deadly missile attack on the presidential palace in Aden, hitting command centres located inside the compound, which is used by government forces and the Saudi-led coalition.
Elsewhere in Yemen, the Saudi-led coalition said its forces were engaged in heavy fighting with the Houthis in Kahboub in the southwest.
A coalition spokesperson said they were trying to repel a large-scale attack and were experiencing intense Houthi bombardment, describing the situation as “very dangerous”.
Clashes are ongoing under “intensive air cover” by coalition and Yemeni forces, the spokesperson said.
In a separate statement, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted five drones launched towards the kingdom, including in the Medina region, home to one of Islam’s holiest cities.
“Four drones launched towards the kingdom have been intercepted and destroyed,” coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki posted on X, adding in a second post that the interceptions took place in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern province as well as Medina.
Al-Malki, who did not specify who was behind the launches, later said another drone had been intercepted in the Eastern province.
The Houthis denied having targeted the kingdom, with Saree saying their forces had not carried out any “deep” operations in Saudi territory.
Fighting in Yemen escalated sharply last month when the Houthis seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast.
Government forces, backed by Saudi Arabia, have been responding with a counteroffensive and have started Operation Dawn of Yemen, which aims to seize and recapture territory from the Houthis, including the capital, Sanaa, which has been under the group’s control since 2014.

Lin Restaurant transforms childhood nostalgia into fine dining
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:02:07 UTC
18:02:07 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Chef Kai-lin Tsai (蔡凱霖) of Lin Restaurant is drawing on childhood memories and family traditions for an autumn menu that reinterprets home cooking and street snacks through contemporary French techniques.
Following the pressure of the Michelin evaluation season, Tsai is taking a more playful, reflective approach. At the heart of the menu is his grandmother’s chicken soup, a source of comfort during difficult times.
The season’s centerpiece is Shanghai-style braised beef with fermented baby Chinese cabbage and chicken jus.
Tsai considers the dish his most complex creation. He spent months refining its braised flavors before finding inspiration at a Shanghai street stall, where he encountered the balance of soy sauce, Shaoxing wine, and savory aromas he sought.
Tsai selected Australian boneless M3 wagyu short rib for its fat content. He omitted Sichuan peppercorns and chilies, instead simmering French chicken jus with Shaoxing wine, soy sauce, and rock sugar.
The accompanying fermented baby Chinese cabbage presented another challenge. To avoid overwhelming acidity, Tsai halted fermentation after one hour, producing a crisp, mildly tart contrast to the beef.
The signature soup, “Hung Chin Hsiu-pao (洪金秀寶),” honors Tsai’s grandmother.
Recalling the comfort of her cooking, Tsai simmers chicken stock with two varieties of ginseng, flower mushrooms, and South African abalone.
Elsewhere on the menu, Taiwanese street snacks and coastal memories inform the dishes.
Inspired by after-school snacks, Tsai uses French pastry techniques to turn scallion pancakes into thin, crisp bases topped with seared beef tartare.
Growing up near Changhua with an uncle who owned a fishing boat, Tsai ate cured mullet roe as a childhood snack. On the autumn menu, it is seared tableside and served with taro cake and garlic potato.
King crab is paired with a French butter sauce flavored with Shaoxing wine and shiso.
Other dishes include a poached egg with traditional dried radish and Comte cheese, and threadfin fish served with a savory broth thickened with sago pearls.
A citrus palate cleanser and chestnut souffle precede a petit four inspired by mian fen jian, a traditional pan-fried batter cake Tsai loved at Changhua markets as a child. Made with peanut butter and toasted buckwheat, it closes the meal with another childhood flavor.
Lin Restaurant's autumn menu. (Taiwan News, Lyla Liu video)

Hong Kong sees last-minute IPO cancellations amid increased regulatory checks, weak market
At least three companies have now shelved their listings in the city after launching share sales since the start of July
Hong Kong’s tougher oversight and weak investor demand have put many mainland China issuers in a dilemma, forcing many small-cap non-technology firms to delay their fundraising plans or even cancel them at the last minute, according to industry players.
On Tuesday Jiangsu Slender West Lake Culture and Tourism (SWL Tour) became the latest such case, when the state-owned aquatic tourism service provider postponed a HK$227 million (US$28.93 million) listing. The company attributed the decision to “several factors, including the prevailing market conditions,” it said just hours after closing its order books.
“Institutional investors are now more cautious about small-cap stocks with limited fundamentals and growth prospects,” said Roy Lo Wa-kei, managing partner at the accounting and consulting firm SW Hong Kong.
The SWL Tour deal did not bring in any cornerstone investor, according to its prospectus, and with the firm opting for the city’s so-called Mechanism B, which caps a public tranche at just 10 per cent, leaving allocation and pricing power more dependent on institutional buyers.

Type 31 support deal being rethought
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:00:53 BST
18:00:53 KST

The Type 31 Through Life Support procurement has been discontinued after a review concluded that the assumptions behind it no longer reflected the right route for supporting the class, and the department is now considering fresh arrangements to meet a requirement it says is unchanged, according to answers given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked by when the Secretary of State will make a decision on the replacement for Type 31 Through Life Support, and was referred to an answer given on 6 October to his earlier question about the corrigendum to the tender published on 22 July.
Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, said in that answer: “The Type 31 Through Life Support procurement was discontinued following a review of the proposed approach. The Department concluded that the assumptions underpinning that procurement no longer reflected the most appropriate route for delivering support to the Type 31 class. Those assumptions included the delivery context for the programme and the way in which future support arrangements should be structured. The requirement to provide effective through-life support for the Type 31 fleet remains unchanged.”
“The Department is now considering the most appropriate arrangements to meet that requirement. Any future procurement activity will be taken forward in accordance with Defence requirements, value for money considerations and established commercial procedures.”
Through life support covers the maintenance, spares, training, documentation and engineering authority that keep a warship class running across thirty years, and it is usually worth more over a ship’s life than the ship cost to build.
Five Type 31 frigates are being built by Babcock at Rosyth under a contract signed in 2019, with HMS Venturer the first of class, and this publication has tracked the programme’s progress towards launch and the build work on Venturer.

Takero Shimazaki upgrades makeshift theatre into permanent "church-like" London venue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Takero Shimazaki upgrades makeshift theatre into permanent “church-like” London venue
A crane tower becomes a soaring beacon at The Yard Theatre in London‘s Hackney Wick, which local studio Takero Shimazaki Architects has revamped and extended using reclaimed materials.
Originally established in 2011 in a converted warehouse and designed by Practice Architecture to last as a three-month project, Takero Shimazaki Architects‘ redesign transforms the theatre from a makeshift space to a permanent performance venue with a bar, backstage facilities and community space.
Aiming to maintain the character of the site, Takero Shimazaki Architects used reclaimed materials to overhaul the existing 110-seat theatre space and extend the venue into the adjacent studios and former brewery with brick walls.
“The core discussion had been about The Yard Theatre ‘growing up’ and for it to have a more permanent presence in the new architecture,” Takero Shimazaki Architects founder Takero Shimazaki told Dezeen.
“The building’s form emerged from the playful idea of creating a civic cultural space by referring to a church-like form made from industrial light-weight materials, as well as the facade brickwork,” he continued.
“The overall architectural form also created stacked boxes on top of the existing warehouse, breaking up the horizontal industrial language and creating a more monumental presence using readily available and sustainable materials.”
Takero Shimazaki Architects retained the brick walls of the former brewery, which now contains a new 224-capacity theatre space with curved amphitheatre seating.
The theatre’s pitched structural frame was made from laminated veneer lumber atop reclaimed tubular steel.
A crane tower was refashioned as a ventilation chimney that rises 23 metres tall, clad in translucent polycarbonate boards to form an eye-catching beacon from outside.
A bar and public foyer occupy the former theatre building, where Takero Shimazaki Architects added a new roof and retained as much of the walls, floors and windows as possible.
The theatre’s backstage facilities are located under the auditorium’s tiered seating, and lifts and stairs were added to connect the bar to the theatre’s upper-level seating.
Materials that were demolished in the construction of the transformation were reused, including exterior bricks used for the stage wall and external infills.
The extended exterior of The Yard Theatre was finished in fibre-cement sheeting, polycarbonate panels and colourful low-carbon named K-Briq, which are made from more than 95 per cent recycled materials.
Atop the roof of the boxy volumes stands a human-shaped sculpture designed by British sculptor Antony Gormley.
Other projects by Takero Shimazaki Architects include a Japan-influenced overhaul of a flat in the Barbican estate and a renovated 1960s house with black-painted brickwork outside of London.

Serbia announced a deal to sell Russia’s stake in NIS to Hungary’s MOL - what it means
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:59:24 EEST
17:59:24 KST

Serbia announced a deal to sell Russia’s stake in NIS to Hungary’s MOL - what it means
Kyiv • UNN
MOL has agreed to purchase Russia’s stake in Serbia’s NIS. The deal is awaiting approval from antitrust authorities, while Serbia’s stake\r\nwill increase to 35%.
The agreement on the sale of the Russian stake in Serbian oil company NIS to Hungarian company MOL has been signed, but still requires approval from antitrust authorities. Serbia's Finance Minister Siniša Mali said this, UNN reports, citing HVG.
Details
In an interview with Bloomberg Adria, Siniša Mali said that the Russian owners and MOL had reached an agreement, and that the Serbian state had concluded a shareholders' agreement with the Hungarian side. The Hungarian minister expects applications for licenses to be submitted to the Serbian and, to his knowledge, Bosnian and Herzegovinian antitrust authorities in the near future, and that the change of ownership could be completed shortly thereafter.
Siniša Mali confirmed that the agreement would increase Serbia's stake in the company. According to him, a written agreement was reached to increase the Serbian state's stake from approximately 30 to 35 percent. He added that Belgrade's goal is to exceed one third.
In early October, Serbian Forbes reported that the negotiations had failed. According to the publication, Russian "Gazprom" clearly does not want to sell its stake in the Serbian state-owned oil company and is merely keeping silent about it to buy time in case the United States lifts its sanctions, which would primarily force it to sell NIS.
Shortly thereafter, information began circulating that American companies might seek to purchase NIS.
What the decision means
By acquiring more than half of NIS, Mol, as the publication writes, could obtain Serbia's only operating oil refinery, as well as the unit in Pančevo, through which the company led by Chairman and CEO Zsolt Hernádi would gain additional oil-processing capacity of 4.8 million tonnes per year, in addition to the combined capacity of its refineries in Százhalombatta in Hungary, Bratislava (owned by Slovnaft) in Slovakia, and Rijeka (owned by INA) in Croatia, amounting to nearly 19 million tonnes per year.
"What makes this deal a real bombshell is that Pančevo covers 80 percent of the country's market demand, and in addition to supplies to its own filling stations and stations bearing the \"Gazprom\" logo, other major consumers also buy from it," the publication states.
If an agreement is reached, Mol could also reportedly become the owner of petrochemical company HIP-Petrohemija, 90% of whose shares have been owned by NIS since 2021.
NIS also has interests outside Serbia. The company explores for oil and gas in Romania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Angola, and also has retail outlets in Bosnia and Romania, as well as in Bulgaria. This means more than 400 filling stations in the region, including household outlets. The company is also involved in electricity trading and is active in the Serbian market, as well as in the markets of Bosnia, Montenegro, Romania, Slovenia, and Hungary.

Turkey says troops will remain in Syria and Iraq until border security is guaranteed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
08:58:39 UTC
17:58:39 KST

Turkish Defence Minister Yaşar Guler said Tuesday that Turkish forces would remain deployed in Syria and Iraq until border security is fully guaranteed and threats to the country’s security have been eliminated.
In written responses to journalists, Guler reaffirmed Ankara’s intention to maintain its military presence in both neighbouring countries, saying any decision to reconsider troop deployments would depend on security developments.
“We are maintaining our military presence in Iraq and Syria,” Guler said.
“Once we are certain that the necessary conditions regarding regional and border security have been met, the status of our deployment sites and our presence in the region will be reviewed.”
Turkey has maintained military forces in northern Syria and Iraq for years, primarily to counter threats from the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) and ISIS.
However, the regional security landscape has changed significantly following the overthrow of former Syrian President Bashar al-Assad and the establishment of a new government in Damascus with close ties to Ankara.
The developments have coincided with Turkish efforts to end its decades-long conflict with the PKK.
READ: Turkiye strongly condemns Israel’s activities in Syria’s Quneitra province
Guler said any reassessment of Turkey’s military presence in Syria would require the complete elimination of security threats, guarantees for border security and the restoration of unified state authority throughout Syrian territory.
“Once the terrorist threat in the region has been completely eliminated, border security is guaranteed, and the authority of the state is fully and uniformly established across all parts of Syria—without exception—the status of our forces will be re-evaluated,” he said.
At the time of Assad’s overthrow, Turkey had an estimated 16,000 to 18,000 troops stationed in northern Syria, according to a Turkish official.
However, updated figures on Turkish troop deployments have not been made available.
A Turkish official said last month that discussions were underway to determine the legal status of Turkish forces operating in Syria.
Guler declined to provide details about possible future military deployments or bases, saying it would be premature to discuss plans that had not been formally announced.
He emphasised that decisions concerning the future of Turkish forces in Syria would be made through consultations with Damascus, taking into account Syria’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.
The process would also consider security conditions on the ground and developments in the threat posed by armed groups, he added.

At least 226 reported killed in Sudan drone strike on crowded market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
08:56:43 UTC
17:56:43 KST

At least 226 people have reportedly been killed in a devastating drone strike on a crowded market in Abyei, a disputed territory between Sudan and South Sudan, according to local authorities. The attack, which took place Monday, October 19, triggered powerful explosions and a massive fire after a fuel depot inside the market was hit, leaving charred buildings, destroyed vehicles and bodies trapped beneath the wreckage. Thousands of residents fled the area as rescue workers struggled to recover the dead, with flames continuing to burn into the following day.
The updated death toll was reported by South Sudan's Eye Radio, citing Yohana Akol Ngor, Abyei's caretaker information minister. According to Ngor, 153 victims were buried in one mass grave and another 73 in a second, bringing the reported total to 226. The figure has not been independently verified. Earlier reports by Reuters and the Associated Press placed the death toll at 153. Ngor said an initial strike also hit a tractor-trailer carrying approximately 26 people, while an estimated 8,000 residents were displaced, some seeking shelter beneath trees and in open spaces.
An eyewitness who spoke to Reuters described hearing five powerful explosions before flames engulfed a fuel storage facility inside the market. As people rushed to evacuate the wounded, many were found suffering from shrapnel injuries to their stomachs and legs. The witness, who requested anonymity for security reasons, said he had seen 28 burned bodies in one location. Images from the aftermath showed scorched vehicles, destroyed buildings and twisted metal scattered across the marketplace, while satellite imagery revealed extensive fire damage.
Doctors Without Borders, also known by its French acronym MSF, reported that more than 20 wounded people were taken to nearby Ameth Bek Hospital, including patients with severe burns and other critical injuries. Dr. Christian Lindauer, the organization's medical activities manager at the hospital, said medical teams were providing emergency treatment, wound care and surgical assistance. Photographs released by the organization showed bandaged patients receiving treatment while lying on the hospital floor. Local officials warned that some bodies had been burned beyond recognition, complicating efforts to identify victims and recover their remains.
Abyei's local authorities and South Sudan's government accused the Sudanese Armed Forces of carrying out the attack. A senior Sudanese military officer subsequently acknowledged to the Associated Press, on condition of anonymity, that the army had conducted a drone strike in the area. However, he claimed the intended targets were fuel tankers arriving from South Sudan and believed to be transporting supplies to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, or RSF, which has been fighting Sudan's army since April 2023. The officer maintained that those killed were RSF members or people involved in fuel smuggling, insisting: "We do not target civilians."
That account was disputed by the Reuters eyewitness, who said he had not seen RSF fighters or other uniformed armed personnel in the market. He described the site as a busy commercial center selling basic goods, including sugar, flour and biscuits, some of which are transported onward into Sudan. Three diplomatic sources told Reuters that the fuel depot struck in the attack had previously been used by the RSF to supply its forces. However, it could not be independently established whether the facility was serving a military purpose at the time of the strike.
South Sudan's Foreign Ministry summoned Sudan's ambassador to protest the attack, condemning the civilian casualties and extensive destruction. The ministry urged Sudan to refrain from military actions that endanger civilians and called for disputes involving Abyei to be resolved through diplomatic channels. United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres condemned the drone attacks in the region, while the UN said women and children were among the victims. The United Nations Interim Security Force for Abyei, or UNISFA, deployed medical personnel, firefighting teams and rapid-response units to help evacuate casualties and prevent the flames from spreading.
Deadly escalation in Sudan's civil war
The Abyei attack came amid a wider wave of deadly drone strikes across Sudan. According to the BBC, the Sudan War Observatory reported that approximately 150 people were killed in two drone strikes Sunday near Al-Dabab in West Kordofan state. One strike reportedly hit a truck carrying about 200 people traveling to a funeral, killing 145, while another five people were killed when a drone struck a tent where mourners had gathered. The organization also reported 150 wounded and assessed that the drones were launched from Kadugli, a city in South Kordofan controlled by the Sudanese army. The figures and attribution have not been independently verified.
The attacks highlight the growing role of unmanned aerial vehicles in Sudan's civil war, which erupted in April 2023 following a power struggle between army chief Gen. Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, widely known as Hemedti. The conflict has devastated large parts of Sudan and created one of the world's worst humanitarian emergencies. According to UN figures cited in the reports, approximately 13 million people have been displaced and more than 33 million require humanitarian assistance. Around 20 million people face severe food insecurity, with aid organizations warning of worsening famine risks in parts of Darfur and Kordofan.
Drone attacks have increasingly targeted strategic infrastructure, supply routes and populated areas. Despite a partial international arms embargo, foreign suppliers have reportedly continued providing unmanned aircraft and other military equipment to both sides. Kordofan, a region rich in oil and gold, has become a crucial battlefield linking RSF strongholds in Darfur with central Sudan and the army-held capital, Khartoum. Control of the region's roads, fuel supplies and trading centers carries significant military and economic importance.
Abyei itself has long been a flashpoint between Sudan and South Sudan. The oil-rich territory's status was left unresolved under the 2005 peace agreement that ended Sudan's previous north-south civil war. The dispute persisted after South Sudan gained independence in 2011, with a referendum intended to determine Abyei's future never taking place because of disagreements over who would be eligible to vote. The Ngok Dinka community generally supports joining South Sudan, while the nomadic Misseriya community favors remaining part of Sudan.
The territory has experienced repeated violence over land, grazing rights and access to resources. Since Sudan's current civil war began, Abyei has also become an important transit corridor for supplies moving toward areas controlled by the RSF. The United Nations warned in May that the presence of RSF members in the region was increasing instability and endangering residents and international peacekeepers. UN spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric has warned that repeated drone attacks and the destruction of essential infrastructure are taking a devastating toll on communities already struggling to survive more than three years of war.

Pope Leo takes to popemobile for first time since cancer surgery
VATICAN CITY, Oct 21 - Pope Leo returned to St. Peter's Square on Wednesday, waving to pilgrims and blessing babies from his open-air popemobile as he held his first general audience at the Vatican since undergoing lung cancer surgery eight days ago.
The 71-year-old pontiff, who pledged on Sunday he would slowly resume his duties as leader of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics, stood in the back of the vehicle as it drove through the square, waving, smiling and stopping to talk to pilgrims.
Leo had the lower lobe of his right lung removed in surgery on October 13 and has been diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer.
The diagnosis, for the youngest pope in decades who was elected only in May 2025, caused shock and raised questions about the future shape of his papacy.
Wednesday's audience, the first held by the pope since October 7, followed a normal format. Crowds began gathering hours ahead of the 9:45 a.m. (0745 GMT) starting time, holding umbrellas under drizzling grey skies.
"The first thing I want to say to you is thank you for the support and prayers," Leo told the crowds in his opening remarks for the 50-minute event, without specifically mentioning his health.
"Thanks be to God for his generosity," said the pope, speaking in a clear voice as cheers broke out in the Square. "Let's renew our trust in the goodness and mercy of God."
PAPAL CALENDAR STILL IN FLUX
After touring the Square on Wednesday, Leo offered a sermon in Italian. In the only major change from previous occasions, he gave brief greetings afterwards in seven instead of nine other languages.
Leo's doctors have said his surgery was completed successfully, without complications. They have not yet disclosed the size of the tumour or whether the disease had spread to nearby lymph nodes, key factors in determining prognosis.
The Vatican has provided no indication of Leo's schedule beyond Wednesday.
The pope is due to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17, in one of the most intense trips arranged for a Catholic leader in decades, but it remains unclear if that trip will go ahead as planned.
Leo's lead surgeon has said the pope could be fully recovered in time for the trip, but the Vatican's secretary of state has indicated the pope may need to adjust the pace of his schedule to aid in recovery. REUTERS

Probe exposes UAH 2.6 mln eRecovery scheme in Mykolaiv
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:48:14 EEST
17:48:14 KST

The State Bureau of Investigation, with the help of National Police leadership, has exposed a scheme of illegally obtaining state compensation under the eRecovery program in Mykolaiv region, the bureau said.
"To obtain a housing certificate, community officials in Mykolaiv region changed the status of a renovated service apartment and registered it as destroyed by Russian shelling," the bureau said on its website on Wednesday.
In March 2022 the Shevchenkivska community in Mykolaiv region came under shelling, and the service apartment of the community's police officer suffered minor damage. Later, the bureau said, the community and charities paid to replace windows and doors in the apartment and repair the building's roof.
However, according to the investigation, the village head, together with his deputy and the community police officer, decided to use the state compensation program for their own benefit.
"First they helped the police officer privatize the service apartment. Because the building was not declared unsafe after the shelling and its residents had already received repair aid, the officials had the village council change the apartment's status and legal address. On paper, the apartment became a separate individual house with a different number," the bureau said.
The commission members then drew up an inspection report on housing allegedly destroyed by armed aggression, which belonged to the police officer and his family members, and stated in the document that the house was ruined and unfit for living, the bureau said.
"On the basis of this report, the police officer received an eRecovery housing certificate for UAH 2.6 million, with which he bought an apartment in Mykolaiv," the bureau said.
The village head and his deputy have been served with notices of suspicion of abuse of office (Part 2 of Article 364 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine), and the police officer with notice of suspicion of aiding abuse of office (Part 5 of Article 27 and Part 2 of Article 364).
All three have been suspended from their posts, and preventive measures have been chosen for them.
The bureau is taking steps to recover the damage caused to the state.
The Mykolaiv regional prosecutor's office is supervising the investigation.

Why Elon Musk Wants to Merge SpaceX and Tesla
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
08:45:59 UTC
17:45:59 KST

The world’s richest man has publicly backed a potential combination of SpaceX and Tesla in what could be the biggest merger in history.
On Tuesday, Elon Musk, the CEO and largest shareholder of both companies, said the electric vehicle maker and the rocket company had formed special committees at the request of shareholders to discuss the idea.
“I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, and there’s a lot to be gained from cooperating,” Musk told SpaceX investors on a conference call.
“I think it would be a good idea, but it’s really up to the special committees of both companies,” he added.
The committees, which are made up of independent directors, would need to agree on the transaction terms of any deal before putting it to shareholders for a vote. Musk said his conflict of interest prevents him from participating in their discussions.
Musk has previously teased a Tesla-SpaceX merger. On a July 22 earnings call, Musk said there was “more and more overlap” between Tesla and SpaceX as the companies expand into artificial intelligence and robotics. Last week, Barclays analysts suggested that a merger could be announced before Tesla’s annual shareholder meeting in December.
Tuesday’s call was the first confirmation that the companies were formally exploring a combination.
A merger could create a company worth around $3.5 trillion, putting it among the world’s most valuable companies. It could also become the biggest merger ever by deal value, potentially surpassing SpaceX’s record-setting $250 billion acquisition of Musk-owned AI company xAI in February. SpaceX is currently valued at about $2 trillion, and Tesla at $1.5 trillion. A deal could also help propel Musk back into trillionaire ranks, depending on its terms and how investors value the combined company. Musk owns around 48% of SpaceX and 20% of Tesla.
The shares of both companies rose in after-hours trading on Tuesday. SpaceX, which went public in June, reported a quarterly net profit of $4.4 billion. Musk told investors he expects annual recurring revenue of between $500 billion and $1 trillion by the end of 2027.
Some analysts, however, have warned of regulatory and geopolitical hurdles, particularly in terms of Tesla’s Chinese operations and SpaceX’s U.S. defence work. Morningstar analysts said a merger could raise U.S. national security concerns involving the combined company’s supply chain. JPMorgan analysts also flagged regulatory approval in China as a potential stumbling block.
Any deal could also face congressional scrutiny, which could intensify if Democrats win control of either chamber in the coming midterm elections. Democratic lawmakers have previously questioned Musk over conflicts of interest and raised national security concerns about reported Chinese investments in SpaceX. Democrats have also challenged major acquisitions in the past on consumer protection grounds. In June, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D, Mass.) criticized SpaceX’s IPO, citing Musk’s concentrated voting power and weak investor protections—concerns that could resurface in a Tesla-SpaceX merger.
Why a merger matters
A merger could bring two of Musk’s biggest businesses under one corporate umbrella, making it easier for the companies to move investments and resources between projects. “This would allow him to run all their operations under one roof without tripping on as many governance issues,” wrote Morningstar analysts Seth Goldstein and Nicolas Owens in June. “For example, Musk could move Tesla software developers or engineers to work on SpaceX AI projects, and vice versa, or have Tesla and SpaceX supply one another without the need for related party transaction disclosures or risking shareholder lawsuits claiming the resources of one firm are being diverted for the benefit of the other.”
Analysts noted that Tesla’s robotaxis could benefit from Starlink connectivity, while its autonomous vehicles and Optimus humanoid robots could more closely integrate SpaceX’s AI technology. SpaceX’s planned orbital data centers, meanwhile, could potentially benefit from access to Tesla’s battery and energy storage products.
A combined company could also mean greater control of several stages of the AI value chain, from chip design and planned manufacturing to computing infrastructure, AI software, and its deployment in vehicles and robots.
The companies already collaborate. In March, they announced Terafab, a joint semiconductor manufacturing project intended to produce chips for Tesla’s vehicles and humanoid robots and SpaceX’s planned AI satellites. SpaceX technologies have also been used in some Tesla products, including the new Roadster prototype, which uses SpaceX-developed thrusters.
David Nicholson, chief technology advisor at market research firm The Futurum Group, told the BBC that a merger also appears to align with Musk’s long-held ambition of colonizing Mars. Musk previously outlined plans to send Tesla’s Optimus robots to the planet aboard SpaceX’s Starship spacecraft.
A merger could also strengthen Musk’s influence over Tesla’s direction. Barclays estimated that a SpaceX acquisition of Tesla could give Musk around 37% of the combined company while controlling around 56% of its voting power. He currently controls around 82% of voting power at SpaceX and 20% at Tesla. That could represent either a benefit or a risk for shareholders, as decision-making would become faster but have fewer checks.
“One thing I don’t think people talk enough about with SpaceX and Tesla as well: You do still have a huge amount of key-man risk here,” wrote Morningstar analyst David Sekera earlier this month. “God forbid anything were to happen to Elon Musk.”

Israeli plans to strike Iran before election raise fears of wider regional war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
08:45:55 UTC
17:45:55 KST

A report that Israel planned to strike Iranian civilian infrastructure earlier this month, only to be stopped by U.S. President Donald Trump, has renewed questions about the strategic justification for another war with Tehran, particularly with Israeli elections less than a week away.
The Financial Times reported Wednesday that Israel had planned to attack Iranian infrastructure on Oct. 10, including power plants, nuclear facilities and other targets associated with the Iranian government, before Trump intervened to prevent the operation.
The report has raised concerns about why Israel would consider launching another major military campaign against Iran when previous rounds of fighting have failed to topple the Iranian government or permanently eliminate its military capabilities.
Israel has spent much of the past three years engaged in intensive fighting on multiple fronts, while damage from previous confrontations with Iran and fighting along its northern and southern borders has yet to be fully repaired.
Iran, meanwhile, continues to demonstrate its ability to disrupt shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, attacking vessels and affecting the global economy. Gulf states have largely absorbed the consequences without launching direct military responses.
Against that backdrop, questions remain over whether Israel has a clear strategic plan for another confrontation and what objectives a renewed campaign could realistically achieve.
Danny Citrinowicz, a former head of the Iran branch in the Israeli Military Intelligence Directorate's Research Division and now a senior researcher specializing in Iran and the Shiite axis at the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), told ynet that there was no immediate military justification for launching another war.
"There's absolutely nothing that justifies a war now, either before the elections or afterward," Citrinowicz said.
"Iran is rebuilding its strength and restoring its missile capabilities. On the nuclear front, there are no indications whatsoever that they have resumed enrichment. There are the same indications that they moved certain materials to Pickaxe Mountain, but nothing beyond that."
Pickaxe Mountain, also known as Kuh-e Kolang Gaz La, is a mountainous site near Iran's Natanz nuclear complex that has attracted international scrutiny over suspected underground nuclear-related construction.
Citrinowicz questioned why Iran remained capable of launching substantial missile attacks after two previous wars that Israeli officials had described as major military successes.
"We also need to understand why, after two wars against Iran, we're still seeing them launch dozens of missiles," he said. "Apparently, they're not afraid for their arsenal."
'No justification for another campaign'
Citrinowicz said the reported Israeli interest in attacking Iran's energy infrastructure appeared to rest on two possible strategic assumptions, neither of which he considered convincing.
"What is the strategic objective of another war?" he asked. "According to various reports, Israel wants to attack Iran's energy facilities for one of two reasons: Either they think that will bring down the regime, which it won't, or they want to turn Iran into a failed state. And it's clear that would lead to a very broad Iranian campaign against Israel."
He said Iran's continued military buildup did not, by itself, justify an immediate attack.
Iran has continued replacing senior officials killed in previous confrontations, including some whose successors have adopted even more hard-line positions.
Earlier this week, Mehrdad Akhlaghi was appointed Iran's new defense minister. Like his predecessors, he warned that Iranian forces remained ready to respond to threats.
But despite the rhetoric and continued rearmament, Citrinowicz said there had been no dramatic change in Iranian behavior in recent months.
He argued that Iran's efforts to rebuild its capabilities were comparable to those of other Israeli adversaries, including the Houthis in Yemen, Hezbollah in Lebanon and pro-Iranian militias in Iraq.
Another war against Iran, he warned, could reignite fighting across all those fronts.
"The point is that there is no justification requiring a military campaign at this time," Citrinowicz said. "We need to monitor the situation and see what develops. If Iran makes a breakout toward a nuclear weapon tomorrow, then we need to attack. But right now, nothing is happening."
He described the possibility of an Israeli strike just two weeks before the election as deeply troubling.
"What's happening now is sheer madness — attacking two weeks before elections. For what?" he said.
"Iran is not on the verge of developing a nuclear weapon, and with all due respect to its missile arsenal, it still hasn't returned to where it was before Operation Rising Lion and Operation Roaring Lion," he added, using the Israeli names for the previous bouts of direct fighting against the Islamic Republic.
"There is no operational or strategic need to attack now," Citrinowicz said. "There is an attempt to incorporate political considerations, and that is serious."
The former intelligence official also questioned the lasting achievements of the previous military campaigns, noting that Iran's leadership remained in power and its military continued rebuilding.
"Yes, another strike would cause damage, but the consequences for the international system would be insane," he said. "They would set the entire Gulf ablaze."
He criticized what he described as an apparent willingness to launch another campaign without first examining why earlier operations had failed to achieve their declared objectives.
"It's as if we don't care. Just attack again. But for what?" he said.
"And this is after we were promised tremendous, unprecedented achievements in two wars, that we had 'pushed the threat back for generations.' How did we push the threat back for generations if they can attack again?"
He added that Israeli officials had previously emphasized achievements against Iran's missile capabilities, yet Iranian missiles continued to pose a threat.
"The most serious thing is the mixing of political considerations," he said. "Ultimately, there is no justification for launching a campaign two weeks before elections."
US midterm elections complicate diplomatic efforts
The prospect of another confrontation also comes as Washington approaches its midterm elections in early November, a political milestone that Citrinowicz said could influence both Iranian calculations and Trump's willingness to pursue military action.
"The elections in the United States are extremely significant because the Iranians want Trump to lose," he said. "They want to demonstrate the price of confronting them to any American president: Mess with us and you'll lose the elections."
Citrinowicz said Tehran remained open to a negotiated agreement but continued to insist on conditions unacceptable to the Trump administration.
"The Iranians are prepared to return to an agreement, but the conditions they're presenting are conditions Trump will not accept," he said.
He dismissed recent reports in the Qatari newspaper Al-Araby Al-Jadeed suggesting a diplomatic breakthrough was imminent.
"With all due respect to the reports in Al-Araby Al-Jadeed, there is no diplomatic breakthrough whatsoever," he said.
He pointed to remarks made Tuesday by Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, during a meeting with Pakistan's army chief, Asim Munir.
According to the account, Rezaei insisted that all enriched nuclear material would remain in Iran.
"All enriched nuclear materials will remain in Iran," Rezaei said, describing them as "a central asset and national wealth of the Iranian people, intended for use within the country."
Rezaei also said Iranian officials and the public agreed that negotiations should not resume until Washington took steps to rebuild trust.
"The Iranian people and officials agree that there will be no negotiations as long as the United States does not take confidence-building measures," he said, adding that the prerequisite for restoring trust was meeting Iran's stated conditions.
Citrinowicz said the statements underscored the distance between Washington and Tehran despite those reports of diplomatic progress.
He also warned that the period between November's U.S. elections and the seating of the new Congress in January could prove especially volatile.
"I think the period between November and January is very dangerous because it's the transition between Congresses," he said. "During those two months, Trump will want to do something."
However, he suggested Trump's preferred course of action might differ substantially from Israel's reported objectives.
"Perhaps he wants to deliver a single blow, then end the whole affair and declare victory," Citrinowicz said. "I'm not sure he wants to return to the idea of toppling the regime."
He described the possibility of Israel initiating another military campaign under the current circumstances as highly irresponsible.
Israeli fighter jet activity raises escalation fears
Citrinowicz also expressed concern over a Fox News report that Israeli fighter jets had flown over Syria and Iraq toward Iran as part of a military exercise.
He warned that such activity, if accurately reported, could be interpreted by Tehran as preparation for an imminent attack, potentially provoking an Iranian response.
"If that's true, it's an extremely dangerous development," he said. "We're on the brink of war, and we're conducting a simulated strike in Iraq?"
Citrinowicz questioned the logic of staging an exercise resembling an attack on Iran during a period of heightened tensions.
"Do we want to force the Iranians to fire missiles at us?" he asked.
"There's no logic in simulating an attack on Iran at the height of tensions, other than a desire to push the Iranians into attacking us, to have them fire the first shot so we'll have an excuse to respond."
He warned that another Israeli-Iranian confrontation would almost certainly spread beyond the two countries.
"Any war with Iran will once again be a regional war," he said. "Certainly involving the Houthis, certainly the militias in Iraq, and I believe ultimately Hezbollah as well."
Citrinowicz said the regional security environment had changed in ways that could make another confrontation particularly dangerous.
He pointed to the absence of a U.S. military presence in Iraq, which he said would make it easier for pro-Iranian militias to operate, as well as the presence of Houthi elements in the country.
"We'll once again find ourselves stuck in a regional war," he said.
He also highlighted concerns about Israel's and the United States' supplies of missile interceptors, which would be essential to defending against sustained Iranian attacks.
"We know we have a problem with interceptors. That's no secret. And the Americans have a problem with interceptors as well," he said.
Those shortages, he suggested, could become particularly consequential in a prolonged conflict involving multiple fronts and repeated missile barrages.
'We cannot separate Netanyahu's political considerations from Israel's strategic interests'
Citrinowicz said his central concern was the possibility that domestic political calculations were influencing decisions with potentially far-reaching consequences for Israeli national security.
"The most serious aspect of this entire situation is that it's impossible to separate Netanyahu's political considerations from the strategic considerations of the State of Israel," he said.
"That's extremely dangerous. This would be another war with Iran."
He warned that previous confrontations had demonstrated the economic and social costs of fighting Iran, with military operations disrupting daily life and economic activity across Israel.
"We know that every war with Iran paralyzes the Israeli economy and brings activity here to a standstill," he said. "And for what? What strategic objective would this war serve?"
He argued that another campaign would be especially difficult to justify given the limited prospects of removing Iran's leadership through airstrikes alone.
"We understand very clearly that we are not going to topple this regime from the air," he said.
Rather than rushing toward another confrontation, Citrinowicz called for a thorough examination of Israel's previous campaigns, including the objectives they failed to achieve and whether additional military action would serve the country's long-term interests.
"Launching a campaign two weeks before elections is madness," he said.
"Before Israel launches a campaign for which there is currently no immediate need, we must ultimately analyze what we failed to achieve in the previous campaign and why."
He said policymakers should also consider whether military force was the only available option and whether another confrontation would advance Israel's strategic interests.
"Is the kinetic solution the only one, and will it serve the interests of the State of Israel?" he asked.
Citrinowicz emphasized that Israel should preserve close strategic coordination with Washington, describing it as the foundation of Israeli policy toward Iran.
"We certainly need to maintain strategic coordination with the United States," he said. "That's a significant issue because it's the basis of all Israeli policy toward Iran."
But he stressed that coordination with Washington should not replace an independent Israeli assessment of the risks and benefits of military action.
"With all due respect to the Americans, the State of Israel needs to examine what's right for it," he said.
He concluded that Israel should not embark on another potentially more dangerous war without first understanding why previous operations had failed to achieve their stated objectives.
"Right now, it's clear that the war's objectives were not achieved," Citrinowicz said.
"Before we analyze why they weren't achieved, we shouldn't jump into another campaign, one that could potentially be even more dangerous than the previous one, because it would be extremely violent and the Iranians are learning from every confrontation."

Two Russian men who say they secretly worked with Ukraine’s intelligence services have given accounts of operations they claim to have carried out against military assets and personnel inside Russia, in a BBC Eye documentary for the BBC World Service, according to the BBC.
Shadowmen: Russians working with Ukraine premieres on BBC iPlayer and the BBC World Service YouTube channel on Monday 19 October, and airs on BBC Two on Monday 26 October at 23:00.
The Polish journalist Marcin Mamoń spent two years developing contact with a network of Russians who say they have been working covertly in support of Ukraine from inside Russia. Among them is a man the film calls Ivan, who describes himself as a patriot and says he wants Vladimir Putin’s government removed from power, arguing that supporting Ukraine’s war effort could help achieve that.
Another operative, given the name Foma and exiled in Poland, runs a network of volunteers inside Russia who carry out surveillance on senior officers that Ukraine’s military intelligence service, the GUR, is tracking.
The documentary raises the possibility that some operatives claiming to work for Ukraine could in fact be acting on behalf of Russia.
Monica Garnsey, the BBC executive producer, said: “Marcin Mamoń has used the incredible access he gained to tell a story that is not about heroes or villains, but about men who have crossed a line many will never face, and who are living with the consequences. Shadowmen asks difficult questions about acts of war, patriotism, and loyalty, and there are no simple answers.”
The BBC said the film examines the motivations of Russians who say they oppose the Kremlin and the risks they say they have taken, and that it explores the difficulty of independently verifying some of the claims made, with many of those involved unwilling to share further detail for security reasons.
Sabotage inside Russia has been a feature of the war almost since it began, and attributing any individual incident has been close to impossible from outside. Railway lines serving the front have been cut, recruitment offices burned, fuel depots set alight and military figures killed, with the GUR and the Security Service of Ukraine claiming some of it, Russian partisan groups claiming more, and Russian authorities frequently describing perpetrators as recruited over the internet for money.

Russia's destruction of satellites in orbit would also harm its own spacecraft – space law expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Russia's destruction of satellites in orbit would also harm its own spacecraft – space law expert
Anna Hurova, who holds a PhD in law specializing in space law and is a postdoctoral researcher at the Chair of Space Studies (Chaire Espace) at the École normale supérieure (ENS–PSL) in Paris, said this in an interview with Ukrinform.
"The principle of proportionality applies in humanitarian law. Even if they call a satellite a legitimate target, destroying it could cause disproportionate harm to other countries. The technical aspect must also be considered: the debris would threaten other satellites, and their owners could respond economically, politically, or in other ways," Hurova explained, commenting on Moscow's threats against Western commercial satellites that help Ukraine.
According to her, space debris would also threaten Russian satellites, forcing them to expend resources on collision-avoidance maneuvers.
Nevertheless, Moscow blocked efforts to establish a legal framework for space debris removal during negotiations on the Code of Conduct for Outer Space Activities.
"Russia objected to establishing a legal framework for this activity, arguing as follows: another satellite approaches and grabs an object – that is military activity, aggression," Hurova said.
The legal expert explained that removing a defunct satellite requires reaching an agreement and obtaining written consent from the country that owns it.
She also cited the example of Russia's destruction of one of its own satellites in November 2021, which generated a cloud of space debris.
According to Western media, on October 18, the Russian military satellite Kosmos-2612 made a dangerously close approach to Finland's ICEYE-X36 reconnaissance satellite, which provides imagery to Ukraine. Russia has repeatedly described such commercial satellites as potential military targets.
