Raushan Kazhibayeva on TRC’s 30th anniversary, its media outlets and creating content about the President
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
08:38:51 UTC
17:38:51 KST

Raushan Kazhibayeva on TRC’s 30th anniversary, its media outlets and creating content about the President
The Television and Radio Complex of the President of Kazakhstan is marking its 30th anniversary. In an interview with Tengrinews.kz, TRC Director General Raushan Kazhibayeva spoke about how the media organization is changing, discussed Kazakhstani content and shared her views on the impact of artificial intelligence, reports a Qazinform News Agency correspondent.
- Thirty years is a considerable age for a domestic media organization. How has it changed over these three decades?
The Television and Radio Complex of the President of the Republic of Kazakhstan was established by a government resolution on December 29, 1996, just before the New Year.
In its early years, the Television and Radio Complex mainly filmed official events, prepared video materials for state and commercial channels, and began filling what used to be called the “archive shelves.” At the time, production was analogue, and footage was stored on tapes. Today, we are completing the digitization of the archive, with servers and metadata offering descriptions and convenient searches replacing shelves of tapes and index cards.
By the late 1990s, TRC had begun making its first documentaries and videos, which were broadcast on Kazakhstani television channels. This new area of activity was formalized by a separate government resolution dated August 17, 1999. At the same time, TRC was transformed from a state institution into a closed non-commercial joint-stock company.
- TRC has changed its status several times over the past 30 years. Was this a search for the ideal management model?
I believe this was primarily related to changes in the country’s legislation. TRC has been a state institution, a closed non-commercial joint-stock company and simply a non-commercial joint-stock company.
Since 2019, work to develop TRC has been underway on the President’s instructions, with systematic support from the Presidential Administration of Affairs, of which TRC is a part.
- TRC is described as a presidential media resource. What meaning do you attach to this definition? Does it reflect the scale of production or new approaches to your work?
Above all, it means a systematic approach. TRC is a factory producing content about our President. And our main newsmaker is the President!
For me, a strong media system is one in which speed, editorial work, visual quality and distribution do not exist separately. They are linked by a shared responsibility for results. TRC is a cross-media company that, without false modesty, sets trends in television, international media and the digital space. We film, write and distribute content both in Kazakhstan and abroad.
Our main television outlet is Jibek Joly. Like TRC itself, Jibek Joly is a unique channel. Around a quarter of its daily airtime is broadcast live.
We were the first in Kazakhstan’s market to stop importing foreign series carrying an ideology alien to us. Their place in the broadcasting schedule was taken by our own original projects: Zhaña Uaqyt; Novoye Vremya; Taldau: Analytical Review; Bügin.Live; Senim Studiyasy; Dämdi.Life and others. Audiences have grown to love our projects, and the channel has retained its position among the country’s leading television channels.
We have accepted that one-way communication with audiences is gone for good. Today, viewers want to interact with the media outlet they have chosen. Live projects make precisely this possible. We are pleased that our audience does not watch passively but actively participates in creating content. Viewers become studio guests, can ask questions in real time and interact with presenters and show participants. In some projects, we have replaced traditional sets with live, dynamic footage from the capital’s streets.
Of course, we also remember that television remains the most widespread and accessible form of family leisure. Original shows, large-scale projects, films and animation bring thousands of viewers together every day in front of screens showing Jibek Joly.
This combination of live broadcasting, sought-after content and a balance of subjects and genres builds what matters most: viewers’ trust, which we value.
Our organization comprises six media outlets. Jibek Joly television’s work in the domestic market is complemented by a radio station of the same name, which also broadcasts in an interactive format. Listeners to our radio station, which broadcasts in Astana on 101.4 FM and is available online, also become guests in the studio and on air.
In recent years, Qazinform International News Agency has regained its status as the country’s leading news agency. Today, it ranks among the top three news outlets and has restored and expanded its network of international partners. It has become the region’s principal trusted hub, with its materials cited daily by global media from Japan to the United States.
Alongside Qazinform International News Agency, the channels under the Silk Way umbrella brand, Silk Way, Silk Way Cinema and Silk Way Prime, operate in the international information space.
These are the only international channels not only in Kazakhstan but throughout Central Asia, broadcasting abroad in six languages and reaching more than 120 countries. The channels have around 300 rebroadcasters and 22 official distributors abroad.
We also have a digital laboratory, a team of professionals of a new generation. They understand an audience that grew up with smartphones in their hands. Under the TRKLAB brand, they create vertical content, generate unique projects using AI and interact with readers across all relevant platforms. In total, we have several dozen accounts.
Our Documentary Film Center has also been modernized. For us, the center is the heart of our company, our qara shañyraq.
The team makes films for festivals, produces original content in foreign languages and was the first in the Central Asian market to release documentaries in a vertical format, an area it continues to develop.
Documentary projects in English, Chinese and French are broadcast by our foreign partners, while those in Kazakh and Russian are shown not only on national channels but also on more than three dozen regional channels.
- At the recent Astana Media Week, there was active discussion about how to make Kazakhstani content global and why translating it into a foreign language does not work. What do you think?
For us, this has been standard production practice since the launch of Silk Way. Since the revamped channel launched in 2022, all new projects for its broadcasts have been produced originally in English. We clearly understood that literal translation was a thing of the past and assembled a team of professionals who became the first in Kazakhstan and Central Asia to produce studio news and analysis in English.
In 2024, Qazinform’s English-language news moved to a global domain, qazinform.com. As the saying goes, “Content is King, but distribution is Queen.”
This year alone, materials produced by Silk Way and Qazinform have been cited by media in dozens of countries. Alongside neighboring Russia, Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan and Turkmenistan, these include the United States, China, Japan, Korea, India, Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Spain, Czechia, Hungary, Serbia, Bulgaria, Türkiye, Indonesia, Pakistan, the UAE, Qatar and many other countries in Europe, Asia and the Middle East, and even media in Peru, Chile, South Africa and Togo.
In total, content from our English-language media outlets, Silk Way and Qazinform, has been cited by foreign media around 6,000 times in 2026.
- Traditional television channels, news agencies and conventional media in general are often fairly conservative organizations that approach new technologies, especially artificial intelligence, with caution. How do things stand at TRC?
TRC combines the best traditions of conventional media, new media and technology, current trends and content formats, which together give us a cross-media approach and the ability to work across multiple formats.
Neural networks help us optimize routine tasks, freeing up time for creativity, and create unique content for broadcast and online platforms. The possibilities here are truly limitless.
Back in 2024, TRC was the first to make a short film in a vertical format. The capabilities of neural networks, unique at the time, allowed us to “bring to life” photographs of our President, many of which had originally been taken on ordinary photographic film.
Responsible and sensible use of AI allows us to accomplish a wide range of tasks for the public good. Last year, we used AI to create sign language interpretation for the animated series The Fixies for our broadcasts. This was our way of caring for our youngest viewers with special needs.
In addition, Jibek Joly aired 100 video lessons on digital literacy in 2025. All 100 episodes were created entirely through generation, without a single frame of live footage.
At Qazinform and in our newsrooms, AI searches for and initially processes information, transcribes audio and video, and creates images to illustrate articles. AI helps analyze large volumes of information, monitor foreign-language sources, conduct basic fact-checking and perform technical checks to ensure texts comply with the rules of the publication language.
At TRKLAB, our newsroom of a new generation, work with neural networks focuses on creating generative content and adapting materials from the news agency and television channels for a new type of reader who quickly tires of long articles and tends toward click-driven, short-form media consumption. AI helps shorten narratives and make them more concise without making them any less informative.
It is important to say that AI-based projects require substantial human involvement and are not created using just one neural network. We follow the Head of State’s principle: “Intelligent systems should not replace humans; they are intended to complement and enhance their capabilities.”
- What does “responsible and sensible use of AI” mean to you?
Our President has declared 2026 the Year of Digitalization and Artificial Intelligence, and Kazakhstan is one of just five countries in the world [Editor’s note: the others are the UAE, the United Kingdom, Canada and Albania] where a Ministry of Artificial Intelligence has been established on the President’s instructions.
Meanwhile, many of our colleagues around the world are debating the future of journalism. They ask whether neural networks will replace humans and whether news journalism will become overwhelmed by synthetic content. Will we find ourselves immersed in an endless expanse of deepfakes?
We see AI as offering enormous potential and opportunities, rather than threats and scare stories. Of course, all these risks can materialize if we fail to exercise reasonable caution and approach our profession carelessly. But that is in our hands.
- Astana recently hosted the first global generative film festival, the Astana AI Film Festival. We watched the finalist entries and, we must say, were impressed. This is further evidence that Kazakhstan is one of the pioneers in adopting and using AI.
The idea for the festival belongs to Vice President Erlan Karin, while its implementation was the work of Almas Zhali and Aizatulla Khusein, young and talented leaders in Kazakhstan’s creative industry.
The festival received a total of 8,067 entries from 125 countries, amounting to more than 100,000 minutes of generative content. This is a truly world-class event with a substantial prize fund.
Without a doubt, this global project will become a regular event, as will the international televised music competition Silk Way Star, the first project by Kazakhstani creators to reach a global level. The first season attracted more than one billion viewers worldwide and was broadcast in nine countries. Citizens of 43 countries took part in the voting, while media in 60 countries cited news about the competition.
This year, together with our partners at China Media Group (CMG), we completed filming the second season in Yiwu, China. It will soon air on Jibek Joly. In China, the project is already being broadcast by two of the country’s leading television channels, CCTV 3 and CCTV 15.
The third season will be filmed in Kazakhstan next year.
- In your previous interview, you spoke about a regional television channel for Central Asian countries based on Silk Way. This October, at the Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia and Azerbaijan in Awaza, our President emphasized the importance of creating a shared information space. How is this project progressing?
A regional channel for Central Asian countries based on Silk Way is one of our promising projects.
Today, colleagues from Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan are working alongside us to provide regional content for Silk Way. We have signed several bilateral agreements with national broadcasters and the relevant authorities of partner countries.
In October, on the sidelines of the Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia and Azerbaijan and the CIS Council of Heads of State in Awaza, Turkmenistan, we signed a historic agreement establishing a permanent Kazakh-Turkmen media council. This is the first document of its kind in the history of media cooperation between the two countries and in the region as a whole.
The pace of cooperation naturally varies, but it is sufficient to fill the first dedicated programming block on Silk Way devoted to Central Asia.
We continue working on a comprehensive interagency agreement between the relevant authorities of the region’s countries that would pave the way for systematic coordination and a full-fledged intergovernmental agreement. I hope we can bring this unfinished task to completion together with our colleagues at the Ministry of Culture and Information and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
- This year, Astana hosted two major events: CMG Week and the second Al Jazeera Week. On what terms do you work with the world’s largest media companies?
Today, we have 70 agreements with television and radio companies and news agencies from around the world. Our partners include Al Jazeera, China Media Group, TRT, Xinhua, Jiji Press, Kyodo, Yonhap, Aju News Corporation, Anadolu Agency, Agenzia Nova, Adnkronos, Belga News, VNA, ANI, Azertac, Petra, IRNA, WAM, Saudi Press Agency and many others.
We are also members of several international industry organizations and associations. TRC is a member of the technical committee of the Organization of Asia-Pacific News Agencies, the Council of Heads of State and Public Television and Radio Organizations of CIS Member States, and the Interstate Information Pool. It is also an active participant in the Union of News Agencies of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation.
For our partners, TRC has become a hub for reliable and timely news from Kazakhstan and Central Asia, and this is their main reason for working with us.
To answer your question directly, we do not buy airtime or print space abroad. We have no financial relationships with any of our partners, and we have not paid for a single news story picked up by global agencies.
- In our previous conversations, you repeatedly spoke about problems in the country’s media market. You raised the near-monopoly in television advertising, weaknesses in the television audience measurement system and the need to protect domestic broadcasters. What is the situation now?
Indeed, over decades of operation, the country’s television, advertising and broader media markets accumulated numerous imbalances. Some have been eliminated through joint efforts, primarily by the regulator and market participants.
The television advertising market has become competitive, new players have emerged, and channels now have a genuine choice between advertising sales companies and the ability to negotiate terms. We have also significantly improved the television audience measurement system.
Thanks to the efforts of the National Media Association, of which TRC is an active member, audience measurement now covers the entire country, from major cities to small towns. We finally know what all Kazakhstanis watch and prefer, rather than only residents of large cities. Work is underway to integrate data from cable television operators into the audience measurement system.
- What, then, is the problem? Why are television channels complaining about falling revenues, while ratings are steadily declining? What needs attention?
The regulatory framework needs fine-tuning to protect the domestic information space in a rapidly changing market.
Today, domestic television operates under fairly strict regulation. We have requirements concerning the volume of domestic programming, language balance, and limits on the amount of advertising per day and per hour, as well as its content.
These requirements do not apply to foreign broadcasters. Yes, they do not earn advertising revenue in Kazakhstan, as this is prohibited. But they compete for our viewers’ attention while earning incomparably greater sums in their much larger home television advertising markets and receiving state support from their own countries.
There are no restrictions at all on the internet. We all watch content on YouTube, and what do we see? The number and duration of advertisements keep growing without any limits. This is despite the fact that most videos also contain advertising integrated by the creators themselves.
In practice, this means that a domestic advertiser paid the video hosting platform for an advertisement, the platform placed it, and a Kazakhstani viewer saw it, while YouTube itself and the content creator received the money. In other words, the money left Kazakhstan’s market and went abroad. Essentially, we are subsidizing content production by foreign creators while domestic producers are forced to cut costs, reduce spending on programming and face another wave of viewers leaving.
Domestic online outlets face a similar situation. We visit a foreign website and see advertisements for Kazakhstani companies. The advertiser has reached its audience, but the money has once again gone abroad, to the foreign outlet and the Google or Meta advertising network.
Numerous foreign online streaming services operating in Kazakhstan also remain outside the regulatory framework.
E-commerce platforms are a separate issue. E-commerce aggregators, which have never been media outlets, provide advertising services while producing no content for audiences. The advertising revenues of some are already comparable to the size of the entire television advertising market.
- But this is a global trend. The boundary of the information space is gradually disappearing and content is becoming a global product…
The trend is that content is becoming global while advertising money remains national. We have already discussed that trying to stop progress is impossible. We need to manage it properly, create a legal framework suited to current realities and fine-tune regulation in the interests of domestic media.
- How are you celebrating your anniversary?
We are trying to make our anniversary year beneficial to society and the industry as a whole. As you noted earlier, this year TRC organized two large-scale projects for media professionals and future journalists: CMG Week and Al Jazeera Week.
Leading professionals from two of the world’s largest media organizations spent a week sharing their experience and best practices, delivering lectures and conducting practical sessions.
From May to September, a nationwide film screening and lecture program was held in every region, allowing audiences to watch around 30 of our best documentaries free of charge on the big screen. Particular emphasis was placed on regional screenings, where, with the support of local administrations, projects about the Head of State’s activities and working people in Kazakhstan were shown. There was not a single empty seat at any screening.
Throughout the year, TRC’s senior managers delivered lectures to future journalists at the country’s leading universities, including Al-Farabi Kazakh National University, L.N. Gumilyov Eurasian National University and Maqsut Narikbayev University.
An exclusive photo exhibition featuring more than 200 unique photographs of the President’s activities, along with several other large-scale events, is planned before the end of the year.
- And a final question. Working alongside our President allows you to see things that do not always appear in official coverage. Which personal qualities of the Head of State particularly impress you?
I admire his rare combination of intellectual depth and tact. The President sees issues in a broad context while always paying attention to details that may affect an individual’s life. His incredible capacity for work and exceptional breadth of knowledge cannot fail to impress.
The task of the President’s TRC creative team is to strive to meet the high standard personally set by the Head of State.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that Kazakhstan’s President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev will deliver his annual State-of-the-Nation Address on October 28.

Nearly half of Dutch MPs use AI to write speeches in parliament
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
08:35:52 UTC
17:35:52 KST

Nearly half of Dutch MPs use AI to write speeches in parliament
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Nearly half of Dutch MPs used artificial intelligence to help write speeches and statements delivered in parliament, according to an investigation based on the AI detection tool Pangram.
A scan of debates and committee hearings revealed that 68 of the 150 MPs from across the political spectrum used AI at least once. Most of the members admitted using artificial intelligence tools when asked by De Groene Amsterdammer and investigations website Investico.
The real number is likely to be higher because only contributions that were found to be more than 50% AI generated were included in the results.
Top of the list was former Pro MP Esmah Lahlah, who is now a member of Amsterdam city council’s executive after leaving parliament in June. The analysis found evidence of AI in her contributions to four debates on poverty and the law on jobseekers.
Lahlah said she sometimes used AI to summarise conversations she had with people during working visits. “Sometimes it was hard to condense those stories into a few minutes’ speaking time, so I used AI,” she said.
Most MPs wrote their own material for big set-piece debates such as the recent debate on the king’s speech, known as the Algemene Politieke Beschouwingen, which kicks off the parliamentary year. But more than half of contributions to committee hearings showed evidence of AI use, the analysis found.
“Rolled out by Chat”
Other frequent users included Rachel van Meetelen of the far-right PVV, who said she used it to make her statements more concise and effective. “I would never say anything in Parliament I didn’t support,” she said.
The heaviest users were right-wing parties such as Gidi Markuszower’s DNA group of former PVV MPs. Only the Socialists (SP), the animal rights party PvdD and Volt showed no use of AI at all.
Harmen Krul of the centre-right CDA also said he used AI to edit his speeches, but not generate content. “I would be dismayed if this created the impression that my contributions were rolled out by Chat,” he said.
Last month an analysis of 28,000 questions in parliament by national broadcaster NOS, again using Pangram, found that around a quarter showed stylistic features of AI.
Prime minister Rob Jetten also had to admit that he used AI to write social media posts, including personal reflections on sensitive subjects such as the mistreatment of Moluccan war veterans who came to the Netherlands in the 1950s.
He defended the practice at the time, saying: “Like three-quarters of Dutch people I sometimes use AI to make things better.”
Some MPs also dismissed the concerns raised by the latest analysis. Henk Vermeer, leader of the farmers’ party BBB, said AI was useful for small parties, after Pangram detected traces in 30% of speeches by his three MPs. “We also use calculators, mobile phones and even coffee makers,” he said.

Norway has introduced a comprehensive new sanctions package against Russia, aligning its national measures with the European Union’s 21st sanctions package.
The updated restrictions take effect on October 21, following regulatory adjustments enacted by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, European Pravda reported.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The new measures establish broad economic restrictions targeting key pillars of the Russian economy.
Under the expanded framework, strict curbs apply to financial institutions, oil projects, cryptocurrency platforms, and military-industrial facilities supporting Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Norwegian officials stated that these policies aim to apply further financial pressure on Russia and restrict its capacity to fund ongoing aggression.
On October 8, 2026, the European Union extended sanctions against individuals and entities linked to Russia’s destabilizing activities abroad for another year, maintaining the measures until October 9, 2027, as announced by the Council of the European Union.
The restrictions applied to 80 individuals and 20 entities, subjecting them to asset freezes and travel bans, while prohibiting EU citizens and companies from making funds or economic resources available to them.
Official statements noted that the decision reflected Russia’s continued and intensified hybrid operations across Europe, which included foreign information manipulation, cyberattacks, sabotage, and interference targeting the EU, its member states, and partner countries.

Australian MP loses both legs in vehicle attack as suspect appears in court
Independent lawmaker Helen Haines is in stable condition, her husband says, as suspect charged with three offences.
Australian independent lawmaker Helen Haines has had both of her legs amputated after being rammed by a car outside her electoral office, her husband said, as the suspected attacker appeared in court.
Doctors amputated the MP’s left leg after an attacker hit her twice with his car in Wangaratta, northeast of Melbourne, on Monday, Phil Haines said. They tried to save her right leg but failed to do so, he told a news conference on Wednesday.
“The good news in all this is Helen is alive, and she’s stable,” he told reporters. “That is the most important thing for our family.”
The suspect in the attack, revealed to be a 43-year-old man called Brendan Nugent, made a brief court appearance on Wednesday.
He has been charged with three crimes: dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing injury and causing harm to a public official.
He was also charged with the cultivation and possession of cannabis, according to court filings.
The suspect’s lawyer said he has a rare neurological condition called idiopathic transverse myelitis and is also recovering from a concussion, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation reported.
Police are still investigating the motive for the attack. Australia’s federal police commissioner Krissy Barrett said there was no intelligence suggesting any threat to Haines.
“What I can say is we didn’t have any specific intelligence that would have indicated something as atrocious as happened on Monday afternoon,” she told reporters.
Haines had worked in nursing, midwifery and academia before being elected to parliament in 2019 for the rural seat of Indi, which she retained in 2022 and 2025.
Attacks on politicians are rare in Australia, but concerns have been growing in recent years as online abuse and threats against elected officials have risen.

UNHCR and Vinnytsia Regional State Administration strengthen cooperation to support displaced people and regional recovery
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:34:36 EEST
17:34:36 KST

© Vinnytsia Regional State Administration
Today, UNHCR, the UN Refugee Agency, and the Vinnytsia Regional State Administration signed a Memorandum of Understanding to strengthen support for internally displaced people, returnees and others affected by the ongoing war, while contributing to the region’s recovery.
Since the start of the full-scale invasion in February 2022, Vinnytsia region has provided shelter and assistance to people forced to flee their homes. Today, the region hosts around 144, 000 internally displaced people. Alongside immediate assistance, displaced people need access to stable housing, essential services, and opportunities to rebuild their lives. Through their cooperation, UNHCR and the regional administration aim to address these needs, support the communities hosting displaced people, and help families find lasting solutions.
© Vinnytsia Regional State Administration
“Displaced people bring skills, experience and determination to the communities that welcome them. Practical barriers, from finding suitable housing to restoring documents and accessing services, can make it difficult to start again. By working with the Vinnytsia regional authorities, we can help remove these barriers so people can regain independence, make decisions about their future and take an active part in community life,” said Bernadette Castel-Hollingsworth, UNHCR’s Representative in Ukraine.
“UNHCR is an important partner for Vinnytsia region in supporting people affected by the war. Russia has intensified its attacks on civilian and critical infrastructure, including in our region. At the same time, Vinnytsia continues to host around 144,000 internally displaced people, for whom access to housing remains a pressing need.
The memorandum we have signed will strengthen our joint efforts to develop long-term housing solutions for people who have moved to the region because of the war, repair damaged homes and assist families affected by Russian attacks. I thank UNHCR for its partnership and readiness to continue supporting those who need it most,” said Natalia Zabolotna, Head of the Vinnytsia Regional State Administration.
© Vinnytsia Regional State Administration
Housing is a central area of cooperation, especially through repairs to homes for displaced women, men, girls and boys and the search of sustainable housing solutions for people accommodated in collective sites. This year, UNHCR resumed support for home repairs for displaced people in the region, with work on 40 private homes underway. The memorandum also covers legal assistance, psychosocial support, access to social services, cash assistance, essential household items and winter support. This cooperation builds on assistance already delivered across the region. Since 2022, UNHCR and its partners have provided legal assistance to more than 44,000 people and psychosocial support to more than 30,000. Over 77,000 people received essential relief items between 2022 and 2024.
UNHCR has also supported repairs to 142 homes for displaced people in 2023–2024 and the creation of temporary housing for 14 households in Shypynky in 2024–2025. Repairs to 40 private homes currently underway are scheduled for completion by the end of 2026.
© Vinnytsia Regional State Administration
In Lukashivka, Ladyzhyn community, the QTochok pilot project will provide fully equipped homes on communal land for 10 displaced families comprising more than 50 people, with completion planned by the end of 2026. Designed for families unable to return home for the foreseeable future, the new settlement will offer long-term housing close to services and employment opportunities in nearby Ladyzhyn.
UNHCR also supports IDP Councils through strategic planning, advice and information activities. Under the memorandum, UNHCR and the regional administration will strengthen links with humanitarian, recovery and development partners and international financial institutions, helping connect emergency assistance with longer-term recovery and lasting solutions for people affected by the war.

‘People are starving’: Survivors recount horrors of Ukrainian siege (VIDEO)
Ukrainian forces have effectively laid siege to the frontline town of Alyoshki in Russia’s Kherson Region, leaving civilians facing acute shortages of food, water, and medicine, residents who managed to escape have told RT.
Located on the left bank of the Dnieper River opposite the Ukrainian-held city of Kherson, the town has been largely cut off from essential supplies and basic services for months. Russian authorities estimate that between 1,500 and 2,000 civilians remain trapped there, including elderly residents and around 15 children.
Kherson Governor Vladimir Saldo has accused Kiev’s forces of deliberately choking off humanitarian deliveries to Alyoshki by remotely mining access roads and targeting vehicles carrying food, fuel, and medicine. Strikes have also damaged the town’s energy and communications infrastructure, deepening the humanitarian crisis.
Russian forces have partially broken through the blockade by clearing some roads, but continued shelling and drone attacks hamper regular aid deliveries. Regional children’s rights commissioner Irina Kravchenko said on Tuesday that aid is reaching the town, but remains woefully insufficient.
Russian Ambassador-at-Large Rodion Miroshnik earlier described the situation as a “medieval blockade using modern methods,” accusing Ukrainian troops of preventing civilians from fleeing and obstructing the recovery of bodies.
The crisis has also reached the highest diplomatic levels. Russian President Vladimir Putin and his US counterpart, Donald Trump, discussed the situation during a phone call earlier this month. Russia’s human rights commissioner, Yana Lantratova, has said she is in contact with US First Lady Melania Trump’s team, which has expressed willingness to help civilians.
Moscow has accused Kiev of deliberately creating the humanitarian emergency while attempting to shift the blame onto Russia. Saldo has invited international organizations to visit Alyoshki and witness the conditions firsthand.
Residents who escaped the town have given harrowing accounts of hunger, destroyed homes, dwindling food supplies, and drones terrorizing civilians.
“The town is burning. There’s nothing left intact,” one evacuee said, describing a destroyed water pump and food prices soaring beyond residents’ reach. She claimed no food supplies have entered the town since May, leaving people “starving.” RT spoke exclusively to Alyoshki evacuees about their struggle to survive and the desperate plight of those left behind.

Council of Europe sees Ukraine gains on Roma, LGBTI rights
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:32:01 EEST
17:32:01 KST

Ukraine is making significant progress in the legislative protection of Roma and LGBTI people, but gaps remain in areas such as equality, hate crime and integration, the Council of Europe's European Commission against Racism and Intolerance (ECRI) said in a new report published in Strasbourg on Wednesday.
ECRI, "recognizing the exceptional circumstances caused by Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine, identifies the legislative and policy progress achieved and the gaps that remain in three main areas: effective equality and access to rights, hate speech and hate-motivated violence, and integration and inclusion," it said.
The report welcomes several positive developments, ECRI said. The Verkhovna Rada Commissioner for Human Rights stepped up work on non-discrimination and strengthened cooperation with civil society.
"More training and guidance has been provided to police on investigating hate crimes, including through stronger international cooperation. New strategies and policies on Roma inclusion have been adopted, and good examples of proactive work with Roma communities have been given. ECRI also welcomes a number of political commitments made on LGBTI equality," it said.
At the same time, ECRI noted remaining problems, particularly on the situation of Roma and LGBTI people.
"Despite positive developments, some issues are of concern. Roma and LGBTI people appear to be particularly affected by hate speech, even if a decline in the overall number of hate speech cases since the start of the full-scale war is reported," it said in a press release.
According to the report, many hate incidents continue to be misclassified and not treated as such by police and prosecutors. Access to health care for LGBTI people, especially transgender people, also remains a problem. Gaps were found in school curricula on including Roma history and culture and LGBTI-related topics in a sensitive and age-appropriate way. Incidents involving allegations of racist or LGBTI-phobic misconduct by officers of the National Police, the State Border Guard Service and the Armed Forces were reported.
ECRI listed 15 recommendations for the Ukrainian authorities. Among them, the authorities should take measures to ensure access to quality education for Roma children, for example through information and awareness initiatives with Roma mediators and families. ECRI also recommended measures to combat and prevent LGBTI-phobic bullying in schools, and to improve equality and hate crime legislation by explicitly including sexual orientation, gender identity, sex characteristics, ethnic origin and skin color in the list of protected characteristics.
"ECRI stresses the need for priority implementation of two recommendations. The first says that the authorities should, in cooperation with civil society, carry out nationwide information campaigns aimed at preventing hate speech, including against LGBTI people and Roma. The second calls on the Ukrainian authorities to set up an inclusive working group to proactively identify Roma who lack proper identity documents and provide them with appropriate support. This involves further simplifying administrative procedures and, where needed, providing targeted assistance to overcome administrative barriers," it said.
The report covers the period from June 2017 to March 2026 and follows a visit to the country in September 2025. Interim monitoring will be carried out within two years of the report's publication to assess measures taken by the authorities to implement the two priority recommendations.

Can China turn national power into world leadership?

Can China turn national power into world leadership?
China has all the signs of world-topping national strength but whether other countries accept its leadership will depend on what’s on offer
As turbulence grows in many countries, it is tempting to ask if there is a global hegemon that can sort everything out fairly.
Our latest projections of national strength for 2027 take into account resources, territory, economic strength and military power. They still put China in first place, with its lead over other countries widening. But when might China move beyond leading the ranking to exert decisive influence over the world’s trouble spots and become a global arbiter?
To explore that question, we should first look at how states have assessed national power. Ancient rulers counted people, revenues, troops, ships and resources but these were separate assessments, not a single measure of national power.

US sanctions target Iran's rail sector as Tehran shifts cargo from sea routes to overland corridors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
08:30:00 UTC
17:30:00 KST

Can Iran's rail network offset expanding US sanctions?
October 21, 2026
The United States has opened another front in its economic pressure campaign against Iran, this time targeting the railways Tehran increasingly relies on as maritime trade becomes more difficult.
On October 1, the US Treasury sanctioned three Iranian railway companies alongside seven automakers and five foreign suppliers of automotive parts as part of its Operation Economic Outcast.
Washington says Iran's rail and automotive industries provide revenue and logistical capacity to the state and are connected to networks involving the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
The timing of the move is significant. Since the US maritime blockade sharply restricted Iran's southern trade routes, Tehran has tried to move more goods through its land borders and railway connections with China, Central Asia, Russia and Turkey.
Rail transport has become more important just as Washington decided to target it.
Iran expands regional rail links
Shahriar Naghizadeh, director general for foreign trade at Iran's railway authority, was quoted by the semi-official Mehr news agency as saying that the country has around 15,000 kilometers (9,300 miles) of main and secondary railway lines, more than 35,000 wagons and nearly 500 diesel locomotives.
The network carried around 44 million tons of freight in the Iranian year ending in March 2026, up from about 40 million tons the previous year, according to Naghizadeh. And authorities are targeting 54 million tons this year.
Iran is linked to neighboring markets through 13 rail crossings, providing overland access to Turkey, Azerbaijan, Afghanistan, Pakistan and onward routes to Central Asia and China via Turkmenistan.
The new US sanctions raise questions about how foreign railway operators, freight forwarders, banks and insurers will continue dealing with Iranian rail companies.
China-Iran rail traffic expands
Bloomberg reported in May that freight trains traveling from the Chinese city of Xi'an to Tehran had increased from around one per week before the US blockade to roughly one every three or four days.
In September, a train left China carrying automotive parts, consumer goods and other cargo. It ran through Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan before entering Iran at Sarakhs with an expected transit time of 14 to 16 days.
For Iran, such services offer a route to Chinese suppliers that avoids the area around the Strait of Hormuz. But advertised transit times do not necessarily reflect what an importer experiences.
Delivery date cannot be guaranteed
A Chinese freight company told DW that actual delivery times can stretch far beyond advertised schedules because of border inspections, customs procedures and train availability.
It estimated that rail transit along the main route from western China to Tehran would take 50-60 days under current conditions. Road transport along a similar route is around 22 to 25 days.
The gap between a scheduled 14-day transit time and commercial estimates of up to 60 days highlights one of the central challenges facing Iran.
Customs inspections, gauge changes, payment problems and sanctions can all be another potential point of delay.
Increasing the number of trains also requires more locomotives, wagons and cooperation from several transit countries.
Rail works best for critical inputs
Alireza Salavati, managing director of London-based Middle East Analytica, said rail is increasingly useful for Iran but should not be mistaken as a replacement for maritime trade.
"A workable overland route now links China and Iran, but I would not call it a replacement for sea freight," he told DW.
Under normal conditions, ships can move far larger quantities at lower unit costs. Rail becomes more attractive for goods where speed and continuity matter more than the cheapest transport.
That includes automotive components, machinery, electronics and industrial inputs, whose absence can stop an entire production line.
When delays become a cash problem
Salavati argues that the effect on companies cannot be measured only in freight charges.
For a manufacturer importing $1 million (€890,000) worth of inputs every 30 days, a 30-day journey means roughly a million dollars of inventory may be tied up in transit.
Cutting the journey to 15 days could reduce that amount significantly, depending on payment arrangements. The reverse can be much more damaging.
If input costs rise while delivery times stretch from 30 to 45 days, companies need more working capital simply to maintain the same production flow, the expert explained, pointing out that a factory can have customers and orders but still have to reduce production because too much cash is trapped in goods that have not arrived.
"Reliability matters as much as speed," Salavati said. "A 15-day train is little use if the container waits a week to depart, or if the bank or insurer will not touch it."
The new US sanctions add another source of uncertainty to that calculation.
Sanctions push trade toward other corridors
Optimizing its railway use would give Iran more options than having to rely on southern ports alone, but the overall scale remains limited.
Washington's sanction strategy is designed to isolate Iran by closing maritime, financial, aviation and now railway channels.
Still, Salavati argues that the same pressure may accelerate Iran's integration with alternative networks.
"Washington's efforts to isolate Iran may also be pushing it deeper than at any point in recent years into China's economic orbit and closer to Russia's wartime strategic system," he said.
That does not mean China or Russia can make up for the economic cost of US pressure, since Iranian importers still need insurers, banks and customers able to absorb higher prices.
Container trains can only carry a fraction of what a large cargo vessel can transport, so for now, rail provides Iran with a limited alternative trade channel.
Its wider success depends on better financing and becoming more reliable — but even then it is not a wholesale substitute for sea freight.

====================================================================================================

Can Europe Build Data Centers Without Giving Up Its Climate Goals?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
08:30:00 UTC
17:30:00 KST

Earlier this year, the German government laid out an ambitious plan: By 2030, it would double the scale of the country’s data center fleet, and quadruple the amount of compute available for running artificial intelligence models. The idea was to minimize Germany’s dependence on the United States for access to AI—a point of concern across Europe—and boost its faltering economy.
However, Germany has found that its AI ambitions are butting up against its climate commitments. EU member states have committed to cutting greenhouse gas emissions by 55 percent by the end of the decade. But policies meant to help meet that target are interfering with attempts to trigger a data center building frenzy.
As part of its broader climate commitments, the previous German administration voted through the Energy Efficiency Act in 2023. Among other things, it required all new data centers to recycle a portion of the waste heat generated by their computer equipment, ideally into nearby municipal heating systems. It seemed like a no-brainer, says Patrick Graichen, who served as a senior official at Germany’s Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy at the time, before resigning over cronyism allegations.
“We need clean heat, and data centers are a source of clean heat,” Graichen tells WIRED.
In June, a month before the rules were due to finally take effect, the German federal government walked them back. Data center firms had complained that the requirements made it almost impossible to build in the country; the German Data Center Association characterized an early version of the bill as a “data center prevention act.” Under an amended bill, which will be put to the German parliament for ratification imminently, data center operators would no longer be obligated to reuse waste heat, only to scope out the possibility.
Graichen and others have accused the German government of sacrificing climate targets for a chance to ride the AI wave. But countries across Europe find themselves pulled between these same two poles, under simultaneous pressure to cash in on rapid growth in the energy-intensive AI sector—and limit dependence on the US—and to protect the climate.
The German Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy did not respond to a request for comment.
Among data center developers, the chief objection to the original Energy Efficiency Act was the chance it could land them in an impossible bind, obligated to reuse waste heat even when there was no available offtake—whether a municipal heating system or an industry, like greenhouse agriculture. “Some of the things they had to comply with were outside of their control,” says Barbara Smitten, associate director for critical systems at consulting firm Cundall. “It felt that [the burden] was all on the data center.”
In the last 18 months, multiple data center proposals have fallen through in Germany: Stack Infrastructure canceled a $3 billion facility in Hesse, and state-owned Komm.ONE withdrew from a project in Baden-Württemberg. Though precisely what causes a data center development to fold is rarely clear, Komm.ONE pointed directly to the burdens of the Energy Efficiency Act.
Graichen claims that the industry’s objections are groundless. He says the availability of a heat offtake should become a default criterion for any developer searching for a new site. “Stop complaining,” he says.
When an offtake is available, recycling heat produced by a data center is straightforward. “There is no technical reason why a data center cannot use its waste heat. The technologies and concepts are well known,” says John Booth, managing director at IT consultancy Carbon3IT, who helped to devise EU-wide energy efficiency targets for data centers. “There is absolutely no reason except the will of the organization to do it.”
Nevertheless, under the amended Energy Efficiency Act, data center developers are required only to assess whether recycling heat is economically and technically feasible. If not, they are exempt. “With practical rules for data centers, we are creating the conditions for digital sovereignty and economic growth,” wrote Katherina Reiche, federal minister for economic affairs and energy, when the cabinet approved the change.
The amendment may unlock pent-up demand among data center developers to build in Germany, whose geographic centrality makes it easy to route data efficiently into Western and Eastern Europe. “It lessens the risk of people not seeing the German market as attractive,” says Smitten.
But in a roundabout way, it could also undermine the aim to spark a building frenzy, inviting the type of climate-focused activism that has led to permitting freezes and data center moratoria in the US. Already, in February, the city council of a small German town voted to block the construction of a $2.5 billion data center development, partly over climate concerns.
As policymakers contend with conflicting ambitions to improve domestic AI capabilities and meet climate objectives, some say the swelling public unease about that trade-off will complicate things yet further in Europe. In the last year, the attitude toward data centers “has switched completely,” claims Graichen. “First and foremost in the US, but the same will happen in Europe.”

Ebola outbreak spreads to Nigeria as Kenya reports ninth case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
08:29:49 UTC
17:29:49 KST

Nigeria has confirmed its first Ebola case in the latest outbreak, while Kenya reported its ninth infection, raising concerns about the spread of the deadly disease across Africa.
Nigeria’s case involves a woman who travelled from Uganda to the capital, Abuja, and was diagnosed after receiving treatment at a private hospital for several days, Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate said on Tuesday. She is in isolation and receiving medical care, while authorities have identified 44 close contacts for monitoring.
Kenya’s latest case is a 24-year-old man who tested positive while in quarantine after developing symptoms. He is a close relative of the first confirmed patient, who died in Nairobi on October 5, the Health Ministry said.
Kenya has recorded nine cases, including one death. Authorities said all infections remain within a single cluster, with no evidence of transmission beyond it. They have traced and quarantined 134 of 135 identified contacts and said eight surviving patients were responding positively to treatment.
The outbreak, caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, now affects four countries — the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria — and has so far infected about 9,400 people and killing at least 4,500, according to figures cited in reports.
‘Most geographically widespread outbreak’
Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), warned that the outbreak had become the most geographically widespread Ebola outbreak in history, affecting multiple countries across three African regions.
“With mortality approaching 50% in DRC, we face an extremely serious threat,” Kaseya said on X, urging the international community to provide funding, medical supplies and health workers.
There is no approved vaccine or drug for the current strain, and the World Health Organization (WHO) has warned that the outbreak continues to outpace efforts to track and contain it.
The first clinical trial of a potential vaccine is expected to begin by the end of October, according to WHO.
Ervebo, a vaccine already approved for use against the more common Zaire strain of Ebola, will undergo a full-scale human trial in the DRC to see if it offers any cross-protection against Bundibugyo.
Two vaccines specifically for Bundibugyo are also being developed, one by the University of Oxford and another by the US-based Moderna group. They are currently in the early stages of testing in smaller-scale clinical trials.
Capobianco, director of global health security at Gavi, told RFI they have the potential to save lives in this and future Ebola outbreaks.
Psychological toll on communities
Beyond the immediate health risks, the outbreak is worsening the hardships faced by communities in eastern DRC, where conflict, crisis and severe malnutrition have already left many people vulnerable.
Mirella Riccardi, a mental health specialist with Doctors Without Borders, said Ebola had compounded the psychological distress of people living in areas already devastated by conflict and deprivation.
A Congolese teacher whose family experienced suspected Ebola symptoms recalled feeling abandoned as neighbours kept their distance until responders took sick relatives to a clinic and disinfected their home.
“It felt as though we were living all alone because of the illness,” she said. “It has caused severe trauma within our family.”
The psychological effects of Ebola outbreaks can persist long after the immediate crisis, according to the WHO, with survivors and affected families experiencing anxiety and mood disorders.

Judge Oded Shaham said the court would not dictate what prosecutors wrote in their response, leaving the defense to decide how to address it.
The judges agreed that the response would not be scanned into the court file so Mandelblit would not be exposed to it. Prosecutor Yonatan Tadmor said prosecutors would not add quotations from the records of discussions to their response, and that any further material they considered necessary to disclose would be provided after a court decision.
The exchange followed Tuesday’s questioning about the distinction between Mandelblit’s approval to investigate Netanyahu and the wording police used to tell the prime minister what he was suspected of doing.
That dispute centered on Case 4000, in which prosecutors allege that Netanyahu advanced regulatory measures benefiting telecommunications company Bezeq in exchange for intervention in the Walla news website’s coverage. In that case, Netanyahu faces charges of bribery, fraud, and breach of trust and denies wrongdoing.
Mandelblit testified Tuesday that he remembered approving Netanyahu’s questioning as a suspect in all three cases against him. However, he could not recall whether he had explicitly approved using the word “bribery” in the warning given to Netanyahu before questioning in Case 4000.
Hadad pointed to a document describing the approved investigation into Netanyahu as concerning public-integrity offenses, while explicitly referring to bribery in relation to Shaul Elovitch, the businessman at the center of the Bezeq-Walla case. Hadad argued that the difference showed Mandelblit had authorized questioning Netanyahu on suspicion of fraud and breach of trust.
'Using discretion between bribery and breach of trust'
Mandelblit maintained that Case 4000 involved suspected bribery, while acknowledging that the wording shown to him more closely suited breach of trust.
“I wanted to leave myself discretion between bribery and breach of trust,” he said Tuesday.
Judge Moshe Bar-Am questioned whether it was appropriate to use such convoluted wording when warning a prime minister before questioning. Mandelblit said the formulation could encompass offenses beyond breach of trust.
The disagreement concerned what investigators were authorized to examine and what Netanyahu was told at the time.
Netanyahu also faces fraud and breach-of-trust charges in Case 1000, involving expensive gifts from wealthy businessmen, and in Case 2000, involving discussions with publisher Arnon Mozes about favorable coverage in Yediot Aharonot in exchange for steps against rival newspaper Israel Hayom. He denies wrongdoing in all three cases. His trial began in May 2020.

====================================================================================================

Europe's growing rebellion against the ICC could change the game for Israel - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
08:26:12 UTC
17:26:12 KST

On October 9, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced sweeping, full-blocking financial sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC). It was an unprecedented escalation in the clash between sovereign states and international institutions, and a direct challenge to the Hague-based tribunal.
The decision came amid a turbulent October. Demonstrations and riots were intensifying in major cities, instability was widespread, and conventional diplomacy was under strain. The sanctions risk dismantling the postwar architecture of international justice.
Washington calls the sanctions a defense of national sovereignty against what it sees as the Court’s political overreach. The dispute, however, goes back years. The US has long objected to ICC investigations involving American personnel and the actions of close allies, particularly Israel. Now the breach between Washington and the Court has widened, giving fresh momentum to critics in Europe.
Their objections go beyond US policy. They question the neutrality, selectivity, and professionalism of the Court’s personnel. Critics argue that an institution founded to judge the gravest international crimes has become a vehicle for political agendas. Much of their attention has centered on Luis Moreno Ocampo, the ICC’s first prosecutor, who served from 2003 to 2012.
Ocampo’s activities since leaving office have fueled allegations of commercialization and political activism. Between 2023 and 2026, he became a vocal critic of Israeli military operations in Gaza, describing them as a "risk of genocide" and suggesting that arms supplies from allied states could constitute complicity.
Ocampo maintains his independence. His critics say that such statements, coming from a former head of ICC prosecution, objectively intensify political pressure on Israel and undermine the perceived neutrality of the Court’s former leadership.
In April 2026, Newsweek România reported on recordings purportedly featuring Ocampo and his son discussing private funding, ways to influence the European Parliament, and efforts to pressure European Commission leaders over EU policy toward Azerbaijan and Armenia.
Whatever the eventual legal assessment, critics see a former chief prosecutor using his reputation and connections in ways incompatible with the independence expected of international justice.
The concerns are not new. In 2017, a joint investigation by major European news organizations revealed Ocampo’s use of offshore structures and a multimillion-dollar consulting contract with a Libyan businessman linked to the Gaddafi regime. To those who regard the ICC as an instrument of geopolitical interests, a former chief prosecutor becoming what they call a "legal gun for hire" is not an isolated professional lapse.
Signs of systemic institutional degradation
It is a sign of systemic institutional degradation. Calls for a full review of former ICC prosecutors’ financial and lobbying activities have become central to the debate.
The Court has also faced questions about its own leadership. In May 2024, allegations of sexual misconduct involving a female ICC staff member were referred to the Court. The initial process ended when the complainant declined to participate, but a second referral followed in October.
The United Nations Office of Internal Oversight Services investigated the matter from November 2024 to December 2025 and reviewed thousands of pages of evidence and testimony. The allegations concerned the Court’s then-chief prosecutor, Karim Khan. On July 24, 2026, the Assembly of States Parties removed him from office after finding serious misconduct and a serious breach of duty. Khan denies the allegations.
This criticism now has a prominent voice in the European Parliament. Harald Vilimsky, head of the Austrian Freedom Party (FPÖ) delegation and vice chair of the Patriots for Europe group, wants the EU to follow Washington’s lead. After the U.S. sanctions announcement, his party called for a "decisive shift in thinking" and urged the EU to impose sanctions on the ICC.
Vilimsky points to the Court’s actions against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, beginning with a 2024 arrest warrant request, as evidence of what he sees as political motivation.
"International institutions have clearly defined tasks to fulfill and must not elevate themselves to the status of political actors who disregard the sovereignty of states and interfere in their affairs," he said in his October 12 German-language statement. In his view, the ICC increasingly acts as a "self-appointed moral and political authority," making unconditional European support untenable.
Vilimsky has influence in certain political circles, but the EU remains divided. Senior EU officials reaffirmed their commitment to the Court as a cornerstone of the rules-based international order at the October 15 and 16 summit. That official position has not silenced Vilimsky and others who challenge it. Their pressure suggests that the consensus behind the ICC is fracturing.
His intervention carries particular weight in Israel. Vilimsky has been warmly received there, and ministers Amichai Chikli and Miri Regev have publicly welcomed the political rapprochement he helped advance. That has raised his standing as a European voice on Israel and the ICC. The debate over the Court is not simply legal. It is also about alliances, sovereignty, and competing views of accountability.
Together, US-led sanctions, scrutiny of past institutional conduct, and political opposition in Europe have placed the ICC in an existential crisis. The current unrest, marked by street riots and a pervasive sense of instability, reflects a broader climate of uncertainty in which confidence in international institutions is increasingly being questioned. It remains unclear whether this is a temporary setback or the permanent dismantling of the existing order.
The court faces a stark choice. It can continue its current course, risking further isolation and the loss of support from major global powers. Or it can undertake a profound, transparent review of its governance, the conduct of former officials, and its operational mandate. Without that transformation, the ICC risks being seen permanently not as an independent court but as a political instrument. That would signal the end of an era of international accountability that began at the turn of the century. The future of international justice itself is at stake.
Dr. Philip Levy is a member of the International Dialogue Circle, a forum focused on international affairs, geopolitical engagement, and collaborative initiatives.

Researchers identify new subtype of depression linked to body clock
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:25:39 CST
17:25:39 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Researchers in Australia have identified a subtype of depression linked to disruptions in the body's internal 24-hour clock that regulates the sleep-wake cycle, potentially paving the way for more targeted behavioral and medical treatments.
The study analyzed clinical and genetic data from more than 10,000 Australians with severe, recurrent or persistent depression, identifying nearly a quarter of participants as having what researchers termed "circadian depression," according to a statement released Wednesday by Australia's University of Sydney.
The subtype is characterized by symptoms including seasonal patterns of illness, longer sleep when depressed, waking feeling exhausted, and being a night owl, according to the study published in the British Journal of Psychiatry.
People with circadian depression were more likely to develop the illness earlier in life and had more severe symptoms, including higher levels of suicidal thoughts. They also had higher genetic risks for inflammatory and cardiovascular conditions and major neurodevelopmental disorders, including attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, the study showed.
Researchers said the subtype is more resistant to treatment by common serotonin-based antidepressants, but is more responsive to behavioral and medical therapies targeting the body clock's unique brain circuits, such as melatonin, melatonin-targeted antidepressants and light therapy.
The researchers warned that not recognizing circadian depression in young people often led to early treatment failures and more side effects. ■

World Insights: Cost-of-living protests highlight mounting economic, social pressures across Europe
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:25:25 CST
17:25:25 KST

FRANKFURT, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Recent protests across Europe have brought social and economic strains into sharper focus, reflecting concerns that extend beyond prices to housing, incomes, public services and economic security. Governments face growing pressure to respond, but high debt, tight budgets and long-standing structural problems leave few quick or easy solutions.
DEMONSTRATIONS ACROSS EUROPE
Holding a cardboard sign reading "I am 81 and being evicted," retiree Maria Teresa Faleiro joined crowds in Lisbon protesting against soaring living costs and a deepening housing crisis.
Despite never missing a payment on the 724-euro (813-U.S. dollar) monthly rent for the home she has lived in for 22 years, Faleiro faced eviction after her landlords refused to renew her lease. With nowhere else to go, she plans to appeal the court-ordered eviction, she said.
Faleiro's struggle highlights the growing plight many pensioners in Portugal face in securing affordable housing. It also reflects a broader cost-of-living squeeze across Europe, where thousands have taken to the streets to protest rising housing, food, fuel and energy costs, even as headline inflation has eased.
In France, protests that began with students demanding better school conditions and more teaching staff broadened into nationwide demonstrations over rising living costs and wider social grievances. Violence soon erupted on the sidelines of some rallies, with clashes, looting and arson reported in several cities. The historic city hall in Limoges was largely destroyed by fire.
In Spain, more than 50 protests took place in Madrid and dozens of other Spanish cities on Oct. 3, demanding action on soaring rents, evictions and housing affordability after the government failed to pass emergency housing legislation.
Elsewhere, protests in Italy and Belgium have reflected a broader mix of concerns over wages, prices, public services and fiscal tightening. In Milan, hundreds of black-clad demonstrators besieged Piazza del Duomo on Saturday, throwing firecrackers and bottles at police. At least four officers and 20 protesters were injured, while about 50 demonstrators were detained, according to the Italian news agency ANSA.
ECONOMIC SECURITY UNDER STRAIN
Beyond higher daily expenses, mounting financial pressures are fueling a broader sense of economic insecurity across the continent. Although inflation has eased from its peak, households continue to feel the cumulative impact of earlier price increases.
The European Central Bank said food prices across euro-area countries were already 20 percent to 57 percent higher in August 2025 than at the end of 2019. Renewed energy pressures have added to the squeeze, with euro-area consumer energy inflation reaching 18.9 percent in September 2026, according to Eurostat.
Housing pressures are particularly acute among young Europeans. Data released by Eurostat showed that in 2025, 26.9 percent of young people aged 15 to 29 in the European Union (EU) lived in overcrowded households. And 9.1 percent of them lived in households spending at least 40 percent of their disposable income on housing, way above the 7.7 percent recorded for the total population.
Similar pressures are visible beyond the EU. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, property prices have risen by about 70 percent over the past five years, real estate agent Haris Kadic told the Federation News Agency (FENA).
Local media also reported that some residents are borrowing money or relying on help from children and friends to cover basic expenses as housing and fuel costs rise.
Emmanuel Conte, Milan's city councilor responsible for housing, told Italian daily la Repubblica this month that when people who keep a city running can no longer afford to live there, housing is no longer just a social and economic issue but a political one.
Similarly, Jean Faniel, director general of Belgium's Centre for Socio-Political Research and Information, told Belgian media outlet BRUZZ that violence accompanying recent protests should be understood in the context of mounting social frustration.
Faniel said peaceful demonstrations and violent confrontations are potentially interconnected rather than entirely separate phenomena, noting that successive austerity measures have placed mounting pressure on people's living conditions, generating frustration and resentment.
STRUGGLE TO BALANCE FISCAL, SOCIAL NEEDS
European governments have introduced housing, energy and income support, but high debt, aging populations and competing demands for defense and investment are narrowing their room for further action.
As the European Commission expects France's deficit to reach 5.1 percent of GDP in 2026 and public debt to reach 118.1 percent, Oliver Nachtwey, a sociologist at the University of Basel, said the country's efforts to contain public debt through spending cuts leave governments with less room to invest in schools, teachers and other public services.
Experts said the challenge is to reconcile fiscal discipline with social stability. Thomas Decreus, a scholar at the Department of Philosophy at Tilburg University, warned that weakening basic social protections could undermine social peace. "A budget must be sound, but social investments are also necessary," he said.
Former Croatian Economy minister Ljubo Jurcic told Xinhua that price freezes can help contain immediate pressures, but governments must consider who ultimately bears the cost. In the longer run, stronger productivity and a better economic structure offer more sustainable protection for households, he said.
While subsidies and price controls can provide relatively quick relief, expanding housing supply, improving public services and raising productivity can take years, analysts said.
The challenge lies in how governments should respond to demands for immediate results while pursuing reforms that may take much longer to deliver tangible benefits, they said. ■

====================================================================================================

China Focus: One keystroke, a new career: AI reshapes China's film and TV industry
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:25:22 CST
17:25:22 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- At a film and television industry park in Suzhou, east China's Jiangsu Province, Qin Wenshan sits glued to his computer screen, watching as visuals, sound effects, subtitles and special effects fall into place on a video timeline.
With a single press of the Enter key, a team of AI agents springs into action, analyzing the script, designing characters and building scenes frame by frame.
Qin entered the field in late 2023, after stumbling across AI-generated content (AIGC), leading him to experiment with AI video production in his spare time. Before that, he had worked as a safety management officer in the local rail transit sector.
After his short-video series racked up hundreds of millions of views, Qin turned his hobby into a business, putting together a team focused on AI-powered content production.
His journey offers a glimpse into a broader transformation sweeping China's film and TV industry, where advances in AIGC video technology are changing not only how content is made, but also who can make it and at what cost.
PRODUCTION GETS A RESHUFFLE
Making a film or TV series used to require large teams of screenwriters, directors, cinematographers, production designers, editors, and visual effects artists, with all hands on deck. A crew could range from a few dozen people to several hundred and beyond.
The bigger the spectacle, the higher the bill. Productions involving animation, sci-fi or fantasy often come with high costs, particularly when they feature complex settings and elaborate visual effects.
AI is changing the math.
Qin's team put AI to work on "PandaPawz," a sci-fi animated short featuring futuristic settings and intense fight scenes, completing the film in just 28 days at a cost of around 30,000 yuan (about 4,464 U.S. dollars).
Industry data shows that AI can dramatically shorten production schedules, cutting timelines that once stretched over months or even years to just days. Some short-form drama episodes can now be produced in just hours, while efficiency in visual effects and previsualization has increased threefold to tenfold.
Yet AI's role goes far beyond generating images. Li Nan, a creator of AI-generated animated dramas, said the process begins with refining the story outline and developing detailed storyboards. AI tools then generate frames with consistent visual styles and character designs, which are turned into videos and combined with AI voice-overs and automated editing to create finished episodes.
This streamlined workflow enables small teams to handle work that once required extensive collaboration. In April, Li formed a two-person team dedicated to AI-generated animated dramas. Since then, its account has amassed more than 140,000 followers.
"Film and TV production used to be a massive team effort. Now, one person can do the work of an entire department, with AI as the backbone," Qin said.
GROWING DEMAND
The rapid expansion of AI-generated dramas is evident in both output figures and market projections. Official data released in September showed that 430,000 micro-dramas had been released nationwide in the first eight months of this year -- 13 times the total for all of 2025 -- with AI-made productions accounting for more than 90 percent.
The country now has more than 800 million viewers of micro-dramas -- series whose episodes run for less than 20 minutes. The market was worth more than 100 billion yuan in 2025.
The demand is expected to grow further. According to a report by DataEye, an industry data platform, China's AI-generated drama and animation market alone is projected to reach 40 billion yuan in 2026, a year-on-year increase of 138 percent.
The boom, however, also raises questions about content quality and the protection of rights and interests. The National Radio and Television Administration (NRTA) has acknowledged that AI is creating new opportunities for creative expression and more cost-efficient micro-drama production, while also highlighting the challenges the technology poses.
"Our position is clear: live-action dramas are the mainstay of quality productions and should receive strong support," said Wang Xiaoliang, an official with the NRTA, at a September news conference on the development of radio, television, and the online audio and video sector over the next five years.
At the same time, the administration said it will guide and regulate the innovative use of AI across the entire production process of audiovisual content in the coming years.
For industry leaders, the future may lie not in choosing between AI and traditional filmmaking, but in combining the two. Gong Yu, founder and CEO of iQIYI, a leading online entertainment platform, believes the use of AI in film and drama production will be common in the future, and that a hybrid approach combining live-action filming with AI may be the way forward.
The Chinese company is already exploring the potential of AI in longer productions. In July, it premiered "Mystic Tales: The Spider Lady's Vendetta," an AIGC internet feature film running over 60 minutes, which brings Chinese supernatural folklore to life, on both its domestic and international platforms.
Recently, it unveiled a trailer for "Immortals Over Mortal Love," its first full-length, multi-season drama combining AI filmmaking with live-action performances by professional actors. The first season of the series is produced on NadouPro, the company's film and TV production platform empowered by large models.
The move toward AI-generated long-form dramas signals a new stage in the technology's development, industry insider Hu Jie said, adding that these productions may face a tougher test of their storytelling, visual quality and ability to strike an emotional chord with audiences. ■
