Musk chose to restrict Ukraine's access to SpaceX network, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
00:35:05 UTC
09:35:05 KST

Musk chose to restrict Ukraine's access to SpaceX satellite network, sources say
A decision by Elon Musk led to restrictions on Ukraine's use of SpaceX's satellite communications network, people familiar with the matter told CBS News.
The satellite service, which is used for drone operations, hitting certain targets and protecting sites in Ukraine, was slowed significantly last week.
Musk held multiple conversations with administration officials leading up to the order, the sources said. He wanted clarity on the president's thinking on the matter. Musk has expressed distaste with his company being seen as profiting from the continued war between Russia and Ukraine.
It's not clear how Musk's order to curtail service was executed.
Musk licenses SpaceX's Starshield technology to the U.S. government. He said last week the U.S. controls who can access the technology and what level of service those users receive.
"Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," Musk, the world's richest person, wrote on X.
Musk did not reply to a request for comment. CBS News has reached out to the White House and the Pentagon for comment.
The Wall Street Journal was first to report on Musk's order.
The temporary restrictions came as a surprise to some officials inside the administration, who said neither Mr. Trump nor the Pentagon specifically ordered any limits meant to deliberately disrupt drone operations and battlefield communications.
Mr. Trump said Monday he was seeking details on who ordered the slowdown.
"I don't know who it was, but I'd like to find out," he said.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Tuesday the Pentagon has not manipulated the service.
"We haven't pulled anything back. There are terms of service that ultimately need to be complied to. And that's where Starlink has the option to make those decisions, but nothing's changed from our view. We haven't made any directives or anything like that," Hegseth told reporters, adding that "we wish the Ukrainians, obviously, success."
Zelensky told NBC News on Sunday there were still limits on Ukraine's Starshield service.
What is Starshield?
Starshield is a military-grade satellite network made by SpaceX for the U.S. government and its partners. It runs on similar technology to its civilian sister, Starlink.
The U.S. government pays to use Starshield and controls who can access the technology. Its use has been limited to Ukraine and occupied territories. It is not available in Russia
Starshield is essential to Ukraine's armed forces as it allows personnel to communicate and carry out strikes, including by maintaining contact with drones across long distances.
There is no working alternative to Starlink, which has put a massive constellation of low-earth satellites into orbit, and no direct competitor comes close.
What happened in Ukraine?
Ukrainian officials and soldiers told CBS News the country's military began experiencing sudden difficulties with Starshield equipment late Tuesday, including a throttling effect that made it more difficult to carry out missions with fast-moving drones. Sources in Ukraine's Ministry of Defense said SpaceX had unilaterally imposed the Starshield restrictions.
Regular Starlink terminals have a 70 km/hr speed cap, that is, the speed at which internet can be used in a vehicle in motion. At rates faster than the cap, the internet degrades and is no longer usable.
Starshield has no artificial speed cap and is known to work at speeds of at least 160 km/hr. Strike drones equipped with Starshield cruise at 160 km/h or higher, and they're the backbone of Ukrainian mid-range strikes.
Ukrainian units reported link drops at speeds as low as 90 km/hr, making those drones inoperable. The degradation of Starshield is estimated to have cost Ukraine tens of millions of dollars in losses, according to an analysis by Dimko Zhluktenko, a drone pilot and analyst in the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
Zelensky said Saturday the speed limits had prevented Ukraine from using Starshield to shoot down Shahed attack drones.
The Ukrainian leader wrote on X last week that "the Russians are trying to take advantage of the problems with Starlink in Ukraine, as our interceptor drones depend on this connection among other things."
Zelensky has suggested there are still some restrictions. He told NBC News over the weekend the maximum speed was 161 km/hr, and he said Tuesday that he'd spoken with Secretary of State Marco Rubio about "the situation with Starlink/Starshield, which needs to be restored."
The apparent restrictions drew swift pushback from U.S. lawmakers, with a bipartisan group of senators asking the Defense Department's internal watchdog to investigate last week.
"There needs to be an investigation, we need to find out who these people are because lives are at risk and lives are lost over these things," Republican Rep. Mike Turner of Ohio said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" over the weekend.
Why have Trump and Zelensky clashed?
Beyond the Starshield disruptions, Zelensky has said in recent days that Russia struck Ukraine without warning from the U.S., and deliveries of key interceptor missiles to Ukraine have slowed down.
A senior Pentagon official told CBS News on Monday there had been "no change to Department of War policy regarding intelligence sharing or any capabilities we are enabling Europeans to provide to Ukraine."
Mr. Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with Zelenskyy in recent weeks, accusing him of not doing enough to seek an end to the Russia-Ukraine war.
The U.S. president argues the war is responsible for high energy prices. His administration waived restrictions on buying Russian diesel earlier this month in an effort to ease pressure on the price of the commodity, a move Zelenskyy argued could embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin. Mr. Trump also waived sanctions on Russia last week.
Mr. Trump said earlier this month that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop striking each other's energy infrastructure — announcing an "energy ceasefire." Zelenskyy initially said Ukraine was willing to abide by such an agreement, but that Russia's strikes never ceased, and several days later he told the Financial Times his country would no longer hold off on striking Russian refineries because Russia was still attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
The Russian government never confirmed that it had agreed to a ceasefire.
In a Newsmax interview late Thursday, Mr. Trump called Zelenskyy "not a good guy for us to deal with," and argued Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries would be a "disgrace," as he urged both sides to make a deal while adding that the Ukrainian leader is harder to deal with than Putin.
"I'm not a big fan of Zelenskyy," Mr. Trump said.

NASA advances lunar rover development for future Moon Base
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
08:34:50 CST
09:34:50 KST

LOS ANGELES, Oct. 20 (Xinhua) -- NASA on Tuesday provided an update on the development of crewed and robotic lunar rovers to support its planned Moon Base initiative, highlighting efforts to develop the surface mobility capabilities needed for future exploration and sustained human operations on the Moon.
NASA's Volatiles Investigating Polar Exploration Rover is scheduled to embark on a mission to the lunar South Pole region in 2027 to explore permanently shadowed craters in search of water and other potentially valuable resources that could support sustainable lunar exploration.
The rover will be delivered to the lunar surface by Blue Origin's Blue Moon Mark 1 lander and is expected to travel more than 30 kilometers, collecting data on local temperatures, lighting conditions and terrain.
NASA said the data could help scientists better understand the origin and distribution of water on the Moon and assess how lunar resources might be used to support future exploration.
Meanwhile, NASA has awarded task orders to Astrolab and Lunar Outpost to build the first phase of Moon Base rovers capable of carrying crew, called lunar terrain vehicles (LTVs), which are intended to reach the Moon ahead of crewed Artemis missions.
Blue Origin has been tasked with delivering the rovers to the lunar South Pole region by 2028 through NASA's Commercial Lunar Payload Services initiative.
The LTVs will allow astronauts to explore geologically diverse areas near the lunar South Pole, collect samples and transport equipment. They will also be remotely operated from Earth to map the lunar surface before astronauts arrive, NASA said.
According to NASA, the LTVs are designed to travel up to 10 kilometers on a single battery charge, support up to three moonwalks per Artemis mission, and carry up to 80 kilograms of lunar samples and tools.
"Lunar rovers are central to our surface mobility strategy," said Robert Pickle, director of NASA's Surface Mobility Office within the Moon Base Program.
Their performance will help lay the groundwork for the mobility systems needed to build, operate and expand infrastructure for long-duration lunar exploration, he said. ■

Germany’s most popular party targeted by unknown hackers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
00:33:14 UTC
09:33:14 KST

Hackers target Germany’s most popular party
Germany’s most popular party, Alternative for Germany (AfD), has suffered a massive cyberattack, with unknown hackers reportedly stealing and publishing hundreds of thousands of internal emails, while the country’s political establishment seeks grounds to outlaw the opposition party.
The breach, which was first reported by Bild on Tuesday, reportedly exposed 421,179 emails totaling 281 gigabytes, including correspondence involving AfD co-chair Alice Weidel, honorary chairman Alexander Gauland, and other senior party figures.
The leaked material reportedly includes photographs of identity documents, bank statements, invoices, membership applications, and internal party lists. Bild said it examined a small sample of the files, including an identity card belonging to Markus Frohnmaier, the deputy leader of the AfD parliamentary group in the Bundestag.
The identities and motives of the hackers are unknown, and the authenticity of the published material has not been independently established.
The AfD confirmed that a hosting provider working with the party was hacked in September, but disputed suggestions that its current communications systems was compromised.
“Only a few email inboxes were unlawfully copied, most of which had not been used for years,” a party spokesman told Bild, adding that current federal party email accounts were unaffected.
The AfD condemned the breach as an “attack on the German party system and therefore on democracy” and said it reported the cyberattack to the security authorities.
No statement from investigators or condemnation of the breach by senior government officials has emerged as of early Wednesday.
The leaked correspondence has already drawn scrutiny from activists seeking to outlaw the party. Valentina Chiofalo, a representative of the German civil liberties organization Gesellschaft fuer Freiheitsrechte, told taz that the stolen emails could help strengthen the case for banning the AfD, while their publication and journalistic scrutiny could also shape public opinion against the party.
The attack comes amid an escalating campaign by Germany’s established political parties to isolate and potentially ban the AfD. The Euroskeptic party, which advocates stricter immigration controls and opposes Berlin’s military support for Ukraine and sanctions on Russia, has surged to 30% support in the latest INSA poll for Bild, opening a 12-point lead over Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s CDU/CSU bloc, which has slumped to 18%.
Earlier this month, the AfD secured the presidency of Saxony-Anhalt’s state parliament for the first time, breaking through the political ‘firewall’ maintained by establishment parties. Its rise prompted Social Democratic parliamentary leaders to demand the creation of a federal-state working group to examine a possible ban, accusing the AfD of threatening democracy from within and promoting extremism.
Germany’s domestic intelligence agency has also sought to classify the party as a confirmed right-wing extremist organization, but a Cologne court blocked the designation in February pending further legal proceedings.
The AfD has rejected the accusations, portraying the proposed ban as an attempt to overturn the will of millions of voters and eliminate political competition.

21 October 2026•Update: 21 October 2026
The Lebanese army on Tuesday rejected Israeli accusations that it had failed to disarm Hezbollah and dismantle its military infrastructure south of the Litani River as required under a November 2024 ceasefire agreement, accusing Israel of spreading misinformation to undermine its credibility amid ongoing negotiations. 
In a statement, the army dismissed Israeli claims casting doubt on its ability to fulfill its mission in southern Lebanon, stressing that its operations were documented by the committee overseeing the cessation of hostilities.
The dispute centers on a military facility in the town of Kfarra in Bint Jbeil district, where Israel accused the Lebanese army of failing to prevent Hezbollah activity.
The army said its units began work at the facility in December 2025 but suspended operations on March 16 following Israeli threats to strike the site.
It said the suspension was requested by the monitoring committee, which was informed that weapons and ammunition remained inside. Israel subsequently struck the facility.
The army said Israel repeatedly blocked efforts to resume operations until work restarted on Aug. 15 in coordination with the committee.
The facility was cleared and permanently closed on Oct. 16, it added.
The army also disputed Israeli footage purportedly showing Hezbollah transporting weapons, saying it was filmed on July 3 near the southern town of Seddikine shortly after a framework agreement was signed.
It said its actions were fully documented by the monitoring committee.
The army reaffirmed its commitment to existing agreements while accusing Israel of continued attacks and violations.
Earlier Tuesday, Israeli military spokeswoman Ella Waweya accused the Lebanese army of failing to curb Hezbollah activity south of the Litani River.
She claimed that Hezbollah had continued operating at the Kfarra facility and moved weapons and equipment from the site, sharing footage she said showed the group transporting arms by truck.
Israel has carried out attacks on Lebanon since March 2, killing and injuring thousands of people and displacing over 1.5 million residents.
On June 26, Lebanon and Israel signed a US-sponsored framework agreement providing for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese territory, the deployment of the Lebanese army and the disarmament of the Hezbollah group.
Despite the agreement, Israel has continued its attacks on southern Lebanon. Israeli forces also continue to occupy Lebanese territory, including areas held for decades and others seized during more recent wars and military operations.

Why former FDLR fighters are returning to Rwanda
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
00:25:43 UTC
09:25:43 KST

Why former FDLR fighters are returning to Rwanda
From the forest to Mutobo, former fighters face the challenge of rebuilding their lives after leaving the armed group.
Musanze, Rwanda – Jean Claude Hategekimana feared that returning to Rwanda could cost him his life. After years with the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), he decided to leave the armed group and return home. At Rwanda’s Mutobo Demobilisation and Reintegration Centre, he began preparing for civilian life.
Born in 1996 in Rutsiro District, in western Rwanda, Hategekimana moved to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) with his parents and grew up in an area controlled by the FDLR. He joined the group in 2018, underwent military training and eventually reached the rank of captain.
“I arrived at the Mutobo Centre after fighting to defend Goma. Following our defeat, I fled to Masisi. After realising that I was fighting for nothing, I decided to return to Rwanda. I came back on February 24,” he told Al Jazeera.
Hategekimana said FDLR members had been taught that anyone who returned to Rwanda would be killed.
“Upon arriving in Rwanda, I realised that the FDLR had been lying to us. For me, returning home felt like embarking on a suicide mission,” he said.
His experience illustrates the challenge of reintegrating former fighters whose beliefs and fears have been shaped by years in an armed group.
Rebuilding civilian life
Francis Musoni, secretary-general of the Rwanda Demobilisation and Reintegration Commission, said the Mutobo centre, located in Musanze in Rwanda’s Northern Province, was established in 2001 to receive members of the FDLR and other Rwandan armed groups returning from the DRC.
The FDLR emerged in the aftermath of the 1994 genocide against the Tutsis. After the genocide, members of the former Rwandan armed forces and militia groups fled to what was then Zaire, now the DRC. The Rwandan government accuses the FDLR of carrying out attacks against Rwanda and contributing to cross-border insecurity.
At Mutobo, the rehabilitation programme includes medical care, psychosocial support, civic education and assistance with reconnecting with families. Returnees can also contact relatives and friends through a telephone service, Musoni said.
“We help them to build confidence among themselves, build trust, and empower them to go back into the community and contribute to the development of the country together with their families,” he said.
The centre also allows visitors and media representatives to meet returnees. Musoni said those undergoing rehabilitation can visit their communities for short periods to help rebuild their confidence in returning home.
“They can travel to their communities [during rehabilitation]. They are given written permission for a week or two, and we even facilitate transport,” he said.
Different journeys home
For the former commanders interviewed by Al Jazeera at Mutobo, the decision to leave the FDLR was shaped by family ties, disillusionment and concerns about personal safety.
Major-General Anastase Munyaneza served in the former Rwandan armed forces in Kigali’s Kicukiro District during the 1994 genocide. He said he left Rwanda after the genocide and later joined the FDLR, eventually commanding its South Kivu sector.
Although he had come to accept the group’s beliefs, Munyaneza remained in contact with his family in Rwanda. News of their lives made him question his own circumstances.
“I was the only one who had fled to the DRC. I regularly received news about them. I knew they were still alive, attending school, working for the government and improving their lives. I began asking myself what I was doing in the forest,” he said.
He added that seeing other members return safely encouraged him to consider going home.
Munyaneza said he contacted personnel from the United Nations Organisation Stabilisation Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUSCO), who transported him from South Kivu to Bukavu and then to the Congolese-Rwandan border. He subsequently proceeded to Mutobo.
Lieutenant-Colonel Idrissa Bizimana, who was responsible for ideology, propaganda and recruitment within the FDLR, said his decision to return followed a change in his convictions.
“I no longer believed in the ideology I had been promoting. After receiving verified information about what was happening in Rwanda, I decided to return home,” he said.
Bizimana said he had been in contact with a MONUSCO general who had offered to help him return. Using a satellite phone equipped with GPS, he sent his location and the date. A helicopter was then dispatched to retrieve him, he said.
Lieutenant-Colonel Emilien Mpakaniye, who joined the FDLR in 1998 and was responsible for economic affairs at its headquarters, said he began questioning the organisation after becoming disillusioned with what he described as its lies.
Colonel Augustin Nshimiyimana, a former FDLR intelligence commander, returned to Rwanda in 2022 and underwent rehabilitation at Mutobo. He said he decided to leave after another commander accused him of working with Rwanda following a disagreement over a mission in Bujumbura.
Nshimiyimana said the accusation made him fear for his life.
“When they accuse you of working with Rwanda, it means they consider you a Tutsi, and the next step is to kill you,” he said.
Preparing for a new life
At Mutobo, former fighters receive education and practical support to prepare for life after discharge.
Febronie Mukankiko, a teacher at the centre, said teaching people who grew up in the forest required a different approach.
“Our students are different from ordinary students. They are adults who grew up in the forest, so teaching them requires special skills. We undergo additional training to ensure that we can teach them effectively,” she said.
She added that completing their studies could be a significant achievement for those with limited access to formal education.
“When they graduate and receive their certificates, they are very happy,” she said.
Musoni said the average stay at the centre was five months, after which returnees completed a formal discharge process. He said assistance could include financial support, vocational training, formal education and help establishing income-generating activities. The commission also follows up with former residents to assess how they are adjusting to life in their communities.
For those who have spent years away from Rwanda, leaving Mutobo marks the start of another transition: finding work, reconnecting with family and adjusting to civilian society.
For Mpakaniye, disillusionment came partly from the contrast between the lives of senior commanders’ families and those of ordinary fighters.
“First, their family members live in Rwanda and in Europe, while ours are in the forest,” he said.

One year on: Has Kenya’s opposition lost its way without Raila Odinga?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
00:22:19 UTC
09:22:19 KST

One year on: Has Kenya’s opposition lost its way without Raila Odinga?
Odinga’s legacy faces a test as ODM splits over its alliance with President Ruto.
Nairobi, Kenya – One year after Raila Odinga’s death, the political movement he led for decades is struggling to define its future. Within the Orange Democratic Movement (ODM), a bitter dispute over cooperation with President William Ruto has exposed divisions over the party’s identity and independence. The struggle raises a question that extends beyond ODM’s leadership: Can Kenya’s opposition remain a credible force without the man who helped shape it?
Raila’s death prompted tributes and commemorations celebrating a political career defined by the struggle for multiparty democracy, constitutional reform, freedom of expression and social justice. Yet the divisions now confronting his party reveal the difficulty of sustaining a political movement built around one dominant figure. His legacy remains a source of inspiration, but also a point of contention over what ODM should stand for and how it should exercise power.
At the centre of the dispute is ODM’s relationship with Ruto’s administration. The removal of Secretary-General Edwin Sifuna, who opposed closer cooperation with the president, has become a flashpoint in a wider struggle over the party’s direction. The disagreement is about more than personalities: It raises questions about whether ODM can work with the government while retaining the independence to challenge it.
A vacuum at the heart of the opposition
For decades, Raila occupied a central place in Kenya’s reform movements, challenging successive governments and campaigning for political change. To his supporters, he represented resistance and the promise of a more accountable political system. His influence, however, also meant that the opposition’s ability to unite often depended on his personal authority, political networks and capacity to negotiate competing interests.
Political analyst Professor Herman Manyora argues that Raila’s absence has left a vacuum that the opposition has struggled to fill.
“One year after Raila’s death, he is larger than life. I think there’s a way in which people thought Raila was not going to die. We had immortalised Raila,” Manyora says.
He argues that the opposition has yet to find a figure capable of bringing its competing interests together.
“The opposition is in disarray. There isn’t a figure that people can rally around,” he says.
The assessment points to a challenge that predates Raila’s death but has become more visible since it: A movement can inherit a leader’s political legacy without necessarily inheriting the authority that held it together. Whether that vacuum becomes a lasting weakness will depend on the ability of other leaders to build trust, establish a common agenda and organise beyond individual loyalties.
The alliance that divided his legacy
Raila’s decision to work with Ruto in 2024, amid nationwide protests against the Finance Bill, remains one of the most contested chapters of his political career.
The protests, driven in large part by young Kenyans, developed into a wider expression of anger about taxation, governance and political accountability. As pressure mounted on the government, Raila’s move towards cooperation with Ruto raised questions about whether dialogue could deliver meaningful change or whether it risked drawing the opposition closer to the establishment it had long challenged.
Manyora views the intervention as a decisive moment for Ruto’s administration.
“What happened then was that Raila came to the rescue of President William Ruto because, had he not come to rescue Ruto, I think the government would have collapsed,” he says.
Although Manyora’s assessment of the political consequences of the alliance is debatable, his interpretation captures the significance of Raila’s decision: A politician long associated with opposition politics had become a partner in an arrangement with the president against whom many Kenyans were protesting.
For some young Kenyans, the alliance was a betrayal of the political struggle that had made Raila a symbol of resistance. The Gen Z-led protests emerged largely outside traditional political structures, driven by demands for accountability and frustration with established political elites. Many protesters rejected the idea that their movement should be absorbed into negotiations among familiar political figures.
Joshua Okayo, a lawyer and human rights activist who identifies with the Gen Z generation, says Raila’s decision left him feeling betrayed.
“As a Gen Z, I recognise the kind of politics he fought for. I recognise the years he put into fighting for social justice, democracy, rule of law, constitutionalism, and many good things. But I also have a spot in my heart where I feel he betrayed the generation,” Okayo says.
That criticism captures the tension at the heart of the debate about Raila’s legacy: whether political compromise was a pragmatic attempt to stabilise the country and pursue reform, or a retreat from the principles that had defined his career.
Supporters of cooperation argued that dialogue offered a route towards addressing national challenges without prolonged confrontation, while critics saw the partnership as evidence that opposition politics risked being absorbed into the very political establishment it was meant to hold accountable. The question is not simply whether Raila compromised, but whether the arrangement delivered enough to justify the political cost.
ODM’s struggle to define its future
That debate now confronts ODM as it tries to establish its direction without Raila’s authority. His ability to negotiate alliances and manage competing interests helped hold the party together. In his absence, disagreements over cooperation with Ruto have become harder to contain, exposing divisions over the party’s identity and its role in national politics.
Sifuna’s removal has brought those divisions into sharper focus. His opposition to closer ties with the president has raised questions about how ODM makes decisions, whose interests its leadership represents and whether the party can maintain its independence while working with a government it once opposed.
Catherine Omanyo, identified as ODM’s new secretary-general and a member of Parliament, argues that the party’s cooperation with Ruto should be judged by its commitments rather than by the symbolism of the alliance.
“ODM’s identity was never just a seat on one side of Parliament. It is democracy, devolution, social justice and the rights of ordinary Kenyans. Raila signed a 10-point agreement with President Ruto. That agreement, not personal loyalty, is the basis of our cooperation with the president,” Omanyo tells Al Jazeera.
Her argument places the emphasis on whether the agreement delivers meaningful results for Kenyans. But the existence of an agreement does not, by itself, establish that the partnership is advancing ODM’s stated principles. Its commitments, implementation and measurable outcomes must be examined alongside the party’s willingness to challenge the government when those commitments are not met.
For a movement whose identity was forged in opposition, the challenge is to demonstrate that cooperation does not come at the expense of accountability. If ODM cannot show tangible progress or explain when and how it will oppose the government, it risks deepening concerns among supporters who fear that the party is drifting away from its founding ideals.
The dispute also presents an opportunity for ODM to define what it stands for beyond its relationship with the president. A credible political movement needs more than a history of resistance or the legacy of a revered leader. It needs clear policies, accountable leadership and the willingness to defend its principles even when doing so carries a political cost.
A legacy still being tested
The stakes extend beyond ODM. Raila’s death has exposed the difficulty of separating a political movement’s principles from the authority of the leader who embodied them. But divisions within one party do not, on their own, establish that Kenya’s wider opposition has lost its ability to hold the government to account. That judgement depends on whether alternative political forces can organise, articulate credible policies and respond to citizens’ demands.
One year on, the question is not simply who can fill Raila’s shoes. No successor can reproduce his political journey or command precisely the same loyalties. The more consequential question is whether the movement he built can sustain its principles without relying on one man to define them.
For ODM, its relationship with Ruto will ultimately be judged not by the language of cooperation, but by what that cooperation delivers. If the party can demonstrate progress on its commitments while retaining the independence to challenge the government, it may defend its decision as a continuation of Raila’s pragmatic politics. If it cannot, the alliance will strengthen the argument that the opposition he helped build is losing its purpose.
The test of Raila’s legacy, therefore, lies not in how often his name is invoked, but in whether the political principles associated with him continue to shape decisions after his death.
“Cooperation that cannot speak up would betray Raila’s legacy. Cooperation that delivers for Kenyans honours it,” Omanyo says.

The head of the United Nations Interim Administration Mission in Kosovo (UNMIK) has warned the Security Council of "increased tensions in Kosovo and the region" over the past six months, whilst welcoming emerging signs that the country's institutional deadlock is easing.
Presenting the UN secretary-general's latest report in New York, Peter Due noted that despite peaceful, inclusive parliamentary elections on June 7—the third vote in 16 months—the period was marked by "political uncertainty and heightened rhetoric."
Due welcomed the election around midnight on 6 October of Justina Shiroka-Pula as President of Kosovo, making her the third woman to assume the role.
"Political disagreement is part of the fabric of democratic life, but prolonged institutional deadlock carries consequences. The formation of the institutions is therefore encouraging," Due said, observing that the prolonged political impasse "seems to have been broken."
Calls for accountability

He stressed that tangible progress requires genuine commitment from both parties in the European Union-facilitated dialogue.
"Our shared responsibility is to work for reconciliation and normalisation, so that all communities in Kosovo can participate fully and confidently in public life, with respect for the rule of law, human rights and Kosovo’s multiethnic character," Due added.
Addressing the Council, Kosovo Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca defended the country's record, stating that "Kosovo continues to remain one of the most stable democracies in southeastern Europe."
Konjufca rejected allegations within the report, criticising "the misuse of ethnic connotations and fabrications" and accusing critics of misrepresenting standard law-enforcement measures as ethnically motivated violations.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has repeatedly touched on the need for a "flexible" approach to energy and is believed to be in favor of more drilling where licenses already exist in the North Sea.

The controversial projects have faced years of debate, legal wrangling and public consultations. Licenses for the fields were granted by the Conservative government in 2022 and 2023, prompting legal challenges from environmentalists.
Last year, the Court of Session in Edinburgh, Scotland, ruled that Rosebank and Jackdaw had been unlawfully approved because the government had failed to take into account the climate impact of burning oil and gas extracted from the sites.
The Times reported in July that Burnham and Fahnbulleh were considering approving oil and gas production at the Jackdaw and Rosebank sites in an effort to help reduce energy costs ahead of winter.
Following reports over the summer that Burnham’s government could take a more pragmatic approach to domestic oil and gas production, US President Donald Trump praised the move in posts on Truth Social.
He said: "The People of Aberdeen, in Scotland, are dancing in the streets because the new Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, has stated that he will be opening up, all the way, the invaluable North Sea Oil!"
Meanwhile, climate group Fossil Free London will stage a demonstration at the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero on Wednesday, with participants dressed as giant receipts showing the predicted climate cost in human lives if the government approves the Jackdaw gas and Rosebank oil field projects.

Southeast Asian families tying house move to top schools spur privilege worries
In Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia, a family’s residential address is one of the factors determining admission into schools
4-MIN READ4-MIN
 Listen
Singapore’s recent parliamentary debate over primary school admissions has put a familiar parental strategy in the city state under the spotlight – parents moving house to improve their children’s chances of getting into popular schools.
Speaking with This Week in Asia, property agents say some families in Singapore have been approaching them with the intention of buying or renting particular residences at least two years before their children’s primary school admission.
Living close to a sought-after school does not guarantee entry, however, as a family might still face balloting for a particular school if it is oversubscribed.
The debate comes as Singapore prepares to widen admission to 12 schools in predominantly private-housing neighbourhoods, in a bid to encourage greater social mixing.

What is celebrated on October 21 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
02:58:52 EEST
08:58:52 KST

What is celebrated on October 21 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
October 21 marks Iodine Deficiency Prevention Day and Mass Media Day. Believers honor the Venerable Hilarions.
On October 21, the world observes World Iodine Deficiency Disorders Prevention Day and World Media Day under the auspices of international organizations. According to the new-style church calendar, Venerable Hilarion the Great and Venerable Hilarion, a schema-monk of the Kyiv Caves, are commemorated, while according to the old style, Venerable Pelagia and Venerable Thaisia are remembered, UNN writes.
World Iodine Deficiency Disorders Prevention Day (Global Iodine Deficiency Disorders Prevention Day)
A global awareness day established with the support of the WHO, UNICEF, and the International Council for the Control of Iodine Deficiency Disorders. The event aims to inform the public about the critical role of the micronutrient iodine in the normal functioning of the thyroid gland, children's intellectual development, and the prevention of endemic goiter. The day emphasizes the importance of consuming iodized salt and regularly monitoring iodine levels in the daily diet.
World Media Day (World Media Day)
A day that emphasizes the fundamental role of independent journalism and the media in building a democratic society. The event calls for the protection of freedom of speech, adherence to professional ethical standards, combating disinformation and fake news in the digital space, and ensuring the safety of journalists in areas of armed conflict.
International Nachos Day (International Nachos Day)
A popular unofficial culinary holiday established in honor of a popular Mexican snack made from tortilla chips and melted cheese. The dish's origins date back to October 21, 1943, when chef Ignacio "Nacho" Anaya in the city of Piedras Negras on the border with Texas improvised a dish for the wives of American officers by frying pieces of tortilla with cheddar cheese and jalapeño peppers.
According to the new calendar, Orthodox and Greek Catholic believers commemorate Venerable Hilarion the Great—one of the founders of Palestinian monasticism, who embraced Christianity in Alexandria, lived as an ascetic in the desert alongside Venerable Anthony the Great, and founded numerous monasteries in Palestine and Cyprus. On this day, they also remember Venerable Hilarion, a schema-monk of the Kyiv Caves—a monk of the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra who was a strict ascetic, man of prayer, and companion of Venerable Theodosius of the Caves.
According to the old calendar, believers commemorate Venerable Pelagia of Antioch—a former dancer and prostitute who, influenced by the preaching of Bishop Nonnus, sincerely repented, was baptized, and spent the rest of her life in strict fasting and prayer on the Mount of Olives in Jerusalem. Venerable Thaisia of Egypt is also remembered; after a sinful life, she turned to Christ with the assistance of Venerable Paphnutius the Great and lived as an ascetic in a desert monastery.

Jerusalem church leaders say lack of accountability fuels Israeli occupiers’ attacks in West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
23:55:18 UTC
08:55:18 KST

Tarek Chouiref
21 October 2026•Update: 21 October 2026
Jerusalem’s church leaders said Tuesday that impunity is emboldening Israeli occupiers to carry out attacks in the occupied West Bank, condemning a recent assault on Palestinian farmers and European diplomats.  
In a statement, the Patriarchs and Heads of Churches in Jerusalem denounced Saturday’s attack by masked Israeli occupiers on Palestinians harvesting olives in Taybeh, a predominantly Christian village northeast of Ramallah.
The assault also targeted foreign visitors, including European diplomats and officials who had come to show solidarity with Palestinian communities facing repeated attacks.
The church leaders stressed that the assault was not an isolated incident, warning of widespread violence against Palestinian villages in recent weeks, particularly during the olive harvest season.
They also condemned a recent religious ruling by Israeli Rabbi Dov Lior permitting Jews to take olives from Palestinian farmers, describing it as dangerous and unacceptable.
The leaders welcomed opposition to the ruling from other rabbis and Jewish voices.
Lior issued the ruling last week, claiming that taking Palestinian olives was permissible and even virtuous, according to Israel’s Channel 13.
“Unfortunately, the facts on the ground show that these attacks continue because of the impunity enjoyed by those who commit them,” the statement said.
They urged Israeli authorities to bring those responsible to justice and called on the international community to intensify efforts to protect Palestinians in Taybeh and across the occupied West Bank, as well as foreign visitors expressing solidarity with them.
The Palestinian Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission has documented more than 14,742 attacks by Israeli occupiers across the West Bank over the past three years.

Elon Musk ordered Starlink slowdown that blindsided Ukrainian military fighting Russia: Wall Street Journal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
23:53:03 UTC
08:53:03 KST

Darren Lyn
21 October 2026•Update: 21 October 2026
SpaceX founder Elon Musk ordered a slowdown of a military-grade version of Starlink used by Ukrainian forces, sparking panic in Kyiv and causing confusion within the Trump administration, according to a report Tuesday by The Wall Street Journal (WSJ).
US officials familiar with the situation told the WSJ that Musk capped the speeds of the Starlink satellite internet service used by Ukraine, rendering some of its military drones virtually useless.
Both Musk and President Donald Trump have voiced their anger at Ukraine for attacking Russian diesel refineries in recent weeks, which the president blames for high oil prices. The sources cited in the report said Musk and Trump discussed the Starlink decision both before and after the slowdown became public last week, but the president denied ordering the slowdown.
Musk posted on X hours after the slowdown became public that "any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," the acronym for president of the United States. But Trump told reporters Monday that he didn't know who was responsible for the Starlink slowdown, adding, "but I would like to find out."
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Tuesday that "we haven't pulled anything back," but "Starlink has the option to make decisions concerning its terms of service."
"We haven't made any directives or anything like that," Hegseth added.
After the Starlink slowdown was carried out, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that "Ukrainians could die if the unrestrictive service wasn't restored."
Some US officials told The Wall Street Journal that "Musk acted unilaterally and that Trump didn't specifically order any retribution against Ukraine." However, another person familiar with the situation told the WSJ that Musk "talked to multiple senior administration officials, including with Trump, before imposing the new speed cap," which Ukrainian officials said had allowed Russian missiles to evade their defenses.
The slowdown, which began on Oct. 14, followed several announcements and statements by the Trump administration that Ukrainian officials saw as hostile to Ukraine, including criticism of Zelensky from both Trump and Musk. That led Ukraine to immediately suspect that the order came either from the president or Musk, according to the report.

Netflix Q3 net profit rises nearly 44 pct
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
07:42:24 CST
08:42:24 KST

SAN FRANCISCO, Oct. 20 (Xinhua) -- U.S. streaming giant Netflix reported a nearly 44 percent year-on-year increase in third-quarter net profit on Tuesday, but lowered its full-year advertising revenue forecast amid slowing revenue growth.
According to the company's latest financial report, Netflix posted net income of 3.66 billion U.S. dollars for the quarter ended Sept. 30, up 44 percent from 2.55 billion dollars a year earlier.
Quarterly revenue increased 11.8 percent year on year to 12.87 billion dollars, compared with 11.51 billion dollars in the same period last year. The growth rate slowed from 13.4 percent in the second quarter.
Operating income rose 37 percent to 4.46 billion dollars, while the operating margin improved to 34.6 percent from 28.2 percent a year earlier.
Diluted earnings per share reached 87 cents, compared with 59 cents a year earlier, exceeding analysts' expectations of 82 cents per share, according to Reuters.
Netflix said its revenue growth was driven primarily by higher subscription revenue, reflecting increases in memberships and pricing, as well as growth in advertising revenue and favorable foreign exchange movements.
However, the company lowered its forecast for full-year 2026 advertising revenue to approximately 2.7 billion dollars from its previous projection of about 3 billion dollars, citing a slower-than-expected rollout of certain advertising product capabilities.
For the fourth quarter, Netflix projected revenue of 13.44 billion dollars and net income of 2.79 billion dollars, with diluted earnings per share expected to reach 67 cents, below analysts' expectations of 73 cents.
The company expects full-year 2026 revenue of approximately 51.1 billion dollars, up 13 percent year on year, with an operating margin of 31.5 percent. ■

Conservators breathe new life into ancient relics in China's Hubei
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
07:42:22 CST
08:42:22 KST

This photo taken on Oct. 19, 2026 shows a view of Han slips from Western Han Dynasty (202 BC-25 AD) after conservation treatment at the cultural relics protection center in Jingzhou, central China's Hubei Province.
Established in 2003, the cultural relics protection center in Jingzhou undertakes the conservation of about 80 percent of China's waterlogged bamboo and wooden slips. The center has developed comprehensive conservation techniques for such slips, covering sectors from archaeological excavation and laboratory conservation to display and storage.
To date, the center has provided technical support in cultural relic conservation to more than 130 cultural and museum institutions across the country, and has restored more than 10,000 lacquered wooden artifacts, over 180,000 bamboo and wooden slips, and more than 1,100 textile artifacts. (Xinhua/Xiao Yijiu)

A British ship that sank more than 160 years ago has been found in the Gulf of Finland
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
02:37:09 EEST
08:37:09 KST

A British ship that sank more than 160 years ago has been found in the Gulf of Finland
Kyiv • UNN
Wreckage of the British sailing ship Bedford, which sank in 1865, has been found near Inkoo. All 19 crew members were rescued at the time.
Near the coast of the Finnish town of Inkoo, marine archaeologists identified the wreckage of the British sailing ship Bedford, which sank in 1865. The vessel lay on the seabed for more than 160 years, and archival documents and underwater research helped establish its name. The Finnish broadcaster Yle reports this, writes UNN.
Details
The ship was built in January 1864 in Sunderland, England. It was approximately 45 meters long, and its maiden voyage took it to Hong Kong.
However, Bedford’s maritime history proved to be short. In October 1865, the sailing ship, under the command of Captain M. B. Nattrass, set out from St. Petersburg for the Amur River, carrying 6,000 sacks of rye flour.
How the British sailing ship sank
During the voyage, strong winds caused the vessel to run aground in shallow waters near Rönnshär. Finnish pilots came to the crew’s aid and rescued all 19 sailors.
Part of the cargo was also salvaged. After the accident, the damaged vessel drifted toward Inkoo, where it collided with an island and finally sank.
Experts from the Finnish Heritage Agency examined the wreckage during underwater dives. Comparing the ship’s structural features with registration records and historical documents made it possible to establish its origins.
Archaeologists call the find exceptional. The preserved remains of Bedford and a 3D model created on their basis will help researchers study in greater detail the construction of British merchant sailing ships of the 19th century.

Witkoff could meet with Putin soon – Kremlin
Moscow expects US President Donald Trump’s special envoy, Steve Witkoff, to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin in the near future, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said. US mediators held talks with Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky in the Norwegian capital, Oslo on Tuesday.
Russia highly appreciates US mediation efforts, Peskov said at a news briefing on Tuesday, adding that Moscow sees every meeting between Putin and Trump’s envoys as “very important and well-timed.” He did not provide any details about the date or place of a potential meeting, but said the Kremlin expects Witkoff to inform Moscow about the results of Tuesday’s talks with Zelensky and his European backers.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said on Tuesday that Russia is willing to discuss any economic and financial initiatives Washington puts forward, provided they are “advantageous to us.”
He stressed that Russia will not make one-sided political concessions, warning that any deals with the US might not last beyond Trump’s term in office.
“The history of the American presidency is notable for a well-established political tradition… whereby a new president is not bound by any decisions made by their predecessor,” Lavrov said, adding that this gives the US leverage in talks and that Moscow is well aware that Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, could try to “arrange something” with this in mind.
Russia should not expect “some political favor to carry us through all global affairs,” Lavrov said. “We must rely solely on ourselves.”
Earlier on Tuesday, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, who hosted the meeting between Zelensky and the US negotiators, said Witkoff will travel to St. Petersburg on Wednesday for a meeting with the Russian leadership.
According to Store, the list of proposals Trump’s special envoy could put forward might include a three-way summit between Trump, Putin, and Zelensky. Ukrainian media also reported that other potential proposals included an energy ceasefire.
Last week, the Financial Times reported that Washington proposed unfreezing billions of euros in Russian assets held in the EU to give impetus to Ukraine peace talks during negotiations in Miami with officials from Ukraine, France, Germany, Britain, the EU, and NATO. The idea was vehemently opposed by Kiev’s European backers, including German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Russia has said the stance of Kiev’s European backers is one of the main obstacles to settling the conflict. The EU is still clinging to the idea of “strategically defeating Russia,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov reiterated last month.
Moscow has also rejected the idea of a temporary truce, insisting on a long-term peace deal that addresses the root causes of the conflict. With negotiations stalling and no breakthrough in sight, Ukraine has maintained its megaphone diplomacy, publicly calling for new negotiations and demanding an unconditional ceasefire.
The renewed diplomatic push follows a spat between Trump and Zelensky over Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil facilities. The US president has demanded that Kiev stop the attacks, blaming them for surging fuel prices globally and in the US. The dispute has since widened, with Zelensky accusing Washington of withholding intelligence on Russian missile attacks and restricting Ukraine’s access to the Starlink satellite network.

NATO to send additional patrol planes to Black Sea after drone attacks
The alliance announces after a chain of deadly drone attacks have struck the region.
NATO is deploying additional patrol aircraft and intelligence personnel to the Black Sea, a spokesman for the alliance said, after a series of deadly drone attacks in the region widely blamed on Russia but denied by the Kremlin.
“Allies have or will send additional maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems, explosive exploitation teams, intelligence personnel, drones and more to the Black Sea,” said Colonel Martin O’Donnell on Tuesday.
“The most important thing we can do, however, is to increase our situational awareness in the region through increased sensors and data sharing,” he added.
NATO, along with Bulgaria and Romania, has not directly attributed the recent spate of attacks to any country. Military analysts have said Russia almost certainly carried out the attacks but Moscow has not acknowledged any responsibility.
In an attack on October 5, Romania reported two people dead after their ship caught fire and sank in Black Sea waters. Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Moscow of being responsible.
The announcement came after NATO’s main decision-making body, the North Atlantic Council, discussed security in the Black Sea at the alliance’s Brussels headquarters.
“NATO has already strengthened our posture along the eastern flank, including with counter-drone capabilities,” spokeswoman Allison Hart said earlier in a post on X.
‘Dangerous and unacceptable’ escalation
The European Union’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas on Tuesday said that “six attacks in 10 days by suspected Russian drones marks a dangerous and unacceptable escalation”, adding that the Kremlin likely sought to choke off revenue to Kyiv from grain exports.
Kallas warned that the latest strikes were adding to a “perfect storm” facing global food supplies already being battered by droughts in multiple regions and the war in the Middle East.
Last week, seven sailors were reported missing after drones struck two chemical tankers near Romania’s Black Sea coast, setting them ablaze and raising fresh security concerns along a vital shipping route used by Ukraine.
At least five other cargo vessels were hit near the coasts of Romania and neighbouring NATO member Bulgaria over the previous 10 days, with at least 23 sailors reported missing or dead.

US President Donald Trump's administration has revoked over 300,000 visas during his second term, the State Department said as the federal government continues its immigration clampdown.
The number showed an acceleration in the pace of visa revocations in recent weeks.
In an update issued on August 10, the State Department had put the number of visa revocations since Trump's current term began in January 2025 at over 175,000.

While Trump campaigned in 2024 on stopping illegal immigration, his administration has also made legal immigration more difficult — for example, by imposing expensive fees for certain work visas.
The State Department is also expected to revoke the so-called B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026 to holders who have sought asylum or are now seeking it, according to State Department documents obtained by The Associated Press.
The Department will take this action in coordination with the Department of Homeland Security.

Nigeria records first Ebola case as outbreak spreads across Africa
Nigeria has confirmed its first Ebola case in Africa's latest outbreak, while Kenya reported its ninth infection, raising fears of further spread across the continent. Africa CDC chief Jean Kaseya warned of an “extremely serious threat” and urged the international community to send funding, medical supplies and health workers.
Nigeria said Tuesday it had recorded its first Ebola case of Africa's latest outbreak, as Kenya declared its ninth case, prompting a regional health official to warn of "an extremely serious threat".
The case in Nigeria, Africa's most populous country, was detected in a woman who had travelled from Uganda to the capital Abuja, the government confirmed.
Since a major Ebola outbreak was declared in the Democratic Republic of Congo in May, the deadly viral haemorrhagic fever has spread to several countries across the continent, including neighbouring Uganda.
Kenya's health ministry meanwhile reported its ninth Ebola case of the outbreak on Tuesday.
"This Ebola Bundibugyo outbreak has already become the most geographically widespread Ebola outbreak in history, affecting multiple countries across three regions of Africa," said the director general of Africa CDC, Jean Kaseya.
In several months, the DRC's Ebola epidemic has become the deadliest in the country's history, killing 4,381 people out of more than 9,000 confirmed cases, according to the health authorities.

'Act now'
Kaseya, who heads the African Union health agency, urged the international community to send money, medical supplies and health workers to help.
"With mortality approaching 50% in DRC, we face an extremely serious threat," he posted on X.
"My appeal to the international community is urgent: ACT NOW."
The outbreak has now spread from central Africa to the continent's east and west.
Kenya reported its first Ebola case on October 6 – a businessman in his forties who had lived in the DRC.
Most of the eight cases reported since in the east African country have been among people with a close connection to the first victim, who died in the capital Nairobi on October 5.
The ninth case is a 24-year-old man, described as "a close family member of the first case", and confirmed positive on Monday, the health ministry said.
"He was isolated at the first sign of illness, tested and started on treatment immediately upon confirmation of his positive test result," it said, adding he "was already in quarantine when he fell ill".
The United States on Tuesday warned its citizens against travel to Kenya due to "health risks".

Contact tracing
In Nigeria, the patient arrived on an international flight from Uganda and was admitted to a private hospital, "where she received care for several days before the diagnosis was confirmed", Nigerian Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate said in a statement.
"She is currently in isolation and receiving medical care," he said.
"Contact tracing has commenced with 44 close contacts identified presently," the statement added, "with public health teams identifying and monitoring people who may have been exposed, including healthcare workers, patients, caregivers and travel contacts".
Late Tuesday, the Ugandan Health Ministry said there were "no confirmed active Ebola cases" in the country, and that "travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here".
It is the west African country's first registered Ebola case since 2014.

France formally repeals slavery-era 'Code Noir'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
23:16:20 UTC
08:16:20 KST

Melike Pala
21 October 2026•Update: 21 October 2026
France's Senate unanimously voted Tuesday to formally abolish the Code Noir, a set of royal decrees passed by King Louis XIV in 1685 that legally regulated slavery and defined the rights, duties and restrictions of enslaved people and their owners in the French colonial empire.
The vote confirmed a decision previously adopted unanimously by the National Assembly in May, completing the legislative process to repeal the slavery-era legislation, according to the news portal France Info.
The Code Noir classified enslaved people as movable property, allowing them to be bought and sold.
The legislation also prescribed harsh punishments for enslaved people who attempted to escape, including mutilation, branding and the death penalty.
Although slavery was abolished in France's colonies in 1848, the royal decrees and related provisions were never formally removed from French legislation, despite having become legally obsolete.
The legislation also requires the government to submit a report examining the legacy of colonial-era laws, their lasting effects, particularly in relation to racism, and the teaching of slavery in French schools.
However, the bill does not address demands for reparations for slavery, an issue that continues to be raised in several French overseas territories.

hedley studios shrinks the porsche 550 spyder into a handcrafted electric two-seater
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

hedley studios shrinks the porsche 550 spyder into a handcrafted electric two-seater
limited to 250 examples, the miniature racer revives a 1950s motorsport icon with vintage curves and a 50 mph top speed.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
porsche 550 spyder at 80 percent of its original size
There’s a tiny silver Porsche parked among a sunlit meadow in the English countryside. With its rounded rear fenders and tiny windshield, it’s quite similar to the 550 Spyder that Porsche raced in the 1950s. The proportions are familiar, but something is slightly off. This is the Porsche 550 J, a miniature, fully electric version of the historic race car, recreated by British manufacturer Hedley Studios at roughly 80 percent of its original size.
Developed in collaboration with Porsche to celebrate 75 years of the company’s motorsport history, the 550 J is an officially licensed, handcrafted vehicle limited to 250 examples. The ‘J’ stands for ‘Junior,’ although the little roadster is large enough to accommodate two people. Measuring just 2.9 meters (9.5 feet) in length and 1.2 meters (3.9 feet) wide, it retains the low profile and flowing aluminum-like contours of its predecessor.
a miniature tribute to porsche’s first purpose-built racing car
The original Porsche 550 Spyder holds a special place in the company’s history. Developed specifically for motorsport, the lightweight, mid-engined racer made its name competing against considerably more powerful cars. At the grueling 1954 Carrera Panamericana in Mexico, Porsche drivers Hans Herrmann and Jaroslav Juhan finished third and fourth overall after five days of racing. The two Spyders also won their class, which helped to establish the ‘Carrera’ name that Porsche continues to use today.
For the miniature recreation, the team at Hedley Studios was granted access to Porsche’s corporate archives, allowing the team to study the historic vehicle and reproduce its distinctive form. The round headlights and sculpted wheel arches are immediately recognizable, while the rear bodywork retains the original’s characteristic twin ventilation grilles. Inside, a cream-colored steering wheel sits ahead of a compact dashboard with circular gauges. The open cockpit is wonderfully spare, with just enough contemporary technology to accommodate the electric drivetrain.
an electric drivetrain modernizes the vintage roadster
Beneath its 1950s-inspired bodywork, the Porsche 550 J is powered by a 48-volt electric system, producing approximately 8 kW, or 11 horsepower, in its standard configuration. An optional RS Package doubles that output to 16 kW, or around 21 horsepower. The little racer can reach a top speed of approximately 80 km/h (50 mph), a surprisingly brisk pace for something with such compact proportions. The 550 J is intended as a collector’s vehicle, with public-road driving off limits.
Each example is built by hand at Hedley Studios in Bicester, England, with a selection of finishes drawing from Porsche’s racing history. Alongside the classic silver bodywork, customers can choose bright heritage-inspired colors and racing liveries, including the vivid blue example pictured with white competition numbers. A bespoke program offers further customization.
With just 250 units planned, the 550 J miniaturizes one of Porsche’s most iconic racing silhouettes, while retaining enough power to be driven and enjoyed.

No jeopardy but loads of fun - Champions League sets new goals record
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
00:03:11 BST
08:03:11 KST

No jeopardy but loads of fun - is new Champions League format a success?
- Published
More teams, more games - and more goals.
Since the current Champions League format was introduced at the start of the 2024-25 season, Europe's elite club competition has delivered all of the above and more.
Especially the goals part.
Already trending upwards over the past two campaigns, there has been a genuine goals boom in this year's competition.
The 187 goals scored so far have come at an average of 4.16 per game - the highest in Champions League history.
Meanwhile, the average goals scored per game in the Premier League is 2.9, 3.03 in La Liga and 3.69 in the Bundesliga.
There have also been no goalless draws yet in the Champions League.
"Look how many goals have been scored, it's phenomenal," ex-Manchester United and England winger Ashley Young said on BBC Radio 5 Live. "The attackers are being clinical."
Former Liverpool defender Stephen Warnock described the volume of goals as "incredible" - so how unusual is it?
What the stats say
Ready for lots of numbers?
Not only is the current goals-per-game percentage the highest ever in the Champions League, it is the third highest in European Cup history - behind only 1959-60 (4.19) and 1955-56 (4.38).
While 40 goals were scored across nine games on Tuesday, last week was even more spectacular.
Last Wednesday saw the third highest-scoring day in Champions League history (46 goals), bettered only by the final league-phase matchdays of 2024-25 and 2025-26, when 18 matches took place.
The 78 goals scored across Tuesday and Wednesday last week made matchday two the highest scoring in history.
That was nine more than the total scored on matchday one this season (69) - which, at the time, was the second highest-scoring matchday since the new league phase was introduced in 2024-25.
Will we see the record fall again this week? It's already halfway there.
More entertainment = more quality?
Ever since Uefa announced its plans to alter the format of the Champions League in 2021, the impact on matches has been a hot topic. Scrutiny has only increased since the changes were implemented in time for the 2024-25 season.
After beginning life as a six-team invitational tournament in 1955-56 before growing to a 32-team knockout tournament in 1967, the Champions League as we know it began in 1992.
A group stage was added, with the last 16 entering a knockout phase. There was a brief spell with two group stages, but this was reverted back to the single group-stage format for the 2003-04 tournament.
The group stage previously featured 32 teams in eight groups of four, with the top two sides from each of those groups qualifying for the last 16.
For the start of the 2024-25 season, the group stage was replaced with a 36-team league phase, with each side playing eight one-off fixtures instead of six games against three teams.
The top eight finishers qualify directly for the knockout stages, with those placed ninth to 24th entering a two-legged play-off stage.
The bottom 12 are eliminated, meaning that after eight matches, 24 sides are still in the competition. Some argue that that creates a lack of jeopardy, which encourages teams to play more expansively.
But do more goals equal better quality?
"I think the entertainment has gone up, although I'm not sure the quality has gone up," The Times football writer Tom Allnutt told BBC Radio 5 Live.
"If I'm looking at the games it's brilliant to watch and thrilling because the football itself is fantastic - but what do they mean?
"The lack of jeopardy, why would PSG and Barcelona play for a draw, why not go for it? If you need five wins from the eight games you know you've got some margin there. If you lose it's OK. I think the format allows all the teams to loosen up.
"The entertainment value is there but I think you come away from these matches sometimes and still think 'what does it all mean?'. The lack of jeopardy early on does deliver entertainment."

As has Governor-General Sam Mostyn.

Opposition spokesperson for women Melissa McIntosh said the incident has been hard to comprehend and digest.
"On one hand you feel like crawling up in a ball and on the other you feel really activated to make change, because as we know there's been warnings for some time," she told News 24.

Earlier this year, a survey of Australian women either elected or running for office found nearly 90 per cent had experienced online abuse or intimidation linked to their participation in politics.
The majority (82 per cent) of women reported changing their behaviour because of the abuse they received.
The research by Women for Election, an advisory group working to empower more women to run for all levels of government, included 51 current elected representatives and 53 candidates or aspiring candidates across local, state, territory and federal government.
Half of respondents questioned whether they would run again — or if they should have done so in the first place given what they know now.
For Tracee Hutchison, the hostility was enough to convince her not to run again after contesting the Victorian seat of Nepean as an independent in a by-election earlier this year.
"The verbal harassment I experienced, and that the women my team did, was unlike anything I had anticipated," she said.

"Something has gone horribly wrong in this country," she said.
"Violent attacks on public figures representing their electorates and violence against women are linked."
Victorian MP Georgie Purcell says she's been the target of online abuse tens of thousands of times in six months, even as recently as this week.
"One comment on my post about Helen said they wished it had happened to me," she said.
She said the attack has left her feeling "pretty rattled".
"It does change the way you move about the world. I consider my movements everywhere I go for my physical safety and I can't do a lot of things other politicians, particularly men, can do,'' she told the ABC.
"It is an act of male violence that has happened against a female politician. We're thinking, 'could this happen to us?'
"For me personally, I feel frustrated because we have been begging for action before something actually happened and now it has."
Heading into a Victorian state election, Purcell said state MPs need the same security arrangements as federal members.

Proposed depression subtype involves waking up tired or being a night owl
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
23:01:00 UTC
08:01:00 KST

One in four people with severe depression have dysregulated body clock, study suggests
In short:
A new Australian study suggests about one in four people with severe depression have a proposed subset called "circadian depression".
Symptoms include waking up very tired, sleeping more when depressed and being a night owl.
What's next?
Researchers believe more targeted treatments will improve outcomes for people with circadian depression.
Sam Hockey's mental health journey stretches across more than two decades.
A diagnosis of post-traumatic stress disorder and insomnia at age eight, after being trapped in a house fire,and then being "horribly bullied" in high school had a significant impact on his mental health.
"I overslept as a way of escapism but then I would also not wake up rested," he said.
"I had intense low energy, and when it came to school, my cognitive function wasn't great, then didn't have the mental or emotional capacity to really combat the bullying."
In hindsight, Mr Hockey said these sleep symptoms were the first signs he had circadian depression, a proposed new subtype of the mood disorder from experts at the University of Sydney's Brain and Mind Centre.
A new Australian study, published today in The British Journal of Psychiatry, suggests about one in four people with severe, recurrent or persistent depression, like Mr Hockey, have this subtype.
Researchers say the subtype is linked to the body's internal clock and people with it often report being a "night owl" or waking up feeling very tired.
Lead researcher Emiliana Tonini from the Brain and Mind Centre said the findings had implications for early intervention and treatment.
"Depression is not a uniform illness and understanding the characteristics of different subtypes means that we can give people earlier access to treatments that will be most effective for them," she said.
What is circadian depression?
According to the World Health Organization, about 322 million people globally have depression, a mood disorder which causes persistent sadness, emptiness or loss of interest in previously enjoyable activities.
In this new study, Dr Tonini and her team looked at clinical and genetic data from 11,380 Australians with severe, recurrent or persistent depression who took part in a long-running national depression study.
They found 2,604 people in this group met the criteria for circadian depression as they self-reported three or more of the following:
- Waking up very tired
- Being a "night owl"
- Experiencing a seasonal pattern of illness
- Sleeping later
- Sleeping more when depressed
- Experiencing "social jet lag" where sleep timings vary greatly between work days and free days
Patients with circadian depression also reported "more severe mental health symptoms" than those with non-circadian depression, Dr Tonini said.
This included an earlier age of onset, more severe symptoms like mania, suicidality, weight gain during mental health episodes and more complex mental health trajectories.
The research also suggests people with circadian depression may have a different genetic profile to those with non-circadian depression, including a higher genetic risk for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).
Philip Mitchell, scientia professor of psychiatry at the University of New South Wales who did not contribute to the research, said more research was needed before circadian depression could be classified as its own subtype.
"At the moment it's not reaching the bar where this could enter clinical practice, but I think this is very thought-provoking for the field," he said.
Professor Mitchell said there was overlap between the features of circadian depression and a recognised subtype called atypical depression, which indicated the need for a clearer distinction between the two.
And he added that more international research was needed to support the Australian findings.
How is sleep and depression connected?
The study suggests circadian depression is linked to the body's 24-hour internal clock which regulates the sleep-wake cycle.
Brain and Mind Centre co-director and clinical psychiatrist Ian Hickie said this internal clock underpinned "your mood, your metabolism, your concentration, your sleep-wake cycle and many other key factors as well".
Professor Hickie said light exposure, movement and eating patterns were important to help regulate the body's 24-hour internal clock, or circadian rhythm.
"It isn't just sleep, it's not just about sleeping better," he said.
Shanthakumar Wilson Rajaratnam, professor of sleep and circadian medicine at Monash University who did not contribute to the study, said a dysregulated circadian system could impact a range of different body systems, including cardiovascular function.
Criteria used to define circadian depression, such as being a "night owl" or waking up very tired, might not solely be driven by circadian dysfunction, he said.
Professor Rajaratnam said symptoms that might explain circadian dysfunction could also be explained by disturbed sleep.
"Symptoms and sleep complaints have a high degree of comorbidity and overlap with depression and mood disturbances," he said.
What does this mean for treatment?
According to this study, patients with circadian depression may be less responsive to traditional antidepressants.
However, Dr Tonini said this finding came from self-reported data, which meant more research was needed to test the efficacy of traditional antidepressants in this proposed subgroup.
She said targeted treatments —such as melatonin, melatonin-targeted antidepressants, light therapy and behavioural changes —may improve outcomes for patients with circadian depression.
More than two decades after his first mental health diagnosis, things have greatly improved for Mr Hockey.
As a youth lived-experience researcher with the Brain and Mind Centre, he was one of the co-authors on the new study.
He said that understanding more about his 24-hour internal clock earlier in life would have saved "a lot of grief, a lot of trouble, a lot of money, and hardship".
But learning about circadian patterns and making behavioural changes, such as putting his bedside light on a timer, had helped him regulate his body clock.
Professor Mitchell and Professor Rajaratnam agreed that there was enough evidence in this study to warrant asking patients with depression about their circadian patterns.
But this was in addition to, not instead of, traditional treatment options.
"It's important to address the sleep and circadian complaints in patients that are presenting with psychiatric disorders, including depression, as well as treating the depression symptoms," Professor Rajaratnam said.
