Bavuma's batting masterclass takes control away from Australia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
20:03:42 UTC
05:03:42 KST

A few days before this Test series began, a digitally manipulated image was doing the rounds on social media.
Modelling South Africa's new Test playing kit, a pensive expression on his face, Proteas skipper Temba Bavuma was flanked by teammates Ryan Rickelton and Marco Jansen.
The visual punchline, in this case, was that Bavuma had been shrunk even smaller than his already-diminutive self, dwarfed by his teammates, even though he was standing on a superimposed shoe-shine box. My sides!
Never mind that 5'4" Bavuma's batting inspiration, Sachin Tendulkar, stands only an inch taller, nor that the previous owner of India's "Little Master" moniker, Sunil Gavaskar, is the same height as Bavuma. Nor, indeed, that a certain lad from Bowral who did kind of OK in the 1930s and 40s was only 5'7". None faced quite the same level of condescension or fixation on their physical stature as Bavuma.
In reality, Bavuma is, by a few key measures, as big as anyone in the story of South African cricket in the post-apartheid decades. On the world stage he captained his country to victory in the 2025 World Test Championship decider, banishing years of big-tournament heartbreak.
Australians, apt to wipe such unexpected defeats in crunch games from the collective memory, are thus obliged to bracket Bavuma with a select group of figurehead skippers of recent decades — Clive Lloyd, Sourav Ganguly, Michael Vaughan, Virat Kohli — who've engineered famous and important victories against great Australian Test sides in their pomp.
Now Australia reckons with his batting. On day three of the second Test at Gqeberha, Bavuma played an innings that, for context and quality, ranks among the highest calibre; a towering and important century that any of the all-timers above would envy.
Beginning the day on 41, with his side wobbling away at 5-97, Bavuma finished it with a stunning set of numbers next to his name: 179 runs from 334 deliveries in a total of 9-425 declared.
Due to the rain and delays of the opening stages of this game, Bavuma's epic stretched across three days, clocked in at a shade under 10 hours and required nothing less than the total psychological and physical mastery of the most complete pace attack in world cricket. Australians scoff at the mere concept of moral victories, but here Bavuma and South Africa claimed a resounding one.
It was the highest score of Bavuma's career, his fourth century (out of five all up) since becoming captain and moving up the order, and it means that a game in which Australia fancied skittling the Proteas on a green pitch is very unlikely to be won by the tourists — and possibly worse.
The "possibly worse" part got its preview sequence in the final moments of the day, when South Africa's returning paceman Kagiso Rabada marauded his way through Nic Maddinson to leave Australia one wicket down at stumps. Had bad light not limited Bavuma to the use of spinners in the final three overs of the day, the carnage could have been worse.
It has been said that the Australians respect but don't particularly warm to Bavuma. By this theory, he is aloof, undemonstrative and unlikely to engage in banter, verbal sparring or fun. In that way, he is more like a bowler who always had Australia's measure, Curtly Ambrose. "Curtly talks to no-one," Ambrose once said. It worked out just fine for him, too.
Bavuma's knock was a masterpiece of the kind of tempo batting that makes Test cricket tragics swoon. His watchful first 50, comprised almost entirely of judicious nudges, nurdles and leaves, took 140 deliveries.
His second, which grew to encompass sumptuous on drives, square drives and a cracking pull shot off Pat Cummins to reach his century, took only 86 balls. His third, a by-product of an acceleration phase when he and Simon Harmer removed any thoughts of an Australian victory, came from just 73 balls.
It was hard to believe this was the same player who'd scratched around for a combined total of four runs in 45 tortured deliveries last week in Durban. But like Matt Renshaw in that game, it was not just Bavuma's own runs that turned this contest on its head but the partnerships he forged with his side's highly capable tailenders.
Loading Instagram content
There was a thrilling stand of 132 from 186 with Marco Jansen, whose 85 came at almost a run a ball and, to be fair, presented a truly arresting example of cricket's capacity to attract all shapes and sizes. Paired with the 6'8" beanpole, Bavuma brought to mind the famous photo of NBA basketballers Muggsy Bogues and Manute Bol.
Even more profitable — game-defining, most likely — was Bavuma's union with Harmer, the spinner whose surprising selection reprieve suddenly seemed completely sensible as he hammered his way through a sparkling knock of 82 from 157 deliveries. Their partnership of 183 traversed 46 overs and was South Africa's highest eighth-wicket stand ever — not the sort of record with which this Australian squad likes to be associated.
In the final analysis, 315 runs came after the fall of South Africa's sixth wicket. It was a total wipe-out for the Aussies.
What did Cummins get wrong? There were some indefensibly defensive field placements, in truth, especially in the crucial phase when Jansen went berserk and Bavuma fed him the strike with easy singles to men stationed in the deep.
But as Richie Benaud once said, the best attribute a captain can have is luck, and there wasn't much on offer here for Cummins. Josh Hazlewood, missing with illness on day two, was thus obliged not to bowl for the first two hours of the day. The green pitch, which had promised carnage early in the game, turned docile and offered minimal lateral movement even for Scott Boland. And after the second new ball brought the wicket of Jansen — Boland's fifth — very little else transpired, so the field spread again.
Of the Australian bowlers, Boland was clearly the pick with 5-81 from 29 overs, and the overall picture of gloom rather rubbished the claim that his otherworldly Test statistics could be attributed to being slotted into an attack that was always firing from the other end (and anyway, by that logic, Andy Bichel, as the last backup quick to receive acclaim like that heaped on Boland, would have easily maintained a bowling average far lower than 32).
In the Boland years, as in the Bichel ones, sometimes even great sides have to admit it has not been their day. That was Australia today; at the mercy of the biggest small man in cricket, who doesn't have to open his mouth to say something profound.

Zelensky hails resumption of US advance warning of strikes on Ukraine
OSLO – Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky hailed on Oct 20 the resumption of US intelligence sharing on looming Russian strikes, but insisted Kyiv must be included in any future talks on its fate after meetings with US envoys.
“We are thankful that intelligence works... I’m speaking about early warning, what is very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic is coming,” Zelensky told reporters in Oslo.
After meetings with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner – US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, who took part remotely – Zelensky said it was “important that we keep the conversation going... and work together on the decisions needed to end this war”.
Flanked by Norway’s Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store and Finnish President Alexander Stubb, the Ukrainian president insisted that “Ukraine wants peace more than anyone”.
Trump, meanwhile, said in Washington he wanted Zelensky to “make a deal” with Russia.
Relations between Kyiv and Washington have soured since Trump partially lifted sanctions to strike a diesel-supply deal with Russia’s Vladimir Putin and slammed Zelensky as a warmonger for Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries.
Zelensky has accused the United States of deliberately withholding vital intelligence and delaying military aid, saying on Oct 19 that Ukraine received no early warning of powerful Russian missile strikes that targeted energy facilities in the capital region.
US-led diplomatic efforts to end Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War II have stalled in recent months, as Washington has shifted focus towards the war with Iran.
‘Needed to protect lives’
Ukraine has also reported a reduction in speeds on Starshield, the US military satellite system which it uses for battlefield communications and strikes on Russian-occupied territory.
Trump has denied ordering a reduction in speeds on the US government-owned and -controlled Starshield network after Elon Musk, whose company SpaceX developed it, said the order could only have come from the White House.
Ahead of the Oslo meeting, Zelensky said he held “substantive” and “constructive” talks with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Oct 20, in which he insisted that the Starshield system “needs to be restored” and that ballistic missile interceptors “are needed to protect lives”.
Speaking to reporters in Oslo, he said on Starshield, “we decided that maybe in 48 hours we will have again a connection”.
Zelensky told US senators on Oct 19 that “the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles” already paid for by European countries, and that the shipment was waiting for US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth’s signature.
He said several European countries were ready to transfer Patriot interceptor missiles from their own stockpiles but were still awaiting US approval.
The United States has denied making any changes to intelligence sharing with Ukraine.
Strained relations
The US leader has accused his counterpart of not trying to resolve the conflict with Russia.
Trump said he was ready to meet Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in China in November to discuss denuclearisation, adding that talks could also cover the Ukraine war – fuelling fears in Kyiv that it was being sidelined.
Zelensky insisted on Oct 20 that Kyiv needed to be represented at any meeting regarding Ukraine’s future.
“I don’t know what the trilateral meeting will be about between America and China, and Russia, it’s up to them. But of course, if the are issues about Ukraine, our future, it can be acceptable only when we are at the table of negotiations. It’s absolutely clear,” he said.
Zelensky stressed the need to find a solution quickly.
“Of course we are not losing this war,” he said when asked, “but we are losing people... and time”.
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said Witkoff was headed on to Russia.
“Steve Witkoff will fly tomorrow to St Peterburg, where he will be meeting with Russian leadership and exchange ideas from this meeting and the proposals that have been worked on by European and American colleagues, and possibly pave the way for a meeting at leaders’ level,” he said.
“We hope that it will be possible to arrange a meeting in the very near future, allowing the American negotiators... Mr Witkoff, to brief President Putin on their contacts with both the Ukrainians and the Europeans,” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Oct 20. AFP

Trump and Zelensky appear at loggerheads despite new optimism
- Published
The hug that Trump envoy Steve Witkoff offered Volodymyr Zelensky before talks in Oslo is unlikely to have dispelled the Ukrainian leader's misgivings about the current direction of US policy towards his war-ravaged country.
Zelensky posted a video of the moment on social media, with the message "Ukraine is working for peace. I thank our partners for their support!"
But given everything that's happened this month, does the Ukrainian leader still regard Donald Trump as a partner?
The two men have never been close – that much is obvious – but have they now fallen out once and for all?
Both in rhetoric and actions, the past 10 days have seen evidence of a rupture as deep as any in their fractious relationship.
Just listen to the way they talk about each other.
"Zelensky's not a good guy for us to deal with," Trump told Newsmax last week.
The verbal assault has continued this week.
"Zelensky doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump told a reporter on Monday when asked what he thought of the Ukrainian leader's suggestion that striking a diesel deal with Russia put the US on the wrong side of history.
Such personal attacks are typical of Trump's sledgehammer approach to diplomacy. It's hard to know when to take them seriously.
In June, he lashed out at Israel's prime minister, saying Benjamin Netanyahu "has no f**king judgement". Four months later, he endorsed Netanyahu enthusiastically, calling him a "great warrior prime minister".
"Trump can always do another U-turn," says Ian Bond of the Centre for European Reform. "But this does look bad."
For his part Zelensky has generally been circumspect in how he describes his unreliable but vital American counterpart.
But this month his frustration has been clear. Addressing a US congressional delegation, he spoke of "decisions on the American side that are hard to explain between friends" and voiced the fear that "some political decision has been made to slow down support for us."
Answering Trump's charge that he represented the principal obstacle to a negotiated settlement, Zelensky sounded more exasperated than ever.
"We have welcomed literally EVERY attempt by our partners to end this war with dignity," he wrote on Telegram on Monday.
But rhetoric aside, how bad is the relationship?
In some ways, we've been here before.
After their notorious televised bust up in the Oval Office in February 2025, at which Trump accused Zelensky of "gambling with World War III", the US suspended military assistance and restricted intelligence sharing.
The crisis only lasted a week. And when the Trump administration decided, later that year, that it no longer wanted to finance direct military assistance to Ukraine, a mechanism was put in place for European countries to pay for American equipment instead.
One exception, in the wake of this year's US war with Iran, has been badly needed US-made Patriot air defence missiles.
Amid a global shortage, the supply to Ukraine has slowed to a trickle, making it harder than ever for Kyiv to shoot down Russian ballistic missiles.
The Washington Post, quoting an unnamed Ukrainian official, said "only a couple" of Patriot interceptors remained in Ukraine's stockpile, and that the Trump administration had slowed down the process by which US allies seek approval to transfer their stocks.
Similar concerns have been voiced in the past, but the latest reports – not confirmed by US officials – come against an increasingly difficult backdrop for Kyiv.
Earlier this month, as Ukrainian negotiators arrived in Miami for talks with Trump's all-purpose envoys Witkoff and Jared Kushner, they were blindsided by the news that the president had just struck a deal with Vladimir Putin to open US markets to Russian diesel.
Experts questioned whether it would do much to drive down US petrol prices, ahead of congressional mid-term elections (the apparent motive), but as a signal of US displeasure over Ukraine's campaign of long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries and Washington's willingness to do deals with the Kremlin, it represented a stinging rebuke to Kyiv.
Last Friday, Trump went further, waiving wide-ranging sanctions on Russia just two days before they were due to take effect.
Trump said the sanctions contained in the Graham Act (named after the former South Carolina senator Lindsey Graham, a vocal supporter of Ukraine who died in July) would hinder his efforts to broker peace. But for Kyiv and its supporters this was another alarming sign that the White House was siding with the Kremlin.
"What the Trump administration is doing is providing carrots to the Russians and sticks to the Ukrainians," former US ambassador to Kyiv William Taylor told the BBC.
"It's inexplicable and saddening."
Kiriil Dmitriev, a senior Putin envoy, called it "an important and truly historic moment".
For Moscow, this felt like a welcome return to the "spirit of Alaska", a phrase much touted by Russian officials in the wake of the Trump-Putin summit in Anchorage in August 2025.
Adding to the impression that Trump is turning his back on Ukraine is the allegation – again not confirmed by Washington – that the US has restricted the flow of intelligence and interfered with Ukraine's access to Elon Musk's Starlink satellite internet service.
Amid an escalation in Russia's drone and missile war on Ukraine's cities, Kyiv says advance warning provided by US satellite intelligence has been lacking.
"We didn't receive it during ballistic attacks for three days," Zelensky told NBC News.
On 12 October five Russian S-400 missiles hit Kyiv, reportedly before air raid sirens or mobile alerts had sounded.
The US Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, denied there had been any pause in intelligence sharing, blaming a "software problem" for the temporary lack of early warnings.
Similar uncertainty surrounds Ukraine's access to Starlink.
A week ago, Ukrainian officials reported that the system was being throttled, with terminals unable to maintain connections at high speeds, making it harder for Ukraine's military to intercept fast moving Russian drones.
Since the summer, Ukraine has struggled to cope with a wave of attacks by advanced, jet-powered drones.
It's not clear where any order to limit Ukraine's use of Starlink – or its military grade equivalent Starshield – originated. Reuters reported that it came from the White House.
Rubio said "no-one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet."
But the fact that such suspicions surface so frequently points to the lack of trust that continues to infect US-Ukrainian relations.
Much of this has its roots in Donald Trump's seemingly long-standing mistrust of Ukraine as a whole - and Zelensky in particular.
A decade ago, Trump became convinced that Ukraine had tried to prevent him from becoming US president. Among a number of unfounded allegations was the suggestion that the US Democratic National Committee had a server hidden somewhere in Ukraine.
When Zelensky became president, three years later, he resisted Trump's demands that he investigate charges of election interference.
During a notorious July 2019 telephone conversation, Trump also asked Zelensky to investigate Joe Biden, the man who went on to defeat him in the 2020 presidential election. Again, Zelensky refused.
At the time, the White House was withholding $391m (£290m) in military assistance to Ukraine, a juxtaposition that ultimately led to Trump's first impeachment.
Whether Trump's resentment over these historic slights continues to inform his current policy towards Ukraine is an open question, but it's clear that the roller coaster of US-Ukraine relations has taken another stomach-churning dip.
Following the talks in Oslo, Witkoff is taking a set of updated proposals to St Petersburg. All eyes will now be on Putin.
Jonas Gahr Støre, the Norwegian leader, said the talks in Oslo had helped "to straighten out a few things."
"There's nothing to gain from… digging into what was said yesterday or a week ago," he said diplomatically.
Zelensky said the day had begun with a productive conversation with the US Secretary of State and indicated that the issue of early warning had already been fixed. He also sounded optimistic about Patriot missiles and Starlink.
"I think we will have good results too," he said.
Yet despite the optimistic tone, it's hard to get around the fact that Volodymyr Zelensky and Donald Trump appear, once again, to be at loggerheads.

Brain scans map multiple “low road” fear pathways between the human thalamus and amygdala
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
20:00:28 UTC
05:00:28 KST

Researchers have mapped several direct routes between the human thalamus and amygdala that may help the brain respond rapidly to threatening information, according to a study published in NeuroImage. Connections involving the back of the thalamus were the most consistent, while others were weaker or harder to detect reliably.
Fear responses can begin quickly. When a person hears a sudden noise or sees a possible threat, the brain must evaluate the information and prepare the body to respond. Animal studies have identified short pathways that carry sensory information from the thalamus, a central relay station for incoming sensory signals, to the amygdala, a region involved in emotional learning and defensive responses.
These pathways have sometimes been described as “low roads” because they may transmit basic sensory information without first passing through the cerebral cortex, where more detailed analysis takes place. Although animal studies have characterized them, they had not been comprehensively mapped in the human brain.
Led by Emmanouela Kosteletou-Kassotaki of the University of Barcelona, the researchers studied 113 healthy right-handed volunteers (average age 24.5 years; 65 women).
The team used high-resolution diffusion-weighted MRI, a scanning method that estimates the direction of nerve fibers by tracking the movement of water through brain tissue. They then used tractography, a technique that reconstructs likely fiber pathways from these data, to map connections between several thalamic nuclei and the basolateral amygdala, a part of the amygdala central to fear learning. Their approach was designed to cope with the dense, crisscrossing fibers around these deep brain structures.
A smaller group of 24 participants underwent a second MRI scan about 15 days later on average. This allowed the researchers to examine whether the pathways could be reconstructed consistently across sessions.
The most reliable connections linked the posterior thalamus to the basolateral amygdala. One pathway ran from the inferior colliculus, an auditory hub in the midbrain, through the medial geniculate nucleus, a key auditory relay in the thalamus, to the amygdala, mirroring an auditory fear pathway well documented in rodents. This pathway was found in nearly all participants.
Connections between the amygdala and the medial, inferior and lateral portions of the pulvinar, a thalamic structure involved in visual attention and combining information across the senses, appeared in all 113 participants and were highly reproducible, particularly for the inferior pulvinar. By contrast, connections with the anterior pulvinar were sparse and inconsistent, and a direct route from the inferior colliculus to the amygdala that bypassed the medial geniculate nucleus could not be reliably reconstructed.
The mediodorsal nucleus, located in the medial thalamus, also showed a prominent connection with the basolateral amygdala, with a high number of reconstructed fiber paths and moderate-to-high reproducibility. The authors note, however, that this connection may mainly carry signals from the amygdala rather than to it.
Connections from intralaminar thalamic nuclei, a group of small nuclei near the center of the thalamus, were also identified, particularly from the parafascicular and central medial nuclei. However, these pathways varied more between people and between the first and second scans. This suggests that some connections are robust across people, while others may be weaker, more difficult to detect or more variable in their anatomy.
Different thalamic regions also tended to connect with different subregions of the basolateral amygdala, and several pathways showed more reconstructed fiber paths in the left hemisphere than in the right, although the authors caution that this asymmetry may partly reflect methodological factors. Overall, the results support the idea that humans possess several direct thalamus–amygdala pathways rather than one simple route. These pathways could help transmit sensory and emotional signals quickly, potentially supporting flexible defensive responses.
Kosteletou-Kassotaki and colleagues described the study as providing “a unifying anatomical framework for multiple direct thalamo-amygdala pathways in the human brain.”
Diffusion tractography has technical limitations that should be noted. It can mistakenly identify pathways that are not present or fail to detect pathways that are present, particularly where nerve fibers cross, so the connections will need to be confirmed with studies of brain tissue. The method also cannot show which direction signals travel and provides information about structure rather than real-time brain function, so the link to fear is inferred largely from animal research.
The study, “Mapping the subcortical pathways associated with fear in the human brain: multiple thalamo-amygdala connections revealed by high-resolution tractography,” was authored by Emmanouela Kosteletou-Kassotaki, Liu Mengxing, Martina T. Cinca-Tomás, Pedro M. Paz-Alonso and Judith Domínguez-Borràs.

Ministers set out who can stop a ship in British waters
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
21:00:25 BST
05:00:25 KST

Royal Navy Police may exercise specified maritime enforcement powers in defined circumstances, any exercise of such powers requires a legal basis and must be undertaken by authorised personnel, and the department supports government efforts to secure British territorial waters including primary legislation as necessary, according to answers given in Parliament.
Ian Roome, the Liberal Democrat member for North Devon, put five questions on the subject, asking whether the Royal Navy must obtain the agreement and authorisation of a civilian police force before intercepting or challenging a foreign military vessel suspected of posing a threat to national security, whether the requirement for Royal Navy Police to act only at the request of civilian forces should be reviewed, what assessment has been made of legislative change to give Royal Navy Police consistent powers across England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, how clear the division of responsibilities is between the Royal Navy, the Royal Navy Police and civilian forces, and whether the six-month review of the Maritime Enforcement Powers (Specification of the Royal Navy Police) Regulations 2020, announced on 17 December 2020, was completed.
Louise Sandher-Jones, the Minister for the Armed Forces, gave the same answer to all five: “The Royal Navy works with the Home Office, civilian police and partners across government to protect UK territorial waters, and respond to threats.
“Responsibilities and authorisations depend on the circumstances and proposed action. Defence may support civilian authorities through established Military Aid to the Civil Authorities arrangements, while any exercise of maritime law-enforcement powers require a legal basis and must be undertaken by authorised personnel.
“Royal Navy Police may exercise specified maritime enforcement powers in defined circumstances. Any review or change must reflect operational needs, applicable law and the UK’s different jurisdictions. As the threat picture changes, the MOD supports HMG efforts to ensure the continued security of the UK and our territorial waters, including primary legislation as necessary.”
The maritime enforcement regime comes from the Policing and Crime Act 2017, which gave designated officers powers to stop, board, divert and detain ships, and the 2020 regulations specified Royal Navy Police as a body able to use them. Separate jurisdictions in England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland mean the powers do not apply identically around the coast.
Warships of another state carry sovereign immunity and cannot be boarded without consent, so intercepting and challenging a foreign military vessel is a naval task carried out under rules of engagement and not a policing one.
Britain took powers this year to board and detain shadow fleet vessels in its territorial waters, and this publication reported when the government announced the policy and again when British forces boarded a Russian shadow fleet tanker.

Forbo Flooring spotlights creative possibilities of custom flooring
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
20:00:00 UTC
05:00:00 KST

Forbo Flooring spotlights creative possibilities of custom flooring
From digitally printed floral and graphic patterns to photographic images and precision-cut inlays, flooring brand Forbo Flooring Systems offers custom design possibilities to make flooring an “integral part of the identity and story of a space”.
Across Forbo’s Flotex, Vinyl, Entrance Flooring and Marmoleum collections, the brand offers customisation techniques that incorporate graphics, branding and messaging upon a floor.
Each technique creates custom floor designs that introduce graphic messaging in hospitality interiors, direct visitors to a certain space, or help support orientation in education or healthcare settings.
Forbo’s flooring can also be used in a museum setting, distinguishing one exhibition from another, or used to reinforce a brand identity in a retail or workplace environment.
“The result is a floor that does more than provide a surface,” said the brand.
“It can contribute to the character of an interior, communicate identity, support zoning and wayfinding, and connect different spaces through a coherent design language.”
The brand’s Flotex flooring has a densely flocked design, allowing detailed patterns, graphics and imagery to be reproduced at high resolution. In comparison, its vinyl collection is digitally printed, making it possible to translate more detailed bespoke patterns, graphics and imagery onto the material.
Across its Marmoleum collections, Forbo uses a specific Aquajet technology that uses high-pressure water to precisely cut material, which can then be combined to form detailed designs.
This enables Forbo to adapt flooring to specific colours and patterns to create individual graphics, imagery, logos or wayfinding.
“The technique makes it possible to translate a wide variety of ideas into the material, from geometric patterns and decorative elements to lettering, logos and intricate artwork,” said Forbo of its Aquajet technology.
“Designers can develop their own concept and work with colours from the Marmoleum palette to create an individual composition.”
Forbo also offers Coral Entrance Flooring, allowing a building’s entrance to connect visually with its identity while helping prevent dirt and moisture from entering.
“Digital printing creates extensive graphic possibilities for Flotex and vinyl,” said Forbo of its process. “Aquajet technology enables precise compositions in Marmoleum, while custom techniques for Coral bring individual design into the entrance area.”
Rather than presenting its collections as separate products, Forbo explained that projects often involve different flooring collections as part of one portfolio.
For example, a project might begin with a customised entrance, continue with an individual floor design and use colour, graphics or patterns to define different zones and destinations.
According to Forbo Flooring, the diversity of its collections allows designers the opportunity to choose the flooring material and technique that best suit both their creative vision and the functional requirements of the space.
“The flooring can therefore contribute to aesthetics, identity, orientation and the overall experience of a space, while different products continue to respond to the functional requirements of each area,” it added.
Forbo Flooring explained that customisation can start at different levels. For example, designers can build on an existing Forbo design, adapting its colours, or develop something entirely new.
“Depending on the flooring type, an original graphic, photograph, pattern, illustration, logo or other visual concept can be translated into the floor,” said the brand.
As a result, this flexibility allows flooring to respond more closely to the architecture, identity and purpose of a space.
To learn more about Forbo’s custom flooring, visit its website.
Photography by Forbo Flooring Systems.

Israel Police released 143 draft evaders after IDF personnel failed to arrive in time, document rev
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
19:58:15 UTC
04:58:15 KST

Israel Police reported 143 cases in which draft evaders detained during random encounters with police officers were released because IDF personnel allegedly failed to arrive within the required time, according to a document from the Attorney-General's Office dated Monday that summarized a meeting on draft enforcement.
Military Police representatives said at the meeting that they were unfamiliar with the figures.
The document, which summarized a meeting held on October 14 and chaired by Deputy Attorney-General Dr. Gil Limon, outlined shortcomings in enforcement operations and coordination between the authorities.
The meeting was held ahead of an update to the High Court of Justice in petitions concerning the implementation of its ruling on the conscription of yeshiva students.
According to figures provided by Israel Police, the 143 releases occurred between July 1 and October 12. The draft evaders were released with a "summons to report to the recruitment authorities," rather than being transferred to the Military Police.
Under the procedure described in the document, the IDF had committed to meeting police officers within half an hour.
Limon said the number of people released was high and "could indicate a failure in the implementation of the joint working procedure."
Police were instructed to provide the Military Police with details of the cases so the IDF could investigate them, draw lessons, and take steps to reduce the phenomenon. An update on the matter was requested by November 1.
At the same time, police reported that 14 draft evaders had been arrested during random encounters over the same period. The document does not explicitly clarify the relationship between that figure and the 143 release cases.
Joint arrest operation postponed as police demand for significant reinforcement
Another central finding concerns a joint IDF and police enforcement operation that had been scheduled for October but was postponed for the second time.
According to the document, the postponement followed a police demand for substantial reinforcements, including hundreds of IDF soldiers, as a condition of approving the operation.
IDF representatives said the demand was impractical and inconsistent with the division of responsibilities and authority between the two organizations.
According to the military representatives, the IDF is responsible for carrying out the arrests themselves, while dealing with disturbances of public order falls under the responsibility of Israel Police.
Major gaps in enforcement between Israel Police and the IDF were exposed by the document
Limon emphasized that Israel Police is responsible for maintaining public order during enforcement operations.
He further clarified that, under the court's ruling, enforcement operations cannot be made conditional on the allocation of IDF soldiers to public-order duties, as distinct from assigning the soldiers required to carry out the arrests.
"The situation described is inconsistent with the state's obligation to combat the phenomenon of draft evasion," the document stated.
The IDF and police were instructed to promptly formulate a framework to resume proactive enforcement operations and provide a detailed update by November 1.
Alongside the joint operations, which have not taken place for some time, the IDF said the Military Police conducts targeted arrest operations every week in various parts of the country as part of an organized work plan.
However, the document emphasized that "in practice, these amount to only a handful of arrests."
The document also identified enforcement gaps at border crossings.
According to figures already presented in the summary of the previous meeting, more than 200 people subject to mandatory military service were arrested in September.
In 64 cases, authorities arrested draft evaders at Ben-Gurion Airport upon their return to Israel after they were not identified as subject to military service when leaving the country.
Conflicting reports between authorities about 64 cases at Ben-Gurion Airport
The Population and Immigration Authority said the cases had been referred to the police for investigation on suspicion of "illegal border crossing."
However, in its response to the meeting summary, Israel Police said it was unaware of any such reports having been received from the authority.
The matter is expected to be examined at another meeting involving representatives of the Population and Immigration Authority, the IDF, and Israel Police.
The document further revealed that, despite a request included in the summary of an August meeting, the IDF has yet to provide a document detailing the criteria used to decide whether draft evaders are released at border crossings.
"It has not been clarified what criteria are used to determine which draft evader is permitted to travel abroad or return home and which draft evader is arrested," the document stated.
The IDF was again instructed to provide the document before the next meeting on the matter.

 The UN on Tuesday warned that displaced Palestinians in the Gaza Strip could face serious flood and collapse risks as winter approaches, with aid efforts hampered by funding shortfalls and supply restrictions.
Citing the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), UN spokesperson Stephane Dujarric said at a news conference that "we assessed displacement sites hosting over 650 families in Khan Younis, including 160 families staying in a low-lying pit that used to collect rainwater and is now at risk of being flooded with both rain and sewage."
Dujarric said the UN and its partners assessed five other low-lying displacement sites on Monday hosting about 750 people, also in Khan Younis.
"We also assessed a sixth site hosting a number of families on the edge of a cliff overlooking the five low-lying sites," he said. "We are concerned that soil erosion this winter could cause the ground beneath the tents there to collapse."
Across Gaza, partners are undertaking "drainage clearance, sandbagging and ground-levelling to support such communities. But efforts are held back by funding shortfalls and restrictions on the entry of a range of critical supplies."
Dujarric added that shelter partners said that "the supplies currently available are only enough to partially support less than a fifth of the nearly 300,000 families in need of winter shelter assistance."

Despite a ceasefire that has been in effect since Oct. 10, 2025, Israel has continued shelling, shooting and demolishing Palestinian structures, further expanding the destruction.

Türkiye, Qatar, Pakistan, and Indonesia to ink defense industry pact
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
19:47:01 UTC
04:47:01 KST

By Firdevs Bulut Kartal, Emir Yildirim, and Mucahithan Avcioglu
20 October 2026•Update: 20 October 2026
- Türkiye seeks to build on existing partnerships with the 3 countries as defense production and exports expand
Türkiye, Qatar, Pakistan, and Indonesia will sign a new memorandum of understanding in Doha to strengthen defense industry cooperation, Türkiye's Defense Industries Secretariat (SSB) announced.
The memorandum will build on existing defense projects among the four countries, marking a new step in Türkiye's approach to multilateral cooperation.
Efforts coordinated by the secretariat focus on moving beyond the supply of military platforms to joint production, technology transfer, interoperability, and the integration of supply chains.
In a statement, the secretariat said defense industry partnerships pursued with the support of Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan are among the strategic elements supporting Türkiye's foreign policy. It added that efforts focused on mass production and exports have gained momentum under Haluk Gorgun, the secretariat’s head.
 
- More than 55% of defense exports since 2012 took place in last 4 years
According to the Defense and Aerospace Industry Exporters' Association, Türkiye's defense and aerospace sector saw approximately $54 billion in exports from 2012 through the first nine months of 2026.
More than $30 billion of that total took place in 2023-2026, meaning the last four years accounted for more than 55% of the sector's exports over the period.
Defense and aerospace exports rose 48% year-on-year in 2025 to top $10 billion, while exports over the latest 12-month period surpassed $11 billion for the first time.
According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), Türkiye boosted its arms exports 122% over the last five years, becoming the world's 11th-largest arms supplier. NATO allies account for 56% of Türkiye's defense and aerospace exports.
Joint production and technology transfer with Qatar
Qatar, one of the parties to the planned memorandum, has a longstanding defense industry partnership with Türkiye.
Bayraktar TB2 armed drones, armored vehicles, and fast attack craft supplied to the Qatari Armed Forces are among the prominent examples of bilateral cooperation.
Barzan Holdings, a subsidiary of Qatar's Defense Ministry, has also signed cooperation agreements in previous years with Turkish defense companies including Aselsan, STM, and MKE.
BARQ, a joint venture established in Qatar by Aselsan and Barzan Holdings, has begun local assembly, production, and calibration activities for SARP remote-controlled weapon systems and electro-optical equipment.
Projects carried out by Turkish companies in Qatar also enable the provision of defense industry solutions to third countries.
Corvette partnership with Pakistan, joint tank production with Indonesia
The PN MILGEM Babur-class corvette project is a leading example of defense industry cooperation between Türkiye and Pakistan.
Under the four-corvette project, led by main contractor Asfat, the first two vessels were built in Istanbul and the other two at Karachi Shipyard in Pakistan.
The project modernized Karachi Shipyard's production infrastructure and transferred shipbuilding and outfitting engineering capabilities to the local workforce. It thus contributed to Pakistan's domestic production capacity alongside the supply of naval platforms.
The KAPLAN MT medium-weight tank development project is a prominent example of Türkiye's defense industry cooperation with Indonesia.
Launched under an intergovernmental agreement between the secretariat and Indonesia's Defense Ministry, the KAPLAN MT was jointly designed and developed by Turkish defense company FNSS and Indonesia's PT Pindad.
Prototypes and the first series-production tanks manufactured by FNSS were delivered to Indonesian users. Production is continuing at PT Pindad in Indonesia under a technology transfer arrangement.
Multilateral cooperation in defense diplomacy
The memorandum planned for signing in Doha aims to strengthen Türkiye's separate defense industry partnerships with Qatar, Pakistan, and Indonesia within a multilateral framework.
The secretariat's defense diplomacy approach prioritizes not only defense system exports but also the development of joint production infrastructure, technology transfer, and long-term strategic partnerships.
The four-country memorandum is expected to help expand existing cooperation and pave the way for new joint defense industry projects.

'A duty of national honor': Ben-Gurion’s historic 1949 radio address resurfaces ahead of elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
19:41:33 UTC
04:41:33 KST

A historic 1949 speech by Israel's first prime minister, David Ben-Gurion, resurfaced about a week prior to Election Day, in which the country's first leader discussed the importance of citizens' participation in the act of voting.
"It is not merely a right, but a duty, a duty of national honor," Ben-Gurion said in the speech, delivered as a radio broadcast on January 24, 1949, the evening before Israel's first Knesset elections.
The address, titled "To the People and the Army," was released on Tuesday by the Ben-Gurion Heritage Institute and the Ben-Gurion Archives at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev. The speech was also broadcast to displaced persons camps in Cyprus, where many Jewish refugees had been deported by the British.
"Every man and woman to whom the law has granted the right to vote must not be absent from the polling station," Ben-Gurion emphasized. "This is a great right, a historic right for which generations have yearned with messianic longing... In it, our responsibility and political maturity will be embodied."
Israeli newspaper stresses importance of voting in 1949 editorial
An editorial from the Israeli newspaper Davar echoed Ben-Gurion's sentiment on the morning of the 1949 elections.
"Never before has the right (of voting) been as much a duty as it is today," the editorial read. "The man and woman in whose hands the decision has been placed to shape the character of the Jewish state for generations to come have a duty to participate in that decision. This duty was placed upon them by all the generations that longed to achieve what this generation has achieved."
The first prime minister further stressed that every Israeli citizen should feel "as though his vote would tip the scales in determining the course ahead," but still retain national unity despite political disagreements.
"If, amid the storm of debate, there was a departure from the bounds of an educational and civilized discussion, let us put the words of quarrel and provocation out of our minds, and once again see one another as fellow citizens, partners in the state that is dear to us all, and accept the verdict of the entire electorate with love and loyalty," he said.
"We came to this land not to be Ashkenazim, Russians, Poles, or Romanians," he added. "On the contrary. Because we did not want to be these things, we did two things: We created equality in labor, and we revived the Hebrew language."
"When we came to this land, we established Jewish defense," he continued. "And in that, too, there was no distinction between one community and another. There was no distinction between Shimon the Kurd, Yitzhak Nadaf the Yemenite, and Yehezkel Nissanov the Caucasian, and Israel Giladi the Ashkenazi. Language, labor, and defense united them all, and when one of them fell, he did not fall as a Yemenite, Sephardi, or Ashkenazi, but as a Jew."
Ben-Gurion addresses IDF soldiers fighting in Israel's War of Independence
The former leader also addressed IDF soldiers serving at the time in Israel's War of Independence, saying that they should vote as free citizens.
"Without any restriction of military discipline, you will determine the course together with all the other citizens," he told the soldiers. "Each of you... will vote solely according to the dictates of your conscience... And even if you differ in your choices, your collective loyalty to military discipline, and the fighting brotherhood... will not be impaired."
Ben-Gurion Heritage Institute CEO Eitan Donitz noted the importance of Ben-Gurion's words, saying that, for the first prime minister, "elections were an expression of every citizen's responsibility for the future of the state and the deep partnership between us, transcending parties and ideologies."
"The right to vote and influence rests on the understanding that democracy exists when its citizens choose to be involved in it," said Donitz. "His legacy reminds us that even today, the demand for responsibility and partnership rests on the shoulders of each and every one of us."

Trump administration sued by US food importer for 50% tariffs on Canada
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
19:41:31 UTC
04:41:31 KST

Mücahithan Avcıoğlu
20 October 2026•Update: 20 October 2026
US food importer Gellert Global Group filed a lawsuit Tuesday challenging the Trump administration's 50% tariffs on certain Canadian goods, arguing that the duties exceed presidential authority.
The Liberty Justice Center, which represents the company, said it filed the case in the US Court of International Trade on behalf of Gellert and a proposed class of affected importers.
The lawsuit asks the court to declare the tariffs unlawful, stop their collection and order refunds with interest.
The duties were imposed under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, a provision aimed at addressing foreign discrimination against US commerce.
The lawsuit argues that Congress superseded that provision with Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which established investigations, public participation and other safeguards for responding to unfair foreign trade practices.
It also alleges that the administration failed to observe a mandatory 30-day waiting period when expanding the tariffs.
Canadian cheeses imported by Gellert were added to the tariff list on Sept. 8, but duties began being collected Sept. 15, according to the center.
The center also filed requests for a preliminary injunction to block collection and summary judgment in Gellert's favor.
The lawsuit challenges the administration's reliance on Canadian retaliatory measures and dairy policies governed by the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement, according to the case summary.
It also argues that some targeted products have no connection to the alleged discrimination, including Canadian cheeses subjected to tariffs linked to disputes about alcohol policies and automobile duties.
Gellert, a family-run food business, imports and distributes products in the US and helps American producers reach overseas markets.

U.S. ramps up warnings to Americans in Middle East after deadly Houthi strikes
U.S. diplomatic missions across the Middle East have issued a new round of security warnings to Americans amid escalating attacks by Iran-backed Houthi militants against Saudi Arabia, including an Oct. 10 strike on Riyadh's international airport that killed an American citizen.
The alerts, issued Sunday by U.S. embassies in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and several other countries, warned that hostilities could rapidly and without warning spread beyond areas already affected by the fighting. The advisories urged Americans to exercise vigilance and prepare for possible flight cancellations, airspace closures and other travel disruptions.
"We are actively warning U.S. citizens about the very real threat the Houthis pose and urging them to heed official guidance," Edgar Vasquez, the State Department's deputy assistant secretary for press, told CBS News.
"These alerts are part of a proactive effort by the Trump administration to ensure Americans are aware of potential risks," Vasquez said, adding that the safety and security of American citizens remain the department's "top priority."
The State Department has maintained restrictions on diplomatic operations across parts of the region since the U.S. and Israel went to war with Iran in February. State Department officials have said the restrictions are intended to be temporary and allow embassies to adjust staffing as security conditions evolve.
Under a longstanding "no double standard" policy, embassies are required to share security threat information with private American citizens when the same risks apply to U.S. diplomatic personnel.
The latest alerts follow a surge in Houthi missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, including repeated strikes on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport and oil facilities belonging to Saudi Aramco. The Oct. 10 airport attack killed at least 13 people and injured more than 300, according to Saudi authorities.
The attacks continued Tuesday, with the Saudi-led coalition reporting it intercepted a Houthi ballistic missile targeting Riyadh as well as a drone near the capital.
The escalating attacks have raised questions about the effectiveness of the Trump administration's approach to the conflict. While the administration has provided intelligence and targeting support to Saudi Arabia, President Trump has thus far declined repeated requests from Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman for direct U.S. military intervention. He has left open the possibility of joining in airstrikes but has not announced a decision.
"We may," Mr. Trump said on Oct. 10, after the deadly attack on Riyadh's airport. "We're going to look at it."
The Houthis have continued to make territorial gains in Yemen, where a Houthi attack killed two teenage girls in Taiz on Tuesday. That came a day after a strike on a government military camp killed 73 recruits and wounded more than 200.
In an interview Tuesday with CBS News, Ambassador Marwan Ali Noman, political adviser to the minister of foreign affairs of the government of Yemen, warned that the Houthis would continue expanding their attacks unless confronted. He argued that Yemen's military campaign was intended to protect the wider region as well as its own population.
"We are fighting on behalf of everyone, because the threat and risk of the Houthis will expand," Noman said.
He added that Yemen's government was seeking expanded U.S. and international assistance, including greater intelligence sharing, air defenses and support for its coast guard, but was not asking Washington to deploy ground troops.
The requests come as the Trump administration faces competing demands for air defense weapons. Speaking to reporters in India on Tuesday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio acknowledged that countries including Saudi Arabia and Israel are seeking additional American-made missile interceptors, even as Ukraine presses for more supplies.
"Every country in the world would like interceptors," Rubio said. "It's probably the most in-demand product right now in the defense field."

Backyard find: Egyptian farmer unearths statue fragments  believed to depict Ramesses II
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
19:41:13 UTC
04:41:13 KST

Fragments of two massive statues depicting Ramesses II were discovered by accident by a farmer working on his land in a northern Egyptian village, Egypt’s Tourism and Antiquities Ministry announced last week.
The fragments were found in Behbeit El Hagar, a village and archaeological site that is home to the remains of an ancient temple dedicated to the goddess Isis, known as the Iseion. In antiquity, it served as part of the ancient Egyptian nome of Sebennytos, the Twelfth Lower Egyptian Nome.
After discovering the stone blocks, the farmer, Khaled El-Shahat Khalil, notified the Egyptian Tourism and Antiquities Ministry, which sent a team to the village to conduct rescue excavations of the fragments.
The first fragment is a massive depiction of the head of Ramesses II, standing about 1.60 meters tall, which shows the pharaoh wearing the pschent (double crown) of Upper and Lower Egypt.
The backing of the statue was also found nearby, bearing an inscription of the pharaoh’s Horus name, "Hor Ka Nakht Meri Maat," meaning “Strong Bull, Beloved of Maat.”
Dr. Hisham El-Leithy, secretary-general of Egypt’s Supreme Council of Antiquities, added that the size of the head indicated that the statue may have originally stood at around 8.5 meters.
The second statue fragment, also believed to belong to Ramesses II, stands 2.4 meters tall and has clear, well-preserved facial features.
Missing its legs and base, the fragment portrays the pharaoh wearing the traditional nemes headdress, the top part of which is missing.
Alongside the statue fragments, a pink granite block bearing several hieroglyphic inscriptions, including two of Ramesses’ titles: “Nesu-Bity,” meaning “King of Upper and Lower Egypt,” and "Sa Ra," meaning “Son of Ra.”
Following the discovery and the rescue excavations, Egyptian Tourism and Antiquities Minister Sherif Fathy presented Khalil and his wife with a certificate of appreciation for reporting the finds, stressing the importance of the discovery to the ongoing study of Egypt's history.
Partial statue, inscriptions of Ramesses II previously found
Previously, in August, archaeologists discovered a large, broken sandstone lintel inscribed both with the titles of Ramesses II as well as a reference to restoration work being carried out on a statue belonging to the deity “Horus, Lord of the City of Mesn.”
Earlier this year, archaeologists also found a partial statue of Ramesses II at the Tel Faraon archaeological site near El Husseiniya in the Nile Delta.
The statue was discovered incomplete, missing its legs and base. Even so, Leithy said at the time that, according to initial assessments, the statue weighed about five to six tons and stood around 2.20 meters tall (just over seven feet).
He added that although the statue was poorly preserved, the remaining features “display artistic and royal features suggesting it was once part of a Triad, similar to those uncovered at a number of archaeological sites across Sharqia Governorate.”

A New Path to Peace — What Zelenskyy Will Bring to Ukraine from the Talks in Oslo
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
22:29:51 EEST
04:29:51 KST

A New Path to Peace — What Zelenskyy Will Bring to Ukraine from the Talks in Oslo
Kyiv • UNN
Zelenskyy announced the restoration of U.S. intelligence sharing and discussions on security guarantees and a trilateral meeting. Russia rejected the energy truce.
In Oslo (Norway), talks between the United States and Ukraine that were intended to bring an end to the hostilities and peace negotiations closer concluded on October 20. Official Kyiv was represented by Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy, while the partner country was represented by U.S. presidential envoy Steve Witkoff (who, incidentally, did not stay to speak with the press).
What the allies discussed and what the president of Ukraine told journalists at a press conference following the talks is reported by UNN.
Among the key messages Zelenskyy addressed to the international community and his fellow citizens were possible security guarantees for Ukraine, a ceasefire, the resumption of intelligence-sharing with the United States, the operation of Starlink, and the prospects for a trilateral meeting of the leaders of Ukraine, the United States, and Russia. Separately, the head of state commented on the Kremlin's position regarding an energy truce and stated that Ukraine would not lose the war, but was continuing to lose people and time.
Ukraine proposes a new path to peace and a trilateral meeting of the leaders
In his brief opening remarks, Volodymyr Zelenskyy emphasized that Ukraine, together with its European partners, was continuing to work on diplomatic proposals that could help bring the war to an end. Official Kyiv expects the American side to consider the prepared initiatives and convey them to the Russian leadership. The president also stressed that Ukraine was interested in achieving peace as soon as possible, but that this required concrete decisions, particularly at the highest political level.
"We have a clear vision of how to achieve peace. In these efforts, we are acting jointly with our European and other partners. We want the American side to consider these ideas," Zelenskyy said.
One of the key proposals of the Ukrainian side remains the organization of a trilateral meeting involving Volodymyr Zelenskyy, U.S. President Donald Trump, and Russian leader Vladimir Putin. According to the head of state, there are a number of issues that remain unresolved and require direct discussion between the heads of state. In particular, this concerns territorial issues and the terms for ending the war.
Zelenskyy also confirmed that on October 21, Steve Witkoff was to travel to Russia to discuss the work prepared during the talks in Oslo.
"We will see what Putin says," the Ukrainian leader noted.
Security guarantees: the United States is discussing a mechanism based on Article 5 of NATO
Particular attention during the talks was devoted to future security guarantees for Ukraine. The American side has already confirmed its readiness to work on the relevant mechanisms. In particular, the United States is considering various guarantee options, including a model similar to Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty, as well as a simplified version of it.
"I am grateful to the American side for once again emphasizing that they will be reliable. We have various proposals; we discussed, in particular, NATO, Article 5, as well as the option of \"Article 5 — a simplified version\"," Zelenskyy explained.
The president clarified that various formats of security guarantees were included in the document that the American special representative was to deliver to the Russian side. Zelenskyy also once again emphasized that Ukraine needed reliable security commitments after the end of the war to protect the country from renewed Russian aggression.
Putin rejected an energy truce
Another issue discussed during the talks in Oslo was the possibility of halting mutual strikes on energy infrastructure. According to Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukraine supported the relevant initiative of the United States and proposed several options for an agreement. These included a mutual renunciation of attacks on the most sensitive energy-sector facilities.
"Ukraine immediately supported the American proposal for an energy truce, but Russia responded by continuing its attacks," he said.
The President of Ukraine explained that Kyiv is ready to refrain from striking sensitive Russian energy facilities if Russia stops attacking similar facilities in Ukraine. However, according to him, Putin rejected this proposal. Nevertheless, despite the Kremlin's refusal, the Ukrainian side continues to seek possible solutions that would make it possible to halt attacks on energy infrastructure.
Zelenskyy also emphasized that Ukraine is ready to discuss various formats for a ceasefire and support real steps aimed at de-escalation.
The United States has resumed sharing intelligence with Ukraine
In addition, during a conversation with media representatives, the head of the Ukrainian state confirmed that the Armed Forces of Ukraine are again receiving American intelligence data, necessary in particular for early warning of Russian ballistic attacks. The President emphasized that this information is critically important for protecting the civilian population, as it makes it possible to receive timely signals about approaching missiles.
"We are grateful that intelligence is now being effectively provided. This concerns the early warning system — it is extremely important for our people, for children and adults, because we receive a signal when ballistic missiles are approaching," Zelenskyy said.
He thanked the American side for restoring the relevant cooperation and confirmed that the early warning system is currently operational.
Starlink, Patriot, and new contact with Rubio within 48 hours
Volodymyr Zelenskyy also said that on October 20, while traveling to Oslo, he held a phone conversation with Marco Rubio. The main topics were the operation of Starlink satellite communications, the supply of interceptor missiles for air defense, and intelligence support for Ukraine. The President ultimately described the conversation as specific and positive.
"We discussed sensitive issues, such as Starlink communications, interceptors, which is very important, and intelligence," the head of state noted.
According to him, the parties identified issues requiring an urgent resolution and agreed to continue contacts.
"We shared the things that we need to resolve, and we will resolve them. We decided that we would get in touch again in 48 hours," the President said.
In other words, Ukraine and the United States plan to return to discussing these issues within the next two days.
Ukraine is not losing the war, but it is losing people and time
Answering journalists' questions about the situation on the front and possible concessions during peace negotiations, Volodymyr Zelenskyy rejected claims that Ukraine is losing the war. At the same time, he acknowledged that the continuation of hostilities is causing significant human losses and negatively affecting the lives of Ukrainians.
"Of course, we are not losing the war. But we are losing people because of Russian attacks. We are losing people and time because our children do not see, do not have a real life, a childhood," the President emphasized.
According to him, the need to preserve human lives is one of the main reasons why Ukraine seeks to end the war as soon as possible. At the same time, Zelenskyy emphasized that the resilience of Ukrainian soldiers on the battlefield strengthens the state's position during diplomatic negotiations.
The President also expressed hope for further assistance from the United States and European partners in finding ways to end Russian aggression.
No decisions concerning Ukraine without its participation
Zelenskyy separately commented on reports of a possible trilateral meeting involving representatives of the United States, China, and Russia. The Ukrainian leader emphasized that countries may independently determine the formats of their diplomatic contacts. However, any negotiations concerning Ukraine's future must take place with its direct participation.
He stressed that decisions concerning Ukrainian territories, security, and the end of the war cannot be made without representatives of Kyiv.
At the same time, Zelenskyy characterized the current dialogue between Ukraine, the United States, and European partners as constructive, despite the complexity of certain issues.
What to expect after the talks in Oslo
Further development of the diplomatic process will depend, among other things, on the results of the trip by U.S. Special Representative Steve Witkoff to Russia, scheduled for October 21. During talks with the Russian leadership, he is expected to present proposals that were discussed with Ukraine and its European partners. According to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, this will make Moscow’s position on the proposed formats for a ceasefire, security guarantees, and possible talks at the leaders’ level clearer.
At the same time, according to him, official Kyiv will continue consultations with the United States on military assistance, intelligence, and the restoration of satellite communications.
We remind you
As Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre reported, the U.S.-Ukraine talks in Oslo went successfully. Following them, Washington is preparing a new step toward ending the war.

Housing is flashing warning signs just as the Fed weighs more interest rate hikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
19:28:43 UTC
04:28:43 KST

The Federal Reserve's inflation fight is running into a growing complication: The housing market is slumping even as broader price pressures persist.
Housing data deteriorated further in September, according to separate reports Tuesday, adding to an already complicated policy landscape for the central bank as it contemplates its next move on interest rates.
Things appear poised to get worse before they get better. If the Fed raises short-term rates as expected over the next several months, mortgage rates that are already at 7.43% could push even higher, putting a further damper on affordability. Higher home borrowing costs have coincided with a general rise in inflation and a housing shortage.
"The housing market is about to go into a deep sleep unless Washington can do a 180 on its policies and make the cost of a new home more affordable," wrote Chris Rupkey, chief economist at Fwdbonds. "It is not winter yet but housing is going into a deep freeze."
The National Association of Realtors reported that pending sales, a forward-looking index that measures home sales under agreement but not completed, hit an all-time low in records that stretch back to 2001. The index slid 7.3% for the month and was off 11.3% from a year ago. The Wall Street estimate was for a decline of just 0.4%.
Housing starts, another important metric when evaluating the state of the market, also posted a decline well outside already-muted expectations Tuesday.
Privately owned housing starts fell at a seasonally adjusted annualized rate of 5.2% on the month, against expectations for a decline of just 0.4%, while building permits were off 0.2%, against the Dow Jones consensus outlook for a 2% gain, according to Commerce Department data.
Moreover, single-family permits totaled just 845,000, down 4% from August and the lowest number since 2023.
"Market conditions weakened in September due to fast-rising mortgage rates," said Lawrence Yun, the NAR's chief economist. "Although job growth and income gains can support home purchases, housing affordability is more affected by changes in mortgage rates."
Rising rates weigh on outlook
The rate for a 30-year mortgage was above 7% for most of September, ending the month around 7.6%, according to Mortgage News Daily. Five years ago, rates were closer to 3%, feeding into the Covid-era housing boom that saw an explosion in demand and, consequently, prices.
Outside of the pending sales number, home builder sentiment is at lows not seen in 14 years.
Under some conditions, Fed officials might respond to the housing weakness with easier monetary policy. Lower rates generally help spur demand by lowering borrowing costs.
But the Fed has a bigger fight on its hands in its effort to bring inflation under control. Readings last week on consumer and producer prices provided few signs of optimism, with wholesale final demand goods prices rising 2.6%, the fastest pace in a Bureau of Labor Statistics data series going back to December 2009.
Fed officials have said they are tracking the inflationary effects of the robust investment in artificial intelligence, which is driving up the cost of chips and electronics. At the same time, they believe that benefits from AI investment could offset weaker sectors of the economy such as housing.
However, conditions generally point to a housing market likely to weaken further before stabilizing, Goldman Sachs economist Ronnie Walker said in a client note Monday.
"In 2027, we expect the headwind from affordability—reignited by the recent rebound in mortgage rates—to increasingly dominate, weighing further on activity," Walker wrote. "Sustained higher mortgage rates will continue to have their most pronounced impact on housing turnover, and the recent run-up in rates is likely to push existing home sales lower in the coming months."
More of the same
Several data points tell the story: More than 95% of mortgage borrowers have rates below the prevailing level, and 65% are 2 percentage points below. Goldman forecasts residential investment to decline 2.5%, 4% and 1%, respectively, over the coming three quarters, with a possibility for a steeper decline if mortgage rates don't fall.
The firm sees single-family starts of just 875,000 in 2027, little changed from this year, while existing sales are forecast at 3.9 million, also about the same as 2026 but notably 26% below pre-Covid 2019 levels. Walker attributed the middling levels as a product of the "lock-in" effect in which it's too expensive for current homeowners to move and take on higher borrowing costs while deteriorating affordability weighs on new construction.
"Housing activity has remained rangebound in recent years, capped on the upside by affordability headwinds and buffered on the downside by the longstanding housing shortage," Walker wrote. "In 2027, we expect the headwind from affordability to increasingly dominate, weighing further on activity."
Markets expect the Fed to hold benchmark rates steady when it meets next week. However, futures pricing implies a strong chance of a quarter-point hike in December and another in March 2027, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool.
One point of optimism comes from Yun, the NAR economist, who thinks the trend of mortgage costs running ahead of Fed hikes could mean that rates are topping out.
"Given that mortgage rates have already risen much more than the Federal Reserve's short-term interest rate hikes, mortgage rates could be topping out," he said. "Buyers and sellers may simply be holding back until mortgage rates move favorably."

Türkiye welcomes Libya's parliamentary backing for 2019 maritime deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
19:24:59 UTC
04:24:59 KST

Türkiye has welcomed a decision by Libya's House of Representatives regarding the memorandum of understanding on the delimitation of maritime jurisdiction areas between Türkiye and Libya.
"We welcome the decision adopted today (October 20) by Libya's House of Representatives regarding the Memorandum of Understanding on the Delimitation of Maritime Jurisdiction Areas between Türkiye and Libya, which has been in force since 2019," the Turkish foreign ministry said in a statement on Tuesday.
The ministry said the memorandum, based on the principles of international law and equity, safeguards both countries' mutual rights and interests and further strengthens cooperation.
Türkiye will continue working with all partners to promote trust, stability and peace in the Mediterranean basin, in line with its commitment to respecting international law, the statement added.
What is the 2019 Türkiye-Libya maritime agreement?
On November 27, 2019, Türkiye and Libya's then internationally recognised Government of National Accord (GNA), signed a memorandum of understanding delimiting their respective maritime jurisdiction areas in the Mediterranean.
The agreement established a maritime boundary between the two countries based on Ankara's interpretation of international maritime law.
Türkiye maintains that its extensive Mediterranean coastline entitles it to maritime jurisdiction areas that should not be disproportionately restricted by Greek islands situated close to the Turkish mainland.
The eastern-based House of Representatives opposed the maritime agreement and questioned the authority of the Tripoli government to conclude it without parliamentary approval.
That opposition became a major point of contention, allowing critics to argue that the agreement lacked the necessary domestic political endorsement in Libya.
The latest parliamentary decision therefore marks a substantial reversal, following years of diplomatic efforts by Türkiye to establish working relationships with Libya's rival political and military authorities.
Since the collapse of Muammar Gaddafi's government in 2011, Libya has experienced successive conflicts, rival administrations and competing centres of political authority.

UK universities silencing pro-Palestine solidarity: Human rights group report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
19:23:21 UTC
04:23:21 KST

Burak Bir
20 October 2026•Update: 20 October 2026
A number of UK universities have suppressed pro-Palestinian solidarity as academics and students have faced sanctions, suspensions, and campus bans, a new study said Tuesday.
In its report, titled Silencing Dissent: UK universities’ response to Palestine solidarity on campus, Amnesty International UK said that students and academics at some prominent universities in the UK have faced sanctions, including suspensions, campus bans, and threats to their visa status for actions "as simple as chanting, clapping and wearing keffiyehs."
The study said these sanctions and threats were used to "restrict" solidarity with the Palestinian people among students and academics, including speech that could be perceived as critical of Israel.
Amnesty also found that the restrictions highlighted in case studies documented in the report often didn’t meet the high bar in international and UK law for interfering with political speech and peaceful assembly.
The report which covered events from Oct. 7, 2023 to Sept. 30, 2025, accompanies Defend Dissent, a student-led campaign calling on universities across the UK to sign and implement the Defend Dissent Charter.
"Students who are visibly Muslim and those displaying symbols of Palestinian identity have been disproportionately impacted," according to the findings.
Citing several cases, the report showed that sanctions were imposed before disciplinary hearings had concluded, effectively transforming precautionary measures into punishments and contributing to the chilling effect.
The report found instances of universities treating peaceful protest as trespass, even in spaces such as campus squares, foyers, and union buildings which have been used for protests for decades.
'This is part of a wider crackdown on communities'
"This is an attack on our freedom of speech and the right to protest from the very institutions who are supposed to encourage free thought," said Kerry Moscogiuri, the CEO of Amnesty International UK.
Saying that students and academics care about the victims of Israel's genocide in Gaza, she said some prominent universities see this as a "threat" that requires punitive measures like court injunctions, and harsh punishments that leave students with their lives turned upside down.
"This is part of a wider crackdown on communities coming together to make their voices heard on Israel’s genocide of Palestinians in Gaza and other issues they care about," she said.
The report mentioned a specific case which involved 22-year-old student Usama Ghanem, who was suspended by Kings College London in 2025 over his involvement in pro Palestinian activism, and told to "return to (Egypt) during this period of suspension."
Usama said: "For protesting a genocide, our university was funding and demanding divestment, I was indefinitely suspended, monitored, and threatened with deportation."
His suspension was lifted after review in September 2026.
The report also cited different cases where students and academics faced various pressure over their activism at their universities including the University of Cambridge, the University of Oxford, and the London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE).
