Italian government approves tougher security measures after weekend violence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
19:21:50 UTC
04:21:50 KST

Giada Zampano
20 October 2026•Update: 20 October 2026
Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni’s government approved new security measures Tuesday that would create a criminal offense for violent participation in demonstrations and stiffen penalties for group violence, following unrest in Milan and other Italian cities, according to media reports.
The Cabinet-approved decree introduces the offense of "violent participation in a demonstration," with penalties of up to five years in prison and fines of up to €20,000 ($22,470).
"If during a march or demonstration you join a group of five or more people, start throwing stones, firecrackers or sticks, and endanger everyone’s safety, you risk up to five years in prison and a fine of up to 20,000 euros," Meloni said in a video after the Cabinet meeting.
Penalties would increase if offenders cover their faces or injure someone, she said. The measures also increase penalties for those who take part in group acts of destruction.
Meloni said the measures were a response to violence that erupted in Milan and other Italian cities during the weekend, where shops were looted, storefronts damaged and police officers attacked. She called it “unacceptable” and said they could not be minimized or justified.
The package also includes measures to extend preventive detention to minors and beyond 12 hours, allow delayed arrests of people accused of taking part in group property damage, and prohibit people considered a threat to public order from gathering.
The government also plans to strengthen the existing "Safe Streets" security operation, sending 500 additional soldiers to patrol Milan’s streets.
One sensitive point concerned an initial proposal to give soldiers judicial police functions. That was the only provision the Quirinale, the office of Italy’s President Sergio Mattarella, objected to during consultations between the presidency and the government ahead of the decree’s approval.
After addressing that issue, Mattarella appeared poised to clear the measure, according to Italian media.

The Yemeni army said Tuesday that it had carried out 744 precision attacks against the Houthi group in the last 24 hours, and “neutralized” around 200 of its members.
The army said in a statement that forces continued advancing an offensive under “Operation Yemen Dawn,” conducting “744 precise and direct targeting operations.”
The attacks involved warplanes, drones, field artillery, multiple rocket launchers and sniper units, it said.
Targets included field command and control centers, firing positions, fortified sites, reserve assembly areas, Houthi reinforcements and supply assets, according to the statement.
In the southwestern province of Taiz, the army said forces continued to intensify military pressure and push back Houthi fighters.
Operations on the eastern, southern and western fronts maintained “a synchronized operational tempo” that restricted the movement of Houthi reserves and prevented the group from making territorial gains, it added.
The army said the operations “neutralized around 200” Houthi members and destroyed or damaged 90 vehicles and other military assets.
“Neutralized” is a military term referring to combatants being put out of action, including through death or injury.
There was no comment from the Houthi group.
It came amid escalating hostilities between the Houthis and forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognized government, backed by the Saudi-led coalition.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, and much of the north.

Quick hits: Jansen hit where it hurts as Bavuma grinds Aussies into the dirt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
19:16:26 UTC
04:16:26 KST

Marco Jansen's swashbuckling innings ends with a bang then a whimper and Temba Bavuma grinds Australia into the dirt with one of the great captain's knocks.
Here are the quick hits from day three of the second Test between Australia and South Africa.
1. Bavuma's all-time captain's knock
Watching Temba Bavuma bat on day three, it was hard to believe the South Africa captain was in the process of scoring just his fifth Test-match century.
He was so organised, so composed and just-about chanceless in making his way to a 223-ball hundred.
His face was a picture of steely determination after reaching his milestone, his mouth twisted into a defiant grimace as he held bat and helmet aloft, well aware he was batting his side back into the game.
And he continued on his way after passing three figures, continually blunting the tiring Australian attack, finding runs all over the outfield and driving through mid-on like only the truest of batting talents are able.
It was a captain's knock if ever there was one and eventually ended with a new high-score of 179.
Having initially struggled to find his feet at Test level, Bavuma has averaged well over 50 in the past five years and can now count himself as one of the format's best batters.
2. Jansen gets hit and then gets out
It was a blow that sent winces across the cricketing world.
Scott Boland produced a beauty with the very first delivery of the 80th over, using the new ball to jag one back towards Marco Jansen.
The towering all-rounder was cut in half and completely helpless to the fresh pill thudding into precisely the place he would have hoped to protect the most.
Doubled over and then down an all fours, Jansen pounded the turf in agony as his teammates offered a mixture of sympathy and mirth from the stands.
It was a long, long delay as he picked himself up, regained his composure and received some medical attention.
He was eventually right to continue, but just four balls later, his counterpunch came to an end with a meek chip to Travis Head at mid-wicket.
Jansen's swashbuckling 100-ball 85 was key to South Africa's remarkable revival on day three, but the big man's special knock was over with a combination of bang and whimper.
3. Starc reaches 450 Test wickets
The milestones just keep coming for Mitchell Starc.
With the St. George's pitch offering little during the first half hour of play on day three, Australia's fearsome spearhead managed to conjure something special.
His venomous bouncer had Wiaan Mulder tied in knots on the backfoot, the ball collecting a mixture of helmet, shoulder and willow on the way through to Matt Renshaw in the cordon.
The on-field decision was not out, but a well-taken review revealed the murmur that sent Mulder trudging from the middle.
The wicket was Starc's 450th in Test cricket, making him just the fourth Australian to reach that milestone, after Shane Warne, Glenn McGrath and Nathan Lyon.
Unfortunately for the Aussies, Starc's early breakthrough proved a lone bright spot in an otherwise pitch-black day in Gqeberha.
4. South Africa better Australia's Durban recovery
It was a truly remarkable day of recovery from the South Africans.
Having started the morning on 5-97, Mulder's early dismissal further reduced the hosts to 6-110, a position even more dire than where Australia found itself on day one in Durban.
The Aussies finished the opening day of the series teetering on 6-124, but went on to score 390, with Matt Renshaw starring in a collection of lower-order partnerships to add a further 266 runs.
South Africa's recovery in Gqeberha was eerily similar but even more dramatic, with Bavuma and his more-than-capable lower-order teammates adding a further 315 runs from that initial position of peril early on day three, with Bavuma and Jansen contributing 132 runs for the seventh wicket and Bavuma and Simon Harmer a South African record of 183 for the eighth.
That unlikely Australian rescue-job laid the foundation for a dominant victory in Kingsmead, and the South Africans will be hoping for something similar at St. George's.
But given the amount of time already lost in this game and how placid the wicket still looks to be, the Proteas may well require something very special to eke out a result on days four and five.
5. A final sting in the tail for Australia
With South Africa's innings declared on 9-425 after Bavuma's late dismissal, Australia's opening batters were faced with an excruciatingly short period in quickly fading light after an arduous, demoralising day in the field.
And Nic Maddinson's lazy waft outside off certainly looked like the shot of a man who had spent seven hours being ground into the dirt.
The veteran was nicked off for a duck by returning South African spearhead Kagiso Rabada with the fourth ball of the innings.
Nightwatchman Scott Boland, mercifully, only had to survive the final two balls of that opening over before the umpires determined the light was only good enough for spin.
The Australians will begin day four at 1-3 and, somehow, 422 runs behind.

Explainer-Three issues defining the 2026 US midterm elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
19:16:14 UTC
04:16:14 KST

Explainer-Three issues defining the 2026 US midterm elections
WASHINGTON, Oct 20 - President Donald Trump’s record-low popularity, voter frustration over the cost of living and a fierce immigration fight are shaping the November 3 midterm elections, which will determine whether Republicans keep control of Congress or Democrats gain the power to challenge his administration.
Republicans hold narrow majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take control of each chamber.
The outcome will hinge on a relatively small number of competitive races, but the campaigns are being shaped nationally by Trump himself and voter concerns over affordability and immigration.
Here is a look at the three issues defining the election:
DONALD TRUMP
The president has put himself front and center in the closing stretch of the campaign cycle despite his record-low popularity, with upcoming rallies in Florida, Iowa, Michigan and Texas. Trump's approval rating has fallen to an all-time low 31%, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll. Yet he has repeatedly urged voters to pretend he's on the ballot, an effort that could motivate Democrats and independents to rally against his party despite the message being aimed at increasing turnout among Trump's base.
Democrats have said Trump has broken his campaign promises to lower costs and end wars. They have vowed to tackle an affordability agenda to reduce Americans' cost of living and hold the administration accountable for alleged corruption if voters give them control of either chamber.
AFFORDABILITY
Voters have consistently ranked the cost of living as the top issue this election cycle. Half of registered voters surveyed in a recent Reuters/Ipsos poll cited the cost of living as the most important factor in how they will vote. In the same poll, voters highlighted healthcare, gasoline, food and housing as the top household bills lawmakers should focus on.
Republicans' top legislative achievement was a tax cut extension that slashed roughly $1 trillion in spending for Medicaid, the government health insurance program for low-income Americans, and other health programs. Democrats last year forced a government shutdown over a failed effort to extend expiring health subsidies that benefited 24 million Americans.
Gas prices have spiked since the US and Israel launched military strikes on Iran in February. The national average price of gas is $4.28 — $1.20 higher than it was a year ago, according to AAA. The average cost of diesel is $6.32 — a $2.70 increase from a year earlier.
Grocery costs are up 1.8% over the past year, according to the US Bureau of Labor Statistics data on consumer prices. Federal Housing Finance Agency data show home prices rose 2.1% over the past year. Congress passed a bipartisan housing bill earlier this year. It became law without Trump's signature.
IMMIGRATION
Preliminary data from the Department of Homeland Security showed a 95% drop in migrants apprehended at the southwest border compared to former President Joe Biden's administration. The agency said there have been no Border Patrol releases the entire fiscal year for the first time ever.
But fatal encounters with federal immigration agents have occurred in Maine, Minnesota and Texas. The backlash to the death of two US citizens in Minnesota pulled many Democrats in competitive primaries to the left this year, with some candidates calling for the impeachment of then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and others saying Immigration and Customs Enforcement should be abolished.
Democrats and Republicans sparred over immigration funding this year in a stalemate that forced Republicans to unilaterally pass a $70 billion bill to fund ICE and the Border Patrol for the remainder of Trump's presidency. Republicans counter Democrats' criticism by saying Democrats support open borders.
Federal immigration officials also raided the Washington home of Democratic US Representative Ilhan Omar of Minnesota this month, drawing widespread condemnation from Democrats. A person familiar with the case against Omar told Reuters one potential aim of the investigation could be to strip her of US citizenship and deport her.
OTHER ISSUES
Artificial intelligence and data centers, cryptocurrency, abortion and Israel could also influence voters in individual races. In Ohio's Senate race, for example, Democratic nominee Sherrod Brown has labeled Republican Senator Jon Husted the face of data centers, and the crypto super PAC Defend American Jobs has spent more than $46 million to reelect Husted over Brown, a former US senator who chaired the chamber's Banking Committee.
In Maine's Senate race, Democratic nominee Troy Jackson is hoping voters don't forget that Republican Senator Susan Collins helped confirm Brett Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court, which later overturned the federal right to abortion. Collins is on the election ballot for the first time since the high court made abortion a state issue rather than a federal right.
In Michigan, Republican nominee Mike Rogers has indicated he would accept help from a pro-Israel super PAC that spent more than $30 million backing Democratic US Representative Haley Stevens in her unsuccessful primary against Abdul El-Sayed, who now faces Rogers in the general election. The group has already spent more than $280,000 on mailers against El-Sayed.
Earlier this week, Trump endorsed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection. REUTERS

Türkiye's maritime deal with Libya opens door to ‘long-term’ partnership, says deputy commander in Libya’s east
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
19:13:39 UTC
04:13:39 KST

Rania Abushamala
20 October 2026•Update: 20 October 2026
Saddam Haftar, deputy commander of Libyan forces in the country’s east, said Tuesday that Libya’s maritime agreement with Türkiye offers opportunities to strengthen bilateral cooperation, investment, and a “long-term” partnership.
In a statement on US social media platform Facebook, Haftar welcomed parliament’s unanimous decisions to approve the agreement and repeal previous resolutions against the pact.
He said the measures reflect a willingness to “move beyond past disagreements and address sovereign matters and foreign relations based on Libya’s supreme interests.”
The agreement also opens broader prospects for developing bilateral relations and strengthening cooperation, investment, and a “long-term” partnership, as well as supporting opportunities for understanding on regional issues, he said.
Haftar described the maritime agreement as a tool that “could help protect Libya’s rights and economic interests in the Mediterranean and advance shared interests with Türkiye as an influential regional power.”
He said his position is rooted in principles that included prioritizing Libya’s interests, safeguarding its sovereignty and territorial integrity, preserving independent national decision-making, and rejecting interference in its internal affairs.
These principles, he added, guide relations with all countries and take precedence over political considerations or alignments.
Haftar said Libya’s national priority continues to be ending its divisions, unifying state institutions, and restoring state authority across the country.
Those steps would enable Libya to manage its foreign relations and protect its interests and resources independently, he said.
He added that developing relations with Türkiye forms part of a “broader approach to cooperation with regional and Mediterranean countries.”
“The doors to cooperation and partnership will remain open to all countries with which we share common interests, on the basis of equality, mutual respect, and good neighborliness,” he said.
Haftar reaffirmed his commitment to Libya’s unity, sovereignty, and independent decision-making.
His remarks followed Libya's House of Representatives approving the maritime jurisdiction agreement with Türkiye on Tuesday, reversing its previous rejection of the deal.
Türkiye and Libya signed the maritime delimitation agreement in November 2019, establishing the boundaries of their respective maritime jurisdiction areas in the Mediterranean Sea.

Nigeria reports first Ebola case in a decade in woman who arrived from Uganda

Nigeria reports first Ebola case in a decade in woman who arrived from Uganda
ABUJA, Oct 20 - Nigeria reported its first Ebola case in about a decade on Tuesday after a foreign woman living in the capital tested positive for the viral infection after arriving from Uganda.
A senior public health official told a local television station the woman is "originally from Uganda and so made a quick travel to Uganda."
Uganda's health ministry said she had travelled to Democratic Republic of Congo, which is battling the world's second-largest Ebola outbreak on record with more than 9,000 cases and more than 4,000 deaths so far.
Odianosen Ehiakhamen, the assistant director of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention, told Arise TV the Ebola patient arrived in Nigeria on October 5 and started feeling unwell on October 7.
She sought treatment in a private hospital on October 11 for malaria-like symptoms and was tested for Ebola on October 19, Ehiakhamen added.
Most of the 44 contacts traced so far are healthcare workers and the patient's husband, a Swiss national who lives with her in Abuja.
UGANDA SAYS IT HAS NO ACTIVE EBOLA CASES
Health authorities are also tracing passengers who travelled with her on the same Ethiopian Airlines flights from Uganda but they do not think she was symptomatic while flying.
Nigerian Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate told public broadcaster NTA that the woman was in isolation and receiving quality medical care.
Uganda's health ministry said in a statement that "travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here."
It added that Uganda had "no confirmed active Ebola cases."
Pate said Nigeria had successfully contained Ebola in 2014 and had the systems in place to respond to the new case.
Congo's Ebola outbreak was declared in mid-May but may have started months earlier, caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain.
Uganda reported 20 cases in May and June, mostly imported from Congo, but was declared free of the virus by the World Health Organization in August.
Kenya has reported nine Ebola cases this month, all linked to a person who had travelled from Congo. REUTERS

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio — who is in India for a three-day visit as the two countries seek to resolve trade tensions and deepen energy ties — has defended Washington's relationship with Islamabad, framing the engagement as similar to New Delhi's ties with Tehran.

We're against anybody who sponsors terrorism. In my new role — I'm no longer a senator; I'm the Secretary of State — I have to manage the foreign policy of the United States. And that does require us to have relationships with countries, including those that we may have some disagreements with."
According to an interview transcript released by the US Department of State, Rubio stated that the US maintains ties with nuclear-armed Pakistan, adding that from a geographical standpoint, Washington needs to maintain relations with Islamabad "in much the same way as the Government of India has to have and has a relationship and meets with leaders from Iran."
The American top diplomat added that US-Pakistan ties could help address India's concerns as well.
"I think in a way it could be a positive thing, because if we have a relationship and we can speak to them it could perhaps help us, perhaps puts us in a position to help discourage the kinds of things that India is worried about," added Rubio.
The comments came after Rubio met Indian External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar to discuss topics concerning regional and global issues, including developments in the Middle East.
US-Pakistan ties
The US and Pakistan have strengthened diplomatic and economic ties under the second Trump administration through high-level dialogue, strategic cooperation, and active mediation efforts
Pakistan has historically served as a major non-NATO ally and a key security collaborator in South Asia.
During the height of hostilities between Pakistan and India in May 2025, US President Donald Trump brokered a ceasefire following a four-day armed conflict. India, however, maintains that there was no US mediation in the truce that halted fighting involving drones, missiles, artillery, and fighter aircraft.
Trump then hosted Pakistan's army chief General Asim Munir at the White House for lunch in June in a rare diplomatic development.
Pakistan said it shot down seven Indian warplanes — including three French-made Rafale jets, a Sukhoi Su-30, and a MiG-29 — using Chinese-built aircraft such as J-10s and JF-17s) and PL-15 long-range missiles.
Indian sources initially acknowledged that three Indian fighter jets crashed in India-administered Kashmir. Some Indian officials have acknowledged the losses but have not specified how many aircraft were downed by Pakistan.
Trump maintains that the clashes resulted in 11 jets being destroyed, emphasising that his mediation efforts averted millions of casualties had the conflict escalated between the two nuclear-armed nations. Pakistan nominated the US president for the Nobel Peace Prize.
Meanwhile, Pakistan emerged as a key diplomatic mediator during the US war on Iran, relaying messages and hosting talks between Washington and Tehran, which helped pave the way for a landmark peace agreement praised by global leaders.
The 60-day Islamabad accord expired on August 17, 2026 without a comprehensive deal. Despite diplomatic setbacks, Pakistan continues efforts to revive US-Iran discussions.
On Tuesday as Rubio visited India, Pakistani army chief held talks with Iranian officials in Tehran as diplomatic efforts intensified to avert conflict involving the US and Israel.
Kashmir dispute
Historic rivals India and Pakistan remain locked in a bitter conflict over Kashmir. Both neighbours administer a part of Kashmir and claim the territory in its entirety.
They have fought two of their three wars over the territory since they gained independence from British colonial rule in 1947. China also administers a portion of Kashmir, known as Aksai Chin, following the 1962 Sino-Indian War — making the Himalayan region the world's only nuclear tri-junction.
Rebels in the India-administered Kashmir have been fighting New Delhi's rule since 1989. Many Kashmiri Muslims support deciding the future of the region through a UN-mandated plebiscite.
India claims the Kashmir revolt is backed by Pakistan. Islamabad denies the charge, and says it only offers moral, political and diplomatic support to Kashmiris. Many Kashmiris consider it a legitimate freedom struggle. Tens of thousands of civilians, rebels and Indian troops have been killed in the conflict.
India has deployed more than 500,000 troops to the region, making it one of the planet's most militarised zones.
Following Rubio’s interview that also touched on Russian oil, Ukraine war, trade deal, and anti-India sentiments in US, several Indian social media users expressed disappointment.
Pakistani accounts widely described it as an "embarrassment for Indian media" and insisted Rubio "refused to toe the Indian line," with others noted it was "much to the disappointment of Indian interviewer."

Inherited procurement system was broken, says Pollard
United Kingdom

The procurement system the government inherited was slow, expensive and not fit for a period of warfighting readiness, and procurement segmentation and new commercial pathways are intended to make buying more agile while opening opportunities to small firms and innovators, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Edward Morello, the Liberal Democrat member for West Dorset, asked what steps the department is taking to improve defence procurement.
Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, said: “The procurement system we inherited was broken. Defence procurement was slow, expensive and not fit for a period of war fighting readiness.
“Through our Procurement Segmentation and new Commercial Pathways, we are making procurement more agile, opening up opportunities for SMEs and innovators, and ensuring every pound of defence spending delivers stronger military capability and better value for the taxpayer.”
Segmentation sorts what the department buys into categories and applies different rules and timescales to each, so that a software capability or a drone does not pass through the same approval machinery as a submarine. Major platforms keep the full process, while fast-moving categories run on compressed timelines designed to be measured in months.
This publication reported when the department outlined the reforms and pledged an SME action plan, and the Defence Office for Small Business Growth was launched at the start of this year to give smaller suppliers a route in. Spending with small and medium sized enterprises is published annually by region in the department’s regional expenditure statistics.

Welsh planning inspector appointed for deep space radar

The Welsh Government has appointed a planning inspector to handle the application for the proposed deep space radar at Cawdor Barracks, and the department will continue to engage with the process with a view to reaching a positive decision swiftly, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked what discussions the Secretary of State has held with the Welsh Government on the timely determination of the planning application for the proposed Deep Space Advanced Radar Capability site, following an answer given on 11 September.
Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, said: “The Ministry of Defence has engaged with the Welsh Government at official and Ministerial level. We are pleased the Welsh Government has appointed a planning inspector and will continue to engage with the process with a view of reaching a positive decision swiftly.”
The Deep Space Advanced Radar Capability is a three-nation programme run with the United States and Australia, placing ground-based radars at sites spaced around the globe so that objects in geosynchronous orbit can be tracked continuously instead of being picked up in the gaps between passes. Each site carries an array of dish antennas able to detect and characterise objects more than twenty thousand miles up, which is where most military communications and early warning satellites sit.
Cawdor Barracks near Brawdy in Pembrokeshire was selected as the British site, giving a long-term use to an installation the Army had been due to vacate, and this publication reported that construction is expected to begin in 2027. The Australian site is in Western Australia and the American one in Texas.
Space surveillance has moved up the defence agenda as the number of satellites and the number of manoeuvring objects has grown, with the Defence Investment Plan and the new space strategy together committing billions to the domain.

Dear Heidi Levine, your attack should shame Israel into action - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20

04:00:00 KST

Dear Ms. Levine,
I don’t embarrass easily. I find much of the Israel-Palestinian conflict coverage biased against Israel. Reporters scrutinize Israel’s behavior obsessively while forever undermining Israel’s legitimacy. Still, when I read how masked vigilantes assaulted you and other unidentified journalists and Palestinians, I was – and am – ashamed.
I know that many Palestinians – not just some of their Jewish neighbors – trigger violence. I know the scene was chaotic. But I also know the attack on you was inexcusable, reprehensible. Despite your body armor and large press tags, they barraged you with bats, sticks, and kicks, breaking your rib, bloodying you, and cutting your left hand severely.
What kind of people kick a fellow human repeatedly when she is down – let alone when you posed no threat and were simply doing your job as a photographer?
And what kind of government enables such violence?
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pooh-poohs these thugs as “fringe.” Yet – once again – minimizing the problem maximizes his negligence. If it’s only a “handful of juvenile delinquents” that causes such trouble – and such reputational damage to Israel – does his failure to handle them demonstrate cowardice, fecklessness, or malevolence?
Last week, before the attack, I published a Hebrew article in Makor Rishon detailing the fundamental Israeli, Zionist, and democratic covenants political extremists keep threatening, and many coalition leaders keep violating. The crimes against you compelled me, shortly before Election Day, to sharpen the critique and blast it broadly.
Democracies rely on implicit and explicit agreements that bind citizens to one another and their government in a web of obligations and responsibilities. Israeli society saved itself on October 7 because an active, involved citizenry, today’s Minutemen and Minutewomen, mobilized spontaneously, heroically, saving us all, even when the government flopped catastrophically.
Next government needs to restore trust
On October 27, Israelis shouldn’t just ask “Who are we voting for?” but “What are we voting for?” We need leaders to restore the trust this government has shattered – occasionally abetted by extremists from Right to Left, too.
The seven broken covenants the next government must restore are:
1. The covenant of personal security: Even if you believe that Netanyahu has functioned effectively every day since October 7, the Hamas bloodbath shattered the faith most Israelis had in the government’s and the IDF’s ability to protect them.
That betrayal was exacerbated by Netanyahu’s refusal to allow a commission of inquiry to learn from the mistakes, while scapegoating Israel’s army and security personnel.
2. The covenant of shared burden: Social trust requires equal burden-sharing, especially in a besieged society, not the creation of a protected, heavily subsidized class of Torah scholars.
Meanwhile, soldiers, reservists, and their families keep sacrificing. True, every major political party indulged the ultra-Orthodox over decades. But this government was in charge precisely when it became broadly understood that mass draft evasion is unacceptable.
3. The covenant of Zionist morality: This, Ms. Levine, is the covenant most violated by the wink-wink, nudge-nudge toleration of violent extremists.
Zionism – or any form of nationalism – without morality is like a car without brakes; it hurtles wildly, endangering everyone.
True, extremists from both sides have bullied politicians they hate. We, Israel’s silenced and moral majority, must temper the crazies, demand proper law enforcement, and change the tone.
4. The covenant of human dignity: The right-wing provocateur Yinon Magal’s despicable characterization of Gadi Eisenkot as a “monkey” being manipulated by “elitist Ashkenazim” proves what happens when leaders unleash the demons of demagoguery and disrespect. Evil metastasizes.
And while so many extremists overstep, those in charge are most responsible for setting the tone and reining in the rhetoric.
5. The covenant of shared citizenship: Many of us have long mourned how Netanyahu’s mainstreaming of Itamar Ben-Gvir mocked the liberal and Jewish values of Ze’ev Jabotinsky and Menachem Begin.
But four years of Ben-Gvir’s ministerial antics, with his bigotry riling up other goons, amid the complicit silence of many on our government payroll, has harmed Israel’s democracy.
Whenever ministerial rabble-rousers question any citizen’s equality, liberty, or dignity, every citizen’s rights become conditional, not inherent. A democratic Jewish state cannot put all its citizens on probation, with their rights subject to what the government deems “acceptable” behavior.
6. The covenant of the Jewish people: As anti-Zionist antisemitism intensifies, our government and people must reinforce Jewish unity, not strain it.
While expecting basic loyalty from Jews everywhere, we Israelis, and especially our leaders, should protect Diaspora Jews, respect them, and engage them thoughtfully.
7. The covenant of competence: Finally, although Hebrew lacks an elegant translation for the term “good governance,” the pandemic of corruption, cronyism, and sheer ineptitude on so many governmental levels is unpardonable.
For four years, we’ve endured a government that cannot govern straight, occasionally reflecting softheadedness and usually hard-heartedness.
These repeated affronts threaten our even more essential covenant, of “Hatikvah,” hope. Ms. Levine, I truly regret you got caught in this maelstrom of incompetence and malice. I also hope that whoever triumphs on Election Day will create a government that renews these covenants, showing respect for all citizens and everyone our complicated Jewish state takes responsibility for.
Meanwhile, in that spirit, I call on all citizens to accept the electoral outcome, whether their side wins or loses.
On October 7, 2023, our enemies reminded us of how much unites us, and how intertwined we are. This October 27, let’s remind the world how safe, functional, and inspirational our remarkably successful experiment in the world’s only Jewish democracy continues to be.
The writer is a distinguished scholar of North American history at McGill University and a senior research fellow at the Jewish People Policy Institute. He is the author of nine books on presidential history and nine on modern Zionism, including To Resist the Academic Intifada: Letters to My Students on Defending the Zionist Dream, as well as his latest e-book, The Essential Guide to the US-Israel Partnership: the 250th Anniversary Edition.

For Lula, Brazil's sovereignty is at stake in final election
BRASILIA, Oct 20 - When Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva addressed the United Nations General Assembly last month, he used one of the world’s biggest diplomatic stages to deliver a message that has come to define what is likely the final presidential campaign of his decades-long career.
"Brazil does not fit into anyone's backyard," he said, in a veiled dig at US President Donald Trump's administration, which he believes is challenging Brazil's sovereignty.
Lula has portrayed Brazil's election as part of a wider battle against undemocratic forces, warning of "foreign interference" in a race that concludes on Sunday in a heated runoff against right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro.
In the candidates' first debate days before the vote, Lula accused the Bolsonaro family, headed by former President Jair Bolsonaro, of being "subordinate to American interests," pointing to May meetings between the Bolsonaros and Trump earlier this year before Trump imposed new tariffs on Brazilian products.
In July, Lula said the new tariffs were the result of a "plot" with the Bolsonaros "driven by electoral objectives."
Last year, the senator's brother Eduardo Bolsonaro, who lives in the US, described Trump's tariffs on Brazilian beef, coffee, fish, footwear and other goods as "bitter medicine" aimed at curbing what he called an out-of-check legal offensive against his father.
“The pressure they applied to get the United States to put tariffs on Brazil, and their appeal for Brazil to suffer some harm," Lula said at the debate. "The brother is over there inciting a coup against Brazil."
The family denied the accusations. The State Department has also denied previous accusations of election interference.
HARD PATH TO VICTORY
The election's first round showed the limits to Lula's message. Over 47% of voters backed Bolsonaro, an outspoken Trump ally, nearly 2 percentage points ahead of Lula.
Lula enters the final days trailing slightly in the polls to Bolsonaro, whose father is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a failed coup against Lula's electoral win in 2022.
Although Lula enters the election as the underdog, he is confident he can stage a dramatic comeback.
He has done so before. After spending 580 days in prison in 2018 and 2019 on a corruption conviction that was later overturned, he narrowly defeated Jair Bolsonaro in 2022.
"As long as I am alive, the far right will not return to power in this country," he has said on the campaign trail.
ALLIES VIEW HIM AS BULWARK AGAINST US POWER
Lula and his allies continue to fight what they see as international interference to keep him from a fourth term. His campaign accused US tech giant Meta, which owns Instagram, WhatsApp and Facebook, of manipulating social media days before the vote.
Meta blamed global technical glitches and denied political bias.
Lula has portrayed his opponent as a stand-in for a broader right-wing movement, sharing images linking him to Trump, Argentina’s President Javier Milei and Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
With right-wing parties sweeping recent elections across Latin America, Lula and his allies see Sunday’s runoff as a chance to stem the region's conservative drift.
“Lula is a symbol of the fight against Trump’s imperialism ... of the liberation of Latin America and the world,” Paulo Saboia, a 67-year-old retired IT technician, said at a Lula rally in Sao Paulo. REUTERS

France backs UNESCO drive to involve more young people in political decisions
PARIS, Oct 20 - A UNESCO drive to get more young people into decision-making bodies, including those on how to prevent wars, won the backing of France's foreign minister on Tuesday, as the country faces a wave of student protests, many of which have turned violent.
The appeal, formally adopted by the UN's cultural and education agency after being drafted by 145 young representatives from 135 countries, calls for youth representation in decision-making bodies, conflict prevention and mediation mechanisms.
The initiative comes at a time where student-led protests in recent weeks have highlighted frustration among some young people over their perceived lack of influence on political decisions.
"Young people's voices matter," Jean-Noel Barrot said on X following UNESCO's backing of the appeal.
The UNESCO proposal also urged governments to establish an international framework to govern artificial intelligence, which the signatories describe as a new threat to peace, and to create public mechanisms to monitor implementation of their recommendations.
High school students are due to join a new round of national protests on Saturday vowing to bring the government to account over what they call a dysfunctional system, worsened by spending cuts spurred by France's budget crunch, with student bodies demanding to be heard.
"Peace among nations, like civic peace, rests on the ability of enlightened women and men to settle their differences respectfully, recognising that they share a common future," added Barrot. REUTERS

Oxfam analysis finds Peru’s richest captured 42 percent of all new wealth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
18:53:51 UTC
03:53:51 KST

Oxfam analysis finds Peru’s richest captured 42 percent of all new wealth
Only 1.4 percent of all new wealth created between 2019 and 2025 went to the poorest 50 percent of the population, report finds.
The top 1 percent in Peru captured 42 percent of all new wealth generated between 2019 and 2025, an analysis by the nonprofit group Oxfam has found.
The report, released on Tuesday, highlights growing inequality in the South American country and raises questions about how the government is addressing deepening social divisions.
“Economic inequality in Peru has remained stubbornly high for decades. And when people feel that the same people always win, that nothing changes and nothing can change, inequality starts to look less like an injustice and more like the natural order of things,” said Alejandra Alayza, the executive director of Oxfam in Peru.
“That is a dangerous kind of fatalism, and we must tear it down.”
The nonprofit told Al Jazeera in an email that the 42 percent figure represents an increase from the 2000 to 2019 period, when the top 1 percent captured about 39 percent of all new wealth.
Just 1.4 percent of new wealth from 2019 to 2025 went to the poorest 50 percent of the country’s population, according to the group.
Experts warn the trend bodes poorly for public faith in government and democratic institutions.
Oxfam worked with the Institute for Peruvian Studies, a think tank in Lima, to publish a report this month on Peruvians’ perceptions of inequality in their country.
The groups found that 84 percent of Peruvians believed their country is governed by powerful interests that shape politics to their benefit. More than 75 percent also said that wealthy corporations and individuals avoid paying their fair share of taxes.
The survey also suggested that public opinion was in favour of action to address the issue.
About 70 percent of respondents said they want the government to do more to reduce inequality, which a majority felt had limited access to services such as healthcare, employment, education and justice.
“The undeniable scale of public support for action to reduce inequality leaves no room for complacency,” Alayza said.
“Inequality is not a force of nature; it is made by political choices. And different choices can build a different Peru.”
Political instability
Peru’s rising inequality has been accompanied by a period of political turmoil, particularly in the presidential palace.
A stream of probes, scandals and impeachments has led to Peru being governed by nine presidents in the last 10 years.
The latest, right-wing President Keiko Fujimori, was sworn into office in July after a narrow race that saw voting delays and heated recriminations among the leading candidates.
Experts believe powerful interests have found opportunity amid the political tumult.
“It’s sort of a paradox. How can you have such a rotation among elites but still have a relatively narrow political-criminal-business elite that holds a lot of power? I think both things are true in Peru,” Will Freeman, a fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, a US-based think tank, told Al Jazeera.
Part of the political upheaval has come from clashes between the presidency and Peru’s powerful Congress, which has the power to impeach executive leaders on the basis of “moral incapacity”, an ambiguous term.
The repeated leadership shakeups have weakened Peru’s democracy, according to analysts.
In December 2022, for instance, then-President Pedro Castillo announced that he would illegally dissolve Congress in response to repeated attempts to impeach him.
His subsequent removal and arrest prompted widespread protests. The government of Castillo’s successor, Dina Boluarte, implemented a months-long crackdown on the demonstrations that rights groups say included widespread abuses for which there has been little accountability.
In the years since, the Peruvian government has also taken steps to weaken judicial oversight and hollow out anticorruption watchdogs.
The nonprofit Freedom House, which measures political freedom in countries around the world, ranked Peru as “free” in 2022. But its ranking dropped the following year to “partly free”, in light of the deadly clashes between security forces and protesters.
In its 2026 report, Freedom House maintained that Peru was only “partly free”, citing in part the denial of full political rights to certain groups, including Indigenous peoples.
“High-profile corruption scandals have eroded public trust in government, and the weakening of judicial independence has impacted the country’s governing bodies,” the nonprofit said.
Powerful interests, both licit and illicit, have taken advantage of those changes.
“The groups themselves are unstable and fluid,” said Freeman. “And yet, I think Peruvians are right to conclude that, generally, they are wielding outsized influence in defence of their own commercial interests or political power rather [than] in service of some kind of general welfare.”

Saudi Arabia postpones ‘Davos in the Desert’ due to Houthi strikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
18:50:01 UTC
03:50:01 KST

‘Davos in the Desert’ cancelled over war
Saudi Arabia has postponed its flagship investment forum until next year, organizers have announced, as Houthi strikes have continued to hit the kingdom.
Launched in 2017, the Future Investment Initiative (FII) conference, often dubbed ‘Davos in the Desert’, brings together world leaders, top executives and global investors.
“This decision comes from a deep commitment to our partners, members, speakers, and delegates,” FII Institute CEO Dr. Maha Bint Mishari Al Saud said in a press release on Monday, adding that the new 2027 dates would be announced soon.
The event was set to mark the conference’s tenth anniversary, with financial and tech heavyweights including BlackRock CEO Larry Fink, Alphabet President and Chief Investment Officer Ruth Porat, and Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon expected to attend.
The conflict with the Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah, has caused broader disruptions in Saudi Arabia. Government agencies and businesses in Riyadh, including those at the Kingdom Center and King Abdullah Financial District, have instructed some employees to work remotely, according to Al Jazeera.
The renewed confrontation kicked off in July, when Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces struck the airport in Houthi-held Sanaa, disrupting years of relative calm following a UN-brokered truce in 2022. The Houthis blamed Riyadh for the attack.
The Houthis retaliated with missile strikes and declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia. The move came in response to restrictions imposed by the Saudi-led coalition on Yemen’s Houthi-controlled ports and airports since March 2015, when Riyadh intervened in the country’s civil war.
The Houthis also seized territory along Yemen’s Red Sea coast near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a crucial shipping route for Saudi oil exports, as traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains heavily disrupted by the US-Iran conflict.
The escalating conflict has caused civilian casualties in both Saudi Arabia and Yemen. Multiple Houthi attacks on Riyadh airport earlier this month killed at least 14 people and injured more than 300, according to the Saudi authorities. Saudi strikes have killed 141 people and wounded 395 since September 3, most of them women and children, the Houthi-run Health Ministry said on Monday.

Polish lawmakers back easing the abortion ban — do they face a presidential veto?
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
21:48:56 EEST
03:48:56 KST

Polish lawmakers back easing the abortion ban — do they face a presidential veto?
Kyiv • UNN
Poland’s lower house backed abortion in cases of fetal abnormalities and the decriminalization of providing assistance. The president is likely to block the bill.
Poland's lower house of parliament voted to allow abortions in cases where fetal abnormalities are detected, as well as to decriminalize providing assistance in obtaining an abortion. In this way, lawmakers are attempting to repeal the near-total abortion ban introduced by the previous government, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
However, as the publication notes, the bill will almost certainly be blocked by the nationalist president's veto.
In Poland—a predominantly Catholic country—a near-total abortion ban was introduced in 2021 after the Constitutional Tribunal ruled that terminating a pregnancy due to fetal abnormalities was unconstitutional. The ban sparked mass protests.
The pro-European coalition led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk won the 2023 election, in part because of its promise to ease restrictions on abortion. The president has indicated that he will block any liberalization of legislation in this area.
"The reality is that these legislative acts are only a very limited reform and will not improve the situation for the majority of women in Poland who need access to abortion," Leah Hoctor, vice president for Europe at the Center for Reproductive Rights, said in a comment to Reuters.
A separate bill is currently being considered by parliamentary committees that would legalize abortion at a woman's request up to 12 weeks of pregnancy.
Tusk's government has already taken steps to expand access to abortion within the framework of the current legislation, which allows pregnancy termination, in particular, on mental health grounds.
Under the current law, abortions are permitted only in cases of rape or incest, as well as when there is a threat to the woman's health or life.

Golan to 'Post': Netanyahu 'burned bridges' with US, will do everything to replace him - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
18:45:43 UTC
03:45:43 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government has turned Israel into a “liability” for the United States’ diplomatic efforts in the Middle East, the Democrats Party leader Yair Golan told The Jerusalem Post in a recent interview, adding that his party would do “everything possible” to replace the premier.
Golan told the Post that the government “burned bridges” with both Democrats and Republicans in Washington, leaving Israel “outside the room” for negotiations on agreements crucial to the country’s security.
“This government has burned bridges with Democrats and Republicans in the United States, and even Trump is now making decisions and striking deals on Gaza, Lebanon and Iran without Israel at the table,” Golan said.
“When the American president seeks to shape the Middle East and negotiate agreements while Israel is left outside the room, it is evidence of how this government has turned a strategic asset into an international liability.”
Golan made the remarks in a written response to a wide range of questions from the Post, in which he argued that the Arab party Ra’am should be included in the next coalition.
He also outlined his party’s positions on Palestinian statehood, coalition red lines, and the policies it would seek to implement in the next government.
The left-wing party is one of the major factions in the opposition bloc seeking to replace current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the October 27 elections.
Recent polling shows the Democrats receiving approximately nine seats. The party was formed through a merger between the Labor and Meretz parties. Golan previously served as IDF deputy chief of staff and an MK for the far-left Meretz party.
Golan: Ben-Gvir, Smotrich turned the US against Israel
Sharply criticizing Netanyahu and his far-right coalition partners, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, Golan stated that they had destroyed Israel’s relationship with the US. “Netanyahu, Smotrich and Ben-Gvir have turned Israel from America’s principal regional ally into an obstacle to regional progress.”
The Democrats are the only party in the opposition to openly support the inclusion of Arab parties, namely Ra'am, in a potential coalition.
This position is at odds with the party’s potential coalition partners, some of which hold a hard-line stance against such a move following October 7. When asked whether the opposition bloc would sit with the Arab parties and if this would cause division, Golan said that his party would do all it could to replace Netanyahu.
“The gravity of this moment is clear to everyone. I can assure you that the Democrats will do everything possible to establish an alternative government,” he said.“I cannot speak on behalf of the other leaders in the opposition bloc. That is precisely why it is so important to strengthen the Democrats if we want to ensure meaningful change,” Golan added.
When he was asked if a coalition with the Arab parties was viable after October 7, Golan said that “over 20% of Israeli citizens are Arabs. Excluding them from participating in government just on the basis of their national or ethnic identity is unacceptable.”“In the previous government, in which all the current opposition party heads served, [Ra’am party leader] Mansour Abbas was an excellent political partner.”
“I therefore see no reason why we should rule out working with him again, based on an agreed policy platform, as part of an effort to build a coalition and replace the current government.”Golan did not acknowledge whether the Joint List, which consists of the other three major Arab parties Hadash, Ta’al, and Balad, should be a coalition partner. Regarding other coalition red lines, Golan responded about sitting in coalition with the haredi (ultra-Orthodox) parties that “I have stated this before, and I stand by it: the parties that were part of the government responsible for the failures of 7 October should not be part of the future coalition we seek to build.”When asked how the Democrats would try to integrate haredim into broader Israeli society, Golan said that “sharing the burden is... an urgent national necessity.”
Golan plans to integrate haredim into Israeli society
Elaborating on his party’s plans, Golan said that every citizen would “undergo a state-administered assessment process and be assigned to military or civilian service, with the IDF’s manpower needs taking priority.”
“We will end benefits for those who evade service and redirect government incentives away from non-enlistment and towards service,” Golan pledged, adding that the party would promote reforms to the state education system for the haredi sector.
Beyond his plans for the sector, the Democrats chief stressed that the party would demand the Education Ministry portfolio in the next government. “There are many urgent and consequential challenges in education, and reform in this area must be a national priority,” he said. The Democrats’ predecessors have historically supported a two-state solution, although Golan has in the past called for a more nuanced solution following October 7.
The Democrats' position concerning a Palestinian state
Regarding the party’s current stance on a Palestinian state, Golan said, “the illusion of ‘managing’ the conflict or ‘shrinking’ it cannot continue.” “We must work actively to end the conflict, as part of a comprehensive regional agreement that guarantees Israel’s security and enables separation from the Palestinians,” he said.
When asked who would be in charge of a Palestinian state, and how it would be governed, Golan said that “separation from the Palestinians requires leadership on their side that we can work with, no compromise on our security, and international support.”
Outlining the stages Israel must take, Golan stated that first it is necessary to “restore Israel’s place among the moderate powers in the region and renew our strategic alliances with the US and European countries.” “Second, we must ensure that Hamas is dismantled as a governing force and prevented from rebuilding its tunnel network or preparing another massacre.”“Third, we must combat terrorism in all its forms, including Jewish terrorism in the West Bank,” he added.
How will Yair Golan combat settler violence in the West Bank
In its party platform, the Democrats argue against annexation of the West Bank. Golan underscored this policy, condemning the rise of Jewish settler violence in the area, and urged them to work against it.“We will work to halt annexation efforts to preserve Israel as a Jewish and democratic state... illegal outposts and farms violate the law, drain budgets and are a security liability.”
“Restoring law and order in the West Bank is an urgent priority, so we will adopt a zero-tolerance policy towards terrorism, whether Jewish or Palestinian,” the former IDF deputy chief added, further calling to strengthen security coordination with the Palestinian Authority.
Golan has been a fierce critic of Netanyahu’s military approach following October 7, calling for the government to seek diplomatic solutions over repeated rounds of fighting with its adversaries. Speaking on Israel’s multiple military fronts, Golan argued that diplomatic agreements are “essential” in achieving lasting security, stressing that his party will pursue policies that “combine military resolve with diplomatic initiative.”
He sharply criticized the approach of Netanyahu’s government, stating that it has pursued “a policy of putting out fires rather than taking the initiative, international isolation rather than building diplomatic alliances, and endless war rather than long-term security.”
Despite that, Golan pointed at Lebanon as an “opportunity for significant change,” hailing President Joseph Aoun as the “most promising leader for a generation.” Golan called on the international community to support Aoun’s government in preventing Iranian weapons smuggling to Hezbollah and driving the terrorist organization away from Israel’s northern border.
Golan: Israel needs to guarantee 'freedom of and from religion'
The party has also placed significant importance on the separation of religion and state.
While Golan has asserted that he wants to keep Israel a “Jewish and democratic state,” he has also stressed the importance of allowing citizens to live “according to their own beliefs.”
Golan said the Democrats want “a country that respects Jewish tradition as a source of identity, culture, and belonging, but never uses it as a tool of coercion,” while guaranteeing “freedom of religion and freedom from religion.”
The party leader called for concrete reforms to make this a reality, including recognition of all streams of Judaism and civil marriage, along with an “end to the Chief Rabbinate’s monopoly over conversion and kashrut certification.”
He also called for public transportation to be available on Shabbat and “an end to religious coercion within the IDF.”
Regarding the party’s “day-one” plans for the next government, Golan said that it is “unacceptable” that a state commission of inquiry into October 7 failures has not yet been established.“We should also legislate term limits for prime ministers, and amend the current legislation to explicitly state that those facing criminal charges cannot be prime minister,” he said.
Golan also said he would act to repeal all laws passed by the sitting government as part of its judicial reform, calling for a “longer process of constitutional reform that strengthens our democratic institutions, with the Declaration of Independence at its heart.”

Herzog says Hungary is an ally against Israel's fight against terror

“Hungary has been a friend and an ally on this long and difficult path,” he said.

Israeli hospital launches AI system to enable hospitalized children to communicate without speaking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
18:45:00 UTC
03:45:00 KST

Clalit-Schneider Children's Medical Center and Code for Israel launched an AI-powered system that lets children who cannot speak communicate with medical teams and family members.
The system uses AI to create personalized, printable communication boards in under five minutes, tailored to each child's needs, age, language, gender, and background.
Communication boards can be essential for children who cannot speak to express pain or communicate their needs. Many hospitalized children have pre-existing language difficulties, while others may require ventilation that prevents them from speaking. The children may not yet have learned to write or are too weak to do so. Communication boards allow them to communicate without speaking or writing.
Previously, preparing customized communication boards could take up to several hours. The new system reduces the time to minutes.
Existing boards can also be updated, shared with professionals, and stored within a reusable library.
System designed to allow children to communicate, teams to spend more time with patients
“When a child cannot speak, they don’t just lose their voice - they may also lose the ability to say that they are in pain, that they are afraid, or that they simply want their parents. For us, technology is not the story. The story is restoring children’s ability to communicate, express themselves, and participate actively in their care. This new system allows us to create personalized communication boards within minutes, enabling us to provide this support to many more children,” Dr. Oshrat Sella Weiss, head of the Speech-Language Pathology Service at Clalit-Schneider Children’s Medical Center, said.
The system will also let teams spend more time with patients, CEO of Code for Israel Idan Roll added.

Concerns about corruption have become a potent issue that the right has sought to capitalise on, a dynamic that Lula has tried to turn to his advantage in the closing weeks of the race.
Worries about US interference have also loomed over the race following a series of interventions by the Trump administration in Brazilian domestic matters, and reports that the US social media giant Meta had taken steps to restrict Lula’s online campaign prompted a legal complaint.

Tehran session to explore British composer Malcolm Arnold’s musical legacy
TEHRAN- A specialist session examining the film music of British composer Sir Malcolm Arnold, known for his nine symphonies and Oscar-winning score for “The Bridge on the River Kwai,” will be held at Arasbaran Cultural Center in Tehran on Thursday.
The 12th session in a series devoted to composers of the English school will feature Nasrollah Davoudi, a composer, translator and music critic, who will discuss Arnold’s distinctive musical language and analyze selected examples of his film scores.
The session will include excerpts from Arnold’s compositions, offering an opportunity to explore his approach to orchestration, melody and dramatic expression.
Born in Northampton on October 21, 1921, Arnold became one of the most prolific British composers of the 20th century, producing works across a wide range of genres, including symphonies, concertos, chamber music, ballets, operas and film scores.
He studied trumpet and composition at the Royal College of Music in London and began his professional career as an orchestral musician. He joined the London Philharmonic Orchestra in 1941, later becoming its principal trumpet. In 1948, he left the orchestra to devote himself to composition full-time.
Arnold’s output combined a strong melodic sensibility with colorful orchestration and a musical language rooted in tonality while incorporating modern elements. His works for the concert hall include nine symphonies, more than 20 concertos and a number of concert overtures, among them “Beckus the Dandipratt” and “Tam O’Shanter.”
His stage works include ballets such as “Homage to the Queen” and “Rinaldo and Armida,” as well as the one-act opera “The Dancing Master.” His versatility also extended to music for brass and wind ensembles, chamber compositions and vocal works.
Arnold achieved international recognition through his extensive work for cinema. He composed more than 130 film scores, including music for David Lean’s 1957 war drama “The Bridge on the River Kwai,” which earned him an Academy Award in 1958. Other notable film scores include “The Inn of the Sixth Happiness,” “Hobson’s Choice” and “Whistle Down the Wind.”
His film compositions helped establish his reputation beyond the concert hall, while his symphonies and stage works demonstrated a broader artistic range, encompassing both accessible melodies and more serious, emotionally charged writing.
Arnold was knighted in 1993 for his services to music. He died in Norwich on September 23, 2006, at the age of 84.
The free session will take place at Arasbaran Cultural Center, located on Jolfa Street, north of Seyyed Khandan Bridge, Shariati Street.
