Egypt moves toward sending troops to Saudi Arabia to help defend against attacks by Iran-backed Houthis
Cairo - Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi has asked the country's Parliament to authorize the military to help defend Saudi Arabia after Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels intensified their attacks on the kingdom, targeting airports and oil infrastructure.
Al-Sisi stressed that it would be a defensive mission and only if the kingdom requests assistance.
"Egypt will take any measures requested by Saudi Arabia to protect and defend it," al-Sisi said Saturday during a military graduation ceremony.
Under Egypt's Constitution, the president must consult the National Defense Council and obtain approval from two-thirds of Parliament before deploying the armed forces on a combat mission abroad.
On Sunday, al-Sisi chaired a meeting of the National Defense Council, which reviewed what the Egyptian presidency described as the "grave escalations unfolding in the region" and the "unacceptable attacks" against Saudi Arabia.
The council pledged to provide "all necessary and possible forms of support to the sisterly Kingdom of Saudi Arabia to defend its security and stability, and to safeguard its resources, territorial integrity, and Islamic holy sites."
Egypt has managed, so far, to stay out of all the recent military conflicts in the region and has tried to de-escalate and find political solutions. For some, this is one of al-Sisi's greatest achievements.
But Samir Ragheb, a retired army brigadier and political and strategic analyst, told CBS News that it was time for Egypt to make good on commitments it had made to helping secure the region.
"Egypt has repeatedly pledged to support the security of the Gulf states and has issued numerous statements reaffirming this commitment," Ragheb said. "However, this is a time of war, not politics and statements. If Egypt fails to deliver on these promises, they will lose their meaning and amount to nothing more than empty threats."
"The Gulf states have invested billions of dollars in Egypt. Morally, it's Egypt's turn to return the favor," he said.
Parliament convened an emergency session on Sunday and was expected to approve the resolution on Tuesday, but the vote was postponed until next Monday.
The Egyptian Social Democratic Party instructed its parliamentary bloc to abstain from voting on the resolution, saying in a statement it had not received sufficient information about "the mission's scope, costs, and risks, as well as the arrangements in place to protect Egyptian forces."
Ragheb is certain the region is heading toward a more severe escalation.
"Egypt is not going to defend the kingdom against the Houthis," he said. "The threat is much bigger than the Houthis. This includes Iran, Iraqi militias and sleeper cells within the kingdom itself."
However, he also believes Egypt will lose much of its influence in the region if it doesn't intervene.
"If you want to be a regional player, you must play a role," he said. "Otherwise, you will lose your seat at the table."
Ragheb argued that the United States' refusal to attack the Houthis in support of Saudi Arabia created a vacuum that must be filled by others. He said Egypt should take on the Arab share of that role.
Other regional powers are also trying to fill the vacuum. In August, Saudi Arabia signed a joint defense agreement with Turkey and Pakistan known as the Mecca Accords.
"Even before Saudi Arabia asked for Egyptian support, the Mecca Accords was a death certificate for the idea of relying on America for any form of defense," Ragheb said.

Hundreds of Moroccan personnel trained for Gaza force deployment
Hundreds of Moroccan personnel have undergone training for deployment as part of a multinational stabilisation force in Gaza, according to a Board of Peace official who spoke to The Times of Israel (TOI) on Monday.
Under the Gaza plan envisioned by US President Donald Trump's"Board of Peace" following the October 2025 ceasefire, an International Stabilisation Force (ISF) would be deployed to secure areas following the withdrawal of Israeli forces. The force would also train new Palestinian police units and support the delivery of humanitarian aid.
The plan envisages Hamas stepping down from government and disarming as Israeli forces gradually withdraw from the Strip. However, Israel has refused to leave Gaza, currently occupying close to 70% of the territory and continuing near-daily attacks that have killed more than a thousand Palestinians since the ceasefire was announced.
Hamas has said it was ready to hand over power in Gaza to an interim authority and disarm in line with the ceasefire deal, but says implementation depends on Israel meeting its commitments, including halting attacks and withdrawing its forces.
Morocco, which normalised ties with Israel in 2020, said in February it would join the ISF by deploying police officers and military personnel to Gaza, becoming the first Arab country to publicly announce such a contribution.
While Albania, Kazakhstan and Kosovo have also agreed to contribute troops, Morocco is expected to be the first to put boots on the ground, officials familiar with the Board of Peace's plans told TOI in July.
In comments to the Israeli outlet on Monday, the Board of Peace official said the training of up to 500 personnel began in Morocco around late August. It involved an initial group of officers and instructors, followed by the broader contingent.
The official said the training was conducted by the ISF but could not confirm whether it had been fully completed.
Several initiatives under Trump's ceasefire plan remain on hold because of Israel, the official added. These include the construction of a proposed ISF base near the so-called Yellow Line, which would accommodate around 150 personnel. The Guardian reported last week that Israel was blocking construction of the base, delaying a key part of plans to stabilise and rebuild Gaza.
Israel's genocidal campaign has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians since 7 October 2023, most of them civilians, according to Gaza's health authorities. Thousands more are believed to remain buried beneath the rubble.
Vast tent cities now cover areas where neighbourhoods once stood, while basic services, including healthcare and sanitation, remain largely absent.

The Alliance will deploy aircraft, radars and drones to the Black Sea following a series of attacks on vessels. At least 23 sailors are missing or have died.
On Tuesday, NATO announced its intention to deploy additional maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems, and drones to the Black Sea. The decision was made following a series of deadly drone attacks on vessels in the region—attacks that are believed to be linked to Russia’s war against Ukraine. This became known after the North Atlantic Council—the NATO decision-making body—discussed security in the Black Sea at the Alliance’s headquarters in Brussels, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
According to NATO military spokesperson U.S. Army Colonel Martin L. O’Donnell, in addition to aircraft, drones, and radars, NATO member states have already sent or plan to send intelligence officers, as well as specialists to conduct forensic analyses of explosives.
NATO has not officially attributed the recent series of attacks to any specific country. At the same time, military analysts say Russia is almost certainly behind the attacks, although Moscow denies any involvement.

CAIRO – Iran told Pakistan’s army chief on Oct 20 that there would be no talks with Washington until Tehran’s demands were met, Iranian media reported, underscoring its hardening stance despite mediation efforts by key interlocutor Pakistan.
President Masoud Pezeshkian discussed mediation efforts and regional developments with Field Marshal Asim Munir in Tehran, according to Nournews.
Pakistan is a key intermediary between the United States and Iran.
Earlier mediation efforts helped produce an interim peace agreement in June, but the Islamabad Memorandum quickly unravelled as fighting between Iran and the US resumed weeks after.
Munir also met Iranian Parliament speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, who said Washington could not regain Tehran’s trust until it fulfilled seven conditions Iran set in September for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, according to an Iranian readout of the meeting.
The demands include ending a US blockade on its ports, the lifting of sanctions on its oil exports as well as ending hostilities on all regional fronts.
Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, delivered a similar message during a separate meeting with Munir, saying there would be no talks with Washington until Tehran’s demands were met, according to Iranian media.
Rezaei also said all enriched nuclear materials would remain in Iran, reiterating Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei’s position that near-weapons-grade uranium should not be shipped abroad.
US Vice-President J.D. Vance said earlier this month that Iran must make a “meaningful” reduction in its uranium enrichment capacity to satisfy US demands and end the countries’ eight-month-old war.
Israel, the US and other Western states have long accused Iran of seeking nuclear weapons, including pointing to its move to enrich uranium to 60%, far higher than needed for civilian uses and closer to the 90% needed for a weapon.
Iran denies seeking nuclear weapons. REUTERS

How French police are harnessing social media to identify looters

How French police are harnessing social media to identify looters
French police are turning to social media to identify and arrest suspects linked to last weekend’s looting and unrest. Investigators are scrutinising videos posted online alongside footage from thousands of security cameras to track suspects and gather evidence. The crackdown comes as the government vows to hold those responsible for the violence and damage to shops accountable.
France's police striving to identify and arrest looters who shattered shops in last weekend's unrest are relying on one tool to trigger their forensic follow-up: social media.
"We are working the social networks ... then we go over all that with our own tools, to see if the crimes seen on social media correspond with the crimes we're studying," said an officer seated in a special operations room with 10 screens in front of him.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Watch moreOctober 17 riots in France: Who's responsible?
The officer, identified only by his first name, Bruno, was seated in a gamer-style chair, pushing a mouse around as looked closely at a video.
He said he was convinced he had identified a group of four youths who took part in the looting that had scarred Paris streets.
Using street security cameras as well as cameras installed in the Paris region's transport system, Bruno tracked the four as they carried their haul, almost up to their home addresses.
The officer was one of a dozen specialists carrying out similar digital hunts on screens in the cramped Security Operational Coordination Centre.
Read moreFrance faces reckoning with public order policing after violent protest weekend
Footage and police footwork
The team, at work since Monday, has 80,000 security cameras at its disposal, whose images it can tap into.
Images on TikTok, Instagram, Discord and other social media platforms often provide the first clues.
"Maybe a victim talks about a crime but doesn't go to the police station to report it – they're in shock, they wonder whether it's worth going – but they post it on social media," Bruno said.
"And so from that, we start checks, see about the geolocation... See if we can find the victim and if we can find the crime. If we find the crime, we send that to the criminal investigation unit, which takes over."
Read moreFrench PM blames 'ultra-left' groups for weekend riots, promises 'massive' security deployment
At that point, footage and footwork combine to potentially build a case.
A suspect identified "might say 'no, that's not me', but if we see their face in a video..." another officer in the unit said, implying that images were persuasive evidence.
"It's not the only tool to close a case, but it's one of the very useful tools for investigators," she said.
The process has already been used in other protest-related cases recently, such as in the assault of a trainee police officer in eastern Paris, or when a group of youths threw bricks from a chimney at police in the city.
To help the video sleuths, Michel Lavaud, a security official for the greater Paris region, told his team that a platform had been set up for witnesses to crimes committed in the street during the unrest to upload images they recorded.
200 investigators
Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin has also announced that facial recognition would be used to compare a police database of mugshots with images posted on social media.
The French government, under fire for not having done enough to stop the violence, is underlining its determination to catch perpetrators of the riots and looting.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has ordered more than 200 investigators to work on that.
A specialised national detection unit has been set up, pooling transport security services with the police unit that battles organised crime.
It was scrutinising "all leads but also the available images, from security cameras, cameras in stores and videos on social media", the Paris police prefecture told AFP.
"Our deployment relies on three complementary pillars: dissuasion, through our presence in the streets; stopping crimes in the act; and prosecuting the crimes," the city's police chief, Patrice Faure, said.
Suspected looter nabbed
The painstaking screen-watching and detective work has not been needed in all cases.
In the southern town of Vienne, near Lyon, a 19-year-old man was arrested Sunday when he walked by the police station, masked and carrying bags of stolen clothes, shoes and jewellery.
Police said the man tried to run when he was spotted by officers walking out of the station, but was swiftly nabbed by other officers nearby.
"He admitted stealing some of the items from a store and said he found a bag full of items in the street that he picked up," the prosecutor's office in Vienne told AFP. It estimated the value of the looted items at €4,500 ($5,000).
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Two re-arrested over alleged help to Iranian intelligence
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
17:50:13 BST
01:50:13 KST

Two men have been re-arrested in the investigation into activity close to RAF Fairford last month on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service, with police confirming that the country the investigation relates to is Iran, according to a statement issued by Counter Terrorism Policing.
A 24-year-old United Kingdom national and a 25-year-old dual British and Iranian national, both from the London borough of Westminster, were re-arrested on Tuesday under Section 3 of the National Security Act 2023. The 24-year-old was first arrested on Sunday 27 September near the Gloucestershire base, and the 25-year-old was arrested in Westminster on Thursday 1 October.
Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of National Counter Terrorism Policing in the United Kingdom, said: “Since the events at RAF Fairford on Sunday 27 September, our specialist teams have been working tirelessly to interrogate the many lines of enquiry involved in this hugely complex investigation.
“So far seven men have been arrested in connection with our investigation.
“As a result of the ongoing efforts of our officers, earlier today two of those men were re-arrested for offences relating to Section 3 of the National Security Act, assisting a foreign intelligence service.
“This is very much a live investigation, and our evidence gathering continues, but at this time our position remains the same; we consider it highly likely that there is Iranian state involvement. Our investigators are continuing to examine what that level of involvement was and the ambition behind it.
“Due to their sensitive nature, national security investigations can take time to progress, and I’m grateful to everyone who has given my teams the time and space needed to pursue this work thoroughly and effectively.
“From the outset our priority has been to uphold the integrity of this investigation and hold those who wish to do our country harm, accountable.
“We know the public have unanswered questions. I want to be as transparent as possible and when we are in the position to share more, we will.”
The other five men arrested remain on police bail.
Moving the two men onto Section 3 of the National Security Act marks a shift in how the case is being pursued. Five men in their twenties were arrested near Fairford on 27 September, and the Westminster arrest on 1 October was made under Section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006, which covers preparing terrorist acts, with police saying at the time that they were considering all possible angles including foreign state involvement. The offence now under investigation is one of working for another country’s intelligence service.
Section 3 was created by the National Security Act 2023, which replaced the Official Secrets Acts and built a modern framework around espionage, sabotage and foreign interference. The offence carries a maximum sentence of fourteen years and applies where a person engages in conduct intended to materially assist a foreign intelligence service, including inside the United Kingdom.
RAF Fairford is a standby base operated by the United States Air Force under British ownership, with a runway long enough for the heaviest American aircraft, and it has hosted B-2 Spirit and B-52 bomber deployments to Europe for decades. It has no permanently based flying units, which is precisely what makes it useful when American bombers are sent across the Atlantic at short notice.
Louise Sandher-Jones, the Minister for the Armed Forces, told Parliament this week that security had been strengthened following the events at Fairford and at RAF Molesworth, that the Defence Investment Plan provides an additional £470 million over four years for site protection, and that the department would not hesitate to use the full range of powers available including the National Security Act.
Iran has been the subject of repeated British counter terrorism and national security operations in recent years, with MI5 having said publicly that it has disrupted a large number of plots linked to the Iranian state on British soil since 2022. None of the seven men has been charged.

Will Europe wake up and stop at the edge of a liberal abyss?

Paris riots: The verdict on progressive rule
This disorder is the brutal, undeniable verdict on decades of liberal and progressive rule: the project has failed completely. Mass migration is not simply a generous humanitarian act. It is a deliberate security threat. It is the engine of the left’s cherished dream of erasing European civilization from within – something many conservatives call the ‘Great Replacement’, and many liberals, a conspiracy theory.

Sánchez does not stand alone. Marco Rubio, America’s Secretary of State, saw the challenge during his early October European tour, which included Iceland, Greece, and Portugal. He criticized transnational bureaucracies, mass migration, the massive welfare state that he argued had bred decline, the “climate cult,” and open borders. In February, he had made the argument even more starkly at the Munich Security Conference: the “end of history” and the triumph of liberal democracy? No. A foolish idea. The West, he argued, must build a new Western century.
And the Trump administration is not just talking. It is acting. Funding is being redirected from globalist and woke agendas towards conservative voices, think tanks, and interests across Europe and beyond. If America is prepared to push back against the EU’s accelerating drift towards demographic replacement, political authoritarianism, and economic insanity, this is not simply interference; it is the strongest possible counterpressure – precisely what Europe’s patriots need right now.
Donald Trump was right. Europe needs regime change. Europe needs a conservative revolution.
The cost of liberal failure
The riots, the terror, the spread of antisemitism across Western Europe, the destruction of great monuments, and centuries of culture – Ceuta and Paris stand as stark reminders. The liberal establishment is impotent. It cannot even manage its own cities. It has turned European streets into war zones and its capitals into symbols of surrender.
Let us be clear about the stakes. For centuries, Europe stood at the heart of Western civilization. Now, its pillars are rotting under the weight of progressive dogma. Cultural clashes erupt into the very riots we see today. Antisemitism has surged: synagogues attacked, Jewish communities targeted. These are symptoms of a demographic transformation that left-wing elites frame as “humanism.”

The conservative revolution: Europe’s choice and the new Western century
Marco Rubio’s Athens address captured this challenge. He reminded the world that the West is at an inflection point. It can atrophy, serve hostile interests, or decline into irrelevance.
A return to Christian roots strengthens families and communities. Healthy nationalism fosters loyalty and shared sacrifice. Sovereignty restores democratic control over people’s destiny. These are not inherently divisive principles; they are the very pillars that once made the West great.

Trump’s America is already acting. Europe’s best interests demand the same: counterpressure against globalist networks and liberal elites.
The riots have spoken. Ceuta showed the southern front. Paris showed the domestic front. Western Europe needs to wake up and realize that the liberal experiment is over. And so is the time for complacency. The battle for sovereignty, identity, and civilizational future has begun. The question is no longer whether Europe must change, but whether its leaders will find the courage to lead that change.

Hsinchu City alone has more than 22,000 households that still rely on cylinders. Local reports say elderly people living alone and poor families struggle to pay for a gas connection.
CPC Corp, Taiwan froze cylinder prices in June and again in August. Its formula called for increases of NT$2.8 and NT$3.4 per kilogram. CPC swallowed the difference. The rice cooker depends on a different gas, the liquefied natural gas (LNG) burned in Taiwan’s power plants.
Washington handled its own fuel squeeze differently. On Oct. 9 it waived its sanctions on Russian diesel, three weeks after US President Donald Trump signed a law to harden them. That diesel feeds Russian President Vladimir Putin’s war economy, which kills Ukrainians every day. Diesel costs more than US$6 a gallon [US$1.59 per liter], and midterm elections in the US are weeks away.
Most commentary focused on pump prices in the US and on Ukraine. Taiwan should draw its own lesson.
Taiwan’s partners count on economic sanctions to deter a Chinese blockade. That threat deters only if Beijing expects the sanctions to hold even when they hurt Western voters. Russian diesel offered the easy test and the sanctions lasted 21 days.
Sanctions on China would hit American consumers on day one. Chinese goods run through US supply chains in a way that Russian fuel never did. Beijing can time a crisis for the months before an election in the US. The next presidential vote in the US falls in November 2028.
In a blockade, Taiwan’s fuel prices would climb before any sanctions take effect. Insurers move first. War-risk underwriters canceled or repriced cover around Hormuz this year. Tanker traffic collapsed within days.
Ukraine already knows how unreliable Trump can be on energy. He opened the US market to Russian diesel and told Kyiv to stop hitting Russian refineries.
Taipei already diversifies its gas suppliers. It plans to lift the US share of its LNG imports to 25 percent from about 10 percent by 2029. Taipei should diversify its partnerships the same way, without turning against Washington.
Europe cut its dependence on Russian gas after 2022. Russia supplied 45 percent of the EU’s gas imports in 2021 and roughly one-eighth last year.
EU rules set a 90 percent target for gas storage before each winter. Gas produced 16.7 percent of EU electricity last year and renewables 47.7 percent, according to the think tank Ember.
France burned gas for 3 percent of its electricity last year. Its nuclear reactors supplied 68 percent, according to grid operator RTE. Europe has also kept its ban on Russian refined products since February 2023.
Lutz Gullner heads the European Economic and Trade Office in Taipei, and Frederic Laplanche leads the French Office. Taipei should work with both offices to reach European grid operators and gas storage companies.
I argued in August, for the Central European Institute of Asian Studies, that Europe’s chips depend on Taiwan’s grid.
Taiwan imported about 95 percent of its energy last year, according to the Atlantic Council. The Ministry of Economic Affairs put crude reserves at 140 to 150 days in May. The law requires 90.
The Petroleum Administration Act (石油管理法) sets a separate floor for cooking gas, 25 days of LPG sales. Taiwan holds far less LNG. Gas-fired plants produce about half of Taiwan’s electricity. The law requires only 11 days of LNG stock, and 14 from next year. Qatar supplies about 30 percent of Taiwan’s gas. Inventories were held at about 12 days when the war with Iran disrupted Qatari cargoes. Beijing’s planners know where to aim.
A blockade reaches this family through the plug before the cylinder. Its rice cooker and its fan run on a grid that burns gas for about half its power. Taipower rationed electricity by district during the shortfall of May 2021.
A long blockade forces it to ration again, neighborhood after neighborhood.
Cooking gas lasts longer, on its 25-day floor. CPC then pays a wartime import bill to hold the cylinder price, or the price climbs. Wealthier households can stock up and buy batteries. This family lives on NT$33,000 a month and can afford neither.
Academic research points the same way. Tat-Dat Bui of National Taiwan Ocean University, Tseng Ming-Lang (曾明朗) of Asia University and three coauthors analyzed the attributes of Taiwan’s energy resilience in “Assessing energy resilience under uncertainty in Taiwan: System response ability and energy sufficiency,” Energy Strategy Reviews, vol. 53 (2024), article 101403.
Resilience depended most on the system’s ability to respond and on energy sufficiency. Infrastructure recovery and national energy efficiency planning were among the five criteria the authors found important, but underperforming, and they called for investment there.
Taipei should start with gas storage and treat 14 days as a floor.
Energy Administration officials want to go further and are surveying land for new tanks. CPC is expanding its Taichung and Guantang terminals.
The government should finance a strategic gas reserve from the national budget. That would take storage off CPC’s books and make it a matter of national security.
Taipei has also said it would consider joining an international LNG reserve in Japan or South Korea. Taipei wants a guarantee that the cargoes could still reach Taiwan in a conflict. No treaty can give that guarantee. Taipei can secure it only with tanks on its own soil.
Taipower launched a NT$564.5 billion grid resilience plan in 2022, after a fault blacked out more than 5 million households. The plan aims to decentralize the network and move substations indoors. Taipower should speed it up. A fault would darken one district, not a whole region.
Taiwan needs gas reserves that outlast the first weeks of a blockade. Then Beijing would have to hold the blockade longer, with Chinese exporters paying for every extra week.
Other governments make the sanctions promises on Taiwan’s behalf. Washington on Oct. 9 showed how quickly it can rewrite those promises. Taipei can decide how much gas Taiwan stores and the Legislative Yuan can fund it in the next budget.
Romain Blachier, associate expert at the Fondation Jean-Jaures, teaches and consults on energy policy and international relations.
The most troubling message coming out of Washington for Taipei is not any single statement but the cumulative effect of a series of signals suggesting that US President Donald Trump is rethinking Taiwan’s strategic value while viewing the US-China relationship through the lens of a transactional great-power bargain. The danger behind Trump’s new softness toward Beijing is a potential US-China bargain that undermines Taiwan’s core interests. ====================================================================================================

Why you aren’t seeing results in the gym
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
16:47:10 UTC
01:47:10 KST

We’ve all done it. Launched ourselves head first into a new regime — perhaps as the result of a new year resolution, recent breakup or aggressively unflattering photo.
“You go all in and train five days a week,” says Elizabeth Davies, personal trainer and author of Training for Your Old Lady Body. “Then life happens. You miss a few sessions, then stop completely. You feel deflated that you couldn’t stick to it. Then some time later, motivation strikes again and the cycle repeats itself.”
A better approach is to devise a realistic training schedule that actually aligns with your lifestyle.
Photo: AP
“When getting started, lower the bar,” she suggests. “Aim for two weekly strength sessions done consistently. If you manage that, and have the time, energy and inclination to do more, you can always add in a third. It’s much easier to build on something you’re doing consistently than repeatedly start over with something that’s unsustainable.”
CHANGE YOUR PROGRAM LESS
“There’s an outdated belief that you must ‘keep the body guessing’ in order for it to adapt, by continually switching up your workouts,” says Nick Finney, who has trained Robbie Williams and Jennifer Lopez. “I understand that people want to avoid boredom by changing what they do each workout, but it ends up hindering their progress. You need to practice your technique, become more proficient and give your body time to improve and get stronger. If you keep changing things up, then it’s impossible to measure progress by comparing what you achieved in previous workouts.”
Photo: AFP
Instead, he suggests adopting the principle of “progressive overload”. Simply put, this means gradually increasing the reps or weight of your lift, in order to stimulate your body to react by growing stronger. “There is a very simple formula: you might be able to lift 60kg on a bench press for five reps. If over time you are able to increase this to eight reps you can then increase the load to 64kg, which may then put your maximum reps back down to five. So you keep practising until you can get to eight reps at 64kg, before increasing the load again.”
YOU ARE TOO FOCUSED ON CARDIO
“For decades, people have associated getting fit with running, cycling or other forms of cardiovascular exercise,” says David Vaux, an osteopath and author of Stronger: 10 Exercises for a Longer, Healthier Life. “These activities are excellent for heart health, weight management, joint health and mental wellbeing — but focusing exclusively on cardio means you may be neglecting one of your body’s most valuable aging assets: your fast-twitch muscle fibers. We lose these at a faster rate as we age, which is one of the major contributors to frailty, falls, reduced mobility and loss of independence later in life. For most people, the healthiest approach is to combine regular movement with resistance training two or three times each week.”
Photo: EPA
YOU’RE ADDING JUNK VOLUME
Victorian poet Robert Browning coined the phrase “less is more.” He wasn’t writing about Bulgarian split squats, but he might as well have been.
“People often assume more is better: more weekly sessions, more exercises within each session, more sets,” says Davies. “But you don’t need to cram 10 different movements into a session. This can actually just add fatigue without much benefit.”
If muscle growth is your goal, you need to be training “close to failure” — the point at which you could not manage another good rep.
“If you’re stopping each set when you’re reaching an arbitrary number rather than because the set has become genuinely challenging, you may not be providing your body with enough stimulus to adapt,” she says. “And don’t confuse ‘feeling the burn’ with being close to failure. That burning sensation is largely associated with the buildup of metabolites during exercise, especially very high-rep sets, which are popular in some classes. It can be very uncomfortable, but discomfort isn’t necessarily the same thing as your muscles reaching the point where they could not do another good rep.”
FOCUS ON DIET
Finney warns that bad nutrition is “by far” the most common factor holding gym-goers back from reaching their goals.
“Working out hard all week can be completely negated simply by eating whatever you want. People believe workouts burn tons of calories, but most barely even burn off a balanced meal. You must tackle your nutrition if you are serious about any physical change.”
If your goal is weight loss, you need to be working in a calorie deficit. If you want to build muscle, you need to be eating a surplus of the right kind of calories, including about 2g of protein for every kilo of body weight. And don’t fall into the trap of thinking that a frenzied hour-long workout is the best way to burn off a burger.
“Blitzing a bootcamp-style workout that leaves you feeling like you’re dying may only burn about 150 more calories than doing a calmer, focused weights workout. That’s about the same amount of calories as one and a half apples. And yet the difference in effort and fatigue and potential for injury is huge.”
If your goal is weight loss, he suggests finding a type of exercise you enjoy, and focusing on training at a sustainable pace while eating a deficit of about 500 calories a day.
DON’T DRINK YOUR CALORIES
According to trainer and women’s wellness coach Aimee Victoria Long, “People often focus on what they’re eating and forget about what they’re drinking. Coffees, juices, smoothies, soft drinks and alcohol contain a surprising amount of sugar and calories — they add up incredibly quickly.”
Long is a proponent of everything in moderation, but cautions: “If your goal is fat loss and you’re not seeing results, it’s worth looking at what’s in your favorite drinks.”

Japanese and US troops on Monday started one of their largest joint exercises focusing on the defense of Japan’s southwestern islands and showcasing advanced weapons systems in the face of growing tension in the region.
Minister of National Defense Wellington Koo (顧立雄) yesterday praised the inclusion of a Taiwan-related contingency scenario in the ongoing US-Japan exercises.
Speaking to reporters prior to a legislative session in Taipei, Koo said that maintaining peace and stability in the Taiwan Strait and the Indo-Pacific region has become a strong consensus within the global community.
Photo: Reuters
Democracies should share this responsibility, making the joint drills highly commendable, he said.
About 45,000 Japanese troops and 12,000 US service members are participating in the biennial Keen Sword 27.
Seven other nations from the Indo-Pacific region and Europe are also taking part in some elements of the exercises, five of them — France, Germany, the Netherlands, New Zealand and the Philippines — for the first time, the Japanese Joint Staff Office said.
During the exercises, which run through Thursday next week, the Japanese and US militaries will largely focus on defending Japan’s southwestern islands and waters around its northern coasts as the country faces growing tension from China, North Korea and Russia.
Japan considers China’s rapidly growing military activities in and around Japan, including in the Pacific Ocean, as a threat and has fortified its southwestern region with longer-range missiles and interceptors in the past few years.
The drills include amphibious landing, air and missile defense, mine sweeping, as well as intelligence gathering, logistics and resupply and casualty evacuation on several remote islands, including Tanegashima.
One of the key locations for the exercise is Yonaguni, Japan’s westernmost island just 110km east of Taiwan.
The Japan Self-Defense Force has introduced its first long-range Type-25 land-to-ship missile to Yonaguni during the drill, although no test-firing is planned. The missile has a range of about 1,000km and can reach China.
The US Navy-Marine Corps Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System and the Marine Air Defense Integrated System are also deployed to Yonaguni for the first time for the exercise. A High Mobility Artillery Rocket System has been deployed on the nearby island of Ishigaki.
Japanese Chief of Staff of the Joint Staff General Hiroaki Uchikura denied that the exercises target a specific country.
At a ceremony on Ishigaki, Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force Admiral Tateki Tawara said that what they are trying to defend is not just the territory, but the peaceful lives of the people.
“In order to do so, it is essential to be fully prepared and cooperate with our allies and partners to prevent the crisis,” Tawara said.
Japan’s ties with China came under strain following Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s comment a year ago, when she said Chinese military action on Taiwan could justify Japanese involvement.

Zhen Ding says supply constraints are going nowhere
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
16:47:06 UTC
01:47:06 KST

Zhen Ding Technology Holding Ltd (臻鼎), the world’s biggest printed circuit board (PCB) supplier, yesterday said it expects no near-term relief in the supply of PCBs, related components and materials, as demand remains driven by global cloud service providers’ (CSPs) investments in artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure.
The company’s comments dashed the hope that the supply constraints could be mitigated next year or in 2028. CSPs’ rapid expansion of AI servers is triggering severe supply constraints across the technology industry, spanning AI chips, substrates, PCBs and critical upstream materials such as copper clad laminate, T-glass and glass fiber fabric.
“We haven’t seen any relief in component shortages yet,” Zhen Ding chairman Charles Shen (沈慶芳) said at a media briefing at a trade show organized by the Taiwan Printed Circuit Association in Taipei. “Some people say the material shortage might clear up by 2027 or 2028, but there’s still no sign of it right now.”
Photo: CNA
In addition to PCB-related components and materials, the company experienced extended lead times for manufacturing equipment, with laser tools seeing lead times stretch to 12 months, he added.
Zhen Ding counts Nvidia Corp, Apple Inc and US-based CSPs among its major customers.
The company sees still-strong AI infrastructure deployment by major CSPs despite stock market volatility on concern about rising borrowing costs, which recently hit a 25-year high.
Photo: Lisa Wang, Taipei Times
Asked whether major CSPs would slow down AI server expansion due to surges in funding costs, Shen said the chances are slim.
“Capital remains abundant in the US market now,” he said.
To meet the surging demand for PCBs, the company is aggressively expanding its production capacity through 2030, Shen said.
By then, Zhen Ding expects to operate 59 factories across Taiwan, Thailand and China — more than doubling the current 28, he said.
The company’s capacity expansion matches the growth of the overall PCB market, which according to the Taiwan Printed Circuit Association is expected to surge to NT$130 billion to NT$140 billion (US$3.99 billion to US$4.29 billion) in 2030, compared with NT$80 billion to NT$90 billion last year.
A significant share of that new capacity would be utilized to produce high-density interconnects (HDI) and optical modules, which are used in AI servers, the company said.
Optical modules are a new growth engine, with revenue expected to rise next year from this year, Shen said.
That should boost the revenue share for HDIs to 38 percent in 2030, after surpassing revenue contribution from flexible printed circuit boards in 2028 for the first time, Shen said.
Flexible PCB, which is the company’s largest revenue contributor, should decline to about 20 percent in 2030, followed by rigid PCB to about 10 percent, he said.

Group criticizes celebrities over pro-China statements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
16:47:04 UTC
01:47:04 KST

Twenty-eight Taiwanese entertainers publicly identified the People’s Republic of China (PRC) as their “motherland” around China’s National Day this year, including actors Wu Kang-ren (吳慷仁), Peter Ho (何潤東) and Nicky Wu (吳奇隆), the Economic Democracy Union said yesterday.
Reposting messages from Chinese state media referring to China as the “motherland,” or taking part in official Chinese National Day programs and celebrations, went beyond offering holiday greetings and amounted to public expressions of national identity, the group told a news conference in Taipei.
The entertainers should not enjoy the freedoms and social benefits of Taiwan’s liberal democracy while endorsing Beijing’s political agenda, union convener Lai Chung-chiang (賴中強) said.
Photo: Chen Yi-kuan, Taipei Times
Such endorsements allow Beijing to claim that Taiwan is part of the PRC’s “sacred territory” and that unification is the “holy duty” of all people of Chinese heritage, including Taiwanese, Lai said.
Russia issued large numbers of Russian passports to people in Crimea and eastern Ukraine before invoking the need to protect Russians and defend a “common Slavic homeland” as a pretext for invading Crimea and launching its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, he said.
The 28 entertainers’ comments could put Taiwan on a similar path, Lai said, urging them to retract their statements or relinquish their Taiwanese citizenship.
While Taiwanese are free to identify as Chinese, they should not impose the view that China is their “motherland” on the rest of the population, he added.
Union think tank researcher Huang Cheng-han (黃承瀚) said the group verified that the 23 entertainers had reposted National Day messages from Chinese state media outlets China Central Television (CCTV) and the People’s Daily, either on their personal accounts or through their studios.
The posts included hashtags such as “77th anniversary of the founding of the PRC” and “One person, one wish for the motherland,” encouraging people to post their greetings, Huang said, adding that the wording left no room for ambiguity.
CCTV’s posts explicitly linked “motherland” with the anniversary of the PRC’s founding, so entertainers who reposted them should have understood that they were participating in state-sponsored national identity propaganda, he said.

Air traffic management upgrade plan approved
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
16:47:04 UTC
01:47:04 KST

The Executive Yuan has approved a NT$19.198 billion (US$588.59 million) investment to upgrade the nation’s air traffic management systems, the Ministry of Transportation and Communications said yesterday.
Deputy Minister of Transportation and Communications Lin Kuo-hsien (林國顯) announced the initiative at the International Aviation Safety Management Summit in Taipei, citing two incidents in the US and the UK last month as reminders of the importance of modernizing air traffic infrastructure.
In the UK, a previously unidentified software defect in the national airspace system’s flight-data processing software caused delays, cancelations and diversions of more than 2,000 flights on Sept. 8.
Photo courtesy of the Civil Aeronautics Administration
In the US, an air traffic control communications outage on Sept. 21 affected flights bound for Philadelphia International Airport, Newark Liberty International Airport, Teterboro Airport, John F. Kennedy International Airport and LaGuardia Airport.
The US outage was linked to problems with communications infrastructure, including a fiber-optic cable accidentally severed during construction work in New Jersey.
“Too often, problems arise because the necessary equipment has not been procured or updated, or personnel have not received adequate training before an incident occurs,” Lin said.
The Civil Aviation Administration (CAA) added 322 staff members during the COVID-19 pandemic, including 163 air traffic controllers, Lin said.
“We hope the NT$19.198 billion investment would upgrade the air traffic management systems and enable air traffic controllers to work more efficiently,” he said.
The eight-year initiative would upgrade facilities at air navigation and meteorological service campuses in Taoyuan and Kaohsiung, as well as air traffic control towers at 12 airports nationwide, the CAA said.
The funding would be used to procure next-generation air traffic control systems, air traffic flow management systems, digital voice switching systems, and big-data analytics and intelligent decision-support systems, the agency said.
The initiative would also establish an environment for developing and testing aviation software and systems, as well as to accommodate aviation training simulators, it said.
Air traffic controller operation centers and power equipment rooms in Taoyuan and Kaohsiung would be expanded under the plan, the agency added.
The upgrades aim to accommodate projected growth in air traffic through the Taipei Flight Information Region through 2049 and ensure that Taiwan’s air traffic control systems exceed safety and system availability targets set by the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) and other international organizations, the CAA said.
The systems would be upgraded in accordance with the ICAO’s Asia-Pacific Aviation System Block Upgrades strategy, with robust backup capabilities across systems to improve resilience, it said.
The upgrades are expected to help airlines improve fuel efficiency and increase air navigation service revenue, it said.
Domestic and international air passenger volume in Taiwan is expected to exceed 70 million this year, up from 68.89 million last year, the CAA said.
As of last month, the nation had handled 56 million air passengers so far this year, CAA data showed.

The US government on Monday ordered its agencies to stop using artificial intelligence (AI) tools from Chinese start-up DeepSeek, as the countries race for dominance in the fast-moving sector.
A notice from the US Department of Homeland Security announced the ban on products developed by DeepSeek — and tools created using DeepSeek by third parties — saying they must be removed from IT devices.
The department can issue direction to civilian agencies, but not the military or intelligence services. The US Department of Defense did not respond to a request for comment.
Photo: Reuters
“DeepSeek’s models present multiple threat vectors,” a document attached to the notice said.
Use of DeepSeek AI tools “may result in the transfer of sensitive data to [China] if used by US government employees or vendors,” the department said.
Its servers are in China, where the legal system permits the government “extensive authority” to access private company infrastructure, it said.
DeepSeek, one of China’s top AI labs, shook up the industry in January last year with a low-cost, high-performance chatbot, challenging assumptions of US dominance.
The firm released a long-awaited new model, V4, in April, and this month updated a faster, more lightweight version of V4.
The US has accused DeepSeek and other top Chinese AI firms of systematically stealing the capabilities of cutting-edge models developed by US rivals.
Despite their fierce competition in the field, China and the US in September agreed to set up a “communication channel” for AI incidents.
The topic is expected to arise again when the countries’ leaders meet next month at a summit in Shenzhen, China.

Nine entertainers who turned themselves in and confessed to evading compulsory military service were given suspended sentences, the New Taipei District Court ruled yesterday.
The entertainers were each ordered to pay NT$300,000 to NT$1.3 million (US$9,198 to US$39,857) to the national treasury and perform community service.
They were among 15 defendants indicted in April in the fourth wave of prosecutions in a broader military service evasion case.
Photo: CNA
The other defendants included five civilians and alleged ringleader Chen Chih-ming (陳志明).
All 15 pleaded guilty during the proceedings, the court said.
Among the entertainers, Leo Liao (廖人帥), a former member of the rock group Circus, received a sentence of one year and 10 months in prison, suspended for four years.
He was ordered to pay NT$1.3 million to the national treasury and perform 60 hours of community service.
The other eight entertainers and four civilian defendants also received suspended sentences of up to four years, with fines and community service imposed in most cases.
The remaining civilian defendant was sentenced to six months in prison, which may be commuted to a fine.
Meanwhile, Chen was convicted of 14 offenses that resulted in sentences ranging from one year and four months to two years in prison for each offense, with more than NT$2 million in criminal proceeds ordered confiscated.
The court did not determine a combined sentence, as other cases involving Chen remain under trial.
The case emerged from a broader investigation launched in February last year into allegations that Chen helped conscripts evade mandatory military service by falsifying medical test results to obtain diagnoses of hypertension.
Evading compulsory military service through illegal means is punishable by up to five years in prison.

A Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) cybersecurity tool called ARTEX was used in a spate of recent hacks of Japanese companies, the subsidiary of a major Tokyo-based Internet company yesterday.
Dozens of Japanese companies, from restaurant chains to a car hire operator, have disclosed unauthorized access or data breaches in the past weeks — potentially impacting millions of customers.
The information security arm of GMO Internet Group said it had “confirmed ARTEX was used” having investigated the attacks in collaboration with external organizations.
Photo: Reuters
“It also became clear ... the attacks were almost exclusively targeting Japan,” GMO cybersecurity center director Daiki Fukumori wrote on the company blog.
AI’s ability to find previously unknown ways to hack into computer systems is in the global spotlight, as leading labs release ever-more advanced models.
ARTEX was designed to help organizations enhance their cyberdefenses through AI-powered security testing to find potential weak points, its developer has said.
The Chinese tool this month stopped programmers from accessing its source code, acknowledging misuse by “bad actors” after South Korea linked it to several hacks on financial institutions.
Using ARTEX for cyberattacks was “entirely contrary to” the developer’s intentions, a statement said, adding that the project would no longer be updated.
Fukumori said the GMO subsidiary had discovered six Internet servers launching AI-powered attacks.
Each server was broadly categorized by the industries such as finance, e-commerce and logistics, he added — without giving details of where the servers were located, or who might have been operating them.
“To prevent further damage, we have shared this information with law enforcement agencies,” his GMO blog post said.
The Japanese government has called on companies to enhance their cyberdefenses.
This month, the head of the ruling party’s cybersecurity committee said a “state of emergency” had been reached over emerging threats.

Flu drug policy extended to next month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
16:47:00 UTC
01:47:00 KST

Expanded eligibility for flu antiviral drug prescriptions funded by the government has been extended to the middle of next month, the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) said yesterday.
Local flu activity is slowing, but it is still in the epidemic period, CDC Epidemic Intelligence Center Director Guo Hung-wei (郭宏偉) said, adding that there were 123,820 medical visits for flu-like illness last week, down 5.4 percent from the previous week.
There were 159 severe flu cases and 44 flu-related deaths reported last week, Guo said
Photo: CNA
The dominant flu virus in Taiwan is influenza A(H1N1), accounting for 92.7 percent of influenza viruses detected through laboratory surveillance in the past four weeks, he said.
CDC Deputy Director-General Lin Min-cheng (林明誠) said that as the flu is in an epidemic period, temperatures are dropping and the peak season for respiratory diseases is starting, expanded eligibility for government-funded flu antiviral drugs has been extended to Nov. 15.
Seven groups deemed at higher risk of spreading the flu qualify for the drugs. Doctors can prescribe government-funded flu antiviral drugs if a patient in one of the groups has flu-like symptoms.
The groups are: healthcare and disease prevention workers; residents and staff of residential care and long-term care institutions; preschool and childcare-facility workers, and home-based childcare providers; students from preschool through senior high or vocational school, and years one to three of five-year junior colleges; people living with or caring for those at high risk of severe flu; livestock farming and animal disease prevention personnel; and personnel in other high-density facilities (such as the military) susceptible to cluster outbreaks.
Weekly COVID-19 activity has been below the epidemic threshold for two consecutive weeks, so the epidemic period has ended, Guo said.
However, 25 severe COVID-19 cases and five deaths were reported last week, so people who are at higher risk of developing severe illness from COVID-19 or flu are advised to get vaccinated as soon as possible, he said.
The epidemic period of the seasonal flu might end early next month at the soonest, but it still depends on vaccine coverage and whether community immunity is established, Lin said.
National Taiwan University Hospital Bei-Hu Branch superintendent Chan Ding-cheng (詹鼎正), a geriatrician, said elderly people are more prone to getting flu and developing severe illness, while many studies show that getting vaccinated can reduce the risk of severe illness.
Some people are worried about side effects from vaccines, but those who are not allergic to its ingredients and have previously received flu shots without severe adverse reactions should have no issues getting another shot, Chan said.
Some people experience mild swelling, redness and soreness at the injection site, or headaches, tiredness or mild fever, but they typically resolve on their own within one or two days, he said, adding that the symptoms are much milder than the symptoms from getting the flu or its severe complications.
An elderly woman who has diabetes and lung conditions traveled to Thailand in July and contracted flu there, developing severe symptoms, he said.
She was hospitalized in an intensive care unit for about a month and later transferred to a general hospital room, he said.
The patient spent more than NT$600,000 on medical expenses in Thailand, Chan said, urging those who are eligible to get vaccinated.
Aside from the flu vaccine, COVID-19 vaccines not only reduce the risk of severe illness, but studies also show that they can reduce the risk of stroke and acute myocardial infarction, so he encourages his elderly patients to get flu and COVID-19 vaccines, he said.

Japan probe on its way to Mars moon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
16:46:57 UTC
01:46:57 KST

A Japanese spacecraft was yesterday on its way to one of Mars’ moons on a world-first mission to retrieve samples, potentially helping unlock the origins of the Solar System and life on Earth.
The flagship H3 rocket carrying the uncrewed Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) probe blasted off into a pitch black sky from the Tanegashima Space Center at 4:41am, a live stream broadcast by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) showed.
More than an hour later, JAXA announced via the live broadcast that the probe had successfully separated from the H3 and was “beginning its journey toward the Martian system.”
Photo: Kyodo via Reuters
“I’d dreamt of this day, so I’m incredibly happy,” JAXA scientist Mari Aida said. “Right now I feel really relieved.”
Following the separation, JAXA said it received signals from the spacecraft as expected, confirming it was operating normally.
Despite the early hour in Japan, thousands of people tuned into the live stream, posting messages of encouragement.
The spacecraft is due to arrive near Mars around August next year, where it would orbit one of its moons, Phobos.
A French-German rover dubbed Idefix — the French name for the comic hero Asterix’s dog — would be the first vehicle to travel across Phobos, conducting surface observations aimed at ensuring a safe landing.
Once MMX arrives on Phobos, it would collect at least 10g of material from the surface during its planned three years in the Red Planet’s vicinity.
The mission — which aims to be the first round trip to the Martian region — is a collaboration with US and European space agencies, as well as numerous universities and tech companies.
Scientists hope it would help lay the groundwork for eventual human exploration.
“The samples from MMX will bring forth paradigm-shifting science on the Mars system for generations to come, especially as NASA prepares to send the first humans to Mars,” Nicky Fox, administrator of NASA Science Mission Directorate, said in a message broadcast on the JAXA live stream.
JAXA hopes the mission would reveal how Mars and its two moons formed, a key piece of knowledge in working out how the Solar System was born.
One theory for the origin of the moons — the “giant impact” hypothesis — is that they formed after a celestial body collided with Mars.
Meanwhile, the “capture” hypothesis postulates that the moons are asteroids pulled in by Mars’ gravity.
Determining which theory is correct could help reveal “how a habitable environment for life might have arisen on the terrestrial planets,” JAXA said, referring to the four rocky worlds closest to the Sun — Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars.
JAXA said the mission would also explore the possibility of using Phobos as a “natural space station” by establishing the requirements for a round trip — something “essential for crewed Mars exploration.”
It would also observe the planet’s other moon, Deimos, although it will not land on it.
US and Chinese space agencies have also been vying to be the first to return rock samples from the surface of Mars back to Earth.
NASA’s Perseverance rover, which has been roaming across Mars since 2021, has already collected samples.
However, the return mission was effectively canceled by the administration of US President Donald Trump following a vote by US Congress in January.
China’s Tianwen-3 spacecraft is scheduled for launch around 2028 and hopes to return Mars samples to Earth as early as 2031 — potentially before the Japanese mission’s return.

ByteDance, Alibaba, Tencent place over US$35 bn worth of Nvidia chip orders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
16:46:57 UTC
01:46:57 KST

ByteDance Ltd (字節跳動), Alibaba Group Holding Ltd (阿里巴巴) and Tencent Holdings Ltd (騰訊) have ordered more than 3 million of Nvidia Corp’s new RTX PRO 5500 graphics cards with a collective sticker price of over US$35 billion, two people familiar with the matter said, in a rush for a less powerful but export-compliant chip amid US restrictions on trade with China.
US-based chipmaker Nvidia has told customers and partners it cannot guarantee that it can fill the orders because demand from Chinese technology companies far exceeds planned production, the two sources and a third person familiar with the matter said. They requested anonymity because they are not authorized to speak to the media.
The RTX PRO 5500 is a workstation chip, designed for powerful professional computers rather than the large data center clusters that use Nvidia’s most advanced artificial intelligence (AI) processors. But it is among the most powerful Nvidia chips that are still available to Chinese buyers.
Photo: Reuters
Nvidia’s Blackwell-based B300 data center chip is not allowed to be sold to Chinese buyers under US export controls, while exports of its Hopper-based H200 are reviewed on a case-by-case basis and are subject to licensing conditions.
One source said Nvidia told partners they might receive only 5 percent to 10 percent of the quantities requested. Another said the company had indicated it could produce no more than 3 million RTX PRO 5500 cards globally next year. Total orders from customers in China have exceeded 6 million, two of the sources said.
The three Chinese tech giants’ orders are for cards priced at about US$11,400 each, two of the sources said, giving them a potential combined value of more than US$35 billion.
The scale of the orders, which have not been previously reported, underscores the ongoing appetite among Chinese companies for Nvidia hardware despite the US curbs.
Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang (黃仁勳) has said the restrictions reduced Nvidia’s share of China’s AI data center chip market from a near monopoly to effectively nothing. But demand for the RTX PRO 5500 suggests Nvidia retains a sizeable potential market in China through less powerful products that may still be available.
The surge in demand also highlights how US restrictions have tightened computing power supplies in the world’s second-largest economy as Chinese companies race to develop cutting-edge AI models and propel Beijing’s effort to deploy the technology across its industries.
Washington’s curbs have pushed Chinese firms toward domestic suppliers, while Beijing has encouraged the use of homegrown chips.
Huawei, in particular, has gained market share, though Chinese chipmakers have generally struggled to match leading American products, partly because separate restrictions have limited access to the foreign equipment that is used to make the most advanced semiconductors.
An Nvidia spokesperson said Chinese producers of workstation chips and cards have experienced "unprecedented growth since 2022," when the curbs were first imposed.
"US firms continue to be restricted by a combination of outdated US export controls, which cover gaming products released nearly a half a decade ago, and China’s own limit on US imports," the spokesperson said.
ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent did not respond to requests for comment.
Starting next year, Nvidia is expected to devote much of its capacity at Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電) to Rubin, its next-generation platform for large-scale data centres, rather than products like the RTX PRO 5500, two of the sources said. TSMC declined to comment.
Nvidia has told customers to expect early samples in December, with commercial deliveries beginning in the first quarter of next year, they added.

Unknown

When Real Madrid splashed a club record 140 million euros (US$157.2 million) to sign Yan Diomande from RB Leipzig this summer, it was because of his clear potential to become one of the game’s stars, as showcased at the World Cup.
That talent has begun to unveil itself in the past few matches, with Diomande lashing in a spectacular strike against Sevilla on Sunday in La Liga ahead of a reencounter with his former side Leipzig in the Champions League on Wednesday.
However, Diomande’s sheer potential was not the only reason Madrid forked out.
Photo: AFP
Real Madrid President Florentino Perez pledged to fans during his campaign for reelection in June that he would pay for a new star as Madrid tried to rebuild following two seasons without a major trophy.
Diomande had demonstrated exciting promise, shining with Leipzig during just one season in Germany after emerging at Spain’s Leganes.
The 19-year-old did not join Madrid to fill an obvious vacancy, with his arrival actually exacerbating an overbooking in attack.
On the same day Diomande’s transfer was announced, Brazilian winger Vinicius Junior signed a new deal until 2032 with Real Madrid.
Madrid struggled last season to find their balance with Kylian Mbappe, Jude Bellingham and Vinicius on the pitch together, let alone throwing a new attacking star carrying a record price tag into the mix.
For a combination of those factors, it should not come as a surprise that Diomande is still finding his footing in the Spanish capital.
The youngster has shown flashes of his great quality, without firmly establishing himself as an essential figure for coach Jose Mourinho, although he is improving.
Diomande scored his first goal for the club against Villarreal on Oct. 10, securing Real Madrid a 1-0 win.
The winger’s superb finish was not the biggest news, after Vinicius was dismissed later in the game.
That made room for Diomande to settle in, with the winger starting on the left wing in Sunday’s 4-1 rout of Sevilla, in which he lashed home from long range in the final stages.
Diomande assisted the opener for Arda Guler, in his best performance for the club so far. He has two goals and three assists in 11 appearances across all competitions.
“He has a lot to improve, he’s young, he’s still naive, he’s still not the finished article,” Mourinho said on Sunday. “At Real Madrid, the demands are very high ... but he had a great game, he’s growing.”
Diamonds form under pressure, and in his career Diomande has dealt with it on and off the pitch.
He suffered rejection after leaving Ivory Coast to go to school in Florida, and was unable to reach a deal with MLS sides Charlotte FC and Colorado Rapids.
Eventually the winger’s senior debut came with Leganes against Real Madrid in March last year, and in 10 games for the club he scored twice, earning himself a move to Germany.
Diomande helped Leipzig reach the Champions League with 12 goals and eight assists, and he was named “rookie of the year” in the Bundesliga, before his Madrid move.
The winger said he is spurred on by tragedy from his life. His sister Roxane, who encouraged his soccer career, died at age 15 last year.
At the record 15-time European champions, Diomande has the chance to become the best.
“He has to improve his finishing ... assist better ... but that will come,” added Mourinho.
“I remember when Vinicius arrived [and struggled], and in two or three years Vinicius was a top drawer player.”

The most troubling message coming out of Washington for Taipei is not any single statement but the cumulative effect of a series of signals suggesting that US President Donald Trump is rethinking Taiwan’s strategic value while viewing the US-China relationship through the lens of a transactional great-power bargain. Takaichi has made Japan impossible to ignore
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
16:46:53 UTC
01:46:53 KST

For a leader often accused of dodging the press, there is one ironic thing about Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi: She is front-page material.
Since becoming Japan’s first female prime minister a year ago, she has divided opinion in a way few of her often-staid predecessors have. Critics and backers cannot even seem to agree on the fundamentals: She has been labeled a radical, a reflationist, a neo-militarist, a female prime minister who is holding women back. Most of these labels range from inaccurate to nonsensical. The true Takaichi remains elusive.
What is undeniable is that she has made the prime minister’s office feel relevant to a degree it has not for years. Whether the increased attention, from Washington to Beijing, is welcome or not, few are ignoring Japan anymore.
She has seen threats to decapitate her, a landslide election victory, the “Takaichi Trade,” a historic joint yen intervention with the US, multiple “Liz Truss moments” in the bond markets that refuse to materialize and fictional stories about her befriending a cockroach. In the years since the late Japanese prime minister Shinzo Abe left office, few of Japan’s prime ministers have had such an enduring impact.
However, headlines are not accomplishments. Her mentor Abe’s significance came from converting his personal popularity and political durability into long-lasting policy change. Next September, Takaichi must persuade ruling party lawmakers that she deserves another three-year term as party head. She needs more than media presence to do that.
The prime minister deserves credit for long-term thinking. Her growth strategy has set out a bold new industrial policy vision. Her budget system overhaul would benefit any successor. The biggest national foreign-intelligence reorganization in decades and a revamp of a creaky immigration system have already put in place institutional change that will outlive her.
Predictions of an easy-money policy that would require massive spending have failed to materialize. Japan’s yields are, for once, rising in line with the rest of the world, part of a process of normalizing monetary policy after decades of rates at zero or lower.
Real wages have risen for eight months in a row, while the Bank of Japan is poised to declare that underlying inflation has finally met its 2 percent target, almost 14 years after the goal was set. Takaichi can claim little credit for either, but neither has she got in the way, despite concerns she would interfere.
Getting the US on board to stabilize the yen has been something of a double-edged sword, with US Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent an occasional backseat driver, whose comments can cause more harm than good. However, the yen’s weakening trend has been halted, although not reversed (predictions of ￥200 were not uncommon earlier this year).
She has navigated geopolitical waters, too: Neither Beijing’s economic boycott in the wake of her comments on Taiwan nor the war in Iran has so far derailed the domestic recovery.
One quality she shares with Abe is the ability to drive her opponents crazy, something I have dubbed Takaichi Derangement Syndrome. Both the domestic and foreign media are obsessed with how she goes about things — the number of meetings she has, the dinners she attends and what she does in her own time — rather than what she actually gets done.
Part of this is old-fashioned misogyny; after decades of calls for a Japanese prime minister who does things differently, she is hounded for not having enough smoke-filled backroom meetings with old men.
She has also made missteps. I have highlighted the recklessness with which she speaks. Her woe-is-me lines on how much sleep she gets, housework and time she needs to put on her makeup are grating, but largely inconsequential. Of greater concern is how she communicates on the yen and her fiscal policy, particularly as her administration finally seeks to engage better with overseas investors.
Her real achievements are still limited. She has squandered political capital on largely unimportant bills; the current Diet session would spend much time debating the forthcoming cut in a sales tax for food, a distraction whose benefits for the poorest households are modest.
The resignation of Japanese Minister of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries Kazuo Yana last week is the first serious wobble for her administration, with voters criticizing her slow decisionmaking. Her popularity has fallen from its sky-high peak in February, although polling at this stage of her administration is comparable only to Abe and former Japanese prime minister Junichiro Koizumi, another long-lasting leader. It is far too early to say if Takaichi can join that pantheon.
One concern is that her administration sometimes resembles Abe’s — his disastrous and short-lived first period in power starting in 2006, characterized by strategic legislative mistakes, too much focus on a long-term vision, and an economy that was seemingly normalizing and improving, but ultimately was not to last.
After five years in the wilderness, Abe got a second chance, one he wielded adeptly. Takaichi probably should not hope for something similar. She has to make this time count. The prime minister has shown she can command attention. Now she must prove she can command outcomes.
Gearoid Reidy is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering Japan. He previously led the breaking news team in North Asia, and was the Tokyo deputy bureau chief. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs yesterday said its travel alert for France would remain classified as low risk, meaning exercise normal precautions, but advised people to steer clear of demonstrations.
In France, student protests over school conditions and teacher shortages have spread into a wider confrontation over living costs, public services and frustration with the government, with some protests escalating into violent clashes, looting and fires.
Although the ministry did not change its travel alert level, the Bureau of Consular Affairs added a description advising people to leave the area immediately if they encounter a protest.
Photo: AFP
“As massive demonstrations and protests are ongoing across France, the representative office in France advises Taiwanese international students, overseas compatriots and nationals traveling to France to stay closely tuned to updates regarding the protest activities, avoid locations and surrounding areas where protests are taking place and enhance personal safety precautions,” it says.
Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Chen Ming-chi (陳明祺) said the travel alert would remain at the current level, as the ministry continues to closely monitor the situation.
However, if the situation changes, the ministry would adjust accordingly, Chen added.
Taiwan’s representative office in France would maintain contact with the local government, as well as overseas Taiwanese, Taiwanese international students and Taiwanese traveling in France, he said.
Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) caucus secretary-general Hsu Yu-chen (許宇甄) said that although some European countries have issued advisories, the ministry has not raised its travel alert level.
She said the decision was “completely out of touch with reality” and the ministry has been slow to react.
Asked about the issue at a routine news conference yesterday, ministry spokesman Hsiao Kuang-wei (蕭光偉) said that when the protests broke out, the nation’s representative office in France immediately contacted local overseas communities and international student networks, but so far no request for emergency assistance has been reported.
As local public transportation is expected to be affected, Hsiao advised travelers to make arrangements for alternative transportation in advance.
If people encounter emergencies in France, they can call the local representative office (33-680-074-994) or the ministry’s Emergency Contact Center (0800-085-095) to ask for assistance, he said.
