‘You have to sacrifice’: Trump voters stay loyal as US midterms approach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
15:57:47 UTC
00:57:47 KST

‘You have to sacrifice’: Trump voters stay loyal as US midterms approach
Rising economic pain confronting US voters has not translated into a loss of faith among Donald Trump’s most loyal supporters.
McConnellsburg, Pennsylvania, USA – Calvin Ott, the owner of a landscaping business in a consistent stronghold for United States President Donald Trump, is one of several so-called “MAGA voters” whose support has not wavered – even as life has gotten a lot more expensive since the president returned to office last year.
“I’m 75 years old, and I’m still working,” Ott says as he sips his Coors Light beer under the dim lights of Fulton Pub in McConnellsburg.
The pub, which serves as a watering hole for the town’s approximately 1,000 residents, is where Ott unwinds after his doctor’s appointment before making the one-hour drive back through the Appalachian Mountains to his home in Shippensburg.
“I had quadruple bypasses. I’ve had skin cancer. I have my fingers cut off. I’ve had several heart issues”, Ott said with a bit of pride, showing off his right hand that has fallen victim to decades of chainsaw and lawnmower accidents.
Despite rising medical costs – his medications have more than doubled in price since last year – and his inability to retire as he approaches his 80s, the three-time Trump voter said he will continue to vote for Republicans in next month’s US midterm elections.
“I support him 100 percent,” Ott told Al Jazeera as Foreigner’s song Urgent played in the background of the pub.
In 2016, less than 6,000 people in Fulton County, where the town is located, supported Trump’s presidential campaign. That number rose to more than 7,000 eight years later, helping to fuel Trump’s return to the White House.
For Ott, his support is less a reflection of what Trump has done than what Democrats would do if they were in power.
“He’s the only president that made a promise that he kept,” Ott said. “He hates wars, even though we’re in one. But he’s for America.”
“What the hell did Biden ever give out?” he railed about the economic policies of Trump’s Democratic predecessor, Joe Biden, which included a $1,400 stimulus cheque to Americans through legislation during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Who deserves the blame?
The unrelenting support for Trump among his most loyal supporters runs through Republican strongholds like McConnellsburg.
MAGA voters like Ott make up the backbone of the president’s support: working-class, white, without college degrees, and angry with Washington.
A poll conducted last month by the Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that just 17 percent of US adults approve of Trump’s handling of the cost of living, while slightly more than a quarter of those surveyed approve of his handling of the economy overall.
Trump’s most fervent supporters say their frustrations – and economic burden – have only grown since Trump’s re-election. But unlike most Americans, they don’t blame the president for the country’s economic woes. Instead, they point to Biden, who left office last year in January.
Seated at the bar next to Ott is Rebecca Lashley, a retired nursing assistant who said Trump deserves the benefit of the doubt after Biden’s policies.
“It took Biden four years of screwing up. How’s [Trump] gonna fix it in two years?” Lashley asked.
Ott agreed.
“Do you realise what Biden left that man? He left that man a hell of a big plate”, he said.
It’s a familiar line frequently touted by the White House.
Since his return to power for a second presidential term in 2025, Trump and members of his administration have regularly claimed they aren’t to blame for the nation’s cost-of-living issues. In social media posts last month, the president wrote that “price increases throughout America were caused by Sleepy Joe Biden and the Biden Administration, not by ‘TRUMP.’”
“We’re coming out of years of energy subtraction,” US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in a recent Fox News interview as he blamed the Biden administration for rising fuel prices.
Five hours south of Pennsylvania, in ruby red Amelia County, Virginia, Terry Williams largely agreed with Trump.
After cooking up a Sunday breakfast, the delivery driver sank deep into his well-worn, waterfall-back couch to prepare for a full afternoon of football viewing. But before the day’s first kickoff, he issued a blunt, expletive-laden rant about a “bullshit” economy that larger “deep state” forces were preventing the president from fixing.
“I think that Trump just [blames Biden] because he just can’t come out and tell people the truth,” the self-described “Trump-lican” said as smells of bacon grease emanated from his kitchen. “The reason why I say that is the Federal Reserve. Their answer to everything is to print money.”
“The Federal Reserve Bank, the stockholders of the Federal Reserve, whoever the hell these people are, they’re creating more currency because they don’t have no choice.”
Williams, who voiced support for Trump’s second-term pressure tactics on the Fed to lower interest rates, said policies created by the US central bank have left the country with currency that has no real intrinsic value.
“I just believe that this economy is an illusion and we’re using fake money,” he said.
‘I have to sacrifice’
After Trump campaigned on a promise to bring down stubborn inflation wrought by the pandemic, his second term has consisted of a range of broadly unpopular initiatives that have forced higher prices on much of the country.
His tariff policies, instituted during a “Liberation Day” event at the White House last year, have minimal support. The AP found that nearly 65 percent of Americans blame Trump’s policies for high costs.
The nonpartisan Tax Foundation estimates tariffs put in place under Trump resulted in an average tax increase of more than $1,000 for US households last year. After the US Supreme Court rendered most of the president’s tariffs illegal in January, that estimate is slightly lower at $820 for 2026.
The policy’s impact is felt even more acutely in Virginia, which, according to the National Taxpayers Union Foundation, has paid an estimated $6.2bn extra since Trump’s tariffs were implemented. That breaks down to just under $1,800 per family.
But some of the state’s MAGA voters, like Williams, say despite the extra cost, they “believe” in Trump’s tariff policy, arguing it should be expanded.
“I love the thought of a tariff system. That way, the American people do not get taxed,” Williams said. “I love that concept.”
But it is the war in Iran that could prove to be the most consequential for Trump and Republicans when Americans make their midterm picks.
As the conflict stretches into its eighth month, just 27 percent of registered US voters said last month that they approve of it, according to a New York Times/Siena poll. That number, however, is much higher among Trump’s most loyal supporters: 65 percent.
“If it needs to happen to save our republic, absolutely,” Williams said of Trump’s war on Iran. But he expressed unease at increasing petrol prices wrought by the president’s war.
Since the first US-Israeli attack on Iran was launched in late February, fuel prices in the US have skyrocketed. The national average for regular petrol is $4.29 a gallon (3.8 litres), up more than $1.30 from last September, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA).
Trump has begun to acknowledge the war — and its resulting economic impacts — could cost his party control of Congress.
“Well, it’s possible,” Trump told reporters earlier this month. “Because Iran will not have a nuclear weapon. So when you say, ‘Is it OK for Iran to have a nuclear weapon?’, I would say 100 percent of the people say ‘no’, including worldwide. So, when you say it that way, it would help. If you don’t say that, it could hurt.”
For the sake of US security, most MAGA voters say they’re willing to bear the cost of Trump’s Iran decision — and America, they believe, should, too.
“What would happen if he wouldn’t have done that? What would happen? Nothing good,” Lashley said. “We have to sacrifice to make things better. I don’t care who you are. We’re with him to make that sacrifice.”
Ott explained how the war’s higher fuel prices have forced changes to his landscaping business. He’s had to tack a fuel surcharge onto his customers’ bills and lay off more than a dozen employees.
“I don’t have a problem with it,” Ott said about the war. “I have a business, and I have to sacrifice.”
Trump promises
President Trump has repeatedly promised that Americans will eventually reap the rewards of his policies.
After launching what turned out to be a trade war with US allies, Trump last year promised to use tariff revenue to give Americans what he described as a $2,000 “dividend” payment.
“People that are against Tariffs are FOOLS!” Trump posted to his Truth Social account on November 9, before adding, “A dividend of at least $2000 a person (not including high income people!) will be paid to everyone.”
The Trump administration had refunded more than $100bn as of late August following the Supreme Court ruling. But that money went to businesses, not directly to ordinary Americans.
In the lead-up to the midterms, Trump has made promises of more cash payments. During his speech at the Republican National Committee midterm convention in September, the US president said US adults would receive a $5,000 “Trump dividend” if his party “wins” next month’s elections.
Polling indicates that proposal has backfired, with 45 percent of unaffiliated voters telling NBC News they would be less likely to support a candidate who’s in agreement with it.
But it plays well — extremely well, even — with Trump’s base, whose members believe they’re entitled to a form of compensation from the government.
“I think it’s great if the president can help all people that need it,” Lashley said. “I mean, we got the money. We all contributed in our life to our country.”
“I paid tax all my life. I deserve something back”, Ott said. “They never give me nothing.”
Lashley stood up and replied, “That’s right!”
‘They’re taking everything’
Most Americans say Trump’s economic policies have burdened, rather than benefitted, them.
About seven in 10 Americans, including more than half of Republicans, believe his handling of the cost of living has been “worse than expected”, according to the AP poll.
But MAGA voters say they are sticking firmly with the president, even as his economic agenda faces growing criticism across the country.
To understand why his most hardcore supporters remain loyal, it is important to understand how Trump built his political coalition in the first place.
A study by New America found that Trump’s coalition has been closely bound and heavily driven by resentment towards opposing cultural and political groups. Lashley reflected that sentiment when she blamed immigrants for the country’s cost-of-living crisis.
“They’re taking over the businesses in our country. They’re taking everything,” she said. “I’m not on board with giving people who come here more than what we get. No!”
Lashley went even further, saying she wished Trump could remain president for the rest of his life.
“I wish he could be our president until he died,” she said. “What is going to happen when he’s gone? That’s what really worries me.”
“I trust Trump with my life,” Ott said.
Rising prices alone have not been enough to sever the bond between Trump and some of his most loyal voters.
For many of them, the choice is not simply between an expensive economy and a cheaper one. It is about what – and who – might come after Trump.
“I’m afraid that somebody’s going to get in there that’s not gonna do the job, and then we’re gonna go downhill again,” Ott said. “I worry about the Democrats”.
“Me too. They’re crazy,” Lashley replied.
“What they’re gonna do to this country. We’re gonna be suffering,” Ott said. “We might as well be living in South Africa or somewhere like that.”
That loyalty could prove important in November.
In this year’s Republican primaries, Trump has demonstrated that the GOP primary electorate will follow his lead. A string of victories by candidates he endorsed in the US states of Indiana, Kentucky and Texas has further solidified his grip on the party.
While the president’s political instinct for activating his loyal, but often low-propensity, voters in critical elections has generally been effective, it is less clear whether they can hold back a rising wave of Democratic support.
Progressive and liberal-leaning candidates have coalesced around a message of affordability and lower prices – an approach that has resonated with voters who feel increasingly squeezed by Trump’s policies.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted in August showed that US voters gave Democrats a 36 to 28 percent advantage over Republicans on cost-of-living issues.
While Lashley acknowledged that the issue resonated with her, she said there were no circumstances in which she would consider voting against the president.
More than 70 percent of US voters who identify with MAGA indicated in a September PBS News/NPR/Marist poll that they were voting in this election to support Trump.
For Williams, who said he plans to vote a straight Republican ticket in November, the economy is not his priority. The choice, he said, boils down to a battle he described as good versus evil.
“Look at the s*** that they’re trying to shove down our kids’ throats with these drag shows and the gender changes,” Williams vented as he described some Democrats’ positions on transgender rights. “Now I don’t know about you, but that’s evil right there. And I have a huge problem with that.”
But Ott said he was sticking with Republicans because of his optimism that economic conditions in the US would improve during the second half of the president’s term.
“[Trump] is gonna do more,” he said. “This economy is going to be so much better.”

Israel unveils new space warfare unit amid Gaza genocide
Unknown

2026-10-20
15:57:38 UTC
00:57:38 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel unveils new space warfare unit amid Gaza genocide
Israel has established a new military Space Division to expand its surveillance and warfare capabilities, raising questions about how the technology could be used against Palestinians amid its genocide in Gaza and continuing military occupation of the West Bank.
The Israeli military announced on Monday that Brigadier General "Shin", identified only by his first initial in Hebrew, had been appointed to command the division, which will operate under the military's Planning Directorate.
The new body will oversee space-related military operations, coordinate training and intelligence, and develop capabilities for what Israel increasingly regards as a separate arena of warfare.
The military said the division was established after it concluded that "the space domain has become an active combat domain" and would play an increasingly important role in future conflicts.
Welcoming the announcement on Tuesday, Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz described the initiative as part of his ambition to transform the country into a major military space power.
"The goal set for the IDF and the defense establishment is to make Israel one of the world's leading countries in the field of space security," Katz said, describing the project as "Star Wars, made in Israel."
He said Israel wanted the "ability to monitor, defend and attack from space any target across vast areas", arguing that such capabilities would strengthen its military dominance and deter adversaries.
Satellite surveillance and the war on Gaza
However, the expansion also carries significant implications for Palestinians, who have long been subjected to Israel's extensive military surveillance and intelligence operations.
Israel already operates a network of military reconnaissance satellites whose imagery is processed by Unit 9900, a specialised military intelligence formation responsible for visual and geospatial intelligence.
The unit's work includes identifying military targets and providing intelligence to support Israeli operations, including attacks in Gaza.
Its capabilities form part of a broader Israeli intelligence infrastructure that has been deployed during the war on Gaza, where surveillance technologies and digital targeting systems have come under growing scrutiny over their role in attacks that have killed large numbers of Palestinian civilians.
Human rights organisations have raised serious concerns about Israel's use of digital intelligence and automated targeting technologies during the war, including the reliability of information used to identify suspected targets and the risks posed to civilians.
Human Rights Watch warned in 2024 that Israel's reliance on digital targeting tools in Gaza raised concerns about inaccurate data and the potential for unlawful attacks.
Although the precise responsibilities of the new Space Division remain unclear, an expansion of Israel's satellite intelligence capabilities could further strengthen the military's ability to monitor Palestinian territory, track movements and identify potential targets.
Such technology could also be used to monitor roads, border crossings, infrastructure and changes in the urban landscape across Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
There is no confirmation that the new division will directly oversee operations against Palestinians, but its establishment could consolidate capabilities already used by Israel's military intelligence services.
The distinction is significant because satellite surveillance is not merely a means of observing territory. When integrated with military intelligence and targeting systems, it can contribute directly to decisions about where and when strikes are carried out.
Expanding Israel's military reach
Israel has continued to invest heavily in reconnaissance satellites, including its Ofek series, which provide imagery for intelligence gathering and military planning.
Until now, responsibility for space-related operations, including satellite launches and ballistic missile defence, has largely rested with the Israeli Air Force, while Unit 9900 has controlled military intelligence satellites after their deployment.
The Israeli military has not clarified which responsibilities will be transferred to the new division.
According to the military, several projects involving space-based sensors and space warfare capabilities have already been approved over the past year.
A new frontier for warfare
Israel's announcement also reflects intensifying international competition over the militarisation of space, with the US, Russia, China and India developing technologies intended to protect their own satellites or disrupt those operated by adversaries.
The 1967 Outer Space Treaty prohibits the placement of nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction in orbit but does not comprehensively prohibit conventional military activities in space.
Israel has also identified Iran's developing space capabilities as a potential threat.
During its conflict with Iran in March, the Israeli military claimed to have destroyed a facility in Tehran involved in military satellite development, alleging that it was also working on technology capable of attacking satellites.
The claims could not be independently verified.
Alongside the Space Division, Israel announced the establishment of a new Robotics Division under its Depth Corps, which conducts operations beyond the country's borders.
Military chief Eyal Zamir has also outlined plans to expand the military's use of unmanned systems and artificial intelligence, reflecting a wider effort to integrate advanced technologies into Israeli warfare.
The announcements come as Israel continues to expand its military capabilities despite mounting international scrutiny of its conduct in Gaza and the occupied Palestinian territories.

Chancellor Merz praises Turkish community’s contributions to Germany

Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Tuesday praised the Turkish community's contributions to Germany, helping build the country’s industrial base in the 1960s and continuing to enrich its economy, technology and culture.
“Turkish guest workers helped build the industrial foundation of our country,” Merz said of those who arrived soon after the October 30, 1961, labor recruitment agreement. “They helped build the foundations of our nation. They created the infrastructure of the prosperity in which we live today.”
He spoke at a ceremony in Berlin marking the 65th anniversary of the agreement with Türkiye, which brought hundreds of thousands of Turkish workers to West Germany during the postwar economic boom. Most had planned to return home after a few years, but roughly half stayed, brought their families and gradually became part of German society.
Their children and grandchildren have since produced high-profile success stories, said Merz. Among those, he named German-Turkish footballer Ilkay Gundogan, film director Fatih Akin and BioNTech founders Ugur Sahin and Ozlem Tureci, whose work in oncology and immunology has drawn international attention. He also cited authors Aras Oren and Deniz Utlu.
“These are just the widely known figures -- the particularly spectacular success stories,” he said. “Yet there are thousands of others. They can be found in every federal state, in every sector of our society, across all political parties, within labor unions, and in employers’ associations.”
The chancellor described integration as an ongoing task for any modern pluralistic society, one that requires mutual effort in workplaces, schools and sports clubs. He said people who come to Germany should respect its democratic rules. In return, they should be able to expect equal opportunity and a sense of belonging regardless of their migration background.
Merz acknowledged that many in the first, second and even third generations have experienced being treated as strangers despite their efforts. He pointed to racist violence that marked the 65-year history, including the 1990s attacks in Moelln and Solingen -- murders carried out over years by the neo-Nazi terror group NSU in which eight people of Turkish origin were among the victims -- and the 2020 attack in Hanau.
“Fear of the foreign is poison for every free society,” Merz warned. He said those fears appear to be increasing and are once again being ideologically charged and exploited. On the term “Remigration,” which is used by politicians of the anti-immigrant AfD, the chancellor said it represents “an attack on the modern Germany that we have built together over the past 65 years.”
The ceremony was attended by representatives of the first generation of Turkish guest workers as well as their children and grandchildren
The agreement brought 867,000 Turkish guest workers to West Germany by the time recruitment ended in 1973; about 500,000 later returned to Türkiye. Many others arrived afterward through family reunification.
Germany is now home to a Turkish community of roughly 3 million, largely descended from those early arrivals.

UK and GCC push investment ahead of free trade deal ratification
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
15:56:49 UTC
00:56:49 KST

Breadcrumb
UK and GCC push investment ahead of free trade deal ratification
British and Gulf officials have called on businesses and investors to begin turning a landmark free trade agreement into concrete partnerships without waiting for its formal ratification, as both sides seek to deepen economic ties and expand cooperation beyond traditional trade.
The calls came during the UK-GCC Strategic Dialogue Forum, organised by The Business Year in central London on Tuesday, bringing together senior officials, representatives of Gulf sovereign wealth funds and private sector companies to explore investment opportunities arising from the agreement.
The UK became the first G7 economy to conclude negotiations on a free trade deal with the six-member Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) on 20 May 2026, when the British government announced that talks had been completed following nearly four years of negotiations that began in June 2022.
However, the agreement has yet to be formally signed and ratified, with both sides still working to finalise and legally verify its text before completing the necessary government and parliamentary procedures.
While the deal is not yet legally in force, officials at the forum stressed that businesses could already begin identifying investment opportunities, building partnerships and preparing projects that could benefit from improved market access once it takes effect.
GCC Secretary-General Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi described the agreement as a "significant achievement" in relations between Britain and the Gulf states, stressing that its importance extended well beyond the immediate benefits of trade.
Speaking at the forum, Albudaiwi said the agreement would strengthen economic partnerships, support diversification efforts and improve competitiveness across the Gulf economies, which have increasingly sought to reduce their dependence on oil revenues.
"GCC estimates put total investment between the two sides at $643 billion, while bilateral trade reached approximately $70 billion in 2025," he said.
The agreement is expected to eliminate tariffs on more than 90% of GCC exports to the UK, opening new opportunities for businesses and strengthening the Gulf's position as a major economic partner for Britain.
"The deal would support the GCC's wider economic objectives, including greater economic integration, diversification of production, improving the business environment and empowering the private sector," Albudaiwi said.
He highlighted opportunities in developing smart cities, sustainable living and attracting leading international technology companies, alongside cooperation in healthcare, financial technology, artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing and clean energy.
These sectors have become increasingly important to Gulf economic transformation plans, as governments seek to attract international expertise, develop new industries and create sources of growth beyond oil and gas.
The GCC chief stressed that the success of the agreement would ultimately be measured not simply by its signing, but by the joint ventures, business partnerships and economic opportunities it generated.
He urged business leaders and investors from both sides to seize the opportunities offered by the agreement and begin translating its provisions into practical projects.
UK pledges support amid regional uncertainty
British Trade Minister Lord Anas Sarwar echoed those calls, urging businesses not to wait until the agreement had been formally signed and ratified before exploring new partnerships.
Addressing the forum, Sarwar acknowledged that the Gulf was experiencing a "nervous time" and a "time of challenge", offering assurances of Britain's continued support for its regional partners.
"It is in difficult times that you know where your friends are," he said, explaining that his first overseas visit as trade minister had been to the Gulf.
Sarwar stressed that the partnership was important to the British government and could contribute to economic growth and improved living standards across the UK.
He described the relationship as being about more than signing an agreement, calling for immediate cooperation across sectors including aviation, security systems, financial services and legal services.
He also highlighted opportunities in artificial intelligence and digital infrastructure, pointing to Britain's research capabilities and the Gulf's access to energy and resources needed to support the expansion of data centres and cloud computing infrastructure.
Such cooperation could allow British companies to contribute technical expertise and specialist services to major Gulf development projects, while creating opportunities for Gulf investors to expand their involvement in Britain's technology and infrastructure sectors.
Sarwar said economic cooperation needed to work in both directions, with Britain seeking not only greater Gulf investment in the UK but also increased British investment and exports into Gulf markets.
He also encouraged businesses to explore joint investments in third countries, arguing that UK-Gulf cooperation should extend beyond bilateral projects.
Lord Mayor of London Alderman Sir Alastair King similarly highlighted the potential for British and Gulf investors to combine their resources and expertise to pursue opportunities in other international markets.
The UK hopes the agreement will encourage larger and more sustained flows of Gulf capital into British infrastructure, property and other strategic sectors, while opening one of the world's most important markets to British exporters.
The emphasis on joint investment also reflects a broader ambition to move beyond conventional trade in goods and services towards longer-term partnerships involving technology, infrastructure development and international projects.
Four years of negotiations
GCC chief negotiator Raja Almarzoqi expressed optimism about the agreement's long-term economic benefits, revealing that negotiators from both sides had held approximately 900 meetings before reaching an agreement.
He said one of the most challenging aspects of the negotiations had been securing a unified position among the GCC's six member states, which have different economic priorities and domestic interests.
Almarzoqi cited studies by the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund suggesting that free trade agreements could increase trade between participating countries by 60% to 100% over five to ten years after implementation.
He expressed confidence that the UK-GCC agreement could deliver similar results, although the scale of any increase would depend on how businesses used the opportunities created by the deal.
Kuwait's Trade Minister Abdulaziz Naser Almarzouq also emphasised the importance of economic diversification, saying Gulf countries were seeking high-quality investments capable of supporting sustainable long-term growth.
He described Britain as a strong economic partner and called for existing relations to be expanded through new investment opportunities.
Discussions at the forum also focused on financial markets, investment and the Gulf states' economic transformation strategies, including Oman's efforts to diversify away from an energy-dependent economy.
The free trade agreement is expected to provide British companies with greater long-term access to Gulf markets while giving GCC businesses improved opportunities to expand their activities in the UK.
For businesses, the potential benefits extend beyond tariff reductions to opportunities for new commercial relationships, investment planning and greater participation in sectors targeted for growth by both sides.
However, the agreement's practical benefits will depend on its final provisions, implementation and the extent to which companies are able to take advantage of the new arrangements.
Although the main terms were agreed in May, the final legal text must still be completed and verified before the agreement can be signed. It will then need to undergo the necessary approval procedures in Britain and the GCC states, including parliamentary scrutiny in the UK.

A large-scale museum dedicated to The Beatles will open in Liverpool in 2028
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
18:53:28 EEST
00:53:28 KST

A large-scale museum dedicated to The Beatles will open in Liverpool in 2028
Kyiv • UNN
The Beatles Story will move to St John’s Market and become four times larger. Apple Corps will also renovate the St Johns Beacon tower for Yellow Submarine.
Liverpool is preparing to unveil a new tourist attraction dedicated to The Beatles. It will cover 100,000 square feet (approximately 9,300 sq. m). Musician Paul McCartney called the project "extraordinary," while Andy Burnham, the mayor of Greater Manchester, said it demonstrates "exactly the level of ambition we would like to see more often across the United Kingdom," reports UNN, citing The Guardian.
The opening is scheduled for 2028. The project will be a major redevelopment of The Beatles Story museum, which has operated at Liverpool’s Royal Albert Dock complex since 1990. The attraction is now coming under the ownership of Apple Corps, which belongs to the band’s members. As a result, The Beatles Story will become the first official space for Beatles fans in their hometown.
The museum will also change locations: it will move to the former St John’s Market shopping centre, located near Lime Street railway station. The building has been vacant since it closed in 2024. The new premises will allow the museum to expand to four times its current size.
In addition, Apple Corps announced plans to take over and renovate Liverpool’s second-tallest building — the St Johns Beacon tower (450 feet, or approximately 137 metres, high). It has also stood vacant since 2024, when the observation deck closed and the radio stations that rented space there moved out. The tower, located next to the redeveloped museum, will become a separate tourist attraction dedicated to The Beatles’ fantastical psychedelic animated film "Yellow Submarine". The new version of The Beatles Story exhibition is being presented as a "multi-hour adventure." It will recreate iconic locations from the band’s history: from the Liverpool homes where the musicians spent their childhoods to the legendary Cavern club and the nightlife venues of Hamburg, where they gained their first experience. The exhibition will also include the Abbey Road studio, Shea Stadium in New York — where Beatlemania provoked such a deafening scream from fans that the musicians themselves could not hear their own playing — as well as the building on London’s Savile Row, whose roof hosted the band’s final concert in 1969.
Paul McCartney said: "It is incredible and moving for me that people are still interested in our story. It is very heartening that The Beatles Story and the Beacon complex in the very heart of Liverpool are undergoing such exciting changes. I love Liverpool. It is part of me, part of what The Beatles are. If someone had told us about this when we were just starting out, we would never have believed it."
Ringo Starr also welcomed the plans: "It’s great to be part of this — deep down, I’m still a Liverpudlian (a Scouser). Liverpool was and remains a city of music. And now we’re expanding The Beatles Story… absolutely fantastic! The music lives on."
We should add
A new charitable organisation, the Apple Corps Liverpool Trust, has also been established. It will receive a portion of the proceeds from every ticket sold, which will be used to support initiatives for local musicians.
Andy Burnham praised the plans for Liverpool, noting that they demonstrate "exactly the level of ambition we would like to see across Britain: supporting what our great cities do best and turning their global reputations into new jobs, opportunities and economic growth." He also stressed that the project’s charitable component would help "the next generation of young artists — wherever they grow up — believe that there is a path from their own bedroom, rehearsal room or local music venue to the heights of global recognition."
Liverpool Mayor Steve Rotheram said: "People are already travelling halfway around the world to visit the birthplace of the four boys who shook the planet. These plans take this incredible magnetism to a new level, creating a world-class visitor attraction. It will give millions more fans a reason to make a pilgrimage to their spiritual home, to see the city with their own eyes and experience its music and culture."
The project is being carried out by Apple Corps in cooperation with Liverpool City Council and the Liverpool City Region Combined Authority, with the support of the UK government. Financial details of the project and the terms of the partnership have not yet been disclosed.
Apple Corps chief executive Tom Greene compared the plans to Elvis Presley’s Graceland estate in Memphis or Dolly Parton’s Dollywood theme park in Tennessee: "It will be a world-class destination in the heart of the city — right where it all began."
Greene is also overseeing the creation of another official Beatles attraction: the redevelopment of the building at 3 Savile Row, where their final rooftop concert took place. The seven-storey museum, scheduled to open in 2027, will give visitors access to the roof. It will also recreate the recording studio where the band worked on the album "Let It Be", as well as house exhibitions from the Apple Corps archive and temporary displays.
These plans are part of wide-ranging efforts to preserve and promote The Beatles’ legacy. In particular, they include an ambitious project — a series of four biographical films directed by Sam Mendes, each telling the story of one of the band members. The films, which are currently in production, will be released in 2028, while sets and props from them will be used to recreate historic locations in a new version of "The Beatles Story" exhibition.
The band’s Hamburg period is explored in a separate project — the BBC drama series "Hamburg Days", written by Jamie Carragher (the author of the series "Succession"). At the same time, The Beatles’ music catalogue continues to be reissued: an expanded edition of the album "Rubber Soul" (1965) reached number two in the UK charts at the beginning of this month.
The Beatles are a powerful tourist magnet for Liverpool: according to a 2016 study, the band brings £82 million to the local economy each year. The current version of "The Beatles Story" exhibition — which includes such artefacts as George Harrison’s first guitar and John Lennon’s glasses — has contributed to this success. Over the past two years, the museum has received a "VisitEngland" award for excellence each time.

The police investigation indicates that the suspected motive is a dangerous 'challenge' circulating on social media, including TikTok, in which teenagers steal fire extinguishers from residential buildings and discharge them in public areas."

The three boys caught in the act were each fined 730 shekels (about $236), while the other teenagers and their parents were warned about the seriousness of the incidents and their potential criminal and safety consequences.
"Police emphasize that this is not a prank but dangerous behavior that could cost lives," the police statement said. "Stealing and emptying fire extinguishers leaves residential buildings without essential firefighting equipment. In the event of a fire, this could prevent an immediate response and lead to serious harm to people and property.
"Israel Police takes acts that endanger public safety and security very seriously and will continue working decisively, together with municipal enforcement authorities, to identify those involved and hold them accountable," the statement concluded.
Police also urged parents to remain vigilant about their children's involvement in dangerous social media challenges and to discuss the potentially serious consequences of such behavior with them.
"We call on parents to be alert to their children's participation in dangerous challenges on social media and to talk to them about the serious consequences of these actions. We also urge building committees to secure fire extinguisher cabinets and firefighting equipment against theft while ensuring they remain immediately accessible in an emergency," police said.

Saudi Arabia launches 2026-27 archaeology season in AlUla, Khaybar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
15:52:06 UTC
00:52:06 KST

Saudi Arabia has launched its 2026-27 Archaeology Season across AlUla and Khaybar, focusing on research, excavation and conservation in one of the most significant archaeological landscapes in the country’s northwest, Anadolu reports.
The Royal Commission for AlUla (RCU) said in a statement on Monday that the season builds on previous years of archaeological research, excavation, documentation and conservation and is aimed at advancing knowledge of the region’s history while developing Saudi expertise in archaeology and cultural heritage.
According to the state news agency SPA, the program combines fieldwork, specialized studies, digital documentation, conservation, community engagement and capacity building.
The commission said this year’s research will focus on early human presence, ancient Arabian kingdoms and oasis communities, travel and pilgrimage routes, environmental history and water management, inscriptions and written heritage, material culture and ways of life.
At Hegra in AlUla, researchers will study the ancient settlement center, including plant and animal remains and archaeological finds, to provide greater insight into life at the site across different historical periods.
In Dadan, the second phase of the Dadan Archaeological Project will build on a previous five-year project, focusing on funerary and residential areas to better understand the development of one of AlUla’s major ancient centers, according to the commission.
READ: Saudi Arabia postpones future investment initiative until 2027 following Houthi attacks
Research in Khaybar will examine the relationship between people and the oasis across different periods, including the Neolithic era and Islamic periods, as well as sedimentary records, ancient environments and natural resources that influenced human settlement and cultural change, it added.
The commission also said that studies in southern AlUla will examine historic pilgrimage and trade routes, including forts, railway stations and other archaeological remains linked to travel networks that connected the area with surrounding regions.
Written heritage is another major component of the program. More than 25,000 inscriptions have been documented in AlUla, providing an important record of northwestern Saudi Arabia’s history, languages and cultural interactions, it said.
Specialized studies will also examine animal remains, ceramics, water systems, oasis water management and material culture to shed light on everyday life in past societies.
Saudi university students will take part in fieldwork, laboratory analysis, specialized studies and digital documentation under the supervision of Saudi and international experts.
The program also includes community activities linking archaeological research with local knowledge through museum and laboratory experiences and visits to archaeological sites.
The commission said the initiative forms part of its broader efforts to preserve AlUla’s cultural heritage and strengthen AlUla and Khaybar as centers for archaeological research, cultural exchange and heritage-led development, in line with Saudi Vision 2030.

"The doctor approached me during the match and told me it didn't look good," Terzic said at Tuesday's pre-match press conference.
"Guru had already suffered a similar injury in his other leg [in 2019], so he immediately felt that something was wrong," he added.
Terzic praised the 30-year-old striker's attitude despite the setback.
"His optimism is on another level. Our duty now is to support him so that when he is ready to return, he steps back into a highly successful team."
Athletic has drawn its last three La Liga matches, scoring just once, and Terzic acknowledged that improving the team's attacking effectiveness would take time.
"It's true that we are currently struggling to score, but our opponents also find it very difficult to score against us," he said.
"Being more dangerous and clinical in the penalty area is a process; it isn't solved in a single training session. Today, we look for instant solutions to everything with technology, but we work with human beings, not automated response buttons. You can't just go to Google or ChatGPT for answers."
Terzic confirmed that Sancet would miss Wednesday's match but said Williams could return, stressing the importance of making "smart, long-term decisions" over injured players.
The match was originally scheduled for September 16 but was postponed after torrential rain flooded the pitch at Levante's Ciutat de Valencia Stadium. ■

Roundup: Fueling developing world's energy transition, China takes green energy global
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
23:51:13 CST
00:51:13 KST

An aerial drone photo taken on Aug. 24, 2022 shows a view of the 330-megawatt Phu My Solar Power Plant in Gia Lai province in Vietnam. (Xinhua)
BEIJING, Oct. 20 (Xinhua) -- As developing countries seek pathways to energy transition, China's renewable energy supply chains, engineering capabilities and operational expertise are opening up new possibilities for renewable energy development.
From solar farms in Southeast Asia to off-grid systems in rural Africa, China's clean energy projects are expanding electricity access, creating jobs and building local skills.
In 2021, China pledged to stop building new coal-fired power plants overseas. Green energy has since become a focus of cooperation with Belt and Road partner countries, with Chinese companies involved in solar, wind and hydropower projects that support local energy transitions.
SOLAR PARTNERSHIP DRIVES LOW-CARBON GROWTH
Across Southeast Asia, Chinese-built renewable energy projects are helping meet rising power demand and cut emissions.
In Indonesia's West Java province, the 100-megawatt Karawang photovoltaic project, constructed by China Electric Power Construction Group Hubei Engineering Co., Ltd., began operation in 2024.
It supplies clean electricity to the industrial park in Karawang, cutting annual carbon dioxide emissions by 19,800 tons and saving about 8,800 tons of standard coal.
The project has also strengthened local expertise. During construction, the Chinese team trained more than 300 Indonesian workers, helping build a local workforce capable of independently installing solar systems.
In Vietnam, PowerChina Jiangxi Electric Power Engineering Co., Ltd. built the 330-megawatt Phu My Solar Power Plant in Gia Lai province. Engineers adapted equipment and mounting structures to withstand coastal salt corrosion, high temperatures and typhoons.
The plant generates about 520 million kilowatt-hours annually, reducing carbon dioxide emissions by roughly 400,000 tons a year. Construction has created more than 2,000 local jobs, while training helped develop skills in renewable energy operations and maintenance.
Beyond solar energy, China-Vietnam energy cooperation now spans wind, hydropower and waste-to-energy, broadening the two countries' clean energy partnership.
CLEAN POWER CUTS ENERGY COSTS
In Pakistan, Chinese solar products and technology are helping diversify an energy mix long reliant on thermal power.
As the South Asian country grapples with high electricity costs and unreliable supply, expanding solar capacity has brought clean power to millions of households.
Chinese companies have also introduced flexible installment plans to make solar systems more affordable, helping families lower electricity bills.
The under-construction China-built Mohmand Hydropower Project in Pakistan is expected to generate 2.86 billion kilowatt-hours annually and has created more than 5,000 local jobs, strengthening Pakistan's construction capabilities.
China's green energy projects also support economic development in partner countries. Construction creates local jobs and trains skilled workers, while solar panels and energy storage systems help grow supply chains in infrastructure, logistics and maintenance.
With no fuel costs, wind and solar power offer more predictable long-term generation costs than fossil fuels, helping reduce electricity bills for households and businesses while providing affordable power for local industries.
OFF-GRID SOLAR EXPANDS ENERGY ACCESS
Across Africa's vast landscapes, dispersed populations and complex terrain have made conventional grid expansion costly and difficult. Many rural and pastoral communities remain without reliable electricity.
China has responded with lightweight, easy-to-install off-grid solar and storage systems. Operating independently of main grids, they deliver stable power and help close "the last mile" of energy access.
In Kenya's pastoral areas, remote villages and refugee camps, Chinese solar equipment has replaced costly, polluting diesel generators. It now supports daily life, local festivals and small businesses.
Solar lighting has extended school hours in rural areas, while photovoltaic irrigation pumps have cut farming costs and increased crop yields by about 30 percent in some cases.
Clean, stable and affordable green power is doing more than lighting homes. It is strengthening education, agriculture and small-scale economies, creating steadier income for local people.
China's overseas energy cooperation has shifted from coal-fired projects to green energy partnerships. By combining project construction with technology transfer and talent training, it helps partner countries build self-sustaining green energy systems.
As high-quality Belt and Road cooperation deepens, China is helping developing countries turn wind, solar and water resources into drivers of growth, improving livelihoods while advancing a shared low-carbon future. ■

Israel seeks to cast Lebanon army as 'failing' ahead of US talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
15:51:04 UTC
00:51:04 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel seeks to portray Lebanese army as failing to curb Hezbollah ahead of talks
Hours before Lebanon and Israel were due to resume negotiations in the United States, the Israeli military on Tuesday accused the Lebanese army of failing to curb Hezbollah’s activities in southern Lebanon, in what a retired Lebanese brigadier general described to The New Arab as an attempt to heighten tensions ahead of the talks and put Lebanon on the defensive.
The Israeli military accused elements within the Lebanese army of allegedly coordinating with Hezbollah to obstruct the enforcement of security arrangements, reportedly allowing the group to anticipate operations and move weapons out of targeted areas. It said the Lebanese army had also failed to dismantle a Hezbollah military site in the south, despite announcing that it had taken the necessary measures there.
The Israeli military said that the Lebanese army was responsible for ensuring the full implementation of the security arrangements, saying it expected it to take more decisive and effective measures to prevent Hezbollah from maintaining weapons and military infrastructure in southern Lebanon.
The Lebanese army later rejected the claims, describing them as false and accusing Israel of seeking to undermine its credibility and cast doubt on its ability to carry out its responsibilities in southern Lebanon.
Lebanon and Israel are due to hold technical military talks in Tampa, Florida, on Tuesday, resuming discussions after the last round of talks in Rome in early August. An eighth round planned for September in the Italian capital did not take place.
The Lebanese delegation is expected to reiterate its demands for a full Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon, which continues to come under daily Israeli attack despite a framework agreement signed in June.
Pressure on the Lebanese army
Retired Lebanese Brig. Gen. Bassam Yassin described the Israeli accusations as an attempt to undermine the talks and put the Lebanese army on the defensive.
"The intention is certainly to create tension around the negotiations and put the army in a position where it has to defend itself," Yassin told The New Arab.
He said the Lebanese delegation was expected to focus on technical issues, including the work of the ceasefire monitoring committee, locally known as the mechanism, and demands for an Israeli withdrawal.
The mechanism was established following the November 2024 ceasefire agreement between Israel and Hezbollah.
"All this talk about the army’s failure does not reflect the major successes it achieved south of the Litani River in 2024 and 2025," Yassin said, questioning why the alleged violations had not been raised with the mechanism at the time.
In a statement on Tuesday, the Israeli military said it expected the Lebanese army to take "more decisive and effective action" to prevent Hezbollah from maintaining weapons and military infrastructure in the south.
It alleged that, despite the Lebanese army announcing in December 2025 that it had dealt with a Hezbollah facility in the southern town of Kafra, footage showed members of the group continuing to operate there and attempting to remove weapons from the site months later.
The Israeli military said its forces had subsequently struck and destroyed a truck carrying the weapons. It also accused members of the Lebanese army of coordinating with Hezbollah over enforcement operations, allowing the group to anticipate military activity and move weapons out of targeted areas.
Yassin rejected the suggestion that the Lebanese army was failing to carry out its responsibilities. While the Lebanese government has made dismantling Hezbollah’s military infrastructure and disbanding its armed wing in the south a stated objective, he argued that the army could not be expected to forcibly disarm the group while Israeli forces continued to occupy Lebanese territory and carry out attacks.
"Of course, the army is not going to dismantle Hezbollah’s weapons and infrastructure in the south right now. There is an occupation and aggression on your land. Can the army confront civilians and tell them: ‘I want to dismantle your defences’? That is impossible," he said.
Yassin maintained that the army had taken control of every Hezbollah site it had entered following the November 2024 ceasefire, and said Hezbollah had helped it access many of its former positions.
Some sites were empty when the army arrived, while others were discovered by chance or with the help of local residents, he said. Some of the people responsible for those sites had been killed during the 2024 war, he added, meaning information about their locations was no longer available.
Yassin said the Israeli military's publication of footage now was intended to undermine confidence in the Lebanese army and portray it as weak.
"If there is something old [still there], that does not mean the Israelis can release videos now. The intention is to confuse the Lebanese army and portray it as being in a weak position, when that is not the case," he said.
Lebanese army rejects allegations
In a statement shared with footage on X, the army said its units had begun work on a military facility in the southern town of Kafra in December 2025. They continued working there until 16 March 2026, when they suspended operations and evacuated the area at the request of the mechanism, following Israeli threats to strike the site.
The army said it had informed the committee that the operation was incomplete and that military equipment and ammunition remained inside the facility, which was subsequently targeted by an Israeli strike. It added that repeated requests to secure permission to resume work and remove the remaining equipment had been rejected by Israel.
According to the statement, the army resumed its operation on 15 August 2026 in coordination with the mechanism, eventually completing the work and closing the facility on 16 October.
The Lebanese army also disputed the Israeli military's account of the footage showing a truck carrying weapons being struck. It said the video dated back to 3 July 2026 and was filmed in the village of Seddiqin rather than at the Kafra facility.
The army said all the events and measures it described had been documented with the mechanism, adding that Israel's repeated allegations and disinformation campaigns were aimed at damaging the military institution's credibility locally and internationally, particularly amid the ongoing negotiations.
It reiterated its commitment to carrying out its responsibilities and assigned tasks, while accusing Israel of continuing to violate existing understandings.
No progress on pilot zones
The talks are due to take place under US auspices against a backdrop of continued Israeli strikes and demolitions in southern Lebanon and growing concerns in Beirut about the consequences of a possible wider confrontation involving the United States, Israel and Iran.
A US official, in remarks carried by the US embassy in Beirut, said the meeting would be limited to working-level teams and focus exclusively on security issues within the tripartite framework signed by Lebanon and Israel in Washington on 26 June 2026.
Little progress has been made on the initial pilot areas announced under the arrangements this summer. Lebanese military sources told The New Arab that continued Israeli attacks were obstructing the army’s work in the areas and making the return of residents difficult and dangerous.
Beirut also rejects any direct coordination between the Lebanese and Israeli armies, despite pressure from Washington and Tel Aviv. Lebanon continues to pursue the diplomatic track, viewing it as the only viable option to end the conflict.
Fears of a more devastating war
Lebanese official sources told The New Arab that President Joseph Aoun was monitoring developments in the region and feared the consequences of any escalation for Lebanon. They said these concerns had also been raised by international officials and diplomats visiting Beirut, including Arab League Secretary-General Nabil Fahmy, who met Aoun on Monday.
The sources also expressed concern about Hezbollah’s increasingly confrontational position, warning that it could draw Lebanon into another war.
They said Lebanese officials were holding internal consultations through their advisers to convey their concerns and urged all sides to put Lebanon’s interests above external agendas.
The sources added that officials had received warnings that another war could have even more serious consequences than the previous rounds of fighting in October 2023 and March 2026.
Hezbollah and Israel began exchanging fire in October 2023, with the conflict escalating into a full-scale war in September 2024. Fighting resumed on 2 March 2026 following the start of the US-Israel war on Iran.
Although fighting largely subsided in June following the signing of the tripartite framework, Israel has continued attacks and demolitions in its so-called buffer zone in southern Lebanon, occupying strategic sites and destroying Hezbollah tunnels.
Israeli attacks over the past three years have killed 8,596 people and wounded more than 30,660 others, many of them civilians.

China to advance new legislation on cultural heritage protection
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
23:50:58 CST
00:50:58 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 20 (Xinhua) -- China will work to advance the formulation of a cultural heritage protection law as part of efforts to better preserve and pass on its cultural heritage, an official said Tuesday.
Hu Kaihong, deputy director of the General Office of the Central Commission for Guiding Cultural and Ethical Progress, told a media conference that the move is outlined in the country's first five-year plan dedicated to cultural heritage protection issued in September.
The plan calls for improving the legal and regulatory framework and strengthening legal safeguards for various types of cultural heritage, including historic and cultural districts, said Hu, also director of the office of the central commission for cultural heritage protection.
Hu said the plan for the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030) prioritizes protection, promotes the rational use of cultural heritage and adheres to the principle of minimal intervention, while strengthening systematic protection and unified oversight.
The plan sets a target of fully identifying the country's cultural heritage resources by 2030, with an improved regulatory framework, a stronger body of laws and regulations, and a growing pool of professionals.
China is home to 61 UNESCO World Heritage sites, including the Great Wall, the Mogao Caves and the Beijing Central Axis.
As part of the efforts required in the plan to restore and revitalize cultural relics, China plans to restore 300 historic and cultural neighborhoods and 15,000 historic buildings during the 15th Five-Year Plan period, said Qin Haixiang, vice minister of housing and urban-rural development, at the press conference.
Currently, the Chinese government has designated more than 1,300 historic and cultural neighborhoods, recognized 72,000 historic buildings, and included 8,155 villages on the national list of traditional villages with high conservation value.
"We will encourage more residents of historic neighborhoods to participate in the restoration, with full respect for their opinions," Qin said, adding that efforts will be made to reinforce historic buildings and improve living environments.
The plan also calls for efforts to improve the protection of immovable cultural relics. Deng Chao, deputy head of the National Cultural Heritage Administration, said the country will upgrade its lists of protected sites of cultural heritage based on the results of the fourth survey on immovable national cultural relics, which started in November 2023 and is now in the conclusion stage.
"More than 70 percent of China's immovable cultural relics have yet to be assigned as protected sites by the government, some of which are privately owned and some are in poor condition," Deng said, noting that the administration will improve the protection and oversight system for such relics.
He said the locations of immovable cultural relics will be incorporated into the country's territorial spatial planning, while satellite remote sensing, drones and other technologies will be used to systematically monitor changes in their condition.
According to Deng, 31 provincial-level regions in China have introduced policies requiring archaeological surveys and exploration before local governments transfer land-use rights in areas where cultural relics may be buried underground. The requirement, included in a revision to the country's Law on the Protection of Cultural Relics passed in 2024, aims to prevent damage to cultural relics from large construction projects.
"We will make archaeology fully integrated into urban development, and promote the coordinated protection of aboveground cultural relics and underground archaeological sites," he said. ■

00:50:56 KST

HELSINKI, Oct. 20 (Xinhua) -- Finland's unemployment rate rose to 10.4 percent in September 2026, up from 9.1 percent a year earlier, as the country's labor market continued to struggle despite signs of an economic recovery, official data showed on Tuesday.
According to Statistics Finland's Labour Force Survey, the number of unemployed people aged 15 to 74 reached 298,000 in September, up 39,000 year-on-year, while the number of employed people fell by 11,000 to 2.578 million.
In particular, youth unemployment worsened, with the jobless rate among those aged 15 to 24 climbing to 22.0 percent, up 5.4 percentage points from a year earlier.
Separate data from Statistics Finland showed that the unemployment rate averaged 9.8 percent in the third quarter of 2026, up from 9.2 percent a year earlier, while total hours worked fell by 1.8 percent year-on-year.
Despite signs of economic recovery, improvements in the labor market could take up to a year to materialize, Finnish national broadcaster Yle reported on Tuesday.
Petri Malinen, chief economist of the Federation of Finnish Enterprises, told Yle that ongoing geopolitical uncertainties were clouding business outlooks and prompting companies to postpone recruitment.
He said cautious consumer spending and a slow recovery in consumption were limiting demand for businesses, leaving them with little incentive to hire additional workers.
Jukka Appelqvist, chief economist of the Finland Chamber of Commerce, said in a statement on Tuesday that the latest figures showed the labor market remains under pressure, with a clear positive turnaround yet to emerge.
"The weakening of the labor market is already behind us, but we are still moving sideways rather than seeing clear growth," Appelqvist said, adding that conditions remained particularly challenging in the private sector.
He also noted that an expansion of the labor force accounted for much of the increase in unemployment.
In its latest economic forecast released in September, the Bank of Finland projected gross domestic product (GDP) growth of 1.7 percent in 2026 and 1.6 percent in 2027, with the unemployment rate expected to remain at 10.4 percent this year before easing to 9.8 percent next year. ■

ANKARA, Oct. 20 (Xinhua) -- The Turkish government has submitted the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement to parliament for ratification on Tuesday, local media reported.

The full text of the agreement, disclosed on the same day by the London-based news portal Middle East Eye, does not identify any specific country or region as a threat. It emphasizes mutual support among all parties if the territorial integrity, sovereignty, or internationally recognized borders of any party are threatened or endangered.

Burhanettin Duran, director of the Turkish Presidential Communications Directorate, said on the social media platform X that the submission marks an important stage in the institutionalization of strategic cooperation among the "three brotherly countries."
On Aug. 7, Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement in Mecca. Under the agreement, an armed attack on any signatory is to be considered an attack on all. ■

Chinese Minister of Ecology and Environment Huang Runqiu speaks at the opening ceremony of the China Pavilion at the 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations (UN) Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17) in Yerevan, Armenia, Oct. 19, 2026. Themed "Taking Action for Nature," COP17 runs on Oct. 19-30. During the conference, the China Pavilion will host a series of events, including thematic side events, sessions on local biodiversity conservation initiatives, seminars and an exhibition showcasing China's achievements in biodiversity conservation. (Xinhua/Chen Junfeng)
YEREVAN, Oct. 20 (Xinhua) -- The China Pavilion at the 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations (UN) Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17) opened in the capital of Armenia.
Chinese Minister of Ecology and Environment Huang Runqiu, Armenian Environment Minister and COP17 President Hambardzum Matevosyan, and Astrid Schomaker, executive secretary of the Convention on Biological Diversity, attended the opening ceremony on Monday. The pavilion was officially opened by Huang at the ceremony hosted by China's Ministry of Ecology and Environment.
Huang said global biodiversity conservation had made overall progress since the adoption of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KMGBF) in 2022, but implementation remained below expectations.
As COP17 conducts the first global review of collective progress in implementing the framework, Huang called on all parties to translate their commitments into concrete policies and conservation actions with greater determination and stronger efforts.
Matevosyan said the current pace and scale of global efforts to implement the KMGBF were insufficient to achieve its targets. He called for stronger domestic coordination and international cooperation, improved mechanisms for assessing and reporting implementation progress, and greater integration of biodiversity conservation across government departments and all sectors of society.
Schomaker said the progress reflected in China's seventh national report on the implementation of the Convention on Biological Diversity was encouraging. She particularly commended China's ecological conservation redline system as an example of integrating biodiversity conservation into national planning and development.
Themed "Taking Action for Nature," COP17 runs on Oct. 19-30. During the conference, the China Pavilion will host a series of events, including thematic side events, sessions on local biodiversity conservation initiatives, seminars and an exhibition showcasing China's achievements in biodiversity conservation. ■

łukasz twarkowski turns theater into a live cinematic spectacle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
15:45:13 UTC
00:45:13 KST

łukasz twarkowski turns theater into a live cinematic spectacle
the polish director builds immersive stage environments in which live performance, moving images, and shifting scenography challenge how audiences experience theater.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
Łukasz Twarkowski merges theater and cinema onstage
Before Oracle begins at Onassis Stegi in Athens, a camera captures the audience and projects its image onto a screen. Spectators appear as grainy black-and-white figures, their faces transformed into a strange, almost anonymous collective portrait. Those who have come to watch find themselves becoming the spectacle. It is an introduction to the work of Polish director Łukasz Twarkowski, in which live performance and cinema become inseparable. Twarkowski brings theater and cinema into a shared space, making the process of filming part of the performance. The stage divides horizontally into two visual fields: the live theatrical action unfolds below, while a screen above displays footage captured by cameras operating within the set in real time. The audience watches the actors perform while simultaneously observing how their movements are framed and transformed into cinematic images.
For the director, video is not just an addition to the performance. Theater and cinema happen at the same time, with cameras filming the actors live and projecting the footage onto a screen above the stage. The audience can watch the actors perform or follow the action through the camera, constantly switching between the two.
directing between the stage and the screen
For most of the three-hour-and-40-minute performance, the filming process remains visible to the audience. Camera operators move within the set, framing actors whose actions are simultaneously experienced in the theater and on screen. The projected images offer close-ups and carefully composed perspectives, while the stage reveals the bodies, movements, and technical decisions behind them. The audience is free to move between these viewpoints, but neither provides a complete account of the event. The screen can draw attention away from the physical stage, offering a familiar way of experiencing a narrative through selected frames. Yet looking away from the screen reveals another performance unfolding around the act of filming itself. Twarkowski makes this competition for the audience’s attention part of the experience, exposing how easily the mediated image can take precedence over the reality it represents.
a recurring approach to theatrical illusion
The set is made up of separate modules, each built around a corner with walls and a ceiling. The units can be joined in different combinations, either in pairs or around the center of the stage, creating a range of spatial arrangements. Depending on how they connect and rotate, they can form enclosed rooms, corridors, or a series of open frames that suggest a street or a cluster of buildings.
The lighting further changes how these spaces are perceived, shifting their atmosphere from one scene to the next. The production rearranges the same elements to create different environments and conditions for the action. The transformations remain visible, making the changing structure an active part of the performance.
the spectacle of watching
What makes Twarkowski’s approach relevant beyond the theater is its engagement with a culture increasingly organized around screens, live images, and mediated experiences. In ORACLE, the audience is first transformed into an image and then invited to watch performers undergo the same process. The camera becomes both a tool for revealing detail and an instrument that determines what can be seen.
The subject of the production, which moves between Alan Turing, the history of computing, and the emergence of artificial intelligence, adds another dimension to this inquiry. Its use of thermal and infrared imaging evokes technologies associated with surveillance and military applications, complicating the assumption that images provide neutral access to reality. What appears on screen is always shaped by a system of interpretation.
Twarkowski uses the resources of contemporary theater to examine how images are constructed and how audiences respond to them. His work suggests that spectacle lies in the systems that organize attention, mediate experience, and determine what becomes visible.

The Palestine poppy badge that sparked right-wing fury
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
15:43:13 UTC
00:43:13 KST

Breadcrumb
The Palestinian poppy: Why one doctor is reimagining a British symbol of remembrance
As Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in 2023, people around the world found different ways to express their solidarity with Palestinians. From wearing the keffiyeh to sharing watermelon emojis, these acts of solidarity took many forms.
For paediatrician Dr Abdul Qader Ismail, it was a poppy-shaped badge.
Alongside his work treating children for the NHS and writing picture books, Dr Abdul created the Palestine poppy badge shortly after Israel's war began in the besieged enclave. The badge gave people a way to show support for Palestinians at a time when expressions of solidarity faced growing scrutiny.
"I wanted to take a symbol that was beloved in the West, given the West's integral role in the suffering and injustice endured by the Palestinian people — from the Nakba, and even before it, to the present day, including the current genocide," Dr Abdul tells The New Arab.
Pinned proudly to his chest as he speaks, the poppy badge features the colours of the Palestine flag. He designed the pin himself, drawing inspiration from other designs he saw online.
For Dr Abdul, the poppy’s associations with remembrance, peace and the human cost of war make it a particularly fitting symbol for Palestine.
"If the poppy is there to remember those who fell in war, those who suffered because of war, and to symbolise peace and an end to violence and injustice, then I think Palestinians, who have suffered immensely, deserve the poppy just as much as anyone else," he adds.
He stressed that the badge was not intended to provoke division or hostility towards anyone. "It's not meant to be a symbol against anyone. It's not meant to be something that causes division or hate or anything like that," Dr Abdul shares.
In Britain, the red poppy is closely associated with Remembrance Day, when people honour the service and sacrifice of armed forces members who died in conflict. Over time, it has also become a symbol of national remembrance, and its use in political campaigns has sometimes sparked controversy.
But the poppy's significance extends beyond Britain. Dr Abdul highlighted that it is also a national symbol for Palestinians, arguing that this connection has been forgotten. He also pointed to the tens of thousands of Palestinians who, he said, fought alongside the Allies during the Second World War, as well as the poppy’s longstanding use in pro-Palestine activism.
Backlash from right-wing UK press
Despite Dr Abdul having made the badge in December 2023, it has now caught the attention of right-wing media, who are accusing the doctor of "hijacking" Remembrance Day.
"I suppose like any media outlet, what they want is to publish a juicy story that gets them more readers and more attention and causes anger and debate, and so I suppose that's what media does, isn't it," Dr Abdul says about the backlash.
He strongly rejected any suggestion that he was anti-Semitic, pointing to his support for Jewish Green Party leader Zack Polanski and his longstanding professional relationships with people of different faiths and backgrounds.
He said he had joined the Green Party specifically because of Polanski's outspoken support for Palestinians and his opposition to conflating anti-Zionism with anti-Semitism.
"Whenever people have tried to show support for Palestine, it's always framed by those who don't like it, that you are somehow a terrorist sympathiser or supporter, that you are anti-Semitic, that you're pro-violence, you're anti-peace," the doctor adds.
"It's always framed in that way to silence people, to stop them from speaking out, to stop them from showing their support for the Palestinian people, and this is no different than that."
Boost in sales
While he had anticipated some backlash and personal attacks, Dr Abdul was surprised that the badge had attracted attention nearly three years after its creation.
The controversy, however, has had an unexpected consequence — a sharp rise in sales.
"Since these articles have come out… its sales have gone through the roof to the extent that I've actually run out of stock now," the doctor explains, noting that the sales within the last few months had "dried up."
He said the badge has attracted buyers from a wide range of backgrounds, both online and at pro-Palestine events, with interest extending well beyond Muslim and Palestinian communities.
"I can see the names of the people who are buying from me... They are from all kinds of backgrounds," Dr Ismail explains.
"There's a lot of support for this. People like the badge, people like the concept, and people recognise it for what it is: a symbol of peace and a symbol for showing your support for Palestine and the Palestinian people," he added.
Like the books he has written, the badge itself is not-for-profit, with proceeds going toward producing more badges and supporting charities working on the ground in Palestine or educating people about the cause.
Reflecting on the backlash, Dr Abdul acknowledged that anticipating criticism and experiencing it firsthand are two very different things, as he continues to navigate the attention his work has drawn.
"If [right-wing press] didn't want the badge to be sold or known about, they've done the exact opposite by writing articles about it," Dr Abdul concluded.
Anam Alam is a staff writer at The New Arab. She frequently writes about human rights and social issues, including women's rights and sex education
