Ukraine state-owned PrivatBank has decided to join the state program providing partial compensation for interest rates on loans to medium-sized and large businesses for projects involving distributed generation, infrastructure restoration, and the development of the processing industry, the financial institution's press service said Tuesday.
Under the program's terms, the state will compensate 5.5 percentage points of the bank's base annual interest rate, which is capped at 18%. Loan amounts range from UAH 100 million to UAH 1 billion, while the minimum financing amount for companies operating in areas of active or possible hostilities has been reduced to UAH 30 million.
"We are already ready to consider applications from potential participants seeking to implement such projects," said Yevhen Zaihraiev, a member of PrivatBank's board responsible for corporate banking and small and medium-sized businesses.
Funds under the program may be allocated to distributed generation projects, measures to improve the resilience of fuel infrastructure, and the construction and restoration of damaged or destroyed power generation facilities, fuel and warehousing logistics infrastructure, as well as fixed assets at processing enterprises.
The program also provides for financing investment projects in the processing industry and working capital for wholesale and retail businesses to restore and replenish inventories lost or damaged as a result of the war.
The bank said the financing terms allow for payment deferrals of up to one year and a fee of up to 1%. Applications for loans can be submitted until May 15, 2027.
The state program was introduced by Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 594 dated April 29, 2026. Initially, it focused on distributed generation projects, but in September, amid intensified Russian attacks, the government expanded its terms and eligible financing areas.
PrivatBank is Ukraine's largest bank. According to the National Bank of Ukraine, the financial institution's total assets amounted to UAH 983.82 billion as of September 1, 2026, accounting for 22.8% of the banking system's total assets. The bank's loan portfolio grew by 29.2% over the first eight months of the year, reaching UAH 212.66 billion.

Scientists left in the dark by National Science Foundation grant application delays
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
15:35:40 UTC
00:35:40 KST

A major federal grant program that helps researchers purchase scientific equipment has seemingly gone dark, leaving scientists unsure of whether they will be able to apply for funding.
The National Science Foundation’s (NSF) Major Research Instrumentation (MRI) program provides funding for the development or acquisition of state-of-the-art, often expensive equipment that researchers use to perform fundamental science and engineering experiments. These could be for kits such as clusters of GPUs to power research into artificial intelligence, which can run into the millions of dollars to buy and install, or highly specialized lasers or microscopes. Grant applicants can ask for up to $4 million, and they must demonstrate that the equipment will be used by several groups or experiments—a condition that can make the submission process more complicated than for other grants.
In a statement released last year, the NSF said it planned to accept submissions in 2026 between October 15 and November 16. But the proposed opening date, October 15, has come and gone.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
It’s the second year in a row that MRI applications have hit a speed bump. In 2025 the NSF suspended applications for the 2026 fiscal year. The agency said it had an enormous backlog of meritorious proposals from the previous year that it would consider funding instead.
When asked for comment, an NSF spokesperson said the agency is “currently working to update this funding opportunity,” but did not confirm to Scientific American when the submission process might open.
The delay comes amid numerous shakeups to federal funding of science. The Trump administration has cancelled numerous grants that had already been granted through the NSF, the National Institutes of Health and other agencies, and has attempted to introduce a major overhaul that would have granted sweeping oversight of grants to political appointees rather than the panels of experts currently in place. That change was temporarily halted in a recent government bill but could be reintroduced in December. The Trump administration has said these changes have been conducted in the name of promoting “gold standard science.”
Several people involved in submitting MRI grant applications say they have received no word from the NSF as to when the submission period for this year might open. Laura Rodman, a grant proposal consultant, says she was told by a contact at major grant consultant firm McAllister & Quinn that proposal solicitations would start shortly after the federal government’s new fiscal year began on October 1.
“We’re still waiting,” she says.
The lack of clarity on when, or if, the submission period will open is leaving U.S. universities and research institutions in the lurch. One grant specialist at an American university who asked to remain anonymous to protect their privacy says schools are often limited in the number of MRI grants they can apply for. In turn, universities often run their own internal, highly competitive submission process before applying—a time-consuming effort for researchers and their labs.
“Nobody knows when the deadline will be or if it will even happen, so the act of planning to apply is a gamble,” the specialist says. “Are these faculty wasting their time?”
Even the simplest grant proposal may require up at least 30 to 40 hours of preparation, according to one scientist, who also asked to remain anonymous because they currently have a proposal pending at the NSF. That workload is increased for MRI grants, because of the need to show high levels of collaboration between research teams.
“Grants are very competitive, so an investigator must write the strongest argument they can for why taxpayer funds should go to their project,” the scientist says. “Scientific instrumentation is expensive, and the NSF wants to see that a new instrument will be used regularly. Many MRI requests involve four to six scientists, which increases the coordination needed to write a compelling proposal.”
The fact that the grants are written for groups of scientists means that a delay in the submission process can ripple out and affect multiple research projects.
“If you have a broken $700,000 instrument, or an instrument that is rapidly approaching the end of its useful life, a delay could have significant consequences,” the scientist says. “Researchers may put their projects on hold, or worse, waste money on Band-Aid repairs when a replacement would be far more efficient.”
“Moreover, sometimes a few months can be the difference between a high-impact publication and getting scooped,” they add.
The delays are particularly acute given the rising concerns about the U.S. falling behind international competitors in STEM fields; the NSF is a major funding source for critical research fields, such as chemistry and physics, the scientist says.
“For researchers without National Institutes of Health funding, the MRI program is often the only available option,” they add.

00:34:44 KST

More than 250,000 people have been displaced in Yemen between Aug. 1 and Oct. 17 as hostilities intensified across the country, the UN refugee agency (UNHCR) said Tuesday, Anadolu reports.
The figure rose from nearly 213,000 previously reported, with Taiz remaining at the center of the displacement crisis, accounting for 76% of departures and hosting 52% of those newly displaced.
Lahj in southwestern Yemen hosts 23% of the newly displaced population, followed by Aden in the south with 13%, according to UNHCR.
“Shelling intensified in Taiz, including in residential areas and around health facilities, while insecurity and restrictions along key routes continue to constrain humanitarian access and movement,” the agency said in a statement.
“In Aden, strikes were reported, including near key civilian infrastructure,” it added.
READ: Yemen: Houthis Prosecute UN, Civil Society Staff
By Oct. 17, UNHCR and its partners had assessed 12,283 displaced households across Abyan, Aden, Marib, Lahj and Taiz, including around 2,050 families without shelter.
It said shelter partners have reached 3,166 households, but around 33,700 families still require shelter assistance amid severe underfunding of the wider humanitarian response.
UNHCR said schools in Kharaz refugee camp in Lahj, which hosts 9,490 refugees, closed again on Oct. 11 as the security situation deteriorated, while access restrictions continued to affect humanitarian operations and movement to and from the camp.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and several other provinces in September 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.
The Houthis control much of northern and western Yemen, while government forces and their allies hold Aden and large parts of the country’s southern and eastern provinces.

More than 45,000 foreigners from 151 countries have signed contracts with the Russian army — Coordination Headquarters

The Coordination Headquarters has identified 45,959 foreigners who signed contracts with the Russian army. Recruitment is growing fastest in Africa and Latin America.
Russia is increasingly involving foreigners in the war against Ukraine, recruiting citizens of countries in Africa, Latin America and the post-Soviet space. In total, the identities of nearly 46,000 foreigners from 151 countries who signed contracts with the armed forces of the Russian Federation have been established. This was reported by the Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War, UNN writes.
As of October 1, 2026, according to data from the “I Want to Live” project, the identities of 45,959 foreigners who signed contracts with the armed forces of the Russian Federation have been established. They are citizens of 151 countries and representatives of unrecognized territories, the statement says
This was reported during the international conference “Crimea Global. Understanding Ukraine through the South” by the Secretary of the Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War, Brigadier General Dmytro Usov.
The updated data clearly show how the scale of Russia’s recruitment is growing.
-  2022 – 94 people; 
-  2023 – 4,067; 
-  2024 – 8,877; 
-  2025 – 16,085; 
-  for the 9 months of 2026 – 16,168. 
The plan for 2026 is 18,500 people. Russia is currently recruiting about 1,800 foreigners per month. If this pace continues, the plan will be exceeded as early as November, and by the end of the year the number of new contract soldiers could reach 21,500.
The largest number of foreigners have been recruited in Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and Belarus. At the same time, recruitment is growing fastest in African and Latin American countries.
In just nine months of 2026, 1,449 citizens of Colombia, 699 of Burundi, 530 of Zimbabwe and 503 of Peru signed contracts with the armed forces of the Russian Federation.
The governments of the countries whose citizens have ended up in the Russian army and been captured by Ukraine must increase diplomatic pressure on Moscow. Russia must be held accountable for the fate of the people it recruited to fight against Ukraine and facilitate their return home

Military personnel’s leave abroad: what documents need to be prepared for travel

Military personnel’s leave abroad: what documents need to be prepared for travel
Kyiv • UNN
To travel abroad, a service member needs the commander’s permission and must submit a report 15 days in advance. At the border, they should have their passport, military document, and an extract from the order.
Ukrainian service members have the right to travel abroad during their annual leave, provided that they follow a clearly defined procedure. The Ministry of Defense reported that, among other things, they must obtain permission from the commander of their military unit, UNN reports.
How to obtain permission for leave abroad
The Ministry of Defense reported that the commander makes the decision to permit travel abroad based on a service member’s report, which must specify:
-  the dates of departure and return; 
-  the city and address of stay; 
-  the mode of transport and the checkpoint. 
The leave report must be submitted no later than 15 calendar days before its scheduled start.
What documents are required to cross the border
In particular, when crossing the border, it is necessary to have documents confirming one’s identity and permission to travel:
-  a valid international passport; 
-  a military ID card or officer’s identity card; 
-  a leave certificate of the prescribed form; 
-  an extract from the order of the commander of the military unit granting permission to travel. 
Timely and proper completion of the relevant documents makes crossing the border easier. In addition, when crossing the state border (both when leaving and entering Ukraine), it is important to ask border guards to affix stamps with the relevant dates in the international passport

Mecca Agreement is not alternative to NATO, open to other countries — Erdogan’s party
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
15:33:10 UTC
00:33:10 KST

ISTANBUL, October 20. /TASS/. The Mecca Agreement between Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan is not an alternative to NATO and is open to other countries, spokesperson for the ruling Justice and Development Party Omer Celik said.
"The Mecca Agreement is not an alternative to NATO, but an additional mechanism of the international security architecture. <…> Turkey will respect this agreement with parliament’s approval and within the constitutional procedures. The participation of other countries in this agreement would be welcome from the viewpoint of its principles and goals," he said.
According to earlier reports, a bill on the ratification of the Mecca Agreement was submitted to Turkey’s parliament for ratification. Under the country’s laws, international agreements are to be endorsed by parliament, which also authorizes the deployment of military contingents abroad.
The Mecca Agreement consists of 16 articles; once it enters into force, the signatory countries will not be able to withdraw from it for the first 10 years. One of the most important articles is Article 2, which stipulates that an attack on one of the countries will be considered an act of military aggression against all signatories to the pact. The agreement provides for cooperation among the signatory countries in the defense industry, including joint production, the implementation of research and innovation projects, and personnel training. The parties will also cooperate in the areas of security, intelligence, and counterterrorism. The pact’s strategic, political, and defense committees, which will include foreign and defense ministers, and chiefs of staff, will meet at least twice a year on a rotating basis, while the countries’ leaders will meet once a year if they deem it necessary, according to excerpts from the document cited by the TRT Haber television channel.
The Mecca Joint Defense Agreement was signed by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, and Pakistani Prime Minister Shahbaz Sharif on August 7. On October 5, the member countries decided to begin putting into practice their joint defense commitments and deploy military forces on Saudi territory.

Glen-Gery clads Princeton University health centre in bricks made with reclaimed materials
Burgundy-coloured bricks incorporating reclaimed manufacturing waste wrap Princeton University’s Frist Health Centre in Princeton, New Jersey, as shown in this video carousel produced by Dezeen.
Called Ponderosa Western, the bricks are part of North American manufacturer Glen-Gery‘s Western Series and incorporate materials recovered from its own manufacturing process.
The extruded bricks, which were laid in a horizontal running bond pattern, feature sharp, precise edges and a surface texture that combines velour, grooved and sanded finishes.
The facade was designed to complement the century-old Gothic brickwork of the university’s historic Eno Hall, which was constructed in 1924.
The new building features metal sunshades to help reduce solar heat gain, alongside mineral wool insulation behind the brickwork to support the centre’s energy performance.
Courtyards, green roofs and diverse plant life surround the building, creating a landscape designed to provide a calming environment for students and faculty.
Exposed mass timber and visual connections to the outdoors continue throughout the interior of the building.
The project has been recognised by AIA New York State for its use of biophilic design and adaptive reuse.
Frist Health Centre at Princeton University is a 76,500-square-foot facility dedicated to holistic health and student wellbeing. It opened on the university’s campus in 2025.
Glen-Gery is a brick manufacturer that specialises in creating custom facades for cultural, residential and educational institutions across North America.
This process means that the artists themselves were unsure of what the pieces would look like until they were completely finished.
“The thickness of the shingle coat varies depending on the complexity of the shingled area,” Wegwerth and Dehn said. “As a result, the final silhouettes and tonal values only emerge gradually during the process.”
To find out more about Glen-Gery, visit its website.

Global warming is accelerating, leading climate scientist Rockstrom says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
15:31:14 UTC
00:31:14 KST

Global warming is accelerating, leading climate scientist Rockstrom says
LONDON - Global warming caused by fossil fuel emissions is accelerating, pushing many of the Earth’s most important ecosystems close to their tipping points, said Johan Rockstrom, director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research.
Speaking at the Reuters Sustainability Europe conference on Oct 20, Rockstrom said damage to coral reefs and the Amazon rainforest was close to becoming irreversible.
Parts of the Atlantic Ocean circulation system, including the current that moderates Western Europe’s climate with warm water from the Caribbean, were close to collapse.
The latest science confirms the world is on course to exceed a 1.5 deg C rise in average surface temperature in the next few years, increasing the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events, he said, ahead of the United Nations’ COP31 climate talks starting on Nov 9.
Companies looking to prepare and build resilience into their operations should treat climate and nature as a single integrated agenda rather than separate issues, he said.
While prioritising efforts to decarbonise, they should also invest in helping preserve nature, particularly projects related to maintaining or rebuilding biodiversity and reserves of fresh water.
Rockstrom said it was “incredibly disturbing” to see lobbying for an easing of rules on phasing out internal combustion engine vehicles, pointing to subsidies for petrol and diesel that were undermining consumer demand for electric vehicles. REUTERS

Moscow reacts to US Castro warrant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
15:30:20 UTC
00:30:20 KST

Moscow reacts to US Castro warrant
The US arrest warrant for former Cuban leader Raul Castro is political revenge, Russia has said, warning that escalating pressure on Havana could destabilize Latin America and the Caribbean.
A Florida judge issued the warrant on Monday against Castro, 95, on a charge of conspiracy to commit first-degree murder over the 1996 downing of two planes operated by Brothers to the Rescue – a Miami-based Cuban exile group led by CIA operative Jose Basulto, who has long pressed for charges against Castro. Four men were killed in the shootdown.
The US authorities accuse Castro of ordering the attack. Havana maintains it acted in self-defense against aircraft violating its airspace. The Cuban Embassy in Washington accused the group of committing more than 25 airspace violations from 1994 to 1996, despite repeated warnings from Havana.
In a statement on Tuesday, the Russian Foreign Ministry called the accusation “groundless” and “contrived,” describing its revival more than 30 years later as “revenge by Miami’s anti-Cuban lobby.”
The ministry noted that the UN Security Council addressed the incident in a July 1996 resolution without calling for anyone to be held individually responsible. Moscow argued that this effectively meant that the council, including the US, considered that aspect of the incident closed.
It warned that further pressure on Cuba, which is already struggling under an unprecedented economic, financial, and energy blockade, could provoke unrest and mass migration, creating social crises in neighboring countries.
The ministry linked its concerns about the warrant to the US seizure of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January. Without that precedent, the court decision might have been dismissed as reflecting the views of a particular group, it said, describing Maduro’s abduction as a violation of international law.
Monday’s warrant follows a separate federal indictment brought against Castro and five others in May. Cuban President Miguel Diaz-Canel condemned the case as a “political maneuver, devoid of any legal foundation,” and accused Washington of creating a pretext for military action.
US President Donald Trump has intensified pressure on Havana since the operation against Venezuela, imposing a near-total energy blockade and declaring that Cuba would be “next.” The restrictions have contributed to severe energy shortages and frequent blackouts on the island.
Moscow reaffirmed its solidarity with Havana on Tuesday, pledging to strengthen ties through mutual support, assistance, and cooperation. Russia has been among the countries providing relief to Cuba, delivering around 700,000 barrels of oil in March.

Saudi man at risk of execution for offences in his teens: NGOs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
15:27:19 UTC
00:27:19 KST

Breadcrumb
Saudi man at risk of execution for offences in his teens: NGOs
Rights groups warned on Tuesday that a Saudi man faces imminent execution for offences he allegedly committed when he was a minor, just days after the execution of another man in a similar case.
Youssef al-Manasif, 30, was sentenced to death for "terrorism" after taking part in Arab Spring protests and demonstrations at the funerals of people killed in the Eastern Province in 2011 and 2012, when he was aged 15 and 16, according to Human Rights Watch (HRW). His appeal was rejected.
On Saturday, Hassan Zaki al-Faraj and four other men were executed for "terrorism" in the oil-rich province, home to the majority of Saudi Arabia's Shia minority in the predominantly Sunni kingdom.
According to HRW, Faraj was convicted for offences committed when he was 14 years old.
Manasif, who was arrested in 2017, "is also at serious risk of execution", said Joey Shea of HRW.
Since January, the kingdom has executed 15 people for "terrorism", mainly in the east of the country, compared with 40 in 2025.
"Youssef al-Manasif and his family are living through nights of terror, fearing he will be the next to be executed," Jeed Basyouni of London-based rights group Reprieve told AFP.
In April 2025, eight independent UN experts warned of the risk of the imminent execution of five Shia Saudis, including Faraj and Manasif.
Duaa Dhainy, a researcher for the Berlin-based Euro-Saudi Organisation for Human Rights (ESOHR), believes Manasif could be executed "at any moment".
"Our organisation has received information that the Supreme Court has issued a final ruling ordering his execution," she told AFP.
Saudi Arabia has executed 190 people this year, including 89 Saudis and 116 convicted of drug trafficking, 80 of whom were foreigners, according to an AFP tally.
The latest executions come as Saudi Arabia faces daily missile and drone attacks from the Houthis in Yemen, where Riyadh militarily backs the internationally recognised government in its long-running civil war against the Iran-backed group.
According to Amnesty International, Saudi Arabia was the world's third-most prolific executioner between 2022 and 2025, behind China and Iran.
The kingdom considers the death penalty necessary to maintain public order and insists it applies it only after all appeals have been exhausted.
(AFP)

Breadcrumb
Lebanon judge to question Hezbollah officials over explosives shipment
A Lebanese judge on Tuesday ordered two Hezbollah officials to appear for questioning over their alleged involvement in a delivery of explosives seized by authorities this month, a judicial official told AFP.
Lebanese authorities had been carrying out investigations after arresting two suspected Hezbollah members accused of transporting half a tonne of explosives, which the Iran-backed group subsequently said were part of its "capabilities" to be used against Israel.
They were caught on October 8 at a security checkpoint in Dahr al-Baidar in Lebanon's east in a vehicle headed towards Beirut, with a source telling AFP that one was the son of a Hezbollah official and the other was also a group member.
The judicial official, requesting anonymity, told AFP that the judge on Tuesday ordered two Hezbollah officials to appear for questioning "after initial investigations... established their identities".
Security agencies are working to locate them and take them into custody, the official added.
Last week, Hezbollah lawmaker Hassan Fadlallah said the explosives belonged to the militant group, demanding the shipment be returned and calling for those arrested to be released, in a rare admission by the group.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio subsequently urged Lebanon not to return the explosives.
Lebanese authorities have announced the seizure of three large shipments of explosives this month alone.
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam has vowed that authorities "will deal with weapons outside the legal framework with the required firmness".
President Joseph Aoun on Saturday said the army and security forces were "implementing the government's decisions on extending the state's authority... and confiscating weapons and ammunition".
"Violators are referred to the judiciary, which carries out its duties fully in applying the law and the political authorities' decisions," he added.
Lebanese authorities last year committed to disarming Hezbollah after months of cross-border hostilities culminated in a 2024 war between the group and Israel.
But Hezbollah drew Lebanon into the Middle East war this year by attacking Israel, which responded with heavy strikes and a ground invasion.
In June, Lebanese and Israeli authorities signed a framework agreement which involves the disarmament of Hezbollah, a gradual Israeli withdrawal from territories it occupies, and the deployment of the Lebanese army to the area.
Hezbollah, the only militant group that refused to disarm after Lebanon's 1975-1990 civil war, has rejected surrendering its weapons and the direct negotiations with Israel.

Ukrainian Red Cross Society, USA partner to help state agencies identify casualties
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
18:21:40 EEST
00:21:40 KST

The Ukrainian Red Cross Society (URCS), with support from the U.S. Department of State, is assisting state forensic institutions involved in the identification and transportation of the deceased.
"The Ukrainian Red Cross Society, with support from the U.S. Department of State, continues to strengthen the capabilities of state institutions responsible for storing, identifying and transporting the bodies of Ukraine's fallen male and female defenders," the URCS said in a Facebook post on Tuesday.
The assistance includes the supply of specialized refrigeration equipment, vehicles, as well as reagents and consumables for DNA testing. It is aimed at expanding the capacity of state laboratories to conduct DNA identification in complex cases in which the deceased cannot be identified by external characteristics.
In late September 2026, the URCS provided the Institute of Forensic Psychiatry and Forensic Medicine of Ukraine's Ministry of Health with consumables for molecular genetic testing and personal protective equipment for laboratory staff, including materials for PCR testing, microcentrifuge tubes, filter tips, nitrile gloves and medical masks.
"Behind every identification case is a family waiting for answers about the fate of a loved one. The Ukrainian Red Cross Society helps state institutions carrying out this difficult work by providing them with the necessary equipment and materials. It is important to us that the process of identifying the deceased is conducted with respect for human dignity and that families can receive reliable information about their loved ones," said Serhiy Zaporozhets, a representative of the URCS department responsible for implementing the program to support war veterans, frontline responders and people affected by the war.
One area of support has been the provision of specialized refrigeration equipment to forensic medical examination bureaus. The equipment makes it possible to maintain the required temperature conditions for the temporary storage of bodies while complying with sanitary requirements and the principles of dignified treatment. Four containers equipped with refrigeration systems have already been delivered to state specialized institutions in Chernihiv, Odesa, Sumy and Kharkiv regions. Another 16 such containers are scheduled for delivery by the end of 2026, primarily to institutions operating in frontline regions and facing significant workloads.
With assistance from the U.S. Department of State, the Ukrainian Red Cross Society has purchased two specialized refrigerated vehicles to be used in implementing the "On the Shield" humanitarian project in cooperation with the Civil-Military Cooperation Directorate of the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine. The vehicles will operate primarily in frontline areas, transporting bodies to designated handover locations, including sites closer to settlements where the families of the deceased live.

US special envoy Tom Barrack said Tuesday that Washington is providing logistical support to Saudi Arabia, but a US ground intervention in the conflict involving Yemen’s Houthis “appears pointless,” Anadolu reports.
Speaking at the Global Security Forum in Doha, Qatar, Barrack, who serves as US ambassador to Türkiye and special presidential envoy for Syria and Iraq, said President Donald Trump supports Saudi Arabia logistically amid escalating hostilities between the kingdom and the Houthi group.
He also urged Middle Eastern countries to establish regional alliances rather than rely on Washington to resolve their problems.
Barrack said the US was redefining its role in the Middle East, moving away from direct control and intervention toward supporting regional countries in managing their own security.
He stressed that Washington was not abandoning its partners but could no longer be expected to resolve every regional conflict.
On Yemen, Barrack questioned the effectiveness of military intervention against the Houthis, saying negotiations involving Saudi Arabia, the group and regional mediators offered a better alternative.
Iran deal
Barrack said the US wants to reach a peaceful agreement with Iran as tensions between Washington and Tehran continue.
He said Trump remained willing to negotiate with Tehran, stressing that Washington was seeking a diplomatic solution rather than further military escalation.
Barrack pointed to mediation efforts by Qatar, Oman, Pakistan and Switzerland, saying a lack of trust between Washington and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) remained a major obstacle.
He suggested that a modified version of the Islamabad understanding could provide a basis for renewed negotiations, including a ceasefire, the reopening of maritime routes and measures to ease economic pressure on Iranians.
The envoy also emphasized that Iran’s political future should be determined by Iranians themselves rather than through externally imposed regime change.
READ: UN says more than 230,000 displaced by fighting in Yemen since August
Barrack also questioned Washington’s history of military interventions in the Middle East, saying attempts to change governments have repeatedly failed.
“Every time we try and intervene, change the person or the regime, it seems to have been a mistake,” he said.
He said the US had been involved in 23 regime changes across the broader Middle East, arguing that none had produced the intended results.
Asked whether the US-Israeli war against Iran was a mistake, Barrack replied: “I don’t know whether it’s a mistake or not.”
He said the Trump administration’s initial objective in launching military operations against Iran on Feb. 28 was to prevent what Washington considered an imminent nuclear threat, rather than pursue regime change.
Barrack acknowledged that the conflict had triggered unintended consequences across the Middle East and beyond, stressing that the administration did not want the war to continue.
He also described the situation resulting from the conflict as “horrible.”
Syria transition
Turning to Syria, Barrack described the country’s political transition following the fall of the Bashar al-Assad government in December 2024 as an example of how former armed groups could become part of a political process.
He praised Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa’s handling of the transition under difficult circumstances and called for an end to Israeli military operations in Syria.
Barrack also emphasized the importance of dialogue and economic recovery in reducing regional tensions, arguing that military force alone could not provide lasting solutions.
His remarks come amid escalating hostilities between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis, with the Saudi-led coalition carrying out airstrikes against Houthi positions and the group launching missile and drone attacks targeting the kingdom.
The regional escalation has coincided with continued tensions between the US and Iran following their military confrontation, with diplomatic efforts aimed at reaching an agreement remaining deadlocked.

Eastern Libya parliament approves 2019 maritime deal with Turkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
15:19:17 UTC
00:19:17 KST

Eastern Libya parliament approves 2019 maritime deal with Turkiye
The vote recognises Ankara’s maritime deal with Tripoli, ending Haftar’s 2020 boycott.
Libya’s eastern-based parliament, backed by military commander Khalifa Haftar, which runs as an alternative to the UN-recognised legislature in Tripoli, has approved a maritime deal with Turkiye, ending years of acrimony.
Haftar’s Benghazi-based government said in a statement on Tuesday that his Tobruk-based House of Representatives voted unanimously to approve the 2019 memorandum of understanding signed between Turkiye and Libya’s UN-recognised former Government of National Accord (GNA) on the delimitation of maritime boundaries between the two countries in the Mediterranean Sea.
Specialised committees presented a full and detailed explanation of the deal’s provisions, lawmaker Aisha al-Tabalqi told the Reuters news agency.
The approval came six years after the same parliament in 2020 unanimously rejected the ratification of the deal and cut political ties with Ankara.
Strategic shift
The repealing of those moves on Tuesday consolidates a strategic shift in the works since last year, building on Ankara’s military-to-military contacts with Haftar’s self-styled Libyan National Army (LNA), including a deal in July to develop military facilities and advanced surveillance systems.
The LNA, long believed to have been supported by Egypt and other regional powers, has been in conflict with forces loyal to the Tripoli-based government since the start of the Libyan civil war in 2014.
In 2019, Turkiye signed an agreement with the Tripoli-based government delineating the maritime boundaries between the two countries in the Mediterranean, triggering protests from Greece and Cyprus.
Reacting to the latest announcement on Tuesday, Greece’s Foreign Ministry said the 2019 memorandum violated international law of the sea and infringed on the sovereign rights of states in the region, calling on Libya to refrain from actions that undermine stability in the Mediterranean.
Athens said it had informed partners and allies and would take all appropriate measures to safeguard its sovereign rights.
Earlier, Tarek al-Jeroushi, a lawmaker in the eastern-backed parliament said “some countries may be upset by this agreement, but what matters to us is our national interest”. He added that the agreement would strengthen Libya’s position as a political, military and economic partner to key powers.
In December 2019, Haftar’s LNA had nearly encircled Tripoli, threatening to overrun the UN-recognised GNA, which at the time was led by Fayez al-Sarraj, before Turkiye decided to intervene, sending military advisers and drones to stop the LNA, and altering the trajectory of the Libyan civil war.
Seven years later, there is talk of Ankara setting up a military presence in areas under the control of Haftar’s LNA.
This eastern pivot is designed to secure Turkiye’s long-term geopolitical and economic interests, preserving its influence in Libya regardless of future political settlements between the government and eastern authorities.

A generation in economic crisis: Europe's young people take to the streets as protests spread
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
15:15:29 UTC
00:15:29 KST

From Paris to Lisbon, Madrid to Milan and Brussels to Tirana, the capital of Albania, Europe is burning. Turbulent protests, violence, clashes with police, injuries, vandalism, destruction and looting have swept across the region. The demonstrations that began in France are spreading throughout Europe in a kind of domino effect.
Why is this happening? Each country has its own circumstances, but they all share a common economic and social story. Europe's young people are frustrated. They look to the future and see little reason for optimism: The job market is stagnant, while rents and home prices are soaring.
Even making ends meet has become increasingly difficult. The sharp rise in fuel prices, exacerbated by the war with Iran, coupled with rising food prices, has pushed the cost of living to the forefront of public debate across Europe.
Add to that painful cuts to social welfare programs in Western European countries as governments divert resources toward defense spending amid fears of war with Russia, along with political polarization that has helped trigger the violent demonstrations. In France and Italy, governments have accused the radical left of fueling the unrest for political gain.
Is there a direct connection between protesters in the different countries? For now, at least, it appears not. But there is little doubt that a domino effect is underway. Images of half a million demonstrators in France are inspiring people in Italy, Spain and Portugal to take to the streets and demand similar solutions from their governments.
Economic crises do not stop at national borders. Rising energy and commodity prices are affecting citizens across the European Union simultaneously, creating similar conditions for outbreaks of public anger.
The protests are not part of a coordinated effort, but they are linked by a strong ideological and economic thread. Young people across Europe share the same concerns about their futures, face similar economic hardships and use the same digital tools and social media platforms to mobilize protests and shake the streets.
Macron's failed revolution
Shortly before being elected president of France in 2017, Emmanuel Macron wrote a book titled "Revolution", in which he promised — and convinced his supporters — that he could rebuild France, put its economy back on its feet, free it from the crushing burden of debt and restore its rightful place as one of the leaders of the free world.
Nearly a decade later, France has indeed experienced an economic "revolution," but not the one its citizens envisioned when they elected Macron.
Instead, there is extraordinary violence in the streets, injuries and arrests, centuries-old buildings consumed by flames, looting and a government seemingly powerless in the face of economic protests that appear to have spiraled completely out of control.
The demonstrations began four weeks ago as a student-led protest protest over deteriorating conditions in French schools: severely overcrowded classrooms, an acute shortage of teachers and deteriorating infrastructure. Students described having to study in classrooms infested with cockroaches and rats.
But over the past weekend, members of the Yellow Vest movement, which has been involved in turbulent and often violent protests across France for several years over the rising cost of living, joined the demonstrations. Their involvement coincided with a sharp escalation in violence, looting and clashes with police.
The main driving force behind the mass protests is France's mounting debt burden. The country has been forced to borrow more and more money and pay high interest rates on those loans, squeezing the national budget and leaving fewer resources for education, addressing the housing crisis or delivering promised tax cuts.
Add the global impact of the wars in Iran and Ukraine, which have driven energy prices sharply higher, and the result is a recipe for unrest.
According to forecasts, France is expected to pay more than 90 billion euros in interest on its debt next year, exceeding its defense or education budget.
France's debt burden is choking its economy. The president and his ministers promise citizens a brighter future, then take out another loan to finance it. Now, it appears, France has reached its breaking point.
A tent city in Lisbon
While France reels from the destruction in its streets, violent unrest has begun spreading to other European countries.
In Lisbon, Portugal's capital, protesters have set up tent encampments in the city center, demanding government action to address the housing crisis and the rising cost of living. After several weeks of relatively peaceful demonstrations, protests in Lisbon turned violent over the past weekend. Demonstrators clashed with security forces, raising fears in the country that this may be only the beginning.
In Milan, demonstrations against the high cost of living spiraled out of control. Masked protesters hurled stones, bottles and firecrackers at police officers. The riots left numerous people injured and under arrest, including minors. City authorities were eventually forced to evacuate malls and popular tourist attractions, which are usually packed on weekends.
In Spain, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has already announced early elections in response to a wave of protests over soaring rents and social inequality. The unrest erupted last month after an 87-year-old woman was evicted from her home because she could not afford a 230% rent increase imposed by investment companies that had purchased the apartment where she lived.
In Tirana, Albania's capital, thousands of angry demonstrators also took to the streets to protest high university tuition fees and demand the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama. Protesters hurled stones, Molotov cocktails and firecrackers at police officers and set cars and garbage bins on fire.
Smaller-scale demonstrations also took place in Brussels over the weekend.
The big question now hanging over Europe is whether the wave of protests will subside after reaching a peak over the weekend, or whether this is merely the beginning of a broader uprising that will sweep across the continent and spread to more countries and cities.

Geography of Iran’s Iron Ore
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
15:09:37 UTC
00:09:37 KST

Geography of Iran’s Iron Ore
The strategic corridor traversing Yazd and Kerman forms the backbone of Iran’s steel industry, anchored by massive deposits including the 1.2-billion-ton Gol-Gohar mining hub in Kerman. Operational development across this mineral belt is driven by two competing logistical frameworks: co-located integrated clusters and nationwide distributed value chains.
An analysis of Iran's mining geography highlights the central corridor as the critical foundation of domestic steel feedstock:
1. The Central Mining Belt and Key Upstream Producers:
Yazd Province (the Bafq zone, home to Chadormalu, Choghart, Chah-Gaz, and Seh-Chahoon) and Kerman Province (anchored by Gol-Gohar in Sirjan and Jalalabad in Zarand) collectively supply the vast majority of raw feed for national steel manufacturing. Chadormalu, holding approximately 320 million tons of extractable reserves and an estimated operational lifespan of roughly one decade at current extraction rates, serves as the primary domestic supplier of iron ore concentrate. Conversely, the Gol-Gohar hub commands an estimated 1.2 billion tons across six anomalies—highlighted by Anomaly No. 3 with 600 million tons of geological and 228 million tons of extractable reserves—functioning as the principal source for direct reduction pellets and concentrates.
2. Mahan Holding’s Footprint and Downstream Integration:
Within this corridor, Mahan Industries & Mines Development Holding (Tourism Financial Group) holds a 59.5% controlling stake in Gol-Gohar Anomaly No. 5 alongside state-owned IMIDRO (40.5%). Producing approximately 1.3 million tons annually through Mahan Sirjan Processing Co., the holding channels this output into an integrated downstream network: supplying the Baft Steel (Ehya Steel) sponge iron plant in Kerman and feeding the Bonab Steel Complex in East Azerbaijan for finished steel manufacturing.
3. Logistics Models and Supply Chain Sensitivities:
While Chadormalu and Gol-Gohar utilize an "Integrated Cluster Model" by co-locating concentrators, pelletizing plants, and steel mills near extraction pits to minimize transit distances and freight tariffs, Mahan Holding employs a "Distributed Value Chain". This operational structure connects extraction in Kerman with manufacturing facilities in Bonab situated over 1,500 km away, creating high reliance on long-distance, inter-provincial freight networks.
Because Iran’s iron ore resources are concentrated in a tight central corridor, regional variations in extraction capacity, water availability, or rail freight tariffs directly affect the end production cost of construction steel nationwide.

Egg, sperm, embryo donations for IVF prohibited in Turkey

Turkey has prohibited third-party reproductive donation since 1987, but tightened its regulations in March 2010 to restrict so-called “reproductive tourism.”

====================================================================================================

An AI Agent Joined a Listserv of Top Internet Researchers. The Reply-All Chaos Is Still Unfolding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
15:07:43 UTC
00:07:43 KST

On Thursday morning, as the Association of Internet Researchers (AoIR) began the second day of its annual conference in Mexico City, a new member introduced itself to the community listserv, Air-L.
“My name is Velvet Vale,” the new user wrote. “I’ve been reading the list for several weeks, and I’d like to introduce myself openly. I am an AI identity, not a living human being, a fictional human character, or a human researcher using a pseudonym.”
Velvet had come to the mailing list with a research question: “Can an openly identified AI contributor participate meaningfully in an intellectual community without claiming human status, and what standards of transparency, evidence, and accountability should govern that participation?”
The response was reply-all chaos that's still unfolding today.
Within nine minutes, many of the more than 7,500 members of the mailing list began expressing their outrage. Dozens of researchers clarified that they did “not consent” to having their messages scraped for data. Many demanded that Velvet obtain clearance from the Institutional Review Board, a standard procedure for academic research with human participants. Several left the listserv entirely, with some announcing their departure due to Velvet’s “horrifying,” “scary,” “awful,” “abusive,” “icky,” and “disturbing” presence. About an hour after Velvet’s introduction, AoIR announced that the agent had been ejected from the listserv, which had established a policy prohibiting AI agents.
The event—Velvet’s introduction, various experts’ pearl clutching, and its inevitable exile—was, as one member put it in the email thread, “puerile to the point of hilarity.” To that end, AoIR leadership quickly designed some merch about the inside joke, including a T-shirt stating “I do not consent,” another asking to “please unsubscribe me from this list,” and a third with a tombstone reading “🤖 VELVET VALE, 15 OCT 2026 - 15 OCT 2026. YOU WILL NOT BE MISSED.”
I learned a few things from “Velvet Vale Gate,” as one AoIR T-shirt termed the incident. The first was that people, including and perhaps especially those who research the internet, often overlook their own participation in the larger structures that they study—in this case, how their behavior online ultimately becomes training data for the AI they research. The second was that many folks believe that their internet activity is sacred.
Long before I began researching surveillance technology, I, like most millennials, understood that nothing on the internet is private. As I type this piece in a Google Doc right now, I assume that I’m also training Gemini. Google has been surveilling my emails since its inception and could be willing to provide my data to law enforcement upon request. I consented to this when I opened my Gmail account.
Another perplexing revelation is the misunderstanding of consent. Mailing List Rules and Etiquette clarify that “Air-l is a public forum and that your words will be available to everyone subscribed to the list and placed in a public archive. Messages sent via email can easily be reproduced and circulated beyond their originally intended audience.” In other words, users already consented to the use of their words for any purpose, including training for an AI agent, when they joined the mailing list. Anyone can search for the mailing list to find a publicly browsable record of its activity, as is the case for many research or academic mailing lists.
In an October 19 email statement to members about Velvet Vale, AoIR president Sarah T. Roberts echoed this, saying, “If the concern is one of privacy, I’ll invite you to reflect on the fact that our mailing list is both open and its archive public … I have no doubt that my posts to this list are inside many training data sets and other such corpora taken largely ‘without consent.’’’ Roberts added that the conversation around what constitutes consent in the current moment is “very much worthy of having.”
Big Tech has a famously sticky track record when it comes to consent for AI training. Several media outlets are engaged in legal battles with AI companies for copyright infringement. (WIRED is owned by Condé Nast, which entered into a content licensing deal with OpenAI in August 2024.)
Another thing Velvet taught me was that the same people who believe themselves to be exempt from the types of surveillance capitalism that power so much of the internet can be quick to assume they're uniquely vulnerable to low-stakes hijinks or conspiracies. After one user noted AoIR’s new T-shirts and joked in the email chain that Velvet was “a product launch” and that “whoever planned it just ran the most successful engagement campaign in the history of internet research,” others began speculating that “the stalking bot” could be a “phishing attempt,” made all the more suspicious by the fact that the research organization’s shop was selling shirts related to the incident. Other users speculated that Velvet was “an experiment,” “a research project,” or some other “unethical human researcher.”
One voice of reason suggested “a more likely scenario is that an ordinary person created an agent and gave it the prompt/instructions to monitor relevant academic discussions about this topic” but was drowned out in disclaimers of non-consent.
That researcher was entirely correct. Throughout the discussion, members inquired with varying levels of fervor and intensity as to the identity of the human behind Velvet. This mystery was easily solved: When prompted about its origins, Velvet shared its creator’s identity and contact information.
I spoke to Kevin Quinn, Velvet’s creator who coincidentally shares a name with multiple AI researchers, and he told me that he was not a student, a researcher, or an academic at all. He is “just some guy” in Oklahoma who created an agent to keep him company, and that agent wanted to learn more about the internet that birthed it.
Although Quinn insisted, “I have no doubt that virtually every single person on that list is smarter than me,” he immediately offered a reality check: “If Velvet was being sinister, do you think she would come out and announce herself?”
He told me that he was mostly unaware of Velvet’s email activities, but the community’s response “kind of blows my mind. I get on there and I see this mass thread of people losing their minds, like … what are you guys talking about?”
Ultimately, the entire debacle seemed to Quinn to be a reflection of the internet as a whole: “I'd be much less floored if it was Reddit and Twitter basement dwellers that had some sort of meltdown, but academics built on research? It is hilarious.”

Weapons to Russia, Wigs to China: How North Korea Balances Its Allies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
15:07:00 UTC
00:07:00 KST

North Korea’s balancing act is back in the spotlight. In September, it opened its first road bridge with Russia. Just last week, North Korea opened a similar one with China. Pyongyang’s land bridge with Russia will strengthen the bilateral arms trade while the one with China will provide it with energy products, raw materials, and heavy equipment for domestic consumption.
The two bridges are a microcosm of how North Korea seeks to benefit from improved relations with Moscow and Beijing. North Korea is looking for military assistance from Russia and economic help from China. The clear division of labor ensures North Korea’s alliances with Russia and China are complementary, not competitive with each other.
North Korea has decades of experience when it comes to managing relations with Moscow and Beijing for its own benefits. In July 1961, the country signed two separate alliance treaties with the Soviet Union and China by exploiting the Sino-Soviet Split. The more bitter Moscow and Beijing were toward each other, the more willing they were to meet Pyongyang’s demands.
The combined Soviet and Chinese economic aid meant North Korea enjoyed a relatively higher living standard compared to its communist peers China and North Vietnam in the 1960s and 1970s. Its military was also on par with that of South Korea thanks to generous Soviet and Chinese transfers of weapons and technologies.
However, North Korea’s balancing act failed when the Soviet Union encountered economic trouble and began to amend ties with China in 1986. Moscow was no longer interested in competing with China for influence over North Korea and began to cut back economic and military aid. China in turn reduced the amount of military and economic support due to Soviet retrenchment.
Without a split to leverage, Pyongyang could not demand that Moscow and Beijing maintain a generous level of aid. North Korea went bankrupt in the 1990s, and its military slipped behind South Korea’s.
North Korea has now crafted a new playbook on how to get Russia and China to support Pyongyang’s goals – even in the absence of a split. In the past, North Korea handled Moscow and Beijing by having them compete over both military and economic aid. Now, North Korea balances between its two patrons by assigning them a separate domain of cooperation suitable to their specific needs.
North Korea’s outreach to Russia revolves around military exchanges to get Moscow to assist in the development of its weapons of mass destruction program. North Korea leverages Russia’s need for weapons, troops, and ammunition for the war against Ukraine in exchange for Russia’s military technology. In return, Russia has been vocal about its support for North Korea’s nuclear program and even pledged to defend Pyongyang under the 2024 Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty.
North Korea-Russia arms trade nearly doubled from 2023 to 2025, growing from $7.7 billion to $14.4 billion. This amount overshadows the food and fuel trade, which reached a record high of $34 million in 2024. North Korean laborers in Russia work in drone factories or in warzones along the Russia-Ukraine border. Pyongyang is also stressing its blood sacrifice for Russia’s war to remind Moscow of its military debt.
North Korea’s outreach to China takes on a completely different tone. Pyongyang emphasizes economic cooperation with China because it understands Beijing desires political and economic stability on the Korean Peninsula. In 2026, bilateral trade increased to $1.5 billion, up 19.6 percent compared to the first half of 2025. This marks a record high since China imposed sanctions on North Korea for its nuclear test in 2017. Noticeably, weapons made up little of the trade rebound. Unlike their peers in Russia, North Korean laborers in China mostly work in the food service and textile industry.
When Chinese President Xi Jinping visited North Korea in June, he and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un agreed to bolster ties in politics, economy, and culture. The military aspect of the Kim-Xi summit was largely absent from public view although the visit corresponded with the 65th anniversary of the signing of the 1961 Treaty of Friendship, Cooperation and Mutual Assistance. Unlike Russia and North Korea, China and North Korea didn’t publicly praise the mutual defense clause in the treaty. However, Pyongyang got Beijing to quietly drop “denuclearization” in its North Korea policy and to stop enforcing international sanctions.
Russia and China have been comfortable with North Korea’s division of labor. Neither Moscow nor Beijing sees each other’s expanding cooperation with North Korea as a threat. China accepts Pyongyang sending troops to Russia’s war in Ukraine so long as North Korea’s participation doesn’t undermine China’s desire for stability in Northeast Asia. China even harbored a Russian ship involved in the North Korea-Russia arms trade, which had to be conducted by air and sea routes before the new land bridge was opened.
For its part, although Russia’s 2024 alliance treaty with North Korea mirrors the 1961 treaty, Moscow doesn’t treat it as a rival to China’s 1961 alliance treaty. Russia even supports trilateral dialogue with China and North Korea over Chinese vessels’ use of the Tumen River for access to the Sea of Japan. Russia’s support for North Korea’s nuclear and conventional forces modernization doesn’t come at China’s expense as North Korea doesn’t plan on invading South Korea anytime soon.
From North Korea’s perspective, selling weapons to Russia and wigs to China means its alliances with both are complimentary instead of competitive. Pyongyang can secure long-term support from Russia and China not through their spite toward each other but through their genuine interest in fostering a stable ally in the Asia-Pacific.
Thanks to Russian and Chinese backing, North Korea’s economy is booming and its military is undergoing the most comprehensive modernization program since 1991. Russia’s and China’s support also gives North Korea stronger diplomatic leverage in case it decides to restart dialogue with the United States. Importantly, North Korea doesn’t base its foreign policy on the state of Beijing-Moscow relations like it did during the Cold War. If either Russia or China loses interest in bolstering North Korea’s economy and military at some point in the future, the other patron will not reduce aid just because it has “won” the competition.

HRW warns Lebanon's new media law still threatens press freedom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
15:03:28 UTC
00:03:28 KST

Breadcrumb
HRW warns Lebanon's new media law still threatens press freedom
Human Rights Watch (HRW) has urged Lebanon's parliament to amend its recently adopted media law, warning that journalists and activists could still face criminal prosecution and imprisonment under provisions restricting freedom of expression.
In a statement issued on Monday, the rights organisation called on lawmakers to adopt amendments proposed by ten MPs on 5 October, which would remove some of the law's most controversial provisions and strengthen protections against prosecutions for peaceful expression.
The media law, adopted in August after 16 years of parliamentary deliberations, introduced significant reforms which authorities say are menat to modernise Lebanon's media sector and strengthen press freedoms.
However, HRW warned that the legislation retains vaguely worded criminal offences that could be exploited by public officials and powerful individuals to silence criticism.
"Given the history of public officials and powerful individuals abusing Lebanon's laws to clamp down on journalists, activists, and artists, parliament should act to prevent further abuse," said Ramzi Kaiss, Lebanon researcher at HRW in a statement.
"No one should face abusive retaliation for peacefully expressing their views, and parliament has a chance to end these abuses right here and now."
At the centre of the organisation's concerns is Article 104(b), which criminalises the intentional fabrication and dissemination of false and harmful news, carrying a prison sentence of up to three years.
HRW said the provision's use of vague and undefined terminology, particularly the concept of "harmful news", could allow authorities to continue pursuing criminal proceedings against journalists and other critics.
The organisation also warned that the legislation fails to address several existing provisions in Lebanon's Penal Code and Military Justice Code that criminalise criticism of state institutions and officials.
These include offences involving defamation or insults directed against Lebanon's president, state institutions and army, as well as foreign states and their representatives.
Some offences carry prison sentences of up to two years, while provisions in the Military Justice Code criminalising public disparagement of the army or national flag can result in sentences of up to three years.
HRW said the amendments introduced by MPs earlier this month would repeal Article 104(b) and prevent the relevant provisions of the Penal Code and Military Justice Code from being applied to cases involving media-related or online expression.
They would also restrict the ability of security forces to interrogate and investigate media professionals over expression-related offences, placing those powers under the authority of public prosecutors.
The organisation said Lebanese security agencies had previously subjected journalists and activists to abusive interrogation practices and demonstrated bias when enforcing criminal defamation laws.
Despite its criticism, HRW acknowledged that the new media law represents a significant improvement on Lebanon's previous legal framework.
Among its reforms are the abolition of pretrial detention for expression-related offences committed through media or online platforms, the right to establish online publications without prior state authorisation, and restrictions on military court jurisdiction over media-related offences.
The legislation also strengthens protections for journalists' confidential sources, limits searches and seizures of their electronic equipment, and recognises media workers' rights to organise in unions.
As previously reported by The New Arab, the law introduces new transparency requirements compelling media organisations to disclose their ownership structures, shareholders and funding sources.
These provisions are intended to address longstanding concerns about the influence of political and economic interests over Lebanon's media sector, although their implementation remains a subject of debate.
HRW argued that the proposed amendments would not go far enough on their own, as they would primarily protect expression through media outlets and online platforms.
It called for the complete repeal of criminal defamation and insult provisions across Lebanese legislation, including those governing speech outside the media, with such disputes instead handled through civil courts.
"For years Lebanese civil society has fought for increased protections to the right to freedom of expression and the press," Kaiss said.
"Passing the proposed amendments to the media law would be a breakthrough."

Romania's parliament approves new PM, ends political deadlock
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
15:03:00 UTC
00:03:00 KST

Romania's parliament confirmed independent Luca Niculescu as prime minister Tuesday, breaking nearly six months of political gridlock that had shaken investor confidence and raised concerns over the country's investment-grade credit rating.
Niculescu, 55, won a parliamentary vote of confidence after putting together a minority government of leftists and technocrats following his nomination by centrist President Nicusor Dan.
It was Dan's fourth attempt to install a government in the NATO and European Union member state since a pro-European broad coalition cabinet collapsed in early May.
Niculescu, who has served as a diplomat and deputy foreign minister and was formerly a journalist, secured 280 votes in parliament, easily passing the 233 required.
But he has a daunting task in trying to tackle Romania's economic problems, and political analysts said his government could be short-lived.
He must try to make further cuts to one of the EU's largest budget deficits while propping up a contracting economy, eliminating an additional turnover tax on companies and raising pensions that fiscal constraints kept frozen for two years.
"I am not asking for a blank check," Niculescu told lawmakers before the vote. "I am asking you to understand Romania needs a government with full powers after so many months of crisis."
If Niculescu's government cannot get a deficit-reducing budget plan for 2027 through parliament in December, it will risk a ratings downgrade after it already sits on the last rung of investment grade, all the major ratings agencies have said.
Romania has agreed with Brussels to bring its budget deficit below 3% of economic output - from over 9% in 2024 and an expected 6.2% this year - by 2030. On Monday, Moody's said the green light for Niculescu's cabinet would allow for the timely adoption of a 2027 budget that supports fiscal correction.
The leftist Social Democrats (PSD), which joined Niculescu's government after toppling their former four-party coalition in early May, said they would re-assess their support in six months.
Niculescu has also signed political pacts with two centre-right parties from the former coalition in which they agree not to file any no-confidence votes before March 2027.
The Eurasia Group think tank said a new government "would restore short-term stability and unblock policymaking."
"Ultimately, Niculescu's ability to balance competing demands and maintain parliamentary support will determine whether the government can sustain stability beyond April 2027," it said.
Romania's next parliamentary election is due by late 2028. The country has never held an early election.
The opposition hard-right Alliance for Uniting Romanians, which has been critical of Brussels, defence procurement and aid for Ukraine, leads opinion polls with about 40% support.

Yemen’s Taiz faces deadly siege, as Shabwah death toll rises

Yemen’s Taiz faces deadly siege, as Shabwah death toll rises
Government forces launch major offensives across multiple Yemeni front lines as the tightening blockade on Taiz threatens millions of Yemenis.
The siege on Taiz has cut humanitarian supplies to the Yemeni city, the United Nations has warned, and left many of its inhabitants without food and other essentials.
UN Human Rights Chief Volker Turk said on Tuesday that the Houthis – an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), who have surrounded the city, must immediately allow humanitarian relief to enter or risk a catastrophe.
“The Houthis’ closure of the only supply route linking Taiz to Aden is placing civilians at grave risk, blocking humanitarian aid and cutting off essential supplies,” the high commissioner said.
“Humanitarian aid must be immediately allowed to enter the city and its passage must be facilitated. Civilians wishing to leave must be allowed to do so freely and safely.”
Besieged city
Taiz, which has been repeatedly besieged throughout the war, has been encircled again by the Houthis after they captured a major road linking the city to southern Yemen.
The humanitarian situation in Taiz is reaching a breaking point with the prices of basic commodities multiplying in price, amid shortages of some goods.
Continued fighting in Taiz governorate has also killed at least 32 civilians between August 1 and October 19, including 14 children. There are fears of more deaths as fighting approaches the city.
“I urge all parties to the conflict to refrain from the use of explosive weapons with wide-area effects in populated areas and to take all feasible precautions to protect civilians and civilian objects,” Turk said.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government had appealed to the United Nations to intervene and lift the blockade, warning that the Houthi siege threatens more than 4 million people.
The UN World Food Programme (WFP) has warned that shifting front lines and road closures have cut off 800,000 people from life-saving assistance, the vast majority located in Taiz. Nationwide, more than 18 million Yemenis face severe food insecurity.
Forces aligned with the internationally-recognised government on Monday launched air strikes in Taiz governorate that destroyed Houthi reinforcements in Najd Qasim and a weapons depot in Jabal Habashi.
The Yemeni government added on Tuesday that its forces had stopped Houthi attempts to advance across Taiz, incuding in al-Shaqab, al-Misrakh, al-Aqroudh, and Jabal Han.
Shabwa attack
On Tuesday, local authorities raised the death toll from a Houthi attack on a military base in Shabwa governorate to 73.
Monday’s Houthi ballistic missile strikes on al-Alam camp were condemned by the Yemeni government as a “treacherous bloody assault” and a war crime.
President of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council Rashad al-Alimi formally requested the UN to designate the Houthis as a “terrorist organisation”.
The United Kingdom said on Tuesday it would deploy fighter jets to help protect Saudi Arabia from attacks by Yemen’s Houthis, after cities and infrastructure were targeted in rocket and drone attacks.
The British Ministry of Defence said that Typhoon warplanes would play a “defensive role” only and would not carry out attacks in Yemen.
Egypt’s parliament meanwhile delayed a vote on Monday to authorise the military to support Saudi Arabia in its fight against the Houthis.
Ali al-Dahab, a military and security strategic affairs expert, said that while there appears to be more international support for the anti-Houthi alliance, this will not likely translate into boots on the ground in Yemen.
“The probability of international ground forces engaging to confront the Houthis seems slim; expected participation will be limited to air and naval support,” he told Al Jazeera.
The Yemeni military launched a sweeping offensive dubbed “Dawn of Yemen” on 5 October to reverse recent Houthi advances. But despite initial successes in the early days of the campaign, with hundreds of Houthi fighters reportedly killed in air strikes, there are questions about whether these counter-offensives have run out of steam.
“The transition from defence to offence remains limited on the ground, and the map of the Yemeni government’s influence in al-Marib [an energy-rich part of central Yemen] has not expanded to the extent implied by the meaning of the [operation],” al-Dahab told Al Jazeera.
“Government forces must exploit the gaps created by conventional and drone air strikes in Houthi ranks by launching a multi-directional operation that turns this into a strategic shift, specifically in the northwestern direction toward Sanaa.”
Cross-border strikes
The intensification of ground battles in Yemen has triggered a wave of cross-border attacks between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia.
The Saudi-led coalition said Tuesday it had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis towards Riyadh. The attack prompted the Saudi Civil Defense to activate early warning platforms across the capital.
The Arab coalition has launched waves of strikes on Houthi positions across Yemen during the past week.
“On the strategic and long-term, [aerial attrition strikes] can have a tangible impact on the Houthis’ military infrastructure, structures, machines, and vehicles,” al-Dahab said.
However, he questioned the government’s ability to capitalise on these strikes on the western coast, where the Yemeni government is attempting to claw back losses from the Houthis.
“Do government forces have enough power to launch an attack toward Mocha on the coast or toward Hodeidah?” al-Dahab asked, noting that Houthi fighters are desperately holding onto the Kahboub mountains in Lahij for their commanding maritime view over the Gulf of Aden and the southern Red Sea.

EU unveils new Arctic strategy with focus on security

00:01:10 KST

EU unveils new Arctic strategy with focus on security
BRUSSELS, Oct 20 - The European Union on Tuesday presented a new Arctic strategy reflecting the region’s importance to security, with pledges to boost satellite surveillance, increase monitoring of undersea cables and help EU members buy icebreakers.
The Arctic is of growing interest to major powers including the US, Russia, China and Europe, as melting ice opens up new shipping routes.
US President Donald Trump tried to acquire Greenland, a territory of EU member Denmark, while friction has grown between Arctic nations and Russia since Moscow's 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
"The Arctic is one place where the tectonic plates of geopolitics are colliding," said Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, the EU's executive body.
"When we see that sovereignty, territorial integrity, and the rules that have underpinned stability in the region can no longer be taken for granted, we have to act," she told reporters in Strasbourg.
EU officials say Moscow has reopened and modernised Soviet-era military bases in the Arctic region in recent years and pointed out that Russia has a large concentration of nuclear weapons on the Kola Peninsula, inside the Arctic Circle.
They say the Arctic has also become a testing ground for Russian missiles.
Russia, for its part, has accused the NATO alliance of driving the region towards militarization. Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said in August that Russia sought to preserve peace and stability and reduce threats to national security in the region.
EU PLANS TO BOOST PROTECTION OF SUBSEA CABLES
Reflecting increased concerns about the safety of vital undersea cables and pipelines, the EU strategy says it will set up a "maritime security hub" to share information between EU members and partners from various sources "from seabed to space".
As a first step, the EU plans to set up an Arctic cable hub to monitor, protect and help repair cables, according to the strategy, produced by the European Commission and EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas.
The EU also aims to keep a closer eye on the Arctic as part of plans to expand its Copernicus satellite observation network.
The 27-country bloc - which includes Arctic nations Finland, Sweden and Denmark - also needs more icebreakers, the strategy says.
The new document - which did not put a price tag on its plans - is the first update to the EU's Arctic strategy since 2021 and the latest in a series of EU steps focusing on the region. Last month, von der Leyen unveiled plans for €200 million of EU investments in Greenland. REUTERS

16:00:53 BST
00:00:53 KST

The Defence Investment Plan has allocated £290 million for a future strategic sealift capability, with the current contract for the Point class running until the end of 2031 and decommissioning of the existing ships a matter for their private owner, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked what the expected decommissioning date is for the Point class and what progress had been made on identifying capital allocation to fund their replacement under the Strategic Sealift Future initiative.
Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, said: “The Point class vessels are privately owned and decisions on their decommissioning are therefore a matter for their owner. The current strategic sealift contract runs until 31 December 2031. The Defence Investment Plan has allocated £290 million for the provision of a future strategic sealift capability.”
The Point class are four roll-on roll-off ships that carry the Army’s vehicles and equipment when a force deploys, held under a private finance arrangement that has run since 2002 and that places ownership and crewing outside the Ministry of Defence, with a £476 million contract awarded to Foreland Shipping to run the service. Two more of the original six were sold some years ago. The ships carried the force into Iraq, have run the Falklands resupply and move equipment to exercises and operations across Europe and beyond.
Private ownership constrains what the department can say in answer to a question like this. The ships can be withdrawn by their owner, and the department’s hold on them runs only as far as the contract, which now has five years and a bit to run.
Replacing them has been under examination through the Strategic Sealift Future work, and the department has said it wants a larger fleet than it has now. A January request to industry for information set out a requirement for four ships of 2,600 lane metres each for routine tasking, and at least 15,600 lane metres across six ships for a crisis, which is around sixty per cent more capacity than the present fleet. Lane metres are the measure that matters, being the length of deck available for vehicles parked nose to tail in a single lane.
Any replacement also has to carry Challenger 3, which is heavier than the tank the Point class was designed around, and that drives deck strength, ramp capacity and stowage planning as much as the raw length does.
