====================================================================================================

Some came to Israel to serve the Jewish state. Haredim are rewarded for refusing to help - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
14:34:22 UTC
23:34:22 KST

Over the course of this war, I served as a combat soldier and commander in Maglan. Most of us had a home to return to when we were off duty.
After weeks of combat, we would head to our parents’ homes, eat a real meal prepared by our loved ones, and relax with our families.
Some of us didn’t enjoy any of that luxury. No help with laundry after weeks, no clean sheets, no chauffeuring to the train station on Sunday mornings.
I think about these “lone soldiers” a lot these days – not just because of their strength, resilience, and sacrifice, which I witnessed firsthand, and not just because of what they represent: the very best of what Israel has to offer.
But because their story points to something that has fundamentally broken in our society.
While one group of men and women carries Israel and the burden of its security on their backs – soldiers, reservists, and their families – another group is freeloading and piggybacking on their sacrifice. They carry none of the burden.
And the gap between these groups keeps growing.
Lone soldiers as an example of the gap
In many ways, lone soldiers are the most glaring example of that gap.
There are Israeli-born lone soldiers, a few thousand in number, many from haredi (ultra-Orthodox) or disadvantaged backgrounds, who choose to serve despite immense obstacles, without their families’ support, and often in the face of outright hostility.
Alongside them are lone soldiers from overseas, many of whom were not born here and were under no obligation to enlist. They came out of pure Zionism, many choosing to do so after October 7, aware of the great risks they were taking.
Meanwhile, just a short drive from the IDF headquarters at the Kirya, tens of thousands of healthy young men in Bnei Brak are effectively being paid by the government not to serve. What an absurdity!
How can a sane government allow a situation in which people travel thousands of miles to serve Israel while tens of thousands are, in effect, paid not to serve their country?
This situation is immoral, unfair, and unsustainable. Worse still, it is putting Israel in severe danger.
October 7 fundamentally changed Israel, including its strategic situation and security needs. Three years on, we must abandon the old security conceptzia, our old security paradigm.
We need many more soldiers to secure our borders and perimeters, and we must ensure that the army has the manpower it needs to keep the country safe.
Today, we are short 20,000 soldiers. That is an imminent threat, a flashing red light. We cannot address it unless ultra-Orthodox men begin enlisting en masse.
To put the scale of the issue into perspective: a single new haredi battalion, comprising approximately 600 soldiers, could relieve 12 reserve battalions of a full month of reserves in a single year. That amounts to nearly a quarter of a million reserve-service days.
Our plan is straightforward: flip the pyramid on its head.
Right now, the haredi population faces few incentives to serve and many reasons not to, while the government continues to reward non-enlistment. Politicians love to talk about how much they value our soldiers and reservists, especially lone soldiers, but they do little to change the equation.
Bennett's plan to solve the issue
Naftali Bennett's plan is simple and effective: take the tens of billions of shekels currently directed toward those who do not serve through various tax breaks, stipends, childcare benefits, and other subsidies, and redirect that money to those who have served and continue to serve, both in active duty and in the reserves.
Every single year, this money would go to people who serve, sacrifice, and put their lives on the line.
Changing the incentives is part of the solution. So is funding only those ultra-Orthodox schools that teach math and English and prepare students to participate in Israeli society and the 21st-century economy.
So is building frameworks along the lines of haredi hesder yeshivas, where ultra-Orthodox soldiers will serve in eight-hour patrol shifts, study Talmud for eight hours, and rest for eight hours.
Such frameworks can help integrate ultra-Orthodox men into the army, the workforce, and Israeli society while allowing them to maintain their distinctive identity.
This is how we begin to lighten the burden on the rest of us who serve, especially reservists, many of whom have been called up repeatedly since October 7, 2023.
Any comprehensive program must also deliver on commitments that have already been made. I have seen firsthand how difficult it can be for lone soldiers to receive the benefits they are entitled to.
Civil society organizations have told us how Israeli lone soldiers continue to fall through the cracks before, during, and after their service.
A disproportionate number of lone soldiers, including many reservists, have been among those who did not receive the psychological support they desperately needed after years of combat and trauma. The consequences have too often been tragic.
My friend Shahar Varon, who is also running for the Knesset on Bennett’s party list, and I represent a generation that has carried the load throughout this war. We are developing practical, implementable plans to ease the burden on reservists, including lone soldiers in the reserves.
These are not just plans on paper. We are working with an experienced team of managers to turn them into concrete changes through the Knesset and government ministries.
Bennett is committing to those who serve because that is who he is. He served. He believes in the generation that has fought this war, and he believes that those of us who have sacrificed must be part of fixing what is broken.
That is why I am running for a seat in the Knesset with him.
Our generation, the one so many dismissed as apathetic and glued to our screens, the “TikTok generation,” has carried this country for three years.
On the battlefield, in the reserves, at home, and at work, we kept going while our lives were put on hold, one reserve tour after another.
We took responsibility for Israel when it needed us most. With Bennett, we will make sure the State of Israel finally shows up for us.
The writer is a Knesset candidate for Naftali Bennett's B'Yachad party.

Who is Russian-held US citizen Stephen Hubbard? - explainer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
14:34:21 UTC
23:34:21 KST

US special envoy Steve Witkoff is going to discuss the possible release of American citizen Stephen Hubbard from detention in Russia with Russian President Vladimir Putin this week, according to people familiar with the matter.
Here are details of Hubbard's case:
Hubbard, 74, a retired schoolteacher, grew up in Big Rapids, Michigan, and served in the US Air Force and National Guard, according to military records cited by The New York Times.
He earned a master’s degree in English and lived in Japan for 25 years, where he taught English before moving to Cyprus and then, in 2014, to Izyum in eastern Ukraine with a Ukrainian partner, according to his sister, Patricia Hubbard Fox.
Fox told Reuters in 2024 that Hubbard lived on a pension of about $300 a month and had few connections with locals. The siblings last spoke in September 2021.
How was Hubbard captured in 2022?
Russia launched its full-scale war in Ukraine in February 2022 and captured Izyum two months later. Ukrainian forces retook the city in September 2022, but Hubbard was already in Russian custody by then.
Russian state media said Hubbard had been detained in April 2022 and alleged he had been manning a Ukrainian military checkpoint. Reuters could not independently establish the circumstances of his capture.
Fox said she recognized her brother in a YouTube video showing a man being questioned about his views on Putin and the war. Another video showed him with his hands bound, being struck with a sandal. Reuters could not verify when or where the videos were recorded.
Why did Russians imprison Hubbard?
Following a closed trial, a Moscow court convicted Hubbard of being a mercenary in October 2024 and sentenced him to six years and 10 months in prison. Prosecutors said Hubbard had joined a Ukrainian territorial defense unit, received training, weapons and ammunition, and was promised $1,000 a month. Russian state media said he pleaded guilty to the charges.
Fox questioned the reported confession, however, saying Hubbard held pro-Russian views and was unlikely to have taken up arms in his seventies.
Martin De Luca, his US-based lawyer, told Reuters in June 2025 that Hubbard told him the charges were false and that he was not in any combat or military unit. He cited Hubbard as telling him Russian soldiers had simply grabbed him from his house.
What is Hubbard's current status?
In January 2025, Washington designated Hubbard as wrongfully detained, enabling the US government to pursue negotiations for his release.
The US State Department has said Russia refused to grant American officials consular access.
The NYT reported in February 2025 that Hubbard had been moved through at least five Russian detention centers before his trial.
His lawyer said Hubbard's legal team learned only in April 2025 that he was being held at a facility in the Mordovia region, east of Moscow.

Turkey has submitted a defense pact with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia to parliament for ratification, three parliamentary sources said on Tuesday, moving NATO's second-largest army closer to a formal mutual defense pledge with Riyadh as it faces Houthi attacks.
The three countries signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement in August, under which an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all. A joint statement issued when they signed the deal did not specify each country's commitments.
At an emergency meeting of the alliance in Riyadh earlier this month, they agreed to ensure the "rapid deployment" of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia.

Parliament must ratify the agreement for Turkey to formally approve it.

The commission could debate the agreement as early as Friday, another source said.
Turkish contribution to be limited to equipment, intelligence, official says
A Turkish official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said Turkey's own contribution was expected to be limited to military equipment, intelligence sharing, and weapons systems, adding that no other form of deployment had taken place under the alliance so far.
Asked how Turkey could help Saudi Arabia defend against attacks by Yemen's Houthis, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said that the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement was not an "offensive agreement," adding that Turkey would not send troops to another country to carry out attacks on its territory.

The death of a captain in Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) is leading to questions about rumors of increasing clashes between Iran and a Kurdish opposition group in the mountains on the Iran-Iraq border. The Rudaw media network reported on December 19 that the IRGC officer “was killed in the Qandil mountain range along the Iran-Iraq border on Saturday, according to a local news outlet affiliated with the IRGC, amid heightened tensions between Iranian forces and Kurdish opposition groups operating in the border region.”
The Qandil mountain range is an active area for the Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK). The PKK has had bases there in northern Iraq. “Captain Sina Ahmadi was killed on Saturday, Fateh Urmia reported, without providing details about the circumstances of his death,” Rydaw noted. The IRGC has not said how the officer was killed. However, they are saying he was a “martyr.” Fars News, which is considered close to the IRGC, reported on the death of the soldier.
The mysterious death is leading to rumors and questions. Ahmadi was from West Azerbaijan province, the report from Rudaw says. There are a half dozen Kurdish Iranian opposition groups that operate in Iran. One of them is called the Kurdistan Free Life Party (PJAK), and it is considered affiliated with the PKK. It is essentially seen as the Kurdish Iranian branch of the PKK.
his is a norm for the PKK to establish local affiliates and branches. For instance, in Syria, the local group linked to the PKK is called the People’s Protection Units (YPG), and the Yazidi group linked to the PKK in Iraq is called the Sinjar Resistance Units (YBS).
There are many changes in the region at this time as the PKK has a peace process with Turkey. Recently, the PKK leader Murat Karayilan gave an interview to the Amargi media outlet about the group’s next steps. He didn’t mention PJAK in the interview, but did note that Iran is currently in a conflict with the US and Israel. He compared that to wider global and regional conflicts.
IRGC intensifies attacks against Kurdish opposition groups
Rudaw suggested that the death of the IRGC officer “comes as the IRGC has intensified military operations against the Kurdistan Free Life Party (PJAK), an Iranian Kurdish opposition group, in the Shaho mountain range in western Iran.” The reports indicate that Iran has moved artillery into the mountain areas and is using drones to monitor and carry out strikes.
This comes as Iran has also carried out attacks against Kurdish Iranian opposition groups in the Kurdistan Region of northern Iraq. It has struck Komala, PDKI and Khabat groups in recent weeks. Why hasn’t it struck PJAK?
There are questions about why the IRGC doesn’t seem as capable against PJAK or carry out strikes on the PKK. Some have suggested in the past that the PKK had an accommodation with Iran. On the other hand, it could also be that Iran has found it easier to program its one-way attack drones to strike at known camps and sites of the other Kurdish groups in the Kurdistan Region.
This is because groups such as PDKI maintain camps in places near Koya. These camps are well known, and coordinates can be put into a drone by Iran. However, fighting insurgents in the mountains is harder. The PKK has long known this, and its fighters have used the mountains for years to fight Turkey. Turkey’s army is more modern and capable than the Iranian army or IRGC.
Iranian operations in Shaho mountain range increase
What is known about Iran’s operations in the mountains of northwestern Iran is that Iran is increasing operations in the Shaho range of mountains in areas of the western Kermanshah and Kurdistan provinces, in the Hawraman region. Rudaw notes that “PJAK maintains mobile armed units in the Kurdish areas of western Iran and has been involved in a long-running conflict with Iranian security forces.” It also says that the IRGC targeted an area in Marivan in Iran. Meanwhile, in the KRG in northern Iraq, the Kurdish authorities are concerned about Iran’s threats. They want the Kurdish groups to reduce tensions and not use their area for attacks on Iran. PDKI recently said it would refrain from sending fighters across the border. In Baghdad, Rudaw said that “Iranian Ambassador to Baghdad Mohammed Kazem Al-e Sadegh claimed Monday that Iraq has agreed to either expel Iranian Kurdish opposition groups based in the Kurdistan Region from the country or hand them over to Tehran, following a joint security meeting in Baghdad.”
"As part of security cooperation between the Islamic Republic of Iran and the Republic of Iraq, both sides agreed during a joint security meeting, which the Iranian delegation and the Iraqi national security adviser attended, on expelling separatist groups from the Kurdistan Region or handing them over to Iran,” Al-e Sadegh wrote in a post on X/Twitter.
Iran is clearly pushing hard to get the Kurdish groups to be reined in by Iraq. Iran’s Press TV reported the same information about an agreement between Tehran and Baghdad. Libya's House of Representatives, which met in the eastern city of Benghazi, backed a maritime deal with Turkey that will bring strategic economic, political, and national security advantages, two lawmakers told Reuters on Tuesday.
The backing of the deal overturns a 2020 decision to cut political ties with Ankara.
Control of Libya is split between rival western and eastern administrations, with the east under Libyan National Army Field Marshal Khalifa Haftar. Turkey has in the past been a major backer of the internationally recognized Government of National Accord (GNA) in the west, succeeded by the Government of National Unity, which still holds de facto international recognition and rules from Tripoli.

Libyan national interest is more important than international reactions, lawmaker says
"Some countries may be upset by this agreement, but what matters to us is our national interest," he said.
Lawmaker Aisha al-Tabalqi told Reuters the agreement was approved after specialized committees presented a full and detailed explanation of its provisions.
The parliament unanimously revoked two decisions issued in 2020: one rejecting the ratification of maritime and security memorandums signed by Libya's GNA and Turkey, and another cutting political relations with Ankara.
Greece rejects Libyan approval of Turkey-Libya maritime deal
Greece on Tuesday rejected the decision, saying the deal was without legal effect.
In a foreign ministry statement, Athens said the memorandum violated international law of the sea and infringed on the sovereign rights of states in the region, arguing that Turkey and Libya do not have opposite or adjacent coasts that would justify such a maritime delimitation.
Greece called on Libya to refrain from actions that undermine stability in the Eastern Mediterranean and said it had informed partners and allies and would take all appropriate measures to safeguard its sovereign rights.

U.S. Army turns light tactical vehicle into missile launcher
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
14:33:33 UTC
23:33:33 KST

- U.S. Army soldiers fired 17 Spike NLOS missiles from an Infantry Squad Vehicle – Utility at Dugway Proving Ground, the first launches from that vehicle.
- The demonstration supports the U.S. Army’s Mobile-Long Range Precision Strike Missile requirement, with a production phase planned after another year of testing.
U.S. Army infantry soldiers have fired Spike NLOS long-range missiles from a light, air-droppable utility vehicle for the first time, completing 17 engagements in a three-day live-fire demonstration at Dugway Proving Ground, Utah, Lockheed Martin said.
All of the shots were launched from an Infantry Squad Vehicle – Utility, or ISV-U, a version of the U.S. Army’s light, open-top truck built to move infantry squads. Lockheed Martin, which offers the Israeli-designed missile to the U.S. Army, announced the results on Oct. 20, 2026, without giving the exact dates of the firings or how many hit their targets.
Spike NLOS, made by Israel’s Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, is a precision-guided missile that can hit targets the shooter cannot see directly. It sends live video back to the operator during flight, so soldiers can steer it onto a target hidden behind hills or buildings, or change targets while the missile is in the air. Rafael lists its range from ground launchers at roughly 30 km (19 miles), far beyond the reach of the shoulder-fired Javelin infantry carry today.
Lockheed Martin said soldiers fired most of the 17 shots against simulated targets at different ranges, and that troops completed their training on the system and the live firing in the same week. Some of the soldiers came from the U.S. Army’s Transformation in Contact units, brigades that are testing new equipment and giving feedback before it is fielded more widely.
“This demonstration represents a critical milestone for Spike NLOS, showing that our infantry partners can confidently employ a long-range precision missile,” said Casey Walsh, program director at Lockheed Martin Multi-Domain Missile Systems.
The firings support the U.S. Army’s Mobile-Long Range Precision Strike Missile requirement, an effort to give light infantry formations their own long-range precision strike weapon. The service is converting infantry brigades into Mobile Brigade Combat Teams that ride in light vehicles such as the ISV, and the missile would give those units a way to hit armored vehicles, artillery and command posts well beyond the range of their other weapons.
Lockheed Martin won the first phase of the competition in August 2025, after three Spike NLOS missiles fired from a vehicle at Dugway hit their targets, two of them without a direct line of sight. In October 2025, it received a $30 million follow-on award for the second phase, which covered building hardware for safety testing and integrating the missile on the utility vehicle.
The U.S. Army qualified Spike NLOS for the AH-64E Apache attack helicopter, and The Defence Blog has reported on its integration on the helicopter. U.S. Special Operations Command has also fielded it on the Joint Light Tactical Vehicle.
“The live‑fire data and soldier feedback gathered here will support the shaping of the final M‑LRPSM requirements and accelerate the fielding of a game‑changing long‑range precision strike capability,” said Walsh.
Lockheed Martin said further validation testing will take place over the next year before the program moves into its third phase, when initial production begins and the final prototypes are delivered to the U.S. Army. The company did not say how many systems the U.S. Army plans to buy.

As weight-loss drug users turn to dietary supplements, doctors, regulators raise flags
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
14:31:23 UTC
23:31:23 KST

As weight-loss drug users turn to dietary supplements, doctors, regulators raise flags
NEW YORK, Oct 20 - For Allison Vecchio, 42, GLP-1 drugs were "a reset button on life," but at a price — side effects like gastrointestinal distress, brittle nails, and feelings of weakness so intense that at times she could not leave her bed.
But the Fort Pierce, Florida-based ER nurse said the symptoms eased when she began a cocktail of supplements that included fiber, collagen and electrolytes, a haul that costs $200 to $300 a month. "You really have to take the reins" to turn mere weight loss into improved health, she said.
GLP-1 drugs like Novo Nordisk's Ozempic and Wegovy rank among the biggest medical breakthroughs in years, owing to their efficacy in treating obesity and type 2 diabetes, and reducing the risk of heart disease. Some 10 million Americans used them last year, a figure that could grow to 25 million by 2030, according to JPMorgan research.
Their side effects, though, have caused many to turn to loosely regulated dietary supplements.
US supplement sales have surged in recent years, surpassing $74 billion in 2025, according to the Nutrition Business Journal. While users swear by them, their growing popularity — fueled in part by social media — has doctors raising red flags and regulators considering new rules around how these products come to market.
Vitamins and supplements don't need preapproval by the US Food and Drug Administration, making their scientific credibility hard to gauge. With social media personalities playing a growing role in their promotion, some medical researchers have called for more regulation of online supplement marketing.
Rob Fried, CEO of Niagen Bioscience, which had $129 million in sales last year, cautioned that companies "can hire an influencer, or even hundreds of influencers on TikTok ... to make whatever claims will sell."
SALES OF SUPPLEMENTS SOAR
Vecchio has 25,000 TikTok followers and is on retainer with three brands. She is also a member of TikTok Shop's HealthPro creator program, which is reserved for licensed health professionals.
Pittsburg, Kansas, resident Terri Hart, 52 — a TikToker with more than 12,000 followers — mostly works on commission, perusing products the brands make available to influencers, and promoting the ones she feels helped her the most.
Hart takes magnesium, electrolytes, B12 and other supplements, which she says have helped offset what she called "horrible" nausea, fatigue and constipation after beginning GLP-1s in 2023. They run about $110 a month, costs insurance doesn't cover. TikTok income eases the burden, Hart says.
She says she makes clear she isn't a medical professional, and urges followers to talk to doctors before taking her advice. "I establish my authority through my lived experience," Hart said.
TikTok Shop generated more than $1 billion in dietary supplement sales in 2025, or 5.4% of all e-commerce supplement sales, according to the Nutrition Business Journal, while overall US vitamin and supplement sales grew 5% in 2024 and 7% last year.
The drugs are "bringing in new consumers and expanding existing supplement routines," said Erika Craft, a data analyst at Nutrition Business Journal.
But absent FDA preapproval, people don't know exactly what is in many supplements, said Jonathan Bonnet, a clinical associate professor at Stanford and chief medical officer at the Ardmore Institute of Health in Ardmore, Oklahoma.
"If you can't know what you're taking, it's hard to know what risks you're undergoing," he said.
RETAILERS OFFER MORE SUPPLEMENTS
Nearly half of GLP-1 users started taking new vitamins and supplements after beginning the drugs, according to a Nutrition Business Journal survey, with probiotics, protein and fiber particularly popular.
A consumer survey by Boston Consulting Group this year said GLP-1 users spend roughly 20% more on protein, fiber and collagen, a protein that helps maintain skin structure, than before starting the drugs.
Companies are capitalizing. Target is widening its supplement offerings, while private equity-owned The Vitamin Shoppe has seen double-digit sales growth this year in fiber and creatine, which are both popular with GLP-1 users, said Jack Gayton, senior vice president of merchandising at The Vitamin Shoppe.
Mergers and acquisitions in the space are getting bigger, though with fewer transactions. In 2024, there were 115 deals globally worth $7.3 billion, according to financial data firm PitchBook. In 2025, there were 95 deals worth $16.9 billion. Through October 6 of this year, there have been 68 deals worth $14.6 billion.
Procter & Gamble is set to acquire supplement maker Thorne, while Japan's Kirin Holdings announced in August it will buy Canada's Jamieson Wellness, whose US-based brand youtheory released a product aimed at GLP-1 users in early 2025.
Jamieson spokesperson Ruth Winker said the company sees GLP-1s as a tailwind for growth beyond combating side effects. "As people get healthier, they tend to take more vitamins and supplements," Winker said.
REGULATIONS IN THE OFFING
US Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has proposed tighter regulations. The FDA this year has stepped up efforts to strengthen oversight of new dietary ingredients, issuing new guidance on what submissions for review should include.
Many supplement makers avoid this review process by using a pathway that allows food companies to declare ingredients “generally recognized as safe" without notifying the FDA. But a proposed rule would eliminate that option as part of Kennedy's broader effort to regulate food ingredients.
The proposal has divided the industry. Some support more regulation, lamenting unscrupulous actors who spike supplements with drugs or add only tiny amounts of touted beneficial ingredients.
“At a minimum, a review process should happen prior to launch," says Jacqueline Maslan, CEO of Body of Work, a vitamin startup aimed at women under 40.
But supplement trade group the Council for Responsible Nutrition says the rule would cause months of backlogs as the FDA reviews thousands of ingredients.
Thorne CEO Colin Watts said it's “improbable” the FDA could have the manpower to review new ingredients “at the speed needed to keep up with innovation."
In a statement to Reuters, an HHS spokesperson said the FDA is mulling opportunities "to modernize its regulatory approach to keep pace with an evolving marketplace," adding the agency wants to ensure product safety "while supporting consumer choice." REUTERS

Russian oil refineries under attack by Ukrainian drones: how to intensify the crisis in the enemy’s oil refining industry
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
17:30:47 EEST
23:30:47 KST

Russian oil refineries under attack by Ukrainian drones: how to intensify the crisis in the enemy’s oil refining industry
Kyiv • UNN
The attacks are damaging Russian oil refineries, repairs to which cost hundreds of millions of dollars and are being complicated by sanctions. Experts are calling for intensified strikes and tighter control over sanctions evasion.
Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries (ORPs) are gradually turning one of the budget-forming sectors of the Russian economy into a source of constant financial losses and technological problems. Damage to complex equipment, much of which is manufactured abroad, is forcing Russian enterprises to spend millions of dollars on repairs, search for alternative suppliers, and reduce the production of petroleum products. At the same time, experts interviewed by UNN are convinced that, to increase economic pressure on the Kremlin, Ukraine should maintain the intensity of its strikes on Russian oil refining, while Western partners should increase sanctions pressure and shut down opportunities to circumvent bans on the supply of high-tech equipment, UNN writes.
Russian oil refineries operating in a state of constant repair
Russia’s oil-refining industry, which for decades supplied the domestic market with fuel and generated significant export revenues for the state, is increasingly being forced to operate amid damage to its production facilities. Ukraine’s long-range strikes are creating a problem for Russian enterprises that cannot be solved merely by strengthening air defenses or increasing funding for repair work.
The distinctive feature of this campaign lies not only in the number of enterprises attacked but also in the repeated strikes. Even after individual production facilities are restored, refineries remain vulnerable to new damage. As a result, Russia is forced to spend ever more money maintaining the operability of its existing capacity.
According to Ukrainian long-range weapons manufacturer Fire Point, the Russian oil-refining enterprises that have most frequently been targeted by Ukrainian attacks include the Saratov (20 attacks), Ilsky (19), Ryazan (18), Syzran (15), Afipsky (15), and Tuapse (13) refineries.
In the fifth year of the full-scale war, Russian refineries are increasingly operating in a state of endless repair. One strike is followed by another, equipment cannot be restored in time, and then an FP-1 (a long-range strike drone — ed.) arrives for an unscheduled inspection of the quality of the repair work, the company noted.
To assess the economic consequences of such intensive attacks, it is crucial to determine which technological units were disabled and how quickly they can be restored.
Military expert Bohdan Dolintse explains that it is not necessary to destroy an entire refinery to seriously disrupt its operations.
It is important to understand that an oil refinery is a complex technological system in which all units are interconnected. Even if some equipment remains undamaged, damage to individual critical components may make it impossible for the entire facility to operate normally. Restoring such facilities requires significant financial resources, specialized equipment, and time. That is why the consequences of strikes can be disproportionately large compared with the scale of the physical damage
At the same time, refineries have different structures and production reserves. Large facilities may operate several similar units, allowing them to partially compensate for damage to individual elements. Therefore, it would be incorrect to speak of a complete shutdown of a refinery after every attack.
However, it is precisely the repeated strikes that have a long-term effect on Russia’s oil-refining industry. Enterprises are forced to restore equipment, maintain current production, and adapt to limited access to foreign technologies simultaneously.
Import dependence, which complicates the restoration of Russian refineries
One of the biggest problems facing Russia’s oil-refining industry remains its dependence on foreign-made equipment. Despite having its own production capabilities, Russian companies have for many years used Western technologies to modernize refineries, increase the depth of oil processing, and produce higher-quality fuel.
After international sanctions were imposed on russia, access to some of these technologies, components, and servicing became significantly more difficult. The kremlin was forced to redirect its focus to the Chinese market. Amid regular strikes on oil refineries, this creates additional problems: even when it has the funds, russia cannot quickly purchase the necessary equipment or find a complete replacement.
Military expert Valerii Romanenko, in a comment to UNN, points out that Western technologies, in particular those of the American company Honeywell UOP, were used at many Russian oil refineries.
Another factor is the dependence of Russian oil refineries on foreign equipment. Western technologies, in particular those of the American company Honeywell UOP, were used at many facilities. This equipment is used for the deep processing of crude oil and the production of valuable petroleum products and petrochemicals. Foreign equipment was also used at some facilities, including in the sector of the company "Lukoil." Therefore, damage to such units can create additional difficulties during repairs and the restoration of production
Dependence on imported technologies has not only a technical but also an economic dimension. Modern deep-processing units make it possible to obtain a larger volume of gasoline and diesel fuel from the same amount of crude oil. The loss of such capacity reduces a refinery's efficiency even if it retains the ability to carry out the primary processing of oil.
Energy expert Sviatoslav Pavliuk adds that russia has its own industrial-equipment manufacturing sector, but it is not always capable of providing comparable technological characteristics.
Regarding the dependence of Russia's oil-refining industry on Western technologies, it is necessary to understand that russia also has its own equipment manufacturing. The problem is that Western technologies were often more efficient. The quality of the equipment directly affects the depth of oil processing and, consequently, how many valuable petroleum products an enterprise can obtain from the raw material
In addition, equipment for large oil refineries cannot always be replaced through an ordinary spare-parts purchase. Some units are manufactured to the specific technological parameters of a facility and require complex installation, commissioning, and integration into existing production processes.
That is why sanctions restrictions on the supply of equipment and technologies may intensify the long-term economic consequences of Ukrainian strikes. The more difficult it is for Russian enterprises to obtain the necessary components, the higher the costs and the longer the restoration of damaged capacity may become.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has also repeatedly spoken about the need to strengthen sanctions pressure on russia overall.
We need a strong 22nd EU sanctions package. And, please, we need real sanctions against every company and every individual involved in the production of Russian ballistic missiles, advanced communications systems, and drones, as well as against those involved in the operation of Russia's financial system - the head of state said after it became known that US President Donald Trump had lifted sanctions on russia and Moscow had agreed to a "diesel deal" with Washington.
Repairs Worth Hundreds of Millions of Dollars: Why Damaged Units Cannot Be Quickly Replaced
The difficulty of restoring Russian oil refineries is determined not only by the availability of foreign equipment but also by the specifics of the technological process itself. An oil refinery is a system of interconnected production units, some of which require individual design, specialized materials, and lengthy installation.
The consequences of such strikes for Russian industry are tangible. Restoring damaged equipment can cost tens or, in some cases, hundreds of millions of dollars. In addition, this concerns specialized foreign equipment that, under Russia's sanctions regime, is extremely difficult to purchase, repair, and keep operational. The loss of such capacity may have long-term consequences: depending on the nature of the damage, partial restoration may take months or even several years
Energy expert Sviatoslav Pavliuk names distillation columns among the elements most difficult to restore. This equipment is used to separate crude oil into fractions and plays an important role in the technological process.
According to him, damage to such structures may require not merely replacing individual parts but a large-scale reconstruction of the entire facility. In addition, this equipment is large, which complicates its transportation.
Chinese equipment may partially compensate for the halt in Western supplies, but it will not necessarily provide a comparable level of efficiency. There are also purely logistical problems. Distillation columns are enormous structures that are difficult to transport. They may be transported in sections and then assembled on-site, or delivered in one piece. In some cases, the dimensions of such equipment create difficulties even when passing under bridges. Previously, transporting similar structures sometimes required dismantling certain infrastructure elements
Thus, even if a Russian enterprise finds a supplier of new equipment, this does not guarantee a rapid return to previous fuel production volumes.
From fuel shortages to rising prices
The economic consequences of damage to oil refineries extend far beyond the industry itself. Russia still remains one of the world's largest oil producers, but the availability of crude oil no longer guarantees a stable supply of gasoline and diesel fuel to the domestic market.
When individual refineries shut down or reduce production, supplies must be redistributed among regions. This increases transportation costs, places additional pressure on logistics infrastructure, and may cause localized fuel shortages.
The consequences begin to affect all sectors of the economy. Rising gasoline and diesel prices increase logistics costs, driving up the prices of food, construction materials, and other goods. It should not be forgotten that the Russian army also requires fuel, so the reduction in production also affects the supply of the occupation forces.
Thus, fuel for Russia is not merely a commodity but an instrument of domestic and foreign policy. Strikes on refineries will not completely halt fuel supplies, but they are gradually turning an industry crisis into an economy-wide one. As early as June, fuel problems had affected 83 regions of the Russian Federation
Refineries are the key link between oil extraction and the fuel market. The more refineries are put out of operation, the more crude oil remains unprocessed. It must be stored somewhere, exported, or production must be reduced. And without refining capacity, such quantities of crude oil inside the country are of no use to anyone, so Russia is trying to export it. However, in this case, exports do not compensate for the decline in production or the fuel shortage on the domestic market.
It is worth noting that on September 28, Russian dictator Vladimir Putin signed a decree banning the publication of data on fuel exports and refinery processing volumes.
Ukrainian strikes on Russia's oil-refining infrastructure are extremely painful for Russia for several reasons. First, revenues from the oil and gas sector are critically important to the Russian economy, providing a significant portion of state budget revenues. Second, Russian political elites have for years promised the population a stable supply of energy resources. Therefore, any disruptions in fuel supplies create not only economic but also political problems for the Kremlin
Another important consequence is that Russia is forced to seek opportunities to import fuel and is already supplying it from India, which places an additional burden on the budget.
How to increase the Kremlin’s economic losses
Overall, we must strike at key nodes of the Russian economy. Oil refineries are precisely such targets. This is an effective area because even drones with a relatively small warhead can cause large-scale fires at refineries. High-temperature processes take place there, including cracking, while the technological units operate under high temperatures and pressure. As a result, damage to critical components can lead to serious consequences for production
At the same time, the strikes alone are insufficient to impose long-term restrictions on Russia’s production capacities. The Russian Federation is trying to compensate for the loss of access to foreign equipment and technologies through domestic production and by seeking alternative markets for purchases. However, such equipment does not always provide comparable efficiency, while its manufacture, transportation, and installation may require considerable time. Accordingly, the more difficult access to imported components becomes, the more costly and time-consuming the restoration of damaged plants will be.
For this purpose, Western partners need not only to expand sanctions restrictions but also to strengthen oversight of their enforcement. Above all, this concerns shutting down channels for the re-export of specialized industrial equipment, restricting the supply of components and technological maintenance, and introducing secondary sanctions against companies that facilitate the circumvention of bans. Particular attention should be paid to technologies that Russian manufacturers cannot fully replace with domestic or Chinese alternatives.
The continuation of Ukrainian strikes is already forcing the Russian authorities to spend resources not only on repairing enterprises but also on stabilizing the domestic fuel market and concealing the real consequences.
Obviously, the greatest long-term effect can be achieved by combining continued Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries with strengthened sanctions control over the supply of high-tech equipment. Under such a scenario, every large-scale damage event will create an increasingly complex production and financial problem for Russian enterprises. And it will bring Ukraine one step closer to peace.

Waiting for an Israel that doesn’t exist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
14:29:08 UTC
23:29:08 KST

Breadcrumb
Waiting for an Israel that doesn’t exist
In Paradigm Lost: From Two-State Solution to One-State Reality, Ian Lustick borrows a joke from Woody Allen’s Annie Hall. A man tells his therapist that his brother thinks he is a chicken. Why not have him treated? I would,’ the man replies, ‘but I need the eggs.’
When I interviewed Lustick some years ago, I asked who was still collecting eggs from the two-state solution long after the conditions for it had vanished. He replied: American administrations, the Palestinian Authority, the Israeli government, and what he called the ‘peace process industry’. By that, he meant the international institutions, NGOs, and experts whose careers rest on the promise of a settlement that never materialises.
That joke stayed with me as the West Bank moved to the centre of mainstream media coverage. Journalists have been attacked by settlers on camera. Israeli army commanders and officials have been publicly questioned about settler violence. All of it has unfolded to the sound of an alarm so old it has become part of the furniture: the two-state solution is under threat.
In much of Western politics and media, criticising “extreme settlers” is the cheapest form of criticism there is. One can condemn settler violence, denounce Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, and perhaps blame Benjamin Netanyahu for wrecking the prospects of peace, all without asking more difficult questions about the Israeli state or the support that sustains it.
This kind of criticism leaves room for a comforting assumption: the problem is this government. Remove it and another Israeli partner, ready for peace, may yet appear. With Israelis voting on 27 October, where is that partner?
The leading alternatives to Netanyahu do not fundamentally disagree over settlement or control of the West Bank. Gadi Eisenkot, the former army chief often cast as the man who could lead Israel out of the Netanyahu impasse, has pledged that no Palestinian state will be established under any government he forms.
Naftali Bennett, who now leads Yachad, his joint list with Yair Lapid, once served as director-general of the Yesha Council, the settlers’ umbrella body. He has also proposed annexing Area C, which covers more than 60% of the West Bank. Even Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats and, by Israeli standards, a dove, called talk of a Palestinian state destructive.
Since the Oslo Accords were signed in 1993, the settler population has grown from about 250,000 to more than 750,000. Much of this growth occurred during the peace process itself, under governments the world regarded as moderate.
One of the busiest years for settlement construction was 2000, under Ehud Barak. In 2008, while Ehud Olmert was negotiating with Mahmoud Abbas after Annapolis, Israel began building more settlement homes in the West Bank than in any year under his predecessor, Ariel Sharon. Olmert has since found a second career on Western television warning about the consequences of the first.
Most Palestinians stopped waiting for that partner long ago. Experience has taught us that settlement is not a policy of the Israeli system. It is the system. That doesn’t make Israeli politicians the same; they don't all treat every form of violence against Palestinians the same way. But the real disagreements are about how to manage, regulate, and institutionalise that violence, and how much violence can be used before the political and diplomatic bill becomes too high.
In August, when the Housing Ministry opened bidding on some 1,200 homes in E1, the corridor east of Jerusalem that would cut the West Bank in two, Eisenkot objected only to the timing, while calling a Palestinian state a “grave mistake”. He had no quarrel with the map, only the calendar.
When settler violence is presented as the exception, and reduced to the extremism of Netanyahu and his allies, it becomes possible to maintain the image of another Israel, one that is moderate, merely waiting for its turn to govern and resume the peace process.
That is how the promise of two states outlives every fact on the ground. Its political power never rested on its feasibility. It has always lain in the capacity to sustain a particular political fantasy about Israel. That fantasy separates Israel as a political system, to be allied with, from the ‘incidental’ excesses of that state.
Decades of ‘peacemaking’ and billions in funding have entrenched it so deeply that questioning it now seems harder than questioning Israel’s violations themselves.
This fantasy survives through fragmentation. In Gaza, the genocide is treated as an excessive use of otherwise legitimate force. In the West Bank, the violence is treated as an extremist deviation from Israel’s political order, one that an election result could end at any moment.
And inside Israel, abuses against Palestinian citizens are framed as threats to an established democracy. Read the mainstream Western press on each, or listen to European and even American officials, and you could be forgiven for thinking they were describing three different countries.
Perhaps these are the new eggs in Lustick’s joke. The West can go on condemning what it sees, so long as it keeps waiting for an Israel that does not exist. On 27 October, Israelis will vote, and the wait will be renewed, as it has after every election before. Its arrival was never the point. The longer the West keeps waiting for the Israel it imagines, the less it has to deal with the one that is already here.
Izzeddin Araj is a Palestinian journalist and researcher. He is the Executive Director of Al-Araby Al-Jadeed and the former Editor-in-Chief of the Arabic network Ultra Sawt. He holds a PhD in Anthropology from The Graduate Institute, Geneva (IHEID).

EU not reconsidering Russian gas embargo due to risk of split — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
14:26:01 UTC
23:26:01 KST

MOSCOW, October 20. /TASS/. The European Union is not revising its decision on the Russian gas embargo, despite the unfavorable timing for its implementation, Alexey Belogoryev, Research Director at the Institute for Energy and Finance, told TASS. Reversing the restrictions could cause a split within the EU, as Poland, the Baltic states, and Finland would likely oppose such a move, he added.
The expert noted that most European countries have ruled out the return of Russian gas supplies. According to him, despite the current crisis in liquefied natural gas (LNG) supplies, Europe has not abandoned its plan to introduce an embargo on Russian LNG on January 1, 2027, during the peak of the heating season.
"It is difficult to imagine a more unfavorable moment for introducing an embargo. Nevertheless, we see no changes to this decision, precisely because reversing it is extremely difficult. At the very least, a number of EU countries – Poland, the Baltic states, and Finland – would likely not allow this. This risks a split within the EU, which the European Commission is constantly trying to prevent and overcome," Belogoryev said.
According to the expert, it is currently difficult to predict what fundamental changes in Europe’s political stance would be required to overturn, revise, or ease the decisions on the Russian gas embargo. "The European decision-making system and bureaucracy are structured such that canceling already adopted decisions, even if they are economically disadvantageous, is much more difficult than moving them forward," he concluded.

September data shows housing market in a deep freeze
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
14:18:58 UTC
23:18:58 KST

Fast-rising mortgage rates in September took a harsh toll on the housing market, according to new monthly data released today.
Pending home sales, a measure of signed contracts on existing homes, dropped 7.3% from August and were down 11.3% year-over-year, according to the National Association of Realtors.
This count reflects buyers out shopping in September, when the average rate on the 30-year fixed mortgage rose sharply. It started the month around 6.8% and hit 7.6% by the end of the month, according to Mortgage News Daily.
"Although job growth and income gains can support home purchases, housing affordability is more affected by changes in mortgage rates," said Lawrence Yun, NAR's chief economist in a release.
Regionally, sales dropped across the nation but the biggest month-to-month drops were in the South (-8.2%) and West (-9.2%). The South is usually the most active market and the West is the most expensive.
Home construction also took a hit in September. Both single-family housing starts and building permits fell much more sharply than analysts had predicted. Starts were down 4.56% to 859,000 annualized, according to the U.S. Census. That is the lowest level since September 2025. Building permits, which are a measure of future construction, fell 4% for the month.
"We expect home construction activity to remain moribund into 2027," said Ben Ayers, senior economist at Nationwide Financial in a note to investors. "Many builders are still trying to unload current projects with widespread use of price cuts and incentives cutting into profit margins. Housing starts, especially for single-family homes, could be low for much of the next year as the market adjusts to a higher rate environment – adding a modest drag to economic growth from reduced residential construction."
An October read on homebuilder sentiment Tuesday came in at the lowest level in 14 years, according to the National Association of Home Builders. Current sales, future sales expectations and buyer traffic all fell, with the latter seeing the lowest level.
"Housing remains squeezed by supply-side constraints and significant affordability challenges," said Robert Dietz, NAHB's chief economist in a release. "Demand persists, but higher mortgage rates, elevated construction costs and weaker consumer confidence are keeping more buyers on the sidelines."

Illegal excavations of the &quot;Ancient City of Panticapaeum&quot; — a Russian museum worker has been notified of suspicion and faces imprisonment
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
17:17:36 EEST
23:17:36 KST

Illegal excavations of the "Ancient City of Panticapaeum" — a Russian museum worker has been notified of suspicion and faces imprisonment
Kyiv • UNN
Since 2014, the suspect has been illegally excavating Panticapaeum in Kerch and handing over the finds to an occupying institution. He faces up to 12 years in prison.
An employee of a museum institution of the Russian Federation has been notified of suspicion over illegal excavations of the "Ancient City of Panticapaeum." As reported by the Prosecutor's Office of Crimea, the suspect is conducting illegal excavations on the territory of a cultural heritage site without any permits from the competent Ukrainian authorities, UNN reports.
The head of the Department of Archaeology of the Ancient World at the "Alexander Pushkin State Museum of Fine Arts" has been notified of suspicion. His actions have been classified under Part 2 of Article 28 and Part 1 of Article 438 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine (commission of a war crime by a group of persons acting in prior conspiracy). The article provides for punishment in the form of imprisonment for up to 12 years
Details
According to the investigation, the suspect has been conducting illegal excavations on the territory of a cultural heritage site since 2014 and to this day, without any permits from the competent Ukrainian authorities.
This concerns the archaeological complex "Ancient City of Panticapaeum" — an architectural monument of national significance protected by law, located in the area of Mount Mithridates in the city of Kerch.
During archaeological work on the territory of the ancient settlement, the suspect found fragments of painted bowls and amphorae, ancient slabs, casting molds, a terracotta statuette, and other cultural valuables that are the exclusive property of the state of Ukraine.
Later, he handed these finds over to the so-called "East Crimean Historical and Cultural Museum-Reserve." The head of this occupation institution, who had previously been notified of suspicion of committing a war crime, subsequently facilitated the inclusion of the recovered items in the Museum Fund of the occupying country and also arranged for them to be transferred for display at exhibitions in the Russian Federation.
In this way, in violation of the norms of international humanitarian law, the suspect facilitated the illegal appropriation of Ukraine's cultural heritage and also caused the destruction of an archaeological monument from the ancient period, as a result of which its historical and scientific value has been irretrievably lost.
The pre-trial investigation is ongoing. It is being conducted by the Main Directorate of the Security Service of Ukraine in the Autonomous Republic of Crimea.

Brazil’s Newcastle poultry outbreak unlikely to have major long-term impact, analysts say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
14:16:10 UTC
23:16:10 KST

Brazil’s Newcastle poultry outbreak unlikely to have major long-term impact, analysts say
SAO PAULO, Oct 20 - An outbreak of Newcastle disease in Brazil is unlikely to cause lasting damage to the country's poultry industry if authorities contain it quickly, analysts said, though uncertainty over trade restrictions, particularly from China, remains a key risk for exporters.
Brazil, the world's largest chicken meat exporter, confirmed a case of the disease at a commercial farm in the southern state of Santa Catarina on Monday, prompting containment measures and triggering concerns over poultry trade flows.
Mexico, Brazil's seventh-largest poultry buyer last year, quickly suspended imports, while meat lobby group ABPA said Brazil would impose a self-embargo on shipments to China pending a decision by Chinese authorities on whether restrictions would apply nationwide or only to the affected area.
Shares in major poultry processor MBRF fell more than 4% on Monday, while US-traded peer JBS slipped 1%.
Brazil last reported a Newcastle disease outbreak in July 2024 in Rio Grande do Sul state, which neighbors Santa Catarina.
Chicken exports fell by about 25%, or 100,000 metric tons, during the month affected by restrictions that year, analysts at JPMorgan estimated, but rebounded quickly as markets reopened, causing no material effect on MBRF's and JBS' earnings.
China was the most consequential source of trade disruption as it kept a state-wide embargo in place until January 2026, they noted, but other key destinations such as Mexico, the European Union, Saudi Arabia and Japan either eased restrictions quickly or implemented a localized response.
"This time around, unless we see a widespread event happening (which is unusual for this disease), we think the impact could be even smaller as several countries have changed their restriction protocol to a radius," JPMorgan said.
Santander analysts also flagged China -- which currently accounts for roughly 10% of Brazilian chicken exports -- as the key uncertainty, adding that MBRF is more exposed than geographically diversified JBS to potential disruptions.
They estimated trade restrictions could affect about 15% of Brazil's chicken production under current export protocols.
Prolonged restrictions could force exporters to redirect shipments to alternative markets or the domestic market, potentially weighing on prices and margins, Santander said.
"All in all, we are monitoring the scope and duration of trade restrictions. Lack of visibility on the duration of Chinese suspension is the key risk," they added. REUTERS

Amnesty says Palestinians face 'season of horror' in West Bank amid Israeli settler attacks

The rights group called on states to act against Israeli settlers after the attacks, which recently saw Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine injured, with broken ribs and hand injuries which required surgery.
Amnesty said the attack, and another which targeted European diplomats, "offer a glimpse into a reality of relentless aggression against Palestinians."
In a rare condemnation of Israeli settler violence, US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee called the attack a "despicable act of terror" in a post on X.
Huckabee also condemned settlers seizing property from Palestinian-Americans in August, but has long been an ardent supporter of Israel.
In September, he blamed "biblical illiteracy" for waning support for Israel among American citizens. He said in an interview with NewsNation that Americans will have a more favourable view of Israel if they "look at the truth."
The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said more than 1,600 settler attacks resulting in casualties, property damage or both had been recorded across 275 Palestinian communities by mid-September this year.
Settler attacks were occurring at an average rate of 6.7 a day, up from five a day in 2025, with the violence spreading across an increasingly wide area of the occupied territory.
On Monday, Israeli police made rare arrests of 10 settlers in the West Bank following attacks on Levine, European diplomats, and Palestinians harvesting olives, It rarely prosecutes settlers accused of violent acts and Israeli armed forces often facilitiate settler attacks.
Israeli human rights organisation Yesh Din found that just 3% of the police investigation files it monitored concerning ideologically motivated offences by Israelis against Palestinians between 2005 and 2025 led to full or partial convictions.
Amnesty said in a press release, "States must recognise that settler attacks are not isolated acts, but a central policy of the Israeli state and take concrete measures to respect their obligations under international law."
It called on countries "to avoid complicity in Israeli violations and crimes against Palestinians by halting all trade, investment and cooperation that contribute to maintaining the unlawful occupation, apartheid and the ongoing campaign of ethnic cleansing."
American citizen Mohammed Sakat was also attacked by Israeli settlers on Monday.
US-based Muslim rights group CAIR said of the political response to the attack, "Failing to speak out about this and demand accountability is a betrayal of the American people in favour of a foreign state."
They called on the US government to launch an investigation into the attacks on Sakat, Levine, and all other Americans assaulted by Israeli settlers.
In September, the UK, Canada and France announced sanctions against Israeli settlements, which are illlegal under international law, in a joint move.
As rumours of UK sanctions on Israeli settlers spread, Huckabee accused the UK government of "Jew hate," but US official responses to the sanctions after the country's official announcement were notably muted.
Rather than his signature style of fiery, often personal attacks, US President Donald Trump responded to the sanctions saying, "I understand exactly what's going on, but I want to find out why all of a sudden has that happened."

23:14:36 KST

Türkiye will maintain its military presence in Syria and Iraq until it determines that regional and border security conditions have been sufficiently met, Defence Minister Yasar Guler has told AFP, signalling that Ankara is not ready to withdraw its forces from either neighbour.
“We are maintaining our military presence in Iraq and Syria. When we assess that the necessary conditions have been met in terms of regional and border security, the status of our base areas and our presence in the region will be reconsidered,” Guler said on Tuesday in written responses to AFP questions.
The comments reflect Türkiye’s continued emphasis on preventing cross-border attacks and countering armed groups it considers threats to its national security, while its relationships with both Baghdad and Damascus continue to evolve.
Security concerns underpin cross-border deployments
Türkiye has conducted repeated military operations in northern Syria and northern Iraq, primarily targeting the PKK terrorist organisation and affiliated groups.
Turkish forces have maintained positions in northern Syria following a series of cross-border operations launched since 2016.
Ankara has also established military positions in northern Iraq as part of its campaign against the PKK and Daesh terrorist organisation.
Türkiye says its deployments are intended to prevent armed groups from using neighbouring territories to launch attacks.
Iraq base transfer signals evolving security ties
Guler’s remarks come as Türkiye and Iraq pursue closer security cooperation alongside discussions about the future of Turkish military positions.
In September, Ankara and Baghdad agreed on the gradual transfer of the Bashiqa-Zelikan military camp near Mosul to the Iraqi government, with the process expected to be completed by the end of 2026.
The agreement was presented as part of broader efforts to strengthen Iraqi state authority and address the presence of armed groups in northern Iraq.
The planned handover does not amount to a full Turkish withdrawal from Iraq. Guler’s statement indicates that Ankara intends to reassess individual bases and its wider presence according to its own assessment of security conditions.
Türkiye and Iraq have also expanded official security and counterterrorism talks, with both governments discussing cooperation against armed groups and other threats.
Syria’s changing security landscape
Türkiye’s military posture in Syria is also shaped by developments following the country’s political transition and efforts to integrate armed formations into state institutions.
Ankara has backed efforts to consolidate security structures under a unified Syrian state and has said its military cooperation should support stability and counterterrorism.
Guler did not give a timetable for withdrawing Turkish forces from either country.
Instead, he said the status of bases and deployments would be reconsidered once the required security conditions were met, leaving the timing of any broader change dependent on Ankara’s assessment of developments along its borders.

Hong Kong child sex sentences remain far below maximum life, report finds
Average sentences for sex with a girl under 13 drop from 10-12 years in mid-2000s to under five in recent years
Average sentences for Hong Kong’s gravest child sex crimes have remained below 10 years over the past three decades, far below the maximum penalty of life imprisonment, prompting a call for a sentencing council to issue clearer judicial guidance.
Citing data from 401 publicly available judgments between 1990 and 2025, University of Hong Kong law professor Puja Kapai on Tuesday said her research found six offences – including rape, buggery, and unlawful sexual intercourse – carried average prison terms ranging from four years and six months to nine years and eight months.
Kapai and her team also found that four of the six gravest sexual offences involving children showed a downward trend. This trend was especially pronounced for unlawful intercourse with a girl under 13, where average sentences fell from 10 to 12 years in the mid-2000s to under five years in recent years.

Euclid space telescope has detected a new comet for the first time
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
17:06:30 EEST
23:06:30 KST

Euclid space telescope has detected a new comet for the first time
Kyiv • UNN
The ESA reported the discovery of the comet in images from Euclid in September 2026. The object is 1.3 billion km from Earth.
The European Space Agency's (ESA) "Euclid" space telescope (Euclid) detected a previously unknown comet for the first time in images obtained between September 16 and 24, 2026. The ESA reported this, UNN writes.
Details
This discovery, the agency notes, is remarkable for a mission designed to obtain deep, stable images of distant galaxies rather than track fast-moving Solar System objects such as comets.
Moreover, the rapid identification and confirmation of the results prove that "Euclid" can detect new comets when they are still far from the Sun, potentially providing a suitable target for ESA's future Comet Interceptor mission.
Mikko Pentinen of the University of Helsinki, together with the Solar System Objects Science Working Group of the Euclid Consortium, made the first discovery using software developed by Mikko to detect moving objects while observing small Solar System objects in "Euclid" images.
"I was thrilled to see my software flag a 'streak' smeared across several images—a result of the object's rapid motion. By predicting its position, I was able to identify it in other images, finding it in five sets of images in total. Further examination showed that it was surrounded by a diffuse cloud, indicating an active object such as a comet emitting dust and gas," the researcher said.
The comet is located approximately 1.3 billion kilometers from Earth, equivalent to a distance from the Sun roughly between the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn. However, it does not lie in the same horizontal plane as the planets and is currently "oriented vertically" relative to the Sun, moving in an arc above the Solar System along an orbit whose full revolution will take thousands of years.

In September, Kokoda constituency in Bougainville declared itself “independence ready.” At the ceremony, Ishmael Toroama, president of the Autonomous Bougainville Government, pledged funding for a hospital and a police station.
Similar ceremonies are being held across Bougainville, an autonomous region of Papua New Guinea (PNG). Each carries the same message: the long road from civil war to self-determination is nearing its end.
97.7 percent of Bougainvilleans voted in favor of independence in 2019, but that referendum was not binding. PNG’s parliament has the final say, and seven years later, the wait for a parliamentary decision continues.
This year, Prime Minister James Marape had proposed holding a vote on August 30. Parliament formally received the result on August 27, then adjourned without voting.
Now Peter Tsiamalili Jr, Bougainville’s regional MP and the leader of government business, has announced a two-day debate for October 20-21. That is progress. But it remains unclear whether the sitting will end in a vote, or what will follow if parliament adjourns without one.
Australia has been careful on the issue of Bougainville, with good reason. In 2022, Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles said Canberra’s job was to “support Papua New Guinea.” Bougainville’s leadership took that as a retreat from neutrality, and Canberra had to clarify that it would support whatever the two sides agreed.
Australia is right to keep its distance on what parliament decides, but it can – and should – help nudge PNG to make a decision.
The 2001 Bougainville peace agreement required a referendum within 10 to 15 years after the election of Bougainville’s first autonomous government. The agreement also gave PNG’s parliament authority to make the final decision on independence – but did not set a deadline for parliamentary action.
The 2022 Era Kone Covenant set 2027 as the outer limit for implementing independence or another settlement, but again it failed to fix a date for parliament to vote. The covenant’s one interim deadline – tabling the result in parliament by the end of 2023 – was missed by almost three years.
The lack of a deadline lets Port Moresby postpone a politically difficult decision; meanwhile Bougainville’s leaders must keep persuading supporters to accept the wait. Many who sustained the peace are former combatants who staked their credibility on the promise that politics would produce an answer. Toroama himself was once a rebel commander. He now warns that trust is under strain even as he urges Bougainvilleans to stay patient. Each postponement makes that appeal harder to sustain.
The approaching PNG election compounds the problem. Under the provisional timetable, voting will be held from June 26 to July 9 of next year. If PNG’s parliament does not vote before the election, the decision will pass to a new parliament, which may first need to decide how much of its predecessor’s groundwork it accepts. Bougainville’s leaders have set September 1, 2027, as the “firm timetable” for a further stage of self-government. At that point, the new PNG parliament would be barely a month old.
Without an agreed timetable, Bougainville and PNG are heading back toward potential conflict. “Trust is the foundation of every agreement. Where agreed processes have been departed from, concerns have naturally arisen,” Toroama said while announcing his timetable in June. He added that “recent events violating these existing understandings cannot be ignored or downplayed,” even as he urged the people of Bougainville to “remain patient.”
Australia has a stake in avoiding a new rift between PNG’s central government and Bougainville. Canberra witnessed the 2001 agreement and led the Peace Monitoring Group that helped hold the ceasefire. Under the Pukpuk Treaty that entered into force in July, Australia and the PNG are formal allies, with an obligation to consult on threats to either country’s sovereignty, peace, or stability.
If Bougainville moves on its own timetable in 2027 and Port Moresby treats that as a challenge to its sovereignty, Canberra might be asked to consult as an ally on the dispute. It’s better for Australia to press for a credible timetable now than be forced to take sides later.
Port Moresby may resent even that level of Australian involvement. Marape’s government frames the referendum as a matter for PNG’s constitutional process, and an ally’s question about parliamentary scheduling can easily be heard as pressure on parliament.
But in asking for a concrete deadline, Canberra would merely be aligning itself with voices from within the PNG. When the result was tabled in August, opposition leader James Nomane told parliament the government should “not kick the can down the road” and pressed it to say when MPs would vote. The PNG and Bougainville have already agreed that Marape and Toroama will jointly determine the date. Canberra would simply be holding them to their word.
A hurried vote under contested procedures could deepen mistrust. In June, parliament set the bar for ratification at a three-quarters majority: 89 of 118 members. Bougainville’s leaders dispute the threshold and how the rule was adopted. However, leaving the vote date open-ended risks pushing the issue past the election – and conflicting with Toroama’s timetable.
That is where Canberra can help. Its role is not to shape the outcome, but to help ensure the process does not drag on indefinitely. Through existing ministerial talks, it should seek a date for the vote and a timetable for addressing the disputed voting rules. A deadline alone is not enough; the covenant had one. What matters is what happens if the next deadline is missed. Both governments should then say publicly why it slipped, who must act next, and when parliament will return to the issue.
If a pre-election vote proves impossible, a joint record of what has been agreed, what remains contested, and when talks resume would at least protect the handover to the next parliament. Australia, already a backer of the transfer of powers, could help maintain that record with both sides’ consent.
Kokoda says it is ready for independence. If Bougainvilleans are asked to keep waiting for parliament to act, their governments owe them a clear account of what comes next.

New Series of Philosophical Puzzles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
14:03:45 UTC
23:03:45 KST

PEA Soup is running a new series of posts on philosophical puzzles and thought experiments.
The idea of the series to “try out ideas and for informal discussion of issues and questions in moral and political philosophy.”
The proprietors of PEA Soup write, “All are welcome to join us in this discussion. But beyond that, we would like to invite people to propose their own puzzles for discussion.”
“PEA Soup Puzzles” kicks off with an entry from Victor Tadros (Warwick) with a set of puzzles for those who, like many, think it is wrong to use others to achieve a greater good and permissible to ensure we’re not harmed for the greater good only because we’re useful for doing so.
Here’s a teaser:
First, consider:
Jump: A trolley is heading towards Archie. If it hits him, he will be killed. If he jumps out of the way, it will head on down the track and run over Bella. Those are his only sensible options.
Although Archie acts, and his action results in Bella being killed, it seems permissible for Archie to jump out of the way…
In contrast it seems clearly wrong for Archie to act in:
Pull: A trolley is heading towards Archie. If it hits him, he will be killed. Bella is on the side of the tracks, and Archie can save his life only by pulling Bella in front of him.
Now consider:
Jump Behind: As Jump, except that Archie is only able to jump behind Bella. Doing this will save his life only because the trolley will hit Bella. Had she not been there he would have been unable to save himself.
The full post is over at PEA Soup. Comments are closed here but open over there.

HANOI, Oct. 20 (Xinhua) -- The Vietnamese government has proposed allowing private companies to invest in, build and operate nuclear power plants using small modular reactors (SMRs), under draft amendments to the Law on Electricity submitted to the National Assembly (NA) on Tuesday, local media VnExpress reported.
Under the proposal, the state would retain its monopoly over investment in, construction and operation of nuclear power plants, except those using SMR technology, opening the sector to private enterprises and state-owned companies.
Minister of Industry and Trade Le Manh Hung said the amendments aim to strengthen national energy security, remove bottlenecks in electricity planning and investment, and improve transparency in electricity pricing and market operations.
SMRs are advanced nuclear reactors with a power capacity of up to 300 megawatts per unit, about one-third that of conventional nuclear power reactors. They can be prefabricated and transported to installation sites to reduce construction costs and time.
Regarding the proposal, the NA Committee on Science, Technology and Environment called for clearer conditions governing private-sector participation and stricter safeguards for nuclear safety and security.
The NA is scheduled to discuss the draft amendments on Nov. 3 and vote on their adoption on Nov. 20. ■
