Economic Watch: China establishes data-focused new central SOE to unlock data value
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
22:02:47 CST
23:02:47 KST

XIONGAN, Oct. 20 (Xinhua) -- China National Data Group Co., Ltd., a new state-owned enterprise (SOE) directly administered by the central government, was officially inaugurated at a ceremony in Xiongan New Area, north China's Hebei Province, on Tuesday.
Headquartered in Xiongan New Area, the newly established enterprise is tasked with specializing in the development and utilization of data resources, bringing the total number of SOEs directly administered by the central government to 100.
It is positioned as a national team for data services, a leader in data infrastructure connectivity and a strategic force for national data sci-tech innovation.
The group said it will provide clients with inclusive and secure data services, and industry data governance services.
Focusing on advancing China's "AI Plus" initiative, the group also vowed to provide high-quality datasets and corpora to further the development of the AI industry.
The establishment of the new central SOE comes as data has increasingly become a new type of production factor driving China's digital and intelligent transformation.
Unlike traditional production factors, unprocessed data can hardly generate value. Only data that is connected to real scenarios, addresses practical difficulties and undergoes processing can be transformed into usable resources, analysts said.
China has been bolstering its efforts to develop a data market in recent years. In 2020, the country listed data as a new type of production factor, alongside traditional factors such as land, labor, capital and technology, highlighting its growing role in driving economic growth and digital transformation.
Following the introduction of a three-year action plan in 2024 to boost the development and application of data as a production factor, China has seen the value of data resources continue to be unleashed.
The plan sets out efforts to expand the breadth and depth of data applications across key sectors, foster new industries, business models and growth drivers, and unlock the multiplier effect of data in supporting high-quality development.
In 2025, China's total data output reached 52.26 zettabytes, up 27.28 percent year on year and accounting for about 27.44 percent of the global total, according to a national survey on data resources released in April this year. A zettabyte is the equivalent of about one trillion gigabytes.
Enterprises contributed about 90 percent of incremental data output, while emerging fields such as embodied intelligence and the low-altitude economy saw surging growth in data production, the survey noted.
Traditional sectors such as industrial manufacturing, transportation and logistics, and software and information technology services also posted marked expansion in data output.
To further unlock the potential of data resources, Chinese central authorities have pledged greater efforts to build an open, shared and secure nationally integrated data market, according to a set of guidelines aimed at accelerating the development of new quality productive forces.
Efforts will be made to promote the deep integration of the digital economy and the real economy, and optimize the layout, construction and operation of national data infrastructure, according to the guidelines, which were jointly issued by the Communist Party of China Central Committee and the State Council earlier this month.
As massive amounts of data are scattered across different departments, industries and fields, China National Data Group is expected to overcome challenges including barriers to data circulation, high data governance costs and insufficient supply of high-quality datasets, analysts said. ■

Feature: Chinese hometown of dedicated American son
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
22:02:33 CST
23:02:33 KST

This file photo taken in 2000 shows David Victor Plymire and a CT scanner he donated to a hospital in Huangyuan County, northwest China's Qinghai Province. (Xinhua)
XINING, Oct. 20 (Xinhua) -- In June 2000, an American bowed before a CT scanner newly delivered to a county hospital in northwest China's Qinghai Province.
"This scanner must serve the people of my hometown well," David Victor Plymire said, in the county's local dialect.
Plymire had made three trips to help secure the 350,000-U.S.-dollar machine for Huangyuan County People's Hospital. At the time, few county-level hospitals in Qinghai had one.
The scanner served patients for 15 years. Long since retired, it is now kept on display at the hospital.
Plymire, 95, was born in New York. But the place he calls home is Huangyuan, where he spent 17 years of his childhood and later devoted decades to improving local medical care.
The work began on a return visit in 1987, after 38 years away. He found old friends and familiar streets, but medical services remained limited. Many residents still had to travel dozens of kilometers to the provincial capital, Xining, for examinations.
Then in the late 1980s, Plymire and his younger sister bought an ultrasound machine in Hong Kong and took it to Huangyuan. It was the first of many such deliveries.
Over the next three decades, he made more than 20 trips between China and the United States, helping bring 31 pieces of medical equipment worth more than 6 million yuan (about 893,000 U.S. dollars) to Huangyuan.
Whenever he returned, Plymire also looked forward to the local foods he missed most -- niangpizi (a cold noodle dish popular in Northwest China), yogurt and boiled lamb.
Plymire was an ordinary wage earner, who rallied friends, overseas Chinese and charitable organizations to cover the costs of the equipment, shipping and customs charges, said Huang Jiong, the hospital's director.
"I can do very little on my own," Huang recalled Plymire saying. "It takes many friends to do something for my hometown."
Huang first saw Plymire at the hospital in 2000, though he had heard stories about the American from his elders long before they met.
Plymire's father, Victor G. Plymire, first came to China as a missionary in 1908. He lived in Gansu and Qinghai before settling in Huangyuan, an ancient city on the eastern edge of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, where he learned Chinese and Tibetan and offered medical care to local residents, often free of charge.
In 1932, the family moved to Huangyuan, as the son was barely a year old.
Having grown up in Huangyuan, Plymire played with local children, ate the spicy niangpizi, and learned their dialect so well that residents made up a teasing rhyme about him: "The big-nosed American loves Chinese niangpizi. He adds chili and vinegar, and gets chili all over his nose ..."
After leaving at 18, Plymire kept practicing the dialect, sometimes talking to himself in front of a mirror so he would not forget the words.
His father had spent nearly 30 years in Huangyuan, photographing everyday life. Plymire later donated hundreds of those photographs to local archives. The family's ties to Huangyuan endured: his mother was buried there, while years later, his sister Mary Ann Plymire's ashes were brought from Canada to rest beside her.
Plymire also supported local schools and helped arrange training for English teachers at local schools. Huangyuan named the American its first honorary citizen, and new employees at the county hospital learn about his donations during their orientation.
Earlier this month, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning cited Plymire's story while discussing ties between China and the United States.
People-to-people friendship holds the key to state-to-state relations, Mao said, likening the exchanges between the Chinese and U.S. people to "small streams that ultimately converge to form the vast river of China-U.S. friendship."
Now unable to travel, Plymire still speaks with old friends in Huangyuan on the phone.
During a video call arranged by Huang in September from Plymire's home in Missouri, a conversation planned for 40 minutes lasted more than an hour. Plymire remembered his old friends by name and recalled details of their years together.
He opened an album, running his fingers over a photograph from 1942 with six children on a hillside. Pointing to himself, he said in the dialect he had never forgotten: "I'll always be a child of Huangyuan."
"David, we've got boiled lamb waiting for you," said Wang Shikang, a former hospital director, from the other end of the call.
Plymire's eyes reddened.
"I miss you all, whenever I have a quiet moment," he replied. ■
This undated file photo shows David Victor Plymire (2nd L) and his family. (Xinhua)
This undated file photo shows David Victor Plymire in his early childhood. (Xinhua)

International BASE jumpers take on China's record-breaking bridge

GUIYANG, Oct. 20 (Xinhua) -- More than 30 BASE jumpers from 19 countries and regions gathered at the world's highest bridge in southwest China's Guizhou Province on Tuesday for a four-day international competition.

BASE jumping, an extreme sport in which participants parachute from fixed structures or natural formations, differs from conventional skydiving, which involves jumping from aircraft.
French jumper Ion-Mihael Paquet, who also competed at the 370-meter-high Baling River Bridge, said the greater height of the Huajiang Grand Canyon Bridge offered a different experience.

Chinese premier says SCO should promote regional stability, prosperity, contribute to global development
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
22:02:12 CST
23:02:12 KST

Chinese Premier Li Qiang attends the 25th meeting of the Council of Heads of Government (Prime Ministers) of Member States of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) in Dushanbe, Tajikistan, Oct. 20, 2026. (Xinhua/Shen Hong)
DUSHANBE, Oct. 20 (Xinhua) -- The Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) should strive to promote regional stability and prosperity while contributing to common development worldwide, Chinese Premier Li Qiang said here on Tuesday.
Li made the remarks while addressing the 25th meeting of the Council of Heads of Government (Prime Ministers) of Member States of the SCO in Tajikistan's capital of Dushanbe.
Noting that this year marks the 25th anniversary of the founding of the SCO, Li said the Bishkek summit held in September achieved a series of important outcomes, injecting fresh impetus into the promotion of peace and development.
Meanwhile, factors contributing to global instability and uncertainty continue to increase, he added.
He noted that at the Bishkek summit, Chinese President Xi Jinping pointed out that at the crossroads concerning the future of humanity, the SCO should shoulder its historic responsibility and take the initiative in steering the course of history.
To achieve this, Li said, all parties need to build greater consensus both on the level of underlying principles, including vision, philosophy and thinking, and the level of practical approaches, including operations and implementation.
At the level of underlying principles, he emphasized the importance of having a clear understanding of several fundamental issues and the vision to discern broader trends.
At present, Li said, different schools of thought are interacting and competing on the international stage, but multipolarity and economic globalization remain the prevailing trends.
Li called for embracing a global perspective and a strong sense of responsibility for the world, saying that the SCO should continue to uphold the Shanghai Spirit.
He urged the SCO to demonstrate perseverance in pursuing long-term goals. Noting that SCO countries share a common aspiration to promote friendship, safeguard security and pursue development, Li said all parties should remain steadfast, strengthen solidarity and move forward with resolve.
At the level of practical approaches, the premier said all parties need to strengthen cooperation and pursue practical innovation.
China stands ready to work hand in hand with all member states to enhance the organization's operational efficiency, strengthen and consolidate cooperation projects, and play a leading and exemplary role in advancing the SCO's high-quality development, implementing the four global initiatives proposed by President Xi, and building a community with a shared future for humanity, Li said.
He said China is ready to work with all parties to strengthen coordination and complete, as soon as possible, the institutional frameworks and rules for the four security centers.
China is also willing to sponsor 1,000 medical professionals from SCO countries to come to China for further training, continuously enhancing the well-being of people across the region, the premier said.
In recent years, the international community has seen growing calls to strengthen multilateralism and reform and improve global governance, Li said, noting that the SCO should strive to unite more international partners and play an active role at the global level.
To this end, he noted, it is particularly important to seek common ground while reserving differences and to build consensus while resolving differences.
The SCO should strengthen economic and trade cooperation and promote regional economic integration by leveraging the complementary strengths of its members, build a stable and resilient system of international transport corridors, and safeguard the stability and smooth functioning of global industrial and supply chains, Li said.
The SCO should also seek common interests amid differences in countries' concerns and work together to uphold world peace and stability, while promoting harmony and coexistence amid cultural differences, Li added.
Participants said the SCO has grown steadily and gained increasing international influence since its establishment 25 years ago.
They called for efforts to implement the outcomes of the Tianjin summit and Bishkek summit, further carry forward the "Shanghai Spirit," strengthen communication and coordination, promote the SCO's high-quality development and make greater contributions to regional and global peace and development.
After the meeting, Li and other participating leaders of SCO member states signed and issued a joint communique and approved cooperation documents covering trade and investment, industry and connectivity, as well as resolutions concerning the SCO's development. ■

ADDIS ABABA, Oct. 20 (Xinhua) -- The African Union (AU) on Monday opened a high-level dialogue on gender equality and women's empowerment, calling for a continent-wide effort to address systemic barriers affecting African women's socio-economic participation.
The second Egumeni Dialogue on Gender Equality and Women's Empowerment, running until Wednesday at the AU headquarters in Addis Ababa, the Ethiopian capital, brought together more than 250 participants, including African ministers of women and youth, heads of financial institutions and regulators, development partners, and women entrepreneurs under the theme "Building a Resilient Africa through Accelerated Women Financial and Economic Inclusion."
As part of its core objectives, the event aims to unlock 100 billion U.S. dollars in economic opportunities for at least 10 million African women and youth by the year 2030, it was noted.
"Women across our continent continue to face structural barriers to accessing finance, productive assets, markets, technology, land and business development support," Ghana's Minister of Gender, Children and Social Protection Agnes Naa Momo Lartey said. She stressed that such challenges constrain their economic potential and limit their full participation in addressing Africa's challenges, as well as the continent's inclusive development.
Mozambique's Minister of Labor, Gender and Social Action Ivete Alane said that true women's empowerment requires guaranteed access to skills training, decent work, markets and social protection, as well as a meaningful role in decision-making.
"Africa's prosperity cannot be built while women remain on the margins of the economy. The Africa we want must also be built with women: with their leadership, their talent, and their economic power," Alane said.
As Africa seeks to accelerate women's socio-economic and leadership inclusion, Alane noted that Mozambique has chosen to place women's economic empowerment at the heart of the country's development agenda and zero poverty ambition.
The three-day high-level dialogue is envisaged to galvanize commitments from African countries, financial institutions, and international partners to reform discriminatory policies and scale investments, while also leveraging digital transformation and trade opportunities under the African Continental Free Trade Area agreement. ■

ULAN BATOR, Oct. 20 (Xinhua) -- A massive steppe fire in a strictly protected nature reserve in Mongolia's eastern Dornod province burned 528,765.5 hectares of land, local media reported Tuesday, citing the Ministry of Environment and Climate Change.
The fire broke out on Oct. 8 in the core zone of the Numrug Strictly Protected Area in Dornod province. It was fully extinguished on the morning of Oct. 16. Initial investigations indicate that the fire may have been sparked by a convoy operated by Mobicom, a Mongolian telecommunications company with Japanese investment.
The Numrug Strictly Protected Area is one of eastern Mongolia's best-preserved natural ecosystems and provides habitat for a wide range of wildlife, including endangered and rare species.
The ministry said in a statement that 468,965.7 hectares of the total area affected by the fire fell within the strictly protected area. This means that 79.8 percent of the protected area was affected by the blaze.
The environmental damage, the ministry said, should be assessed not merely in terms of the area burned but also through a comprehensive evaluation of the fire's impacts on soil, water, air, vegetation, wildlife, habitats of rare and endangered plant species, and ecosystem functions, as well as its long-term ecological consequences.
A working group tasked with assessing the damage to the Numrug Strictly Protected Area is currently conducting fieldwork in the affected area.
The group is expected to assess the ecological and property damage caused by the fire, the costs of firefighting efforts, the ecosystem's capacity for recovery, and the protection and restoration measures required. It is also expected to compile and document relevant evidence and information before preparing its findings. ■

Ukrnafta targets 100,000 tonnes oil boost via reservoir pressure support
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
17:01:45 EEST
23:01:45 KST

JSC Ukrnafta is developing reservoir pressure maintenance systems to improve the efficiency of oil field development, the company said Tuesday.
"For fields that have been in operation for a long time and account for a significant share of Ukrnafta's assets, reservoir energy management is one of the key technological areas," the company explained.
During operation, reservoir pressure naturally declines. At the same time, reservoir pressure maintenance (RPM) technologies make it possible to manage this process by injecting water, gas, and other environmentally safe agents. This helps maintain reservoir energy, improve the displacement of oil toward wells, and increase the oil recovery factor.
"For Ukrnafta, this is part of the systematic technological modernization of field development. Our task is to manage processes within the reservoir more precisely and make more efficient use of the potential of our existing resource base," Ukrnafta Board Chairman Bohdan Kukura said.
RPM is currently used at 19 of the company's fields. From December 2022 through September 2026, the team conducted a comprehensive analysis of this area at 16 fields. Modern injection metering equipment was installed at five of them, while flow-diverting compositions were applied in five injection wells at three other fields.
"The practical effect of the optimization carried out during this period amounted to an additional 7,200 metric tons of oil produced," Kukura added.
The next stage involves implementing more sophisticated technological solutions. By 2030, the company plans to implement three key projects: establish an RPM system at one of its most promising fields, expand an existing system at another, and introduce polymer flooding at one of its operating production sites.
According to the company's estimates, the combined effect of these projects could amount to approximately 100,000 metric tons of additional oil recovered over the five years following their implementation.
JSC Ukrnafta is Ukraine's largest oil producer, operating across the full range of upstream activities, including exploration, oil and gas production, and oilfield services. It also operates UKRNAFTA, Ukraine's largest network of gas station complexes.
The company produces hydrocarbons from 1,789 oil wells and 167 gas wells.
Ukrnafta's shareholders are NJSC Naftogaz Ukrainy and Ukraine's Ministry of Defense. The company has been under state management since 2022 and is undergoing a large-scale business transformation.
At the end of 2025, Ukrnafta ranked first in the extractive industry, with revenue of UAH 99.6 billion, according to Opendatabot's Index of Best Companies.
The UKRNAFTA gas station network is Ukraine's largest, comprising approximately 650 filling station complexes and ranking among the country's top three operators by fuel sales volume. The UKRNAFTA brand brings together networks that previously operated under the Glusco, Shell, and U.Go brands.

The Security Service of Ukraine and the National Police exposed a scheme to embezzle more than UAH 65 million worth of state-owned gas and sell it through controlled filling stations. Thirteen people were detained.
The Security Service and the National Police of Ukraine exposed a scheme in Dnipropetrovsk region involving the theft of state-owned gas worth more than UAH 65 million. The suspects sold the stolen gas through controlled filling stations as motor fuel, the SBU reported, according to UNN.
Details
The investigation established that the criminal scheme was organized by the head of the gas measurement and metrology service of the regional office of the state gas company. He involved his subordinate - the head of a division of the respective unit - in the illegal activity.
To conceal the unauthorized extraction of gas from the "pipeline," they disconnected meters at the gas transmission system, falsified accounting data and reporting documents. To carry out the next stage of the scheme, the officials involved 11 accomplices - representatives of an affiliated private enterprise engaged in the wholesale trade of fuel
All 13 detainees were notified of suspicion, in accordance with the crimes committed, under several articles of the Criminal Code of Ukraine:
-  Part 5 of Article 185 (theft committed on an especially large scale by an organized group); 
-  Part 3 of Article 28, Part 2 of Article 362 (unauthorized actions involving information in computer systems, committed by an organized group). 
The detainees are currently in custody; they face up to 12 years in prison with confiscation of property.

Why You Should Turn Your Walk Into a Color Hunt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
14:01:10 UTC
23:01:10 KST

The last time you went for a walk, you might have focused on your favorite podcast, a call to your sister, or the number of calories your Apple Watch said you were burning.
Meanwhile, on a walk around her neighborhood, Kim Bernard noticed everything that was yellow: “A manhole cover, a yellow rain jacket, a fire hydrant, the numbers on someone's mailbox,” recalls the Maine-based artist. A “children at play” sign, part of a Pennsylvania license plate, and even a bucket of cat litter became part of the neighborhood’s palette.
Bernard was on a color walk, a simple scavenger hunt organized around intentionally noticing a certain color—and how much of it is hiding in your ordinary surroundings. We asked experts why you should make the activity part of your routine and how it can brighten an otherwise ho-hum day.
Why a color walk can help you tune in
About a year ago, Bridget Campbell, a content creator in Venice, Calif., realized she had become tethered to her phone. Even as she moseyed along the Venice canals, she brainstormed business ideas instead of admiring the colorful homes and flowers along the water. That’s when she decided to do a color walk, a concept she had stumbled upon on social media.
“It was a way to get out of my mind and come back into my body, slow down, and be present,” she says. While an ordinary walk might leave her mind racing toward work, looking for a particular color gave it something else to do, effectively putting all that other mental chatter on mute.
That’s exactly why color walks work so well: They encourage focused attention, says Cheryl Fisher, a licensed clinical professional counselor in Annapolis, Md., and associate professor of clinical counseling at Alliant University. She describes a “skim-scan-scroll world,” where it’s easy to move through your surroundings without really seeing them. Searching for color gives you a reason to look up from your phone and pay attention to what’s in front of you.
It also gives people who don’t consider themselves particularly creative an easy place to start, says Mari Reisberg, a licensed professional counselor and creativity coach in Boulder, Colo. Choosing a color to focus on provides a bit of structure while leaving plenty of room for discovery.
Reisberg still finds surprises on neighborhood sidewalks she’s traveled many times. “Oh my gosh, I’ve never seen that before,” she’ll think. Even on the most familiar routes, “There’s so much joy that shows up,” she says.
Pick a color that makes you curious
There are lots of ways to play color roulette and figure out which shade to hunt for. You could, of course, opt for your favorite color. Fisher collects paint swatches, cuts them up, and tosses them into a basket so people can draw one before heading out. A teacher once shared an even simpler approach with her: Have kids pick a color from their clothing, then look for matches along the way. You can even choose midway through your walk. Campbell sometimes spots an orange flower and decides that’s the color she’ll look for the rest of the way.
How specific you get is up to you. Finding nine fuchsia objects on a 15-minute walk? “It’s pretty difficult,” Bernard says. Reisberg sometimes opts for a particular shade, like midnight blue or sky blue, to give her eyes a more precise target. On other days, green is plenty. “There’s no right or wrong way to do it,” she says.
Take your usual walk—and see what you’ve been missing
Once you’ve settled on a color, head outside and see where it turns up. You don’t need a picturesque trail or a neighborhood full of flower gardens. Campbell encourages people who think their surroundings are too gray to give it a try anyway: Color can pop out in places you’ve passed countless times without a second glance.
When you find a match, resist the urge to mentally check it off and rush toward the next one, Fisher says. Spend a moment looking at what caught your eye. “The real gift is sitting with it and not just finding it,” she says.
You don’t have to keep your discoveries to yourself, either. “You can do it with a friend, you can do it with your mom,” Campbell says. Searching together gives you something new to talk about.
If you want a souvenir, snap photos along the way. Bernard asked participants in a color walk she led to select their nine favorite images and arrange them into a grid. Together, the collections resembled a patchwork quilt of color. You could make your own collage or save a few pictures to revisit when you need inspiration.
Or simply enjoy the walk. “We live in a day and age where everything is content,” Reisberg says. Sometimes she takes photos to share; other times, the discoveries are hers alone. If the whole thing feels a little silly at first, that’s OK, she says. Adults aren’t always used to indulging this kind of curiosity. “Keep giving it a little more space, a little more opportunity to surprise you.”

Three months of PM Andy Burnham: Can he sustain the ‘hope vibe’?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
14:00:49 UTC
23:00:49 KST

Three months of PM Andy Burnham: Can he sustain the ‘hope vibe’?
The UK’s new prime minister has made big promises and is a popular leader, but there is still talk of an early election.
London, United Kingdom – There was a moment towards the end of Andy Burnham’s conference speech in Liverpool that, through silence, spoke volumes.
The new prime minister and Labour leader fell quiet.
For 20 seconds he stood, saying nothing. He hadn’t forgotten his words. He was gathering his emotions for a passage of the speech he hadn’t been able to make it through in rehearsals without crying.
Burnham’s father had died just a couple of weeks before, and this was the section where he’d talk about it.
As the audience realised what was coming they stood, applauding, and urging him on with shouts of “Come on, lad!’ and “Come on, Andy!”
Thanking them, he composed himself and continued.
Conference speeches are theatre, and contemporary British political standards require that a leader be relatable. But there’s little doubt that Andy Burnham handled this moment with an emotional register that struck many as genuine.
His predecessor Keir Starmer sometimes came across as wooden, almost robotic and uncomfortable in front of cameras. Burnham, the seventh prime minister in 10 years, is more emotional.
He talks big ideas and grand solutions and relishes the opportunity to communicate.
In the vibes-denominated currency of modern political discourse, this matters.
The polls speak for themselves. Politico’s Poll of Polls had the Labour Party retake top spot shortly after Burnham became PM – a position it has not relinquished since. At the end of September, Ipsos found Andy Burnham to be the only politician with a positive net favourability rating.
YouGov’s polling also judges him the most popular politician in the UK at the moment.
But to keep up, Burnham must deliver tangible change before the next general election. Unless he calls one early, that will be 2029.
According to political analyst Sam Freedman, “So many in Westminster keep coming back to an early election, despite Burnham ruling it out … No one can quite figure out how Burnham keeps the hope vibe going for three more years with relatively little visible progress.”
‘Going back to what Labour was in the 50s’
In the Welsh town of Port Talbot, terraces of workers’ cottages cluster beside the UK’s largest steelworks.
Like much of Wales, Port Talbot did vote Labour for a century – until elections for the Senedd Cymru or Welsh Parliament in May.
Labour was beaten to an unprecedented third place behind Plaid Cymru’s nationalists, and the anti-immigration Reform UK.
But that was before Burnham took over.
Myles Lewis, who organises social walks for the town’s elderly, told Al Jazeera that Labour had not convinced people on immigration, and Starmer’s communication wasn’t good enough.
“[But now], it’s kind of going back to what Labour was in the 50s and 60s, where they actually looked after the working-class people. I do believe Andy Burnham can get there because I think he has the interests of the working-class people.”
In his first weeks in power, Burnham delivered a quick flurry of eye-catching, domestic, cost-of-living-focused policies.
He capped bus fares, cut the value-added tax (VAT) on electricity bills, and cut business rates for pubs.
He said that he would end street homelessness, reindustrialise the country, take services back into public control, and start the biggest build-out of social housing since World War II.
The mayor of Greater Manchester for nine years, Burnham supports the devolution of powers from Westminster to the UK’s nations and regions.
In July, he announced mayors could keep a share of business rates from April 2027 and of income tax from 2028.
And his conference speech in September set out the contours of some big political battles to come, including a national social care service, free at the point of use, paid for by changing the UK pensions’ triple lock from 2030. It would arrive next parliament. Burnham also pitched a national commission on electoral reform, with a manifesto commitment to overhaul the voting system. And he delivered a blunt verdict on Brexit: that it “has done more harm than good”. He wouldn’t rule out an in-out referendum, or a pledge for the UK to rejoin the European Union, in Labour’s next manifesto, he said.
On foreign affairs, there is less blue water between Burnham and his predecessors.
When he travelled to Ukraine in August, the UK’s new prime minister came with a headline-grabbing gift – British know-how to build the long-range SCALP missile. He was the fourth British prime minister to visit Kyiv since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and pledge steadfast support.
On Gaza, he has said the Labour government “didn’t get it right” and should have called for a ceasefire earlier. And in September, the Burnham government announced a sanctions package against illegal West Bank settlements.
But there has been no genocide declaration, and no full arms embargo against Israel. And Burnham hasn’t overturned the Starmer government’s proscription of the Palestine Action protest group as a “terrorist” organisation.
Defence spending is also a looming problem.
The government’s formal defence pledge is 3.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2035, and Burnham has declined to say whether he’d pay for it with tax rises or welfare cuts.
John Healey, who resigned as the UK’s defence secretary in June over underfunding, is now chancellor of the exchequer, and will not commit to the 3-percent-by-2030 target he set himself.
Burnham’s first budget comes at the end of this month. A full spending review follows next year. Much will be clearer after these.
His biggest pledges – reindustrialisation, control of public services, a new social care system – are expensive.
Burnham certainly has the vibes. The public likes them, for now. The budget will show whether he can afford them.

But I am now discussing a purely hypothetical scenario.".

College students who use more cannabis are less willing to share it, and less likely to use it with friends
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
14:00:17 UTC
23:00:17 KST

College students who use cannabis more frequently tend to be less willing to share a hypothetical supply of the drug and less likely to say they almost always use it with other people, according to a new study published in Experimental and Clinical Psychopharmacology. The findings suggest that heavier cannabis use tends to go hand in hand with valuing the drug more and consuming it in less social settings. If the pattern holds in clinical samples, a simple sharing task might eventually help flag people at risk of developing problematic use.
Over the past decade, cannabis consumption among young adults in the United States has climbed alongside the expansion of state-level recreational legalization. Between 2013 and 2023, the proportion of young adults aged 19 to 30 who reported using cannabis within the past month rose from 18.3 percent to 28.7 percent. Diagnoses of cannabis use disorder, a condition in which a person is unable to stop using the drug despite it causing health or social problems, have also grown, prompting psychologists to search for behavioral markers that distinguish casual recreational consumption from problematic use.
“Perhaps some people are aware of this, but with increasing cannabis legalization in the United States there has been a parallel increase in cannabis use disorder (CUD) diagnosis,” study lead author Paul Romanowich, an associate professor of psychology and director of the Operant Choice Lab at Gonzaga University, told PsyPost. “That is, cannabis legalization does come at a real cost for society. Earlier and more efficacious treatments for CUD are necessary to deal with this increase in CUD.”
To understand what drives substance use, behavioral economists often examine how people make trade-offs when evaluating rewards. A common method is temporal discounting, which measures how much a person’s valuation of a reward drops when they have to wait for it. People who heavily use alcohol, nicotine, or illicit drugs typically show steep temporal discounting, meaning they strongly favor smaller, immediate rewards over larger, delayed ones.
When it comes to cannabis, however, the connection between usage frequency and impatience for delayed rewards has proven weak and inconsistent across prior studies. Because waiting for rewards does not reliably track cannabis habits, scientists have turned their attention to social discounting. Social discounting measures how a person’s generosity changes depending on their emotional closeness to someone else.
In a standard social discounting task, people are generally willing to share resources with a close friend or family member, but they become increasingly likely to keep the resource for themselves as the recipient becomes a more distant acquaintance. Previous research on cigarette smokers and methamphetamine users has shown that substance use is associated with a faster drop-off in generosity as social distance grows, aligning with one prominent argument that addiction can be understood as a series of increasingly self-focused choices.
Prior neuroscience research has also examined how cannabis relates to social processing and interpersonal experiences in other ways. For instance, a study covered by PsyPost in 2019 found that men with cannabis dependence showed blunted brain reward activity and reported less pleasantness in response to interpersonal touch. Looking at emotional comprehension, research covered by PsyPost in 2024 indicated that regular cannabis users scored higher on tests of understanding others’ emotions than non-users.
Rather than looking at emotional empathy or neural responses to touch, Romanowich and his colleagues at Gonzaga University wanted to see how economic sharing of cannabis itself relates to real-world consumption habits. In a 2024 study, Romanowich and his team had modified a social discounting task by asking people how much hypothetical cannabis they would share with others, finding that current users shared less than people who had never used the drug. Because that earlier work did not measure how often the current users actually consumed cannabis or whether they used it around other people, the researchers designed the new study to test whether heavier use among current consumers is tied to both less willingness to share and less time spent using the drug in social groups.
“We were motivated to replicate and extend our previous study showing that college students share increasingly less hypothetical cannabis as social distance increases and that experience with cannabis (none, past, or current) changes how much hypothetical cannabis is shared,” Romanowich explained. “In that study we didn’t quantify current cannabis use (e.g., how many days have you used cannabis in the past month) or who they typically used cannabis with. Thus, we wanted to replicate this effect with current cannabis users and test whether the social environment changed with increased cannabis use.”
The researchers recruited undergraduate students enrolled in general psychology courses at a small private university in the Pacific Northwest between the spring of 2024 and the spring of 2025. While 100 students initially completed the online survey and reported using cannabis both in their lifetime and within the past 30 days, data from 11 participants were excluded because their answers on the sharing task followed an erratic, inconsistent pattern. For example, if a student said they would give 50 percent of their cannabis to their closest friend, but 75 percent to their second-closest friend, their data was removed for lacking consistency.
This filtering left a final sample of 89 college students with an average age of about 19. Sixty-five percent of the participants identified as female, and 74 percent identified as White. Nearly all of the students, 96 percent, reported drinking alcohol.
Participants first completed the cannabis social discounting task on their personal devices. They were asked to imagine a list of 100 people numbered by closeness, where number 1 was their dearest friend or relative and number 100 was a mere acquaintance. Across seven separate questions corresponding to person number 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, and 100, students slid a marker on a scale from 0 percent to 100 percent to indicate what proportion of a hypothetical amount of cannabis they would share with that specific person rather than keep for themselves.
To convert these seven answers into a single score for each student, the researchers calculated a metric known as the area under the curve. This value ranges from 0 to 1, where higher numbers indicate that a person shared a larger percentage of cannabis across the various social distances, and lower numbers indicate less sharing overall.
Next, the students completed the Cannabis Engagement Assessment, a 30-item questionnaire detailing their usage habits over the past 30 days. The survey asked how many days they had used three distinct categories of products: dried cannabis such as flower or bud, concentrates like oil or resin, and edibles such as gummies or baked goods. It also asked whether they typically consumed cannabis alone or with other people, how they obtained it, and whether they had ever tried to cut back.
To compare lighter and heavier users within the sample, the researchers summed the number of days each student used dried cannabis, concentrates, and edibles over the past month. Across all participants, total usage ranged from 1 to 60 product-days, with a median of 4 days. The researchers split the sample at this midpoint, comparing the 46 students with 4 or fewer combined product-days in the past month against the 43 students with more than 4. Because this cutoff is quite low, the heavier-use group still includes many fairly occasional users.
Across the entire group of 89 students, more frequent cannabis use was moderately correlated with lower sharing scores on the hypothetical task, showing a correlation of negative 0.30. When comparing the two subgroups directly, students above the median of 4 product-days shared a smaller proportion of hypothetical cannabis than those at or below the median. Specifically, the heavier-use group had an average sharing score of 0.46 on the 0-to-1 scale, compared to an average score of 0.57 for the lighter-use group. The difference between groups was medium in size by conventional standards, similar to the gap seen between current users and never-users in the team’s earlier study.
A similar pattern emerged regarding the social environment in which students actually consumed the drug, with usage frequency showing an even stronger negative correlation of negative 0.40 with social use than with sharing scores. Overall, 82 percent of the students reported that they used cannabis always or almost always with other people, consistent with the idea that college cannabis use is largely a group activity. However, as usage frequency climbed, fewer students said they almost always used cannabis with others, with the drop becoming most noticeable around 10 total product-days of use in a month.
Among students at or below the median of 4 product-days, 93 percent (43 out of 46 students) said they used cannabis always or almost always with other people. Among students above the median, that figure dropped to 70 percent (30 out of 43 students). In addition, 61 percent of the lighter users reported getting their cannabis from whatever their friends happened to have on hand, compared to just 35 percent of the heavier users.
“Individuals that use more cannabis also tend to share less cannabis with people they both do and don’t know well,” Romanowich noted. “In addition, individuals that use more cannabis also tend to use cannabis less frequently with other people. That is, what was once social cannabis use becomes solitary cannabis use as cannabis use increases.”
“We were not surprised that cannabis value increased with increased self-reported cannabis use – that was predicted from our previous study and many other behavioral economic cannabis studies,” Romanowich added. “However, it was somewhat surprising that there was also a strong effect for whom those individuals with increased cannabis use reported using cannabis with. We hypothesized this may be the case but didn’t think the effect would be as significant as it was. More generally, we were also surprised that there is not much empirical research on how an individual’s social environment may be related to increased cannabis use.”
The questionnaire also pointed to several differences in consumption methods and habits between the two groups. Students above the median were more likely to have used high-potency cannabis concentrates in the past month, at 60 percent compared to 37 percent of those below the median, and they took an average of 1.77 concentrate hits per day compared to 0.39 hits among lighter users. Heavier users were also more likely to know the specific strain of dried cannabis they used (45 percent versus 23 percent) and its tetrahydrocannabinol, or THC, percentage (29 percent versus 7 percent), though less than half of the students in either group knew these details.
In addition, 63 percent of students above the median reported having tried to reduce or cut down on their cannabis consumption, compared to 26 percent of those below the median. Heavier cannabis users were also more likely to report using e-cigarettes, at 23 percent versus 7 percent of lighter users.
These findings align with behavioral economic principles suggesting that as a person uses a substance more frequently, they place a higher personal value on the commodity and become less willing to part with it. Just as people who are willing to pay higher financial prices for cannabis tend to consume more of it, students who are less willing to give away hypothetical cannabis to friends and acquaintances tend to be heavier users who are less likely to consume the drug consistently in social settings.
“The practical significance of the effects is that we empirically demonstrated two ways that increased cannabis use is related to their social environment,” Romanowich said. “First, college students with increased cannabis use also tend to value that commodity more, as evidenced by significantly less cannabis shared with others. Second, students with increased cannabis use also tend to isolate themselves from other individuals when using cannabis.”
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these results. Because the study captured correlational data at a single point in time, it cannot establish whether frequent cannabis use causes people to become less generous with the drug, or if people who already prefer to keep resources to themselves are more inclined to use cannabis frequently and outside of group settings. The analyses were also not preregistered. The sample was relatively small and consisted largely of White, female college students in a state where recreational cannabis has been legal for over a decade, even though 88 percent of the students were under the legal purchasing age of 21.
In addition, only four participants in the entire sample reported ever seeking treatment for their cannabis habits, meaning the study primarily reflects differences between occasional and regular recreational users rather than people diagnosed with severe cannabis use disorder. All consumption data relied on student self-reports rather than biological urine or saliva tests, and the researchers did not measure mental health conditions like depression, which has been linked to reduced sharing in prior research on smokers.
“First, we don’t know whether the results will generalize to clinical populations, especially individuals at risk for or diagnosed with cannabis use disorder (CUD),” Romanowich cautioned. “Generalizing these results to a clinically relevant population may be important to show that the same relationship exists regardless of the amount of cannabis use. However, there may also be a floor effect whereby individuals diagnosed with CUD never share and/or use cannabis socially.”
The design of the sharing task itself also leaves room for refinement in future work. The survey did not specify an exact gram amount of cannabis to be shared, and it asked students to imagine sharing with seven people on their closeness list without knowing whether those specific friends or acquaintances actually use cannabis. If a student’s closest relative disapproves of cannabis, the student might choose to share 0 percent out of respect rather than selfishness, a factor future studies could address by asking how much time participants spend with other cannabis users.
Future research could also test whether combining social discounting tasks with traditional temporal discounting and price-sensitivity questionnaires improves clinicians’ ability to predict who will transition from casual social use to cannabis use disorder. By tracking diverse populations over time and incorporating clinical diagnostic tools, scientists can better determine whether a reluctance to share cannabis serves as an early warning sign of problematic use.
“Second, we don’t know whether these two social environment measures (cannabis sharing and social use) are predictive for current cannabis users who later develop CUD, independent of other measures,” Romanowich explained. “Showing whether this is the case will help to identify cannabis users at risk for developing CUD earlier for intervention, which should increase treatment efficacy.”
“There is still much we don’t know about who transitions from recreational cannabis use to CUD,” he concluded. “Adding an empirically based social environment level to this research is important to capture the lived experience of cannabis users.”
The study, “Increasing Cannabis Use Is Associated With Increased Social Discount Rates and Decreased Self-Reported Social Use in College Students,” was authored by Paul Romanowich, Celia Connor-Smith, Kendyl Eugenio, and Presley Nelson.

Roche forum highlights health care investment as driver of economic growth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
13:59:20 UTC
22:59:20 KST

Furkan Gençoğlu
20 October 2026•Update: 20 October 2026
Investing in health care innovation can drive economic growth, boost productivity and strengthen national resilience, executives and researchers said at Roche’s 2026 Media Dialogue, emphasizing the need to expand access to innovative treatments and rethink health spending as a long-term investment rather than a cost.
The event, held at the Swiss pharmaceutical company's headquarters in Basel, brought together Michael Oberreiter, head of global external affairs at Roche International, Dennis Ostwald, CEO of the WiFOR Institute, and Jorg Rupp, head of pharmaceuticals for Roche's international regions.
Oberreiter said health should be recognized as a key driver of economic growth and national security, warning that the rising burden of noncommunicable diseases threatens to place further strain on health systems and economies worldwide.
He cited research suggesting that pharmaceutical innovation accounted for an average of 40% of gains in global life expectancy between 1984 and 2000.
Improvements in global health have also been linked to roughly one-third of economic growth in advanced economies over the past century, he said.
Oberreiter pointed to estimates suggesting that investments in preventive care and medical innovation could save 60 million lives by 2040.
"Health care innovation is not a cost to society but an investment that drives meaningful transformation and delivers substantial socioeconomic returns," he said.
 
- Health care as economic infrastructure
Ostwald said the health sector, traditionally viewed as a financial burden, has increasingly become a driver of economic growth and innovation.
He highlighted research examining the economic consequences of migraine in Germany, where an estimated 15.5 million adults suffered from the condition in 2017.
According to the findings, migraines accounted for approximately 836 million headache days annually, resulting in 547 million hours of lost paid labor.
The combined economic impact of lost paid and unpaid time was estimated at nearly 100 billion euros ($116 billion) a year, equivalent to approximately 3% of Germany's gross domestic product in 2017.
"Health is not a cost center. It is essential infrastructure," Ostwald said, calling for greater emphasis on prevention and early intervention.
He argued that addressing health risks early is less costly than treating diseases at advanced stages and urged governments to integrate health considerations into economic, labor and fiscal policy.
“High-value innovations should be adopted to strengthen the resilience of health systems, while investments should be monitored and their impact measured,” said Ostwald.
 
- Aging populations add pressure on health systems
Rupp said scientific advances have helped people live longer but have also transformed health care needs, particularly as populations age and chronic diseases become more widespread.
An estimated 3 billion people worldwide live with chronic conditions, Rupp said and added:
“We need healthy, productive populations to sustain the economic growth required to fund the health care systems of the future. Yet two-thirds of diseases remain inadequately treated or go untreated altogether. Half the world's population lacks adequate access to essential health services, and health inequalities continue to widen. The global population aged 65 and older is projected to triple by 2050, placing even greater strain on health care systems.”
Rupp argued that investing in medical innovation could help governments address those challenges while supporting future economic growth.
He cited estimates suggesting that every dollar invested in preventing noncommunicable diseases could generate $7 in economic returns.
Greater investment in health innovation could also save 60 million lives by 2040 and contribute $12 trillion to global GDP, he said.
"A stable country needs a strong foundation, and that foundation begins with a healthy and resilient population. This enables people to remain in the workforce longer, increases labor force participation and boosts productivity,” he added.

Alberta Voted to Stay in Canada. That Doesn’t Quite Settle the Separatist Debate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
13:58:03 UTC
22:58:03 KST

Albertans voted overwhelmingly to remain in Canada on Monday, but the result may do little to quiet the separatist movement that helped bring the question to the ballot.
Preliminary results early Tuesday showed that roughly 76% of voters rejected beginning the process toward a future binding referendum on separation. While approval would not have authorized Alberta’s independence from Canada, it would have allowed the province to take the next steps in the process of separation.
Even before the vote, most Albertans expected the debate to continue. Polling from the nonprofit Angus Reid Institute, released last week, found that 62% of people in the province think that “there will never be an end to the separatist movement.”
Responding to former Alberta Premier Jason Kenney’s suggestion that the movement should end if the referendum were to fail, Keith Wilson, one of the most prominent separatist leaders, said at a rally on Oct. 17, “That’s not happening."
“We are going to build on our successes, build on our relationships," he added.
Speaking to TIME before the results came in on Monday, Jared Wesley, a professor of political science at the University of Alberta, said that even if the referendum were to fail, “it seems unlikely that separatism as a political strategy, if not an actual objective, is going anywhere soon.”
He added that the next provincial general election is next year, so it’s possible that voters could be faced with a similar question on the ballot then.
“The country is very familiar with western alienation and western grievances—that is a very long-standing political phenomenon in Canada,” Andrew McDougall, an associate professor of political science at the University of Toronto Scarborough, tells TIME. “There’s been a long history of regional tensions in Canada where the west feels disaffected from what, historically, has been the larger and, in many ways, sometimes more prosperous central Canada.”
“The idea, though, of having a vote on separatism—that is a little bit new,” he continues.
The Alberta independence campaign got more traction after the Liberal Party, headed by Prime Minister Mark Carney, won the federal election last year, with many Albertans expressing frustration that their views aren’t sufficiently represented by the Liberal government.
That dissatisfaction, driven in large part by the federal government’s energy policies, comes as Canadian leaders are placing particular emphasis on national unity.
Why did Alberta hold this referendum?
Alberta is an oil-rich province; mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction made up about a quarter of the province’s GDP in 2025. But Albertans have expressed dissatisfaction with the level of support the industry has received from Ottawa, criticizing the federal government for blocking pipeline projects, among other industry initiatives.
The feeling among some residents in the province, McDougall says, is “that central Canada is taking advantage of Alberta; that the central government has, at times, through environmental regulations, for example, hindered the development of the oil resources that exist in Alberta.”
He adds that the independence campaign may also have been fueled by Albertans’ dissatisfaction with representation in the federal government.
Alberta is considered a conservative stronghold, but the Liberal Party has led the country for over a decade. The western province has about 5 million residents, compared to 16 million in Ontario and 9 million in Quebec, which means “it could be difficult sometimes for the West to get representation in the government,” McDougall says.
At the beginning of May, separatists turned in a petition with hundreds of thousands of signatures to push for a vote on leaving Canada, while opponents collected signatures in support of staying. A court ruling on May 13 complicated matters: A judge halted the petition, finding that the province could not advance the discussion without consulting First Nations.
The government instead asked voters whether it should take the steps needed to hold an independence referendum later, leading to this month’s vote. Alberta Premier Danielle Smith supported staying in Canada.
Polling suggests that, for many voters, support for the referendum was not necessarily about wanting to leave Canada—it was a way to underscore dissatisfaction with the federal government.
The Angus Reid Institute found that 60% of respondents who were in favor of holding a future independence referendum said their motivation was sending a message to Ottawa, compared with 37% who wanted Alberta to take the necessary steps toward secession.
As early results emerged Tuesday, Wilson, the separatist leader, observed: “It’s fair to say that at least a quarter of Albertans feel that Alberta needs to be treated better.”
Carney stressed unity amid tensions with U.S.
Alberta’s independence referendum came as Carney’s government promotes national unity amid a trade war with the U.S.
McDougall says that the issues behind the referendum are "longstanding grievances,” but the fact that it advanced at a time of strong pro-Canada sentiment is “a little out of step with the times.”
The trade dispute escalated after negotiations between the two nations broke down in August. On Sept. 8, Canada responded to new tariffs from the U.S. with matching, retaliatory levies.
Tensions have continued to escalate in recent weeks as Trump repeatedly insists that Canada is ripping off Americans and should join the U.S. He said at a rally in Arizona on Oct. 14 that Canada will “end up being the 51st state, because it’s the only way it works.”
The following day, Carney spoke at a rally in Calgary, emphasizing the importance of Canadian unity amid outside tensions, though he did not explicitly reference Trump’s remarks.
“The stakes are high. This referendum, it comes at the worst possible time. The world has become more dangerous and divided," Carney said. “There are some outside our borders who are working to break us, so they can own us.”
The speech was another effort by the Carney government to promote national unity, just days before the referendum in Alberta.
The message became especially poignant that weekend when four service members died in a fire at a military base in Alberta. The nation came together to provide resources and support for the province. At a press conference on Sunday, Carney emphasized that “Canadians come together in crisis.”
Wesley says he believes that “the vast majority of Albertans are viewing this referendum through a broader global lens.”
“They know their votes send a message—not just to governments here in Alberta or Ottawa, but to Washington,” Wesley says. “Albertans are overwhelmingly opposed to Trump’s trade war and even more averse to becoming the 51st state. They know that voting to destabilize Canada makes it harder to weather the economic storm and easier to fall into the American orbit.”
“Albertans made a clear choice,” Carney said Tuesday after preliminary results became available. “They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other. Above all, Albertans chose Canada.”

New AI tool can predict cancer survival chances from selfie: Study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
13:57:58 UTC
22:57:58 KST

Halis Sünnetci
20 October 2026•Update: 20 October 2026
US researchers have developed an artificial intelligence tool that can predict cancer patients' survival chances from a single facial photograph, according to a study published Monday in the journal The Lancet Digital Health.
Developed by researchers at Mass General Brigham in the US state of Massachusetts, the system, called FAHR-Face, analyzes facial features to estimate biological age and mortality risk, potentially helping doctors make treatment decisions.
The model was trained on more than 40 million facial photos and adapted into two tools: FAHR-FaceAge, which estimates biological age, and FAHR-FaceSurvival, which predicts cancer patients' survival directly from facial images without relying on age estimates.
Researchers found that the survival model focused mainly on areas beneath the eyes and around the nose, while the age-estimation model examined facial features around the mouth and temples, suggesting the two systems identify different health-related patterns.
The survival model was trained on images of 34,363 patients and tested on another 3,820, with results independently validated using data from 4,892 cancer patients in the Netherlands.
Researchers found that patients classified in the highest-risk group had more than three times the mortality risk of those in the lowest-risk group, even after accounting for clinical factors.
Patients whose faces appeared at least five years older than their actual age also had a 21% higher mortality risk, while those appearing at least five years younger had a 17% lower risk.
Combining the two models further improved the accuracy of survival predictions, according to the study.
Researchers said the technology could help doctors assess patients' health and guide treatment decisions, although further validation is needed before it can be widely used in clinical practice.

Lebanon doesn't meet minimum standard for eliminating human trafficking, US State Dept. finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
13:57:33 UTC
22:57:33 KST

Beirut is failing to meet the minimum standards for eliminating human trafficking, the US State Department said in a report released earlier this month, explaining its decision to maintain Lebanon’s Tier 2 status.
The Lebanese government reported six trafficking investigations, 14 prosecutions and 13 convictions in 2025, compared with 73 prosecutions and no convictions in 2024.
Of the 14 suspects prosecuted last year, four were accused of sex trafficking, three of forced labor and seven of unspecified forms of trafficking, and a further 20 prosecutions from previous reporting periods remained ongoing.
Acknowledging that Beirut had made efforts to address the issue and that displacement caused by the Israel-Hezbollah war had complicated the situation, the department said Lebanon’s capacity to establish and implement anti-trafficking policies remained insufficient. Lebanon had failed to approve a National Action Plan, provided only fragmented data on trafficking cases and victim identification, and failed to adequately screen potential trafficking victims, leaving them vulnerable to penalties for unlawful acts committed as a direct result of being trafficked.
Lebanon’s parliament has also failed to approve a draft amendment to the country’s anti-trafficking law, despite the Cabinet approving it in October 2023. The proposed amendment seeks to address the burden of proof in trafficking cases, which under the 2011 law can fall on victims to prove they were exploited. The change aims to reduce the risk of victims being treated as criminals or immigration offenders rather than people subjected to coercion.
The department also highlighted the absence of a law prohibiting or penalizing employers who confiscate workers’ passports, a practice recognized as an indicator of potential trafficking. Lebanon’s employer-based visa system further increases migrant workers’ vulnerability to exploitation and hinders authorities’ ability to identify and protect trafficking victims.
Women, girls trafficked from Asia, Africa
Women and girls from southern Asia, as well as increasingly from East and West Africa, are still being exploited in domestic servitude in Lebanon. Many of these women, especially those from Nigeria, the Philippines and Ethiopia, face passport confiscation, withheld wages, excessive working hours, restrictions on their movement, and physical or sexual abuse. The economic crisis has also pushed some migrant workers and Lebanese nationals into prostitution due to a lack of economic opportunities, increasing their vulnerability to trafficking, according to the report.
Despite these shortcomings, Lebanon had introduced comprehensive standard operating procedures (SOPs) for identifying trafficking victims, the department said. The government also expanded cooperation with NGOs and international organizations to train officials in identifying victims and implementing the procedures. Other efforts included strengthening protections for domestic workers through new regulations and taking enforcement action against fraudulent recruitment agencies.
However, Lebanon lacks a dedicated judicial body to review cases referred by the Internal Security Forces’ Anti-Human Trafficking and Morality Protection Office despite increased international coordination. The government also reported no coordination with other countries on law enforcement operations, raising concerns about potential corruption and complicity in trafficking. Notably, Beirut reported no investigations, prosecutions, or convictions of government employees allegedly complicit in trafficking crimes.
Syrian refugees in Lebanon face heightened risk of trafficking
Reports also indicated that forced child labor among Lebanon’s Syrian population increased last year, particularly in agriculture, construction, street vending, and forced begging, with limited government efforts to address the problem.
The report identified non-state armed groups, including Hezbollah, as recruiting and using child soldiers, with Syrian refugee children particularly vulnerable to recruitment.
An estimated 900,000 Syrian refugees in Lebanon face heightened risks of sex and labor trafficking due to restrictions on legal employment and residency permits. Some are reportedly forced to work in exchange for food, shelter, or passage to Lebanon, leaving them vulnerable to debt bondage.
It was also flagged that the Anti-Human Trafficking and Morality Protection Office was reluctant to arrest parents accused of trafficking their children, often for forced begging, due to the lack of social and welfare services. NGOs were required to relocate children to foster families.
Lebanon has also relied on NGOs to provide shelter for adult trafficking victims, offering them only limited legal support. In some cases, foreign embassies housed victims when shelters became full.

Coke Zero or regular Coke: Which is better for your health?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
13:57:27 UTC
22:57:27 KST

Replacing regular Coke with Coke Zero can help habitual cola drinkers cut sugar and calories. It is a familiar choice when ordering food, opening the refrigerator, or browsing the drinks aisle, complicated by warnings about artificial sweeteners, cancer, and weight gain.
For most adults who regularly drink sugary cola, the switch can be a useful step toward reducing their intake. Water remains the preferred everyday drink, and people who already rely on it have no health reason to start drinking Coke Zero.
The first difference is the sugar content
Regular cola contains about 10.6 grams of sugar and 42 calories per 100 milliliters. A 330-milliliter can contains about 35 grams of sugar, nearly nine teaspoons, and roughly 140 calories. Coke Zero contains no sugar and a negligible number of calories. In the product sold in Israel, the sweeteners aspartame and acesulfame K provide the sweetness. Formulations can differ between products and countries, so check the label.
That difference matters. The World Health Organization recommends limiting free sugars to less than 10% of daily energy intake and suggests reducing them to below 5% for additional health benefits. Free sugars include sugars added to foods and drinks, as well as those naturally present in honey, syrups, and fruit juices. On a 2,000-calorie diet, those limits amount to less than 50 grams and, ideally, less than 25 grams a day. A single can of regular cola exceeds the stricter limit.
Does switching to Coke Zero help with weight loss?
It can help when it replaces a sugary drink. A review published in JAMA Network Open that included 17 randomized clinical trials found that replacing sugar-sweetened drinks with low- or no-calorie alternatives was associated with small improvements in body weight and some measures of body fat. The participants were mainly adults with overweight or obesity.
The SWEET study, published in Nature Metabolism in October 2025, also found a modest benefit. Adults who included products containing sweeteners in a reduced-sugar diet maintained greater weight loss after one year, with a difference of about 1.6 kilograms compared with the group that avoided them.
Several limitations are worth considering. The study examined a range of foods and drinks, so its findings cannot be attributed to Coke Zero alone. Only about 60% of the adult participants completed the study, and some researchers disclosed ties to the food and beverage industry. The findings support a possible benefit from replacing sugar with sweeteners; they do not establish that drinking Coke Zero on its own causes weight loss.
Why does the WHO advise caution about sweeteners?
In 2023, the WHO recommended against relying on non-sugar sweeteners for weight control or the prevention of chronic diseases. The recommendation was conditional, reflecting uncertainty about their long-term effects. It addressed their use for those purposes and left existing safety assessments in place. It also excluded people with pre-existing diabetes.
Some concerns stem from observational studies that found associations between diet drinks and disease. Such studies cannot establish cause and effect. People with overweight or a higher risk of diabetes may switch to diet drinks because of their health. Researchers therefore need to distinguish between the health of people who choose diet drinks and the effects of replacing a sugary drink with a sugar-free alternative.
Do sweeteners pass through the body unchanged?
Sweeteners behave differently in the body. Aspartame, for example, breaks down in the digestive system into phenylalanine, aspartic acid, and methanol. Safety assessments consider those substances, the amounts involved, and overall exposure. The fact that a sweetener breaks down does not, by itself, indicate harm. Claims that all sweeteners enter and leave the body unchanged are inaccurate.
Aspartame is about 200 times sweeter than sugar, so only a very small amount is needed. Sweetness alone tells us little about toxicity. Assessing safety also requires more information than whether a substance is described as “natural” or “artificial.”
What does the cancer warning mean?
In 2023, the International Agency for Research on Cancer classified aspartame as “possibly carcinogenic to humans”, based on limited evidence. The classification concerns its potential to cause cancer. It does not establish that a can of Coke Zero causes cancer or quantify the risk at a particular level of consumption.
At the same time, a joint expert committee of the WHO and the UN Food and Agriculture Organization retained an acceptable daily intake of up to 40 milligrams per kilogram of body weight. For someone weighing 70 kilograms, that amounts to 2,800 milligrams of aspartame from all sources combined. This is an amount considered acceptable for daily consumption over a lifetime; there is no reason to aim for that level.
People with phenylketonuria, an inherited condition that requires strict limits on phenylalanine, are an important exception. They need to avoid or restrict aspartame under medical guidance.
Sugar-free cola is still acidic
Coke Zero can also affect teeth. Removing sugar reduces a food source for the bacteria that cause tooth decay, while acids in the drink can still erode tooth enamel. Sipping over several hours prolongs that exposure. Reducing how often you drink acidic beverages, drinking water afterward, and avoiding brushing immediately after an acidic drink can help limit the damage.
When choosing between regular Coke and Coke Zero, Zero has a clear advantage in reducing sugar and calories. For someone switching from regular cola, it can be a useful way to change drinking habits. People who already drink water have no health reason to add it, and water should still account for most of the fluids consumed each day.
