Rashida Tlaib demands arrest of Israeli officer over Hind Rajab
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
12:47:14 UTC
21:47:14 KST

Breadcrumb
Rashida Tlaib demands arrest of Israeli officer in US over Hind Rajab killing
US Congresswoman Rashida Tlaib has called for the arrest of an Israeli military commander accused of involvement in the killing of five-year-old Palestinian girl Hind Rajab in Gaza, after a human rights organisation revealed that he was visiting the US.
Tlaib made the demand on Monday after the Hind Rajab Foundation (HRF) filed an urgent request with the US Department of Justice seeking the investigation, arrest and prosecution of Sean Glass, a former commander in Israel's 52nd Armoured Battalion.
The foundation alleges that Glass commanded the unit responsible for opening fire on the vehicle carrying Hind and her relatives in Gaza City on 29 January 2024.
"As a party to the Genocide Convention and the Geneva Conventions, our government is obligated to arrest and investigate him for these war crimes and acts of genocide," Tlaib wrote on social media.
The foundation said its investigation placed Glass and soldiers from his "Vampire Empire" Company within a few hundred metres of Hind's vehicle during the attack, saying that he most likely gave the order to open fire.
It said the evidence included geolocation analysis and documentation of the unit's movements, alongside statements made by Glass about his military operations in Gaza.
The allegations against Glass have not been established in court.
Hind was travelling with relatives through Gaza City when their car came under Israeli fire. Six-year-old cousin Layan Hamadeh contacted the Palestinian Red Crescent Society for help before she was killed.
Hind subsequently spoke to emergency dispatchers, pleading for someone to rescue her as she remained trapped in the vehicle, surrounded by the bodies of her relatives.
The recordings of her desperate calls for help provoked international outrage.
An ambulance dispatched to rescue Hind was also attacked, killing two Palestinian paramedics. Hind's body and those of the rescuers were discovered days later.
An investigation by the research group Forensic Architecture subsequently found no evidence of the Israeli account of the incident, which claimed that there was an exchange of fire with Palestinian fighters.
The killing became one of the most widely recognised symbols of the suffering of Palestinian children during Israel's genocide in Gaza.
Wider allegations against Israeli commander
The Hind Rajab Foundation also accuses Glass of involvement in other military operations across Gaza, including the assault on Al-Shifa Hospital, the destruction of the headquarters of the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, UNRWA, and the devastation of residential neighbourhoods.
It alleges that his company participated in the seizure and destruction of the Rafah Crossing, which connects Gaza with Egypt.
According to the foundation, Glass publicly celebrated the destruction carried out by his unit, including in statements describing the devastation of areas his soldiers had been ordered to enter.
The organisation said it had previously submitted material concerning Glass and other Israeli soldiers to the International Criminal Court, alongside complaints to national judicial authorities.
Its latest action seeks to establish whether US authorities will pursue allegations against an Israeli military officer present on American territory.
Polish explosives manufacturer faces legal challenge
The demand for Glass's arrest comes as the Hind Rajab Foundation pursues a separate legal challenge in Poland over the alleged supply of explosives used in Israel's military campaign in Gaza.
On Monday, the foundation, alongside the International Federation for Human Rights and the European Legal Support Centre, announced an appeal against a Warsaw prosecutor's decision to dismiss a criminal complaint targeting representatives of Polish explosives manufacturer Nitro-Chem.
The original complaint, filed in June, alleges that the state-owned company supplied TNT used in the manufacture of American bombs subsequently transferred to Israel, potentially implicating its representatives in international crimes committed against Palestinians.
The organisations argue that Nitro-Chem's commercial relationships with US arms manufacturers, as well as its direct sales to Israeli defence companies, warranted a criminal investigation.
They are asking the Warsaw Regional Court to review the dismissal and examine whether company representatives could bear criminal responsibility for supplying materials allegedly used in war crimes and genocide.
The allegations against Nitro-Chem representatives have not been established in court.

A red aurora was spotted over &quot;Vernadsky&quot;, and two neighboring galaxies also appeared in the frame
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
15:39:55 EEST
21:39:55 KST

A red aurora was spotted over "Vernadsky", and two neighboring galaxies also appeared in the frame
Kyiv • UNN
Ukrainian polar researchers photographed a reddish glow near the "Akademik Vernadsky" station. The Magellanic Clouds are also visible in the frame.
Ukrainian polar researchers captured an incredible night sky near the "Akademik Vernadskyi" station — the photographs show not only a reddish aurora, but also two neighboring galaxies, UNN reports, citing the National Antarctic Scientific Center.
Why is the aurora reddish?
The scientific center notes that we usually imagine the aurora as green. In fact, it can take on different colors depending on which atoms and molecules of gases in Earth's atmosphere emit light and at what altitude this occurs.
When high-energy charged particles from the solar wind enter the upper layers of the atmosphere, they ionize atoms and molecules of various gases, causing them to emit light of different colors. Red and green shades are mainly associated with oxygen emissions. At altitudes above 200 km, atomic oxygen often creates a red glow, while lower down it produces a green one.
And what are those two hazy spots among the stars?
In the second photo, if you look closely, you can notice two blurred patches of light. These are the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds — dwarf galaxies that are satellites of our Milky Way.
The Large Magellanic Cloud is located approximately 160,000 light-years from Earth, while the Small Magellanic Cloud is 200,000 light-years away. Both can be observed with the naked eye in the Southern Hemisphere under favorable conditions.
As noted by the NASC, these images combine phenomena of completely different scales. The aurora occurs hundreds of kilometers above Earth, while the light from the Magellanic Clouds traveled through space for hundreds of thousands of years before reaching the camera lens!

- A U.S. Navy P-8A Poseidon patrolled off Bulgaria’s Varna and Burgas, tracking data shows, a week after drone attacks sank a cargo ship nearby.
- Drones hit two ships in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone on Oct. 13, sinking one and leaving 11 crew missing.
A U.S. Navy P-8A Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft flew off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast near the ports of Varna and Burgas, a week after Russian drone attacks sank a cargo ship and damaged another in the area, flight tracking data shows.
Tracking data published by the flight monitoring Itamilradar, using Flightradar24 data, shows the Boeing P-8A crossing Bulgaria from the west near Shumen, passing over the Varna area and heading out to sea, then turning south and circling off Burgas, inside the Black Sea waters bordering Bulgaria and Turkey. The aircraft flew at low altitude and that it was the first such U.S. patrol over that part of the Black Sea in several months.
The P-8A is the U.S. Navy’s main submarine-hunting and maritime surveillance aircraft, based on the Boeing 737. It carries radar that can pick out small boats on the surface, electro-optical and infrared cameras, and sonobuoys it can drop into the water to listen for submarines. Flying low lets crews identify small objects such as drone boats more easily.
The flight follows a string of attacks on merchant shipping off Bulgaria. Early on Oct. 13, drones hit two cargo ships in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone. One of them sank off Krapets in the north of the country near the Romanian border, and Bulgarian officials said 11 crew members were missing. The second, the Ukrainian-owned, Maltese-flagged Chelsea 3, was damaged about 15 to 18 nautical miles off the coast south of Varna, and all 15 of its crew were rescued and taken to Varna.
The crew of the Chelsea 3 said the ship was attacked by three drones. Bulgarian reports described them as aerial drones, while Russian Telegram channels published images of a mark on the ship’s hull that they said was left by an uncrewed surface vessel, or drone boat. It has not been officially established what type of drone struck the ship or where it was launched from.
A week earlier, on Oct. 6, drone attacks in the same zone sank the cargo ship Alfa Watan, with all of its crew believed lost, and badly damaged a second vessel whose crew was rescued.
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said there was no clear evidence of who carried out the attacks, but that “logic indicates that the result is in favour of the Russian Federation.” He called the latest strike “absolutely unacceptable,” said Bulgaria would summon the Russian ambassador, and asked allies to help identify where the drones came from and to strengthen air and sea surveillance off the coast. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said the alliance would adjust its defenses as needed.
Bulgaria’s neighbor Romania has dealt with similar threats this year. In August, a Romanian F-16 opened fire with its cannon on a maritime drone carrying explosives that was found drifting several hundred meters from the Neptun Deep offshore gas platform, about 80 nautical miles east of Constanța, The Defence Blog reported. Romanian F-16s have also shot down aerial drones over the Danube Delta, and in June a sea drone blew up in the port of Constanța, Romania’s largest.

Why Rubio is visiting Reliance’s oil refinery in India, the world’s largest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
12:37:06 UTC
21:37:06 KST

Why Rubio is visiting Reliance’s oil refinery in India, the world’s largest
Reliance is central to Washington’s efforts to punish Russian energy buyers and contain oil prices amid the war on Iran with a crucial midterm election looming.
New Delhi, India — United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio has arrived in India for a two-day visit, during which he is set to tour the Jamnagar refinery complex in Gujarat, owned by billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, a major player in global oil markets.
Reliance’s crude refinery in Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s home state is the world’s largest single-site refinery. In many ways, Reliance Industries’ businesses sit at the crossroads of the ongoing global energy crisis.
The conglomerate is central to Washington’s efforts to punish Russian energy buyers, while also trying to contain oil prices amid the war on Iran, on top of rising diesel costs in the US, where a crucial midterm election looms. Reliance has also only recently committed to a major investment in the US, which President Donald Trump’s administration has cited as an example of its successes in luring global capital.
Rubio is skipping the capital, New Delhi, at a time when the US-India bilateral relationship has been rocky, strained by a string of friction points — and an elusive trade deal.
So why is the top US diplomat visiting the world’s largest single-site oil refinery?
Where is Rubio visiting?
After meetings in Mumbai, India’s financial hub in the western state of Maharashtra, Rubio will fly to Jamnagar in neighbouring Gujarat, near the Gulf of Kutch. Jamnagar opens into the Arabian Sea and is home to Reliance Industries’ refining complex, a major hub for crude processing and fuel exports, which processes 1.4 million barrels per day (bpd).
Rubio had visited India earlier this year too, but this trip “is a little more business-focused”, the US ambassador to India, Sergio Gor, told reporters last week. A readout from Rubio’s office noted that he would “meet with business leaders to promote opportunities for commercial investment and economic cooperation”.
“[At Jamnagar] he will meet some of the folks at Reliance,” Gor said.
What’s in Jamnagar?
The world’s largest single-site oil-refining complex has a combined crude-processing capacity of 1.4 million bpd. That is nearly 1.5 percent of global refining capacity, according to the company.
The complex comprises two refineries: the original facility, commissioned in 1999 with a capacity of 660,000bpd, and a second, export-oriented refinery commissioned in 2008, adding 580,000bpd, which operates in a special economic zone.
Jamnagar imports crude from international suppliers and exports refined products to global markets. The refinery can process heavy, sulphur-rich crude that many facilities cannot handle efficiently, converting oil into higher-value products.
Reliance said last month that the complex has processed more than 216 crude grades, claiming to be “perhaps the only refinery to achieve this feat”.
The Jamnagar refinery’s capacity is also driving a sharp revival in imports of Venezuelan crude — taken over by the US earlier this year after abducting then-President Nicolas Maduro — as Washington seeks to reshape global oil trade.
Reliance is expected to account for roughly 350,000bpd to 370,000bpd of the October intake, according to estimates from analytics firm Kpler. “We will talk with Reliance about refining more Venezuelan crude,” Rubio told reporters in brief remarks on Tuesday.
Why is the refinery significant for global energy supplies?
Reliance is a central player in keeping global oil markets stable, as one of the world’s biggest suppliers of refined petroleum products. In September, for instance, six of the seven large cargo ships that docked at European Union ports carrying oil products were bearing Reliance goods.
Reliance’s biggest export is diesel, which Trump has been particularly worried about, with prices reaching historic highs in the US ahead of midterm elections early next month.
Though the data on exports by category is not public, an analysis by the Reuters news agency from trade sources noted that Reliance Industries exported 21.66 million tonnes of refined petroleum products in the first half of 2025 from Jamnagar. Diesel accounted for the largest share at 9.81 million tonnes, followed by petrol at 6.14 million tonnes and jet fuel at 2.06 million tonnes.
Europe accounted for the biggest share of the company’s exports, making up 28 percent of Reliance’s refined products during the period. Buyers include BP, ExxonMobil, Glencore, Vitol and Trafigura.
The Jamnagar refinery also shipped about $143m worth of oil products to the US last month, according to data cited by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a think tank in Finland.
CREA noted in its report that the EU’s ban on importing petroleum products made from Russian crude from January 2026 does not adequately prevent products from refineries in third countries from entering Europe when those refineries also process Russian crude. The Jamnagar refinery is a prime example of that loophole.
Rubio’s visit to the refinery also comes as Trump faces his worst approval ratings amid inflation and rising fuel prices ahead of the midterm election in November. Just about 31 percent of Americans are happy with Trump’s performance – the lowest-ever number in his two terms, according to a Reuters/Ipsos survey.
The Trump administration has also reportedly been pushing Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop strikes on Russian energy facilities, which have rattled the global fuel markets.
Why the refinery is important for the Russia-Ukraine war
Reliance is also a critical actor in US efforts to influence how much oil Russia sells.
Since the start of Russia’s full-fledged war on Ukraine in February 2022, India has emerged as the second-largest buyer of Russian oil after China. And Reliance is driving that surge in imports. While only 3 percent of its oil was sourced from Russia before 2022, that share rose to 50 percent by 2025.
So when Trump imposed an additional 25 percent tariff on Indian goods in August 2025 to punish New Delhi for the purchase of Russian oil, Reliance was directly affected. It cut back on Russian crude imports significantly in subsequent months, but it still made up a third of the oil processed by Jamnagar’s refinery during the July-September 2026 quarter.
That was under threat when the Trump administration appeared poised to impose a 100 percent tariff on Indian goods because of continued Russian oil imports, under a new law passed last month.
But Trump has since suspended those proposed tariffs, easing concerns for India and Reliance.
Rubio has said India has been diversifying its import mix away from Russian crude, even as it still buys millions of barrels of Russian oil every day. “You’ve got countries like India, for example, that have voluntarily diversified their energy portfolio, but are still getting a substantial amount of energy from Russia because it’s hard to pivot from one day to the next,” Rubio said on Sunday.
“But they’re also an important ally and partner of the United States.”
Is Reliance also investing in the US?
Yes, India’s richest man, Mukesh Ambani, the chairman and managing director of Reliance Industries, is investing in the US, primarily through energy-related projects.
It is backing America First Refining’s planned oil refinery at the Port of Brownsville in Texas, also the first major US refinery in about 50 years, announced by Trump in March.
The refinery is expected to cost $3bn to $4bn and process about 60 million barrels of US crude annually. Reliance has signed a 20-year agreement to buy a large share of the facility’s output, with operations expected to start around 2029.
In November 2024, Reliance’s US subsidiary also acquired a 21 percent stake in helium explorer Wavetech Helium for $12m as part of its low-carbon energy strategy.
Last month, Trump announced that India’s Essar Group — an oil major with knee-deep ties to Russia — is planning an $18bn integrated steel investment in the US through its subsidiary, Mesabi Metallics.
Didn’t Trump’s ally just lock horns with Ambani?
Despite Reliance’s investments in the US and Rubio’s upcoming visit to the Jamnagar facility, Elon Musk, the world’s richest man who is also a key Trump ally, recently hit out at Ambani.
His Starlink space telecommunications firm has struggled for years to secure a licence to operate in India.
In a series of X posts recently, Musk accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government of stalling Starlink’s entry to favour market leader Ambani’s telecom firm, Jio. Musk taunted Ambani directly, addressing him as “Prime Minister Ambani” and asking whether he would “consider allowing Starlink to compete”. Starlink, Musk wrote, was being blocked by “oligarchs” protecting their “monopolistic chokehold” on Indians.
In a statement issued on X, Reliance said it has “never feared competition” and has “grown in an India that welcomes investment and innovation, homegrown or international”.

Astronomers uncover new secrets of the Universe’s first five minutes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
12:34:15 UTC
21:34:15 KST

Astronomers uncover new secrets of the Universe’s first five minutes
Scientists have uncovered an extraordinarily precise chemical fingerprint of the Universe’s first five minutes, revealing new clues about the Big Bang and the laws of physics.
- Date:
- October 20, 2026
- Source:
- University of Minnesota
- Summary:
- Scientists have achieved a major breakthrough in understanding the Universe’s earliest moments, measuring the amount of helium formed in the first five minutes after the Big Bang with unprecedented precision. Using one of the world’s most powerful telescopes, an international team studied 15 remarkably pristine galaxies that act as cosmic time capsules, preserving clues from nearly 13.8 billion years ago.
- Share:
Scientists have measured the amount of helium produced during the Universe's first five minutes with unprecedented precision, offering a clearer picture of the conditions that existed shortly after the Big Bang. The achievement, made by an international research team that includes scientists from the University of Minnesota Twin Cities, represents a major advance in precision cosmology.
The findings, presented in five papers published in The Astrophysical Journal, are based on 130 hours of observations using the Large Binocular Telescope. By analyzing distant galaxies, the researchers reduced the uncertainty in this fundamental measurement to just 0.5%, making it three times more precise than previous estimates.
The improved accuracy provides scientists with a powerful new tool for investigating the origins of the Universe and testing the Standard Model of physics. Such fundamental tests have a long history of advancing scientific understanding and contributing to technological breakthroughs.
"This is a physics experiment on a grand scale and one of the biggest findings in my entire 40-year career," said Evan Skillman, University of Minnesota College of Science and Engineering Distinguished Professor in the School of Physics and Astronomy. "It's a fundamental number that tells us specifically about the conditions of our Universe in its first five minutes. It has diagnostic power that speaks directly to the Standard Model of Physics."
Why Helium Holds Clues to the Big Bang
According to the Big Bang theory, the Universe began expanding from an extraordinarily hot, dense state approximately 13.8 billion years ago. Three major lines of evidence support this explanation: the continuing expansion of the Universe, the cosmic microwave background radiation, and the amounts of light elements such as helium and deuterium that formed during its earliest moments.
Although cosmic expansion and the microwave background have been studied extensively, measurements of primordial helium have historically received less attention. Determining its original abundance more accurately allows researchers to investigate the physical conditions that prevailed when the Universe was only minutes old.
To achieve their new level of precision, the team departed from the conventional method of estimating primordial helium. That approach involves observing large numbers of galaxies and extrapolating the results to determine how much helium existed before later generations of stars altered their chemical composition.
Instead, the researchers selected 15 exceptionally pristine, small, distant galaxies. These galaxies have undergone relatively little chemical evolution, making them valuable cosmic "time capsules" that preserve clues about the Universe's early composition.
Powerful Telescopes Deliver Record Precision
The team used sophisticated spectrographs developed at Ohio State University to examine more than 10 helium spectral lines and 15 hydrogen lines simultaneously. Studying these signals together made it possible to identify and correct subtle sources of measurement error that earlier studies could largely overlook.
Such small effects become especially important when researchers are trying to reduce uncertainty to less than 1%. Accounting for them was essential to achieving the new 0.5% precision.
"The MODS spectrographs took 12 years to build from conception to first light on sky," said Richard Pogge, College of Arts and Sciences Distinguished Professor of Astronomy at Ohio State University. "This is the kind of project we designed them to do, and to see them deliver is enormously satisfying. It's not every day you can help build instruments that measure something fundamental about our Universe."
Testing the Fundamental Laws of Physics
Beyond refining estimates of the Universe's earliest chemical composition, the new measurement provides an important test of the Standard Model of physics. The amount of helium created shortly after the Big Bang depends on the physical conditions at that time, including the types of elementary particles present.
Using their precise helium measurement, the researchers were able to calculate the number of neutrino families in the early Universe. Neutrinos are extremely light subatomic particles, and their behavior plays an important role in scientists' understanding of fundamental physics.
The results therefore do more than strengthen existing evidence for the Big Bang. They also offer a more precise way to check whether established physical theories accurately describe the Universe during its first few minutes.
"We promised a half-percent uncertainty in our proposal, and we got there," added Skillman. "In the unpredictable world of science, that doesn't happen very often."
The international collaboration brought together scientists from the University of Minnesota Twin Cities, Ohio State University, Gonzaga University, Northwestern University, The University of Texas at Austin, Indiana University, University of California Santa Cruz, University of Illinois, Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, and TRIUMF.

Türkiye, Belgium revive ministerial talks in Brussels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
12:34:01 UTC
21:34:01 KST

Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan attended the 4th Turkish and Belgian Foreign Affairs, Justice, and Interior Ministers Meeting alongside Justice Minister Akın Gürlek and Interior Minister Mustafa Çiftçi in in Brussels, Belgium, on Oct. 20, 2026. (AA Photo)
Belgium underscored Türkiye’s strategic importance to European security on Oct. 21, as ministers from the two countries met in Brussels to revive high-level dialogue after a 10-year hiatus.
Seven Belgian and Turkish ministers met at Egmont Palace to discuss strengthening bilateral cooperation, particularly in security, justice and migration.
The Belgian delegation included Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot, Justice Minister Annelies Verlinden, Security and Home Affairs Minister Bernard Quintin and Asylum and Migration Minister Anneleen Van Bossuyt.
Türkiye was represented by Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, Justice Minister Akın Gürlek and Interior Minister Mustafa Çiftçi.
Belgium’s Foreign Ministry described Türkiye as a strategically important partner for Europe, citing its NATO membership and diplomatic influence in regions central to European security.
The ministry said Türkiye plays a key role in Black Sea security and maintains diplomatic contacts with both Kiev and Moscow.
It also highlighted Ankara’s diplomatic engagement in the Middle East, particularly concerning Gaza and Syria, and in Africa, including the Horn of Africa.
“You cannot seriously discuss European security without engaging with Türkiye. It is an important NATO ally, but also a diplomatic player with contacts and influence in regions that are vital to our security,” Prevot said.
“From efforts to bring peace to Ukraine to stability in the Middle East, the Black Sea and the Horn of Africa, Türkiye can help advance diplomatic solutions.”
Security cooperation was among the main issues on the agenda, with both sides focusing on combating terrorism and organized crime, according to a Belgian Foreign Ministry statement.
The meeting was also expected to lead to the signing of a bilateral action plan on police cooperation to strengthen coordination between Belgian and Turkish law enforcement agencies, the statement said.
The agreement aims to facilitate faster information exchange, expertise-sharing and joint training, particularly in combating organized crime and international criminal networks, it added.
Quintin said closer coordination between police services was necessary as criminal networks increasingly operated across borders.
He said the agreement would help authorities combat organized crime more effectively and protect citizens.
The discussions also aimed to improve judicial cooperation while respecting the rule of law and fundamental legal safeguards.
Migration was another focus of the talks, with ministers exploring ways to strengthen cooperation between their administrations on migration and consular matters.
Van Bossuyt described Türkiye as an “important partner” for Belgium and the EU, emphasizing that effective migration management required cooperation beyond the bloc’s external borders.
Belgium also sees opportunities to deepen bilateral cooperation in industry, defense, energy, innovation and trade, according to the ministry’s statement.

Trial by Social Media? The Boundaries of Feminist Teaching in China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
12:33:00 UTC
21:33:00 KST

On September 29, Beijing Institute of Technology (BIT) announced the dismissal of a teacher surnamed Pei, widely identified in reporting as law school assistant professor Pei Yi. The university canceled her eligibility to supervise graduate students, revoked her eligibility to hold a teaching position at BIT, and terminated her employment.
The university said a special working group had investigated allegations against Pei and found serious violations of teachers’ professional ethics and codes of conduct. Its public statement did not specify the conduct or disclose the supporting evidence.
The announcement followed an online controversy surrounding Pei’s elective course, “Protecting Women’s Rights in the Digital Age.” A message in a course group chat attracted accusations that she was insulting male students. Screenshots attributed to her subsequently circulated, broadening the backlash into accusations of “radical feminism.”
The case raises questions that BIT’s statement leaves unanswered: What conduct justified dismissal? How were the allegations assessed? And how should universities distinguish complaints about discriminatory teaching from opposition to feminist discussion itself?
The subject of Pei’s course is a legitimate field of legal inquiry. Women in digital spaces can face harassment, invasion of privacy, and discrimination; it’s important to know both their rights and their access to remedies. Teaching these subjects, however, requires examining unequal distributions of power, including inequalities that students may find uncomfortable or contest.
A video circulating online, purportedly from Pei’s classroom, featured her discussing the online harassment of law professor Lao Dongyan over her public positions on legal issues, including sexual consent. Pei mentioned that such harassment is difficult to counter because attacks come from dispersed individuals rather than a unified group with an identifiable leader. The discussion addressed a substantive question for a course on “women’s rights in the digital age”: how online hostility develops and what makes accountability difficult.
The initial dispute centered on Pei’s description of her course as having a “chocolate attribute” that might make some students uncomfortable. Critics interpreted this as a reference to an internet joke about chocolate being harmless to humans but dangerous to dogs, and therefore an insult to male students. Pei reportedly offered a different explanation, invoking the “Forrest Gump” metaphor of life as a box of chocolates.
The backlash was not simply a demand for clarification. Some commenters celebrated Pei’s dismissal, calling her a “女拳师” (“female boxer”), a derogatory pun on the Chinese word for feminism. Such responses suggest that, for at least some participants, the controversy became an opportunity to celebrate the removal of someone identified with feminism.
Other allegations concerned screenshots attributed to Pei expressing support for men being treated as inferior. Their authenticity and context, however, need to be established rather than inferred from their widespread circulation. Public approval of a dismissal cannot establish the truth of the allegations behind it. That distinction is especially important when hostility toward a teacher’s perceived feminist identity becomes entangled with complaints about her professional conduct.
The controversy surrounding Pei underscores the importance of distinguishing online hostility from substantiated complaints about professional conduct. BIT’s public statement leaves outsiders unable to assess how that distinction was made. For those teaching about women’s rights, that uncertainty may be enough to discourage difficult but necessary conversations.
A controversy in Hong Kong around the same time offers an imperfect contrast. According to students quoted in media reports, Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) academic Chong Tai-leung said that high grades were of little use to women, who would ultimately seek wealthy husbands. He reportedly also advised women against pursuing Ph.Ds, saying their youth was too precious. His presentation slides also discussed the “cost-benefit” of women marrying rich.
Chong later publicly apologized for his remarks. His college said it had reminded him to be mindful of his language and others’ feelings.

Social unrest sweeping through France to Albania sets Europe ablaze
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
12:32:00 UTC
21:32:00 KST

A housing crisis, rising fuel costs and deteriorating public services have sparked a wave of autumn protests across Europe where weeks of demonstrations in France, Italy and Albania have seen arrests and violence, while tent camps have formed in Spain and Portugal to protest unaffordable housing.
Young Europeans are experiencing "a strong sense of uncertainty and a lack of control," said Maria Silvestre, professor of sociology at the University of Deusto in Spain. "And when specific situations come together, a spark suddenly ignites that is capable of channeling that discontent and driving people into the streets."
Cities have turned into battlefields as top EU economies, including France, Italy and Spain, approach pivotal elections, while far-right parties have made electoral gains in Germany and could do so elsewhere. It also comes as Europe faces a critical moment in its support for Ukraine, with President Donald Trump making overtures to President Vladimir Putin even as Russia is blamed for increasingly frequent arson attacks, cyberattacks and other acts of sabotage in NATO countries.
Right-wing politicians have seized on the chaos. While protests in France have appeared broad-based, Trump portrayed immigrants as responsible for the destruction, writing Monday on his Truth Social platform: "The migrants have taken over France. They must CLOSE THE BORDERS, FAST!"
Many of the protests have been fueled by frustrated young people. Other actors, including black-clad, masked agitators, have fomented violence, but French authorities and police have not blamed immigrants.
In France, which has a centuries-old tradition of popular protest, high schoolers have staged blockades and demonstrations for more than three weeks, demanding more resources for schools they describe as understaffed and dilapidated, especially in lower-income neighborhoods.
The protests broadened as France's CGT labor union and other activists joined in while students paused for a fall break. The movement now includes demands over rising living costs and public services.
Despite hundreds of thousands of people marching peacefully, the weekend’s unrest led to 2,400 arrests and serious disturbances in parts of France, including looting in Paris, Marseille, Lyon and Bordeaux.
In Limoges, flames engulfed the 19th-century City Hall and nearly destroyed the building. Some schools were set on fire. As students and rioters threw firebombs and law enforcement responded with tear gas, hundreds have been injured.
French President Emmanuel Macron condemned Saturday’s violence, accusing far-left activists of trying to foment chaos by attacking buildings and police.
"Those who looted will have to pay for the damage, and those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable," Macron said Sunday in a rare televised address.
In Spain, elementary and secondary schoolteachers began an indefinite strike in Madrid last week to demand better pay and working conditions. Discontented teachers staged similar walkouts elsewhere in Spain this year.
In Madrid's central Puerta del Sol, tarpaulin tents have blanketed the square for weeks to protest rising housing costs, sparked by the eviction of María del Carmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman who later died while hospitalized. Smaller protest camps followed in other Spanish cities.
The public pressure led the ruling Socialist government to approve affordable housing measures, but they lacked support in Parliament, leading Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez to call for an early election in November. A general strike also was called for November – the first in 14 years.
Similar housing protests have sprung up in Portugal’s largest cities, Lisbon and Porto and in Barcelona, a focal point of Spain's overtourism and housing challenges.
Spain's minimum wage is 1,221 euros ($1,370), while the average monthly rent for an 80-square-meter apartment is around 1,130 euros (about $1,270), according to an analysis by the business newspaper Expansion.
"Most of my paycheck goes to the rent. My roommate struggles to make ends meet just like I do," said Diana Manzanares, a 20-year-old waitress at the Madrid encampment. "This is my reality and the reality of most of us living in this city."
"Italia in Piazza," or Italy in the Streets, has galvanized thousands of demonstrators, voicing demands for better employment, health care, education and access to housing, as well as higher wages. Inflation in Italy rose to 4.2% in September, surpassing the eurozone’s 3.8%, according to government data.
The peaceful marches were followed by violent riots in Turin and Bologna and in Italy's finance and fashion capital of Milan, where masked rioters clashed with police, looted stores and set property on fire. Milan police said 271 people were arrested - most of them minors - and 14 security officers were injured during two days of unrest.
Now a newly formed group calling itself the "Oct. 17 Movement" has announced what it describes as a "permanent mobilization" to demonstrate every Saturday at 3 p.m. in cities across Italy.
Anti-government protests have stretched over a week in Albania's capital of Tirana, with clashes escalating after high school and university students joined the broad anti-government "Flamingo" movement calling for Socialist Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign.
Rama has condemned the protesters as "ideologized and radicalized" by antifa , an umbrella term for loosely organized far-left militants. President Trump has designated the movement a terrorist organization in the United States.
Ending corruption is a major demand of the movement, which was named for the natural habitat of flamingos in an area where Rama's government agreed to allow a major luxury tourism development linked to Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law. They also want protections for healthcare, education, and public pensions, according to its website.
In Serbia, the university students leading mass anti-corruption protests for nearly two years are challenging an attempted return to power by the Balkan country’s former populist leader Aleksandar Vucic in parliamentary elections.
The former authoritarian president is aiming to be named prime minister after the Oct. 25 vote. The youth-backed Students’ List party is believed to be running close to Vucic’s party, making the outcome uncertain and fueling fears of possible violence.

Who is Stephen Hubbard, the US citizen held by Russia?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
12:31:11 UTC
21:31:11 KST

Who is Stephen Hubbard, the US citizen held by Russia?
Oct 20 - US special envoy Steve Witkoff is going to discuss the possible release of American citizen Stephen Hubbard from Russian detention with President Vladimir Putin this week, according to people familiar with the matter.
Here are details of Hubbard's case:WHO IS STEPHEN HUBBARD?
Hubbard, 74, a retired schoolteacher, grew up in Big Rapids, Michigan, and served in the US Air Force and National Guard, according to military records cited by the New York Times.
He earned a master’s degree in English and lived in Japan for 25 years where he taught English before moving to Cyprus and then, in 2014, to Izyum in eastern Ukraine with a Ukrainian partner, according to his sister, Patricia Hubbard Fox.
Fox told Reuters in 2024 that Hubbard subsisted on a pension of about $300 a month and had few connections with local people. The siblings last spoke in September 2021.
HOW WAS HE CAPTURED?
Russia launched its full-scale war in Ukraine in February 2022 and captured Izyum two months later. Ukrainian forces retook the city in September 2022, but Hubbard was already in Russian custody by then.
Russian state media said Hubbard had been detained in April 2022 and alleged he had been manning a Ukrainian military checkpoint. Reuters could not independently establish the circumstances of his capture.
Fox said she recognised her brother in a YouTube video showing a man being questioned about his views on Putin and the war. Another video showed him with his hands bound, being struck with a sandal. Reuters could not verify when or where the videos were recorded.
WHY WAS HE IMPRISONED?
Following a closed trial, a Moscow court convicted Hubbard of being a mercenary in October 2024 and sentenced him to six years and 10 months in prison.Prosecutors said Hubbard had joined a Ukrainian territorial defence unit, received training, weapons and ammunition, and was promised $1,000 a month. Russian state media said he had pleaded guilty to the charges he faced.
Fox questioned the reported confession, however, saying Hubbard held pro-Russian views and was unlikely to have taken up arms in his seventies.
Martin De Luca, his US-based lawyer, told Reuters in June 2025 that Hubbard had told him the charges against him were false and that he was not in any combat or military unit. He cited Hubbard as telling him Russian soldiers had simply grabbed him from his house.
WHAT IS HUBBARD'S CURRENT STATUS?
In January 2025, Washington designated Hubbard as wrongfully detained, enabling the US government to pursue negotiations for his release.
The State Department has said Russia refused to grant US officials consular access.
The New York Times reported in February 2025 that Hubbard had been moved through at least five Russian detention centres before his trial.
His lawyer said Hubbard's legal team found out only in April 2025 that he was being held in a facility in the Mordovia region, east of Moscow. REUTERS

Iran denies collapse is close as US claims IRGC running out of money
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
12:29:58 UTC
21:29:58 KST

Iran denies collapse is close as US claims IRGC running out of money
Iranian authorities have remained defiant despite the financial strain, saying they want to lift the US blockade and pressure on their terms.
Tehran, Iran – Iranian authorities have rejected claims that Iran is unable to support its regional allies, but acknowledged that the United States’ sanctions and the war have created financial challenges.
US Central Command chief Brad Cooper claimed last week that a combination of military attacks and a naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports “has dealt severe blows” to the country.
The admiral said the US had prevented at least $25bn in Iranian crude exports and helped freeze approximately $350m in cryptocurrency assets. This means the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) are now unable to pay their soldiers and Iran-linked regional groups suffering from financial shortfalls.
“The financial strain on Iran’s military has become so significant that there are reports of Iran-aligned militia groups across the region withholding payments to their soldiers in order to funnel money back to the IRGC, which also is not paying its troops,” Cooper said.
This is being portrayed as a victory for the US in its war with Iran, which so far has shown very few tangible victories for Washington.
Michael Knights, head of MENA research at US-based intelligence and geopolitical risk advisory firm Horizon Engage, said Hezbollah in Lebanon and the Houthis in Yemen have suffered financially during the past few years.
“The national economies feeding the Hezbollah and Houthi movements are badly broken, so they continue to receive stipends and in-kind funding – in fuel products – from Iran,” Knights told Al Jazeera.
Funding the axis
For decades, the IRGC Quds Force has supplied money, weapons, components, training and manufacturing expertise to regional allied groups. It has enabled partners at loggerheads with the US and Israel to assemble or produce a number of weapons locally, according to United Nations experts and US officials.
The axis groups also draw on businesses, including oil exports, as well as donations and local resources to fund their operations. Some Iraqi factions have been integrated into the official security forces and receive government funding through the Popular Mobilisation Forces.
Allied commercial networks in Iraq are selling Iranian commodities and distributing proceeds through intermediaries and exchange houses, the US Department of the Treasury has claimed.
This has put them in a better financial position than their “poorer cousins” in Hezbollah and the Houthis, Knights said, with some money allegedly flowing from Iraq towards Iran in recent years.
“Some Iraqi militiamen and government civil servants are indeed paid late at the same time that Iraqi militias send funding overseas to help Iran, the Houthis and Lebanese Hezbollah,” he told Al Jazeera.
The US Treasury alleged in September that Kataib Hezbollah, a prominent Tehran-backed Shia Muslim armed group in neighbouring Iraq, siphoned Iraqi resources to support Iran.
The Treasury also described substantial earlier transfers from the Quds Force to Hezbollah, depicting flows in both directions.
A report by the Reuters news agency earlier this month cited unnamed sources as saying Hezbollah received $200m from Iran in September. The US State Department rejected the report at the time, saying Hezbollah was “trying to save face with fake stories about cash influxes from Iran”.
Iran says no ‘collapse’ imminent
Iran’s economy has taken hit after hit in recent years due to war, domestic mismanagement and sanctions.
This has led to runaway inflation, low-paying jobs, a depreciating national currency and isolation from the global community for 90 million Iranians.
There appears to be little sign of the situation improving, with the World Bank reporting earlier this month a projected 7.7 percent contraction of the economy in the fiscal year 2026-27.
The authorities emphasise that does not affect their resolve. They have also challenged US Treasury assessments that economic pressure could result in losing control within months.
“Despite all these pressures, the Iranian economy has demonstrated very good resilience, and the claim that Iran’s economy is collapsing is nothing more than an illusion,” Central Bank chief Abdolnaser Hemmati said earlier this month.
Financial problems
President Masoud Pezeshkian acknowledged on Sunday that military attacks and the maritime blockade had created substantial problems for the country. But he said his government was relying on domestic capacities to withstand the pressure.
He claimed consumption management had now removed the need for petrol imports that would otherwise cost $12bn, if US pressure allowed imports at all. The president promised to return revenues from recently increased fuel prices to households by modestly increasing their electronic food vouchers.
Knights said the Iranian authorities were “stuck in an aggressive cycle of escalation with the US government no matter what state Iran’s economy is in”.
“Trump is betting that being poorer will make Iran’s regime more flexible, but that has never been a good bet,” he said.
Negar Mortazavi, a senior fellow at the Washington, DC-based Center for International Policy, said she expected Tehran to continue prioritising its regional allied groups despite the financial strains involved.
“Economic pressure is certainly constraining Iran’s military resources, but that does not mean it will fundamentally change the IRGC’s strategic calculations or force Tehran to surrender,” she told Al Jazeera.

Blame Russia, ignore the money? Israel’s election interference debate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
12:29:35 UTC
21:29:35 KST

Blame Russia, ignore the money? Israel’s election interference debate
As Israel prepares for the October 27 elections, accusations of foreign interference are intensifying. While Israeli leaders have pointed to Iran, Russia, and China, journalist Nick Kolyohin argues that greater scrutiny should be directed at Western funding of Israeli media outlets and civil society organizations, which he believes may be influencing the country’s political discourse.
With election day approaching, political parties are stepping up efforts to attract voters and consolidate their support.
The right-wing camp, led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, is seeking to rally hawkish voters behind him, potentially at the expense of other conservative parties. The opposition bloc is trying to persuade voters to abandon Netanyahu and shift their support to its side.
Yet the battle for the Israeli electorate is not being fought exclusively within the country’s borders. Foreign actors are also seeking to shape the political landscape and influence the outcome of the election.
Foreign meddling
Several days ago, speaking to Channel 14, Netanyahu raised this concern.
“Iran is trying to damage the elections with the help of its terror arms Hamas and Hezbollah. It is totally true – they say it openly that they need to topple me because their real desire is to destroy the State of Israel.”
Iran, however, is not the only country accused of interference. In July, speaking at the Knesset, opposition leader Yair Lapid also accused China and Russia of attempting to meddle.
“The elections are drawing closer. Iran is involved, Russia is involved, and influence operations are running rampant on social media. They want to divide us, strengthen the extremists, weaken the moderates, and sow chaos and hatred.”
Nick Kolyohin, a veteran Israeli journalist and Russia expert, disputes the accusations against Moscow, saying he has seen no evidence of Russian interference in the current or previous election cycles:
“I am not witnessing, neither in the current round, nor in the previous, any influence from the Russian side.”
“I am not even sure which side Russia prefers in this internal dispute between the different political parties. Israeli politicians are not speaking about Russia so it doesn’t even make any sense for Moscow to interfere because it is not clear which government is going to be good or bad for the Kremlin,” he said.
Kolyokhin maintains that the broader relationship between the two countries lends weight to his assessment. Despite periodic setbacks and fluctuations, economic ties and trade have continued. Diplomatic relations and cooperation have also endured through some of the most turbulent periods in recent history, including the Syrian civil war, the Russia-Ukraine conflict, and the Hamas-led attack of October 7, 2023.
Relations between the countries’ leaders have also largely remained cordial. Although then-Prime Minister Yair Lapid strongly criticized Russia over its actions in Ukraine, relations between Moscow and other Israeli prime ministers, including Naftali Bennett and Netanyahu, have been more amicable.
“I know for a fact, including from my sources within the PM office, that the current premier has very good and close relations with President Vladimir Putin. Israel understands that from time to time Moscow needs to slap it [publicly] because it is a part of a broader geopolitical game but in the end of the day this will not sour the relationship between the nations.”
The West dictates
Kolyohin argues that while Russia has come under scrutiny over alleged interference in the upcoming elections, another potential source of foreign influence is receiving far less attention: liberal political circles in Europe and the US.
“For many years, the European Union and the Democratic Party have been pouring money into the Israeli NGOs, news outlets, journalists, think tanks and experts – all of whom are located on the left side of the Israeli political map. So they ended up promoting European interests, which I find outrageous, especially now, when the EU is openly unfriendly towards Israel.”
In recent years, several European countries have recognized Palestine despite Israeli appeals. European governments have also pursued sanctions on Israeli products manufactured in the West Bank and Golan Heights, imposed embargoes on military equipment, and suspended bilateral agreements.
Kolyohin says he has evidence to support his allegations of Western interference. In recent weeks, he says, he obtained three documents that point to substantial financial transfers from Western liberal circles to Israeli left-wing organizations.
The first transfer involved around $48,000 (€43,000). According to Kolyohin, the money came from Canal France International (CFI), a French public media-development agency, and went to the Seventh Eye, an Israeli liberal outlet known for its critical coverage of Netanyahu.
CFI has also reportedly provided hundreds of thousands of euros to another liberal Israeli organization, the Israeli Association of Internet. While the stated objective was to support Israel and combat disinformation, Kolyohin suspects that the underlying motivations extend beyond those publicly declared goals.
The US State Department has allegedly followed a similar approach. Kolyohin says documents in his possession show that the Institute for Israel’s National Studies, one of Israel’s most reputable think tanks, received more than $500,000 from 2023-2025.
“This is one of the ways for the west to censor and control the information in Israel and in this way they can also interfere in the elections, and promote their agenda among the public.”
According to the journalist, the Western agenda extends beyond the promotion of liberal ideas. He argues that another key objective is to foster anti-Russian sentiment in Israel, a goal he believes is advanced through media outlets and think tanks that receive Western funding.
“These journalists and experts learned fast that if they want to be honored, invited to conferences, and get prizes, they need to criticize Russia even if that is contrary to the interests of Israel itself,” Kolyohin said.
“You have to understand: Russia is an important partner of Israel but very often the Israeli government is trying not to flash these tight relations petrified by what the media and the experts are going to say.”
Witch hunt campaign?
Kolyohin says he has personally experienced what he regards as the consequences of anti-Russian sentiment in Israel. Several Israeli news outlets have investigated his alleged connections to the Kremlin. His name is frequently associated with what local outlets describe as Russian propaganda, and he believes these efforts have damaged his professional standing.
In 2025, he was barred from press conferences held by Israel’s Foreign Ministry after asking Foreign Minister Gideon Saar to comment on Ukraine’s glorification of the Nazis.
A year later, he was removed from a plane carrying Netanyahu to Washington, where the prime minister was scheduled to meet with Trump. According to Kolyohin, the Shin Bet, Israel’s internal security agency, wanted to examine his background and ties.
“They are after journalists like me because I am not slamming Russia like the rest of them. They are after me because I dare to speak to the Russian media, I dare to give interviews and do reports. That’s why they want to discredit me, and they are even trying to tilt the PM office and the Shin Bet against me.”
Kolyohin has filed a lawsuit against several Israeli organizations that receive foreign funding and says he is prepared to continue his legal fight to find out the truth: Who funds Israeli NGOs, for what purpose, and how is this money used to shape public opinion?

Iran and Uzbekistan: Where shared history comes alive in Tashkent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
12:29:02 UTC
21:29:02 KST

Iran and Uzbekistan: Where shared history comes alive in Tashkent
TASHKENT, Uzbekistan - As an Iranian journalist visiting Tashkent, I found myself looking at the huge Islamic Civilization Center from two perspectives. I was a visitor discovering the depth of Uzbekistan’s cultural heritage. I was also an Iranian looking for familiar traces of a civilization that has never respected the borders drawn on today’s maps.
I found those traces in the manuscripts, the art and the names of scholars whose lives and work connected Central Asia with Iran and the wider Islamic world. Their presence raised a question that followed me through the galleries: How can a country preserve its own national history while showing that its greatest cultural achievements were often shared with others?
The Islamic Civilization Center offers one ambitious answer. Officially opened in March 2026, the complex stands beside the historic Khast-Imam ensemble, one of Tashkent’s most important religious and cultural sites.
My guide throughout the visit was Mr. Ozod Kuvondikov, Head of the Information Service of Uzbekistan’s Committee on Interethnic Relations, who had also assisted me during earlier visits to other attractions in the capital. He spoke English quite well and approached his role with professionalism, patience and a clear knowledge of the places he introduced me to.
A building designed to tell a story
Even from kilometers away, the center is difficult to overlook. Its four monumental entrance portals, each approximately 34 meters high, draw on architectural traditions from different parts of Uzbekistan. The eastern entrance recalls the Ulugbek Madrasah on Registan Square in Samarkand. The western portal reflects the religious architecture of Bukhara, while the northern and southern entrances incorporate references to other historic regions and cities, including Khiva, Shakhrisabz, Karakalpakstan, Kokand, Tashkent and Termez.
Together, the entrances form an architectural map of the country. They suggest that Uzbekistan’s heritage cannot be reduced to a single city, dynasty or style. It developed through many regional traditions, each contributing its own forms, colors and artistic vocabulary.
Above the complex rises a central dome more than 60 meters high. The building covers more than 40,000 square meters of interior space, making room for exhibition galleries, research facilities, a library, educational areas and conference facilities. Official descriptions place the complex among the country’s largest recent cultural projects.
Inside, the scale becomes more apparent. Broad halls lead into exhibition spaces, and the building’s pale surfaces and monumental proportions give visitors room to pause rather than hurry from one display to another.
Yet the center’s most interesting feature is not its size alone. It is the way the building attempts to turn history into a continuous narrative.
Instead of presenting the past as a series of unrelated treasures, the main exhibition follows a chronological route. It begins with the ancient civilizations of Central Asia, moves through the region’s pre-Islamic heritage, enters the period of scientific and cultural flourishing between the eighth and 13th centuries, and then follows the artistic and political achievements associated with the 14th to 16th centuries. The final section turns to contemporary Uzbekistan and its vision of a new cultural renaissance.
This arrangement makes an important point: the story of Islamic civilization in Central Asia did not begin with the arrival of Islam, nor did it end with the decline of a particular dynasty. It emerged from earlier societies and continued through centuries of exchange, adaptation and intellectual work.
The Hall of Fame: scholars beyond borders
One of the first spaces to command attention is the Hall of Fame, where huge mosaic panels vividly portray some of the most influential thinkers in the history of the Islamic world.
The figures include Avicenna, known in the Islamic intellectual tradition as Ibn Sina; Al-Khwarizmi, whose work helped establish the foundations of algebra; Al-Biruni, the scholar whose investigations ranged across mathematics, astronomy, geography and other fields; and Al-Farabi, the philosopher often called the Second Teacher after Aristotle.
The portraits are assembled from thousands of small pieces of tile. Viewed from a distance, they form monumental images. Seen more closely, they reveal the patience and precision required to bring so many individual pieces into a single composition.
The effect is both artistic and symbolic. Each scholar is presented as an individual whose ideas helped shape a much larger intellectual world.
A peek into the ancient world
The center’s historical journey reaches back much further than the Islamic period. In the galleries devoted to pre-Islamic heritage, archaeological objects present Central Asia as a place of human settlement, artistic production and cultural contact stretching back thousands of years.
Among the countless objects described in the exhibition material are stone tools and arrowheads associated with the Obi-Rahmat site, dating to approximately 80,000 years ago. There are also gold ornaments and other finds linked to ancient Bactria, a historical region that included parts of present-day Uzbekistan, Afghanistan and Tajikistan.
One striking exhibit is the sculpted head known as the Head of the Kushan Prince, dated to the first or second century CE and discovered at Dalverzin-Tepa in southern Uzbekistan. Its features and surviving detail offer a glimpse of the artistic culture that developed under the Kushan Empire, whose territories connected parts of Central and South Asia.
Nearby, a deer sculpture dating to the first millennium BC recalls the symbolic importance of animals in ancient artistic traditions. Its presence gives the gallery a different character from the displays of manuscripts and religious objects elsewhere in the building. Here, visitors encounter societies whose beliefs and artistic languages developed long before the emergence of Islam.
The objects also challenge the idea that the history of Uzbekistan can be understood only through the history of the Uzbek state, which is modern in its present form. The territory has been home to many peoples, languages, religions and political systems. Sogdian, Bactrian, Khwarazmian, Persian, Turkic and other cultural traditions all formed part of the wider historical landscape.
For an Iranian visitor, this part of the exhibition feels especially close. Ancient Bactria and the surrounding regions were linked to the Iranian cultural world through language, religion, trade and political contact. These connections were neither simple nor unchanging, but they formed an important part of the history of the lands that now make up modern Iran and its neighbors.
When technology brings history closer
The chronological galleries are supported by a range of digital installations. Multilingual screens provide information about objects, while digital reconstructions place historic buildings and cities within their former settings. Interactive displays allow visitors to explore historical periods in ways that would be difficult to achieve through labels and glass cases alone.
Some of the most engaging features use artificial intelligence to animate portraits of scholars and present their discoveries in a more personal format. Rather than simply reading a short biography, visitors can encounter a digital representation of a historical figure explaining aspects of his work.
Such displays can make a difficult subject more accessible, especially for younger visitors or people unfamiliar with the history of Islamic scholarship. Mathematics, philosophy and astronomy may seem distant when presented only through dates and technical terms. A digital guide can help turn them into stories about human curiosity, disagreement and discovery.
One of the most effective installations is an interactive map of the Silk Road. The historic trading network is often represented in books as a series of lines connecting distant cities. Here, its routes become visible paths of movement and exchange, helping visitors understand how merchants, religious teachers, diplomats, artists and ideas travelled between regions.
The Silk Road was never a single road with one fixed route. It was a changing network of overland and other connections that linked East Asia, Central Asia, the Middle East and Europe across many centuries. Its importance lay not only in the goods that moved along it but also in the knowledge and artistic practices that accompanied them. That is way it sometimes referred to as the Silk Roads NOT the SilK Road.
Looking at the map, I thought about how often the history of our region is divided into national chapters, even when the historical evidence points towards constant interaction. The roads that connected Samarkand, Bukhara and Khiva also linked them to cities farther south and west, including those of historical Iran.
Other interactive features make the experience more playful. Visitors can try a virtual archery simulation or explore an installation demonstrating how bellows supply air to a traditional tandoor oven. In the gallery devoted to contemporary Uzbekistan, Humo AI acts as a digital assistant, answering questions about the center and the country’s history.
These activities may seem far removed from ancient manuscripts, but they serve a useful purpose when they encourage visitors to ask questions. A museum is not only a place to look at the past. It can also be a place to discover how people lived, worked, cooked, travelled and understood their world.
The Quran Hall and a manuscript’s long journey
The most solemn space in the center is the Holy Quran Hall, which covers approximately 1,200 square meters and serves as the symbolic heart of the complex.
The room is monumental in scale. Pink marble lines the walls, while an extremely vast chandelier hangs overhead. Silk carpets bearing Quranic verses add another layer of craftsmanship to the setting.
Yet the central object is a manuscript, not the architecture around it.
Known as the Uthman Quran, the Osman Quran or the Samarkand Kufic Quran, the manuscript is traditionally associated with the third caliph, Uthman ibn Affan, and dated to the seventh century. It is among the most celebrated early Quranic manuscripts and was inscribed on UNESCO’s Memory of the World Register in 1997.
According to a widely circulated account, the manuscript was brought to Samarkand during the reign of Amir Timur in the late 14th century. It remained there for centuries before being transferred to St Petersburg under Russian imperial rule in the 19th century. After further movement during the revolutionary period, it returned to Tashkent in 1924.
Visitors are kept at a respectful distance from the manuscript, and photography of the original is restricted. Copies and multimedia displays help explain its history, its script and its importance. These limits are understandable: a fragile manuscript must be protected from excessive light, handling and other risks.
Standing in the hall, I was struck by the contrast between the immense space and the modest physical form of the object at its center. The chandelier, marble and carpets create a sense of grandeur, but the manuscript itself is made of pages bearing lines of writing. Its importance rests in the religious meaning attached to it, the history it has survived and the generations who have regarded it as a treasure.
Artifacts that cross cultural boundaries
Elsewhere in the center, the collection widens the story through religious objects, archaeological discoveries, manuscripts, textiles and works of art. Some items come from museums in Uzbekistan; others have been acquired through international auctions or cooperation with foreign institutions. In cases where originals remain abroad, the center uses scientific replicas to make important objects accessible to visitors.
Among the religious exhibits are a fragment of the kiswa, the cloth covering the Kaaba in Mecca, dating to 1859, and historic keys associated with the Kaaba. Such objects reflect the broad geography of Islamic religious life and the artistic traditions that developed around its most sacred sites.
The galleries devoted to the First Eastern Renaissance present manuscripts, coins, architectural models and finely made objects from the period between the eighth and 13th centuries. A copy of Imam al-Bukhari’s Al-Jamiʿ as-Sahih, a major collection of hadith, appears alongside a later manuscript of Al-Farabi’s philosophical work commonly known as The Virtuous City.
The presence of these works connects religious learning with philosophy, science and the study of society. Islamic intellectual history cannot be understood through theology alone. It also includes debates about medicine, mathematics, logic, astronomy, ethics and political life.
The section devoted to the Timurid period takes visitors into another world of artistic ambition. Amir Timur and his successors supported architecture, scholarship and the arts, creating a court culture that drew talent from across a wide region.
The displays include a decree associated with Timur, a silk robe from the first half of the 15th century and miniature paintings from the 15th and 16th centuries. Some of the miniatures are associated with Bukhara and Iran’s Shiraz, an important detail for anyone trying to understand the close relationship between Central Asian and Iranian art.
Shiraz was one of the major centers of Persian miniature painting, book production and calligraphy. Artists, techniques and visual ideas moved between workshops and courts, sometimes under the patronage of rulers whose political territories extended across regions that are now separate countries.
Looking at these paintings, I did not see a simple division between Uzbek and Iranian heritage. I saw an artistic language that had developed through a long conversation among masters, patrons and audiences. The works belong to specific places and periods, but their influence cannot be confined to a single modern border.
The same is true of Persian literature and architecture, which left deep marks across Central Asia. Persian was used widely as a language of literature and administration, while Turkic languages and traditions also played increasingly important roles in the region’s cultural life. These histories overlapped rather than replacing one another in a straight line.
For me, this is one of the center’s most valuable opportunities: to present Uzbekistan’s national history without separating it from the wider world that helped shape it.
A visitor’s experience
The center’s technology and monumental spaces can easily dominate first impressions. Yet the real test of a museum lies in what visitors take away from it.
During the visit, a middle-aged man who was there with his wife and daughter described the experience as something that went beyond looking at objects in display cases. The immersive galleries and multimedia installations, he said, allowed visitors to move through digital reconstructions of historic Uzbek cities and encounter scientific discoveries through digital representations of the scholars who made them.
I would not claim that every visitor responds to the displays in the same way. A conversation with one family cannot represent the views of everyone who enters the building. But the center’s combination of objects, interpretation and interactive learning gives it the potential to reach audiences with different interests and levels of historical knowledge.
Iran in the galleries and beyond them
As I moved through the center, my thoughts repeatedly returned to Iran.
This was not because the building was trying to tell Iran’s story. Its principal purpose is to present Uzbekistan’s heritage, and it does so through the country’s historic cities, archaeological sites, religious traditions and intellectual achievements. But the story it tells cannot be fully understood without acknowledging the larger cultural world in which those achievements developed.
The appearance of Persian miniatures from Shiraz is one example. The lives of scholars such as Avicenna and Al-Biruni are another. The wider influence of Persian literature, calligraphy, architecture and scholarship offers still more connections.
As I left the Islamic Civilization Center, one question stayed with me: Why has Iran, a country with such a rich and diverse historical heritage, not yet established a single public institution of comparable ambition, one that brings together its many civilizational periods through rigorous scholarship, modern museum design and interactive technology?

HAIKOU /China/, October 20. /TASS/. China’s southern province of Hainan has successfully adjusted to a new offshore customs model this year. The Hainan Daily newspaper reported that the country’s southernmost region has been demonstrating high development rates thanks to a broad array of policy favors.
According to authors of the publication, there has been a noticeable improvement in the efficiency of cargo flows running through the island’s seaports since December 18 of last year when the Hainan Free Trade Port officially transitioned to a new trade and investment regime. The province is becoming a “new vanguard of China’s opening-up,” a promising platform for mutually beneficial cooperation and economic globalization, the paper said.
It cited official statistics, which show that following the transition to a new customs model in early 2026 the number of new commercial entities registered in Hainan climbed by more than 71% in annual terms (including a 31% rise for enterprises with foreign capital, and a 47% surge for foreign trade companies). The province has started attracting global resources much more actively, implementing more landmark projects with other countries’ participation.
The new customs regime serves as one of the key catalysts for increasing Hainan’s economic openness, according to the publication. Amid those changes, the province has been demonstrating an impressive increase in its external trade turnover, which soared by 49.8% in January-September to 285.44 bln yuan ($42.47 bln at the current exchange rate of the People’s Bank of China). Trade in services with other countries and regions rose by 11.7% in the reporting period to 56.95 bln yuan ($8.47 bln). Despite the mounting scale of economic interaction with other countries, the time required for customs clearance of imported goods on the island has decreased by around 20%, with low-risk shipments undergoing procedures “in a second.”
Hainan’s shift to a new customs regime has spurred progress in the area of international transport links that has been registered by authorities. Specifically, the province’s border checkpoints have inspected 16,000 aircraft and 4,000 vessels since the middle of last December. Those figures gained 23% and 9% year-on-year, respectively.
On December 18, 2025, Hainan transitioned to a new customs system, under which the list of products exempt from import duties upon entry into the province expanded from 1,900 to 6,600 items (up to 74% of the entire range of products). The preferences cover “almost all enterprises, institutions, and private non-profit organizations on the island that have a genuine need for imports.” Unlike freight, all passenger flows are subject to existing regulations: individuals heading to the island for business or tourism do not require any additional documents.
